title: AI Development Timeline
caption: **AI Development Timeline**: The red curve tracks how often published books mention artificial intelligence, a measure of attention rather than capability, and the light-brown bands mark the two AI winters. Callout boxes place milestones such as Turing's 1950 paper [@turing1950], the Dartmouth conference [@mccarthy1955dartmouth], the Perceptron [@rosenblatt1958], ELIZA [@weizenbaum1966], Deep Blue [@campbell2002], and GPT-3 [@brown2020language] against that curve. Adapted from @michel2011quantitative.
alt: Timeline from the 1950s to the 2020s with a red line showing AI publication frequency. Light-brown bands mark two AI winters. Callout boxes mark milestones including Turing's 1950 paper, Dartmouth conference, Perceptron, ELIZA, Deep Blue, and GPT-3.
context:
@Fig-ai-timeline traces attention to AI across seven decades of published literature and shades two "AI winter" intervals (1974--1980 and 1987--1993) marked by funding cuts and unmet expectations.[^fn-ai-winters-systems] These setbacks reflected gaps between expectations and what systems could deliver. Later advances combined changes in algorithms, data, and computing resources; the sections below examine how those changes shifted the limiting constraint.

[^fn-ai-winters-systems]: **AI winters as systems failures**\index{AI winters!systems failure}: The first AI winter (1974--1980) unfolded amid funding cuts; the 1973 Lighthill Report criticized the gap between AI promises and delivered results [@lighthill1973artificial]. The second winter (1987--1993) involved a market and funding collapse around expert systems and specialized Lisp machines as general-purpose workstations undercut their economics [@hendler2008avoiding]. These episodes involved technical limitations, unmet expectations, and economics; hardware capacity alone does not explain them.

title: AlexNet Architecture
caption: **AlexNet Architecture**: Two parallel GPU streams process $224{\times}224$ input images through convolutional layers (green blocks) that extract spatial features at decreasing resolutions, converging through three fully connected layers to 1,000 output classes. Because each stream holds half of the network, the figure also shows how the model was partitioned across two GPUs. Adapted from @krizhevsky2012imagenet.
alt: 3D diagram of AlexNet with two parallel GPU streams. Green blocks show convolutional layers decreasing from 224x224 input. Red kernels overlay green blocks. Right side shows three dense layers converging to 1000 outputs.
section: The deep learning era and the infrastructure bottleneck {#sec-introduction-deep-learning-era-infrastructure-bottleneck-2f02}
context:
Redesigning hand-crafted feature extractors for every new domain could not scale, so **deep learning**\index{Deep learning!first use} [@lecun2015] moved feature extraction inside the model itself. A neural network computes in layers, stages of arithmetic on learned weights in which each layer transforms the output of the one before. Instead of receiving features designed by humans, deep networks with many such layers learned representations directly from raw inputs such as pixels and audio waveforms. The training process could now shape both the representation and the decision boundary, enabling "end-to-end" learning.

The breakthrough was not algorithmic alone. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), whose convolutional layers slide small learned weight patterns called filters across an image to detect the same feature at every position, existed earlier [@lecun1989; @lecun1998]. AlexNet paired architecture and training with **systems co-design**\index{Systems co-design!definition}, choosing the model, training procedure, and hardware mapping together [@krizhevsky2012imagenet]. Its parallel matrix operations matched GPU capabilities. With `{python} AlexNetBreakthrough.alexnet_params_m_str` parameters distributed across two GTX 580 GPUs\index{GTX 580!AlexNet training}, AlexNet achieved `{python} AlexNetBreakthrough.alexnet_top5_error_pct_str` top-5 error, a `{python} AlexNetBreakthrough.alexnet_relative_improvement_str` relative improvement over the next-best entry that year. The hardware partition in @fig-alexnet carries the immediate systems lesson: the network divided work between the two GPUs and exchanged intermediate results only at selected layers to limit communication across the link between them [@krizhevsky2012imagenet]. Model structure and machine organization were designed together.

title: The D·A·M Axis Triad
caption: **The D·A·M Axis Triad**: Each vertex is one diagnostic axis, and each double-headed edge is a path along which a relaxed bottleneck can reappear on the neighboring axis.
alt: Triangle with circles at vertices labeled Algorithm at the top, Data at lower left, and Machine at lower right. Double-headed purple arrows connect all three, showing bidirectional dependencies. Icons depict a neural network, database cylinders, and a cloud server.
context:
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that the three axes are independent. Changing from a simple classifier to a larger model can require more memory, different serving infrastructure, and a broader data distribution. Because changing one of Data, Algorithm, and Machine can change the requirements imposed on the other two, every edge of the triangle in @fig-dam-axis-triad-intro points both ways.

:::

title: The D·A·M Intersection Landscape
caption: **The D·A·M Intersection Landscape**: Each circle lists the concerns that belong to one axis, and each pairwise overlap is titled with the question that axis pair must answer jointly. The central region, where all three circles overlap, is labeled ML systems engineering.
alt: Three-circle Venn diagram labeled Data, Algorithm, and Machine. Data lists storage formats, data quality, distribution properties, and labeling. Algorithm lists loss functions, architectures, optimization mathematics, and gradients. Machine lists silicon, memory hierarchy, peak FLOP/s, and power envelope. The Data–Algorithm overlap is titled What to Learn From, the Data–Machine overlap is titled How to Move Information, and the Algorithm–Machine overlap is titled How to Execute Efficiently. The central overlap is labeled ML systems engineering.
context:
An operational diagnosis earns confidence only when an intervention validates it, that is, when relaxing the identified constraint improves full-system behavior. Resolving one bottleneck frequently migrates the binding constraint across an adjacent edge of @fig-dam-axis-triad-intro, so interventions rarely end the optimization process. Upgrading to faster accelerators (Machine) leaves execution units idling if storage I/O cannot stream input batches quickly enough (Data). Conversely, expanding dataset volume (Data) exposes model architectures that lack the expressive capacity to absorb new patterns (Algorithm). Scaling model capacity to close that gap (Algorithm) soon exceeds accelerator memory, triggering out-of-memory faults or expensive paging across the PCIe bus (Machine). Engineering an ML system therefore requires identifying the currently binding constraint while anticipating where the bottleneck will migrate once that constraint is relaxed.

While the triad separates the three axes to simplify initial diagnosis, practical systems operate at their boundaries. Data formats govern memory traffic, model architectures dictate hardware functional unit utilization, and deployment budgets reshape both data representation and algorithmic design. @Fig-ai-triad partitions these interfaces into a three-set Venn diagram whose pairwise overlaps each pose one question: what the system can learn from ($\text{D} \cap \text{A}$), how information moves ($\text{D} \cap \text{M}$), and how computation executes efficiently ($\text{A} \cap \text{M}$).

caption: **Algorithmic Efficiency Trajectory**: Each point shows how much less training compute an ImageNet architecture needed than AlexNet to reach AlexNet-level accuracy, so height measures algorithmic progress with hardware speed held out. alt: Scatter plot of training efficiency factors from AlexNet in 2012 to EfficientNet-B0 in 2019. Red dots rise from AlexNet at 1x, with VGG-11 just below it, to EfficientNet-B0 at about 44x. A dashed exponential trend line fit through the points curves upward.
context:
```

The historical trajectory of computer vision models isolates the compounding effect of architectural design. @hernandez2020measuring held accuracy fixed at the AlexNet level and asked how much training computation successive architectures needed to reach it. Because they counted operations rather than seconds, hardware speed does not enter the measurement. Between AlexNet in 2012 and EfficientNet in 2019, the required compute fell by `{python} EfficiencyGainsMetrics.algo_efficiency_max_mult_str`, a halving roughly every `{python} EfficiencyGainsMetrics.algo_halving_months_str` between those two endpoints (@fig-algo-efficiency). The dashed line in the figure is an exponential fit to those measured points. The reduction measures algorithmic progress at fixed task quality. Comparing it with hardware progress would require a matching measure of useful throughput or energy efficiency; Moore's law describes transistor integration,[^fn-moores-law-baseline] which alone does not determine either quantity.
```

title: Distributed Intelligence Spectrum
caption: **Distributed Intelligence Spectrum**: Deployment tiers form a continuum governed by physical constraints, spanning nine orders of magnitude in power. Moving from centralized cloud infrastructure to on-device TinyML trades raw computational capacity and elastic scale for shorter communication paths, data locality, and network independence.
alt: Horizontal spectrum showing five deployment tiers from left to right: ultra-low-power devices and sensors, intelligent device, gateway, on-premises servers, and cloud. Arrows indicate TinyML, edge AI, and cloud AI spans across the spectrum.
section: Four Deployment Regimes Across Nine Orders of Magnitude {#sec-ml-systems-deployment-paradigm-framework-0d25}
context:
Three physical constraints (latency, power dissipation, and memory) organize four deployment paradigms.[^fn-paradigm-deployment-tradeoff] The categories overlap—edge describes proximity to data, while mobile and TinyML further distinguish local devices by their resource envelopes—and the combination of a workload and its target platform determines which constraint binds first. Centralizing computation in Cloud ML\index{Cloud ML!characteristics} provides elastic compute and large memory capacity, at the cost of wide-area network latency on every inference. Moving workloads to Edge ML\index{Edge ML!latency benefits} eliminates that network round trip and keeps sensitive data on premises [@shi2016], but it caps available compute at local site power and cooling budgets. Stepping onto battery-powered devices, Mobile ML\index{Mobile ML!energy constraints} delivers responsive interaction directly on handsets and tablets, within a passive thermal envelope where sustained computation triggers throttling. At the low-power extreme, TinyML\index{TinyML!always-on sensing} runs on microcontrollers [@janapa_reddi2022] whose milliwatt power budgets and kilobyte memories require compact models and integer arithmetic. Along the way, the memory constraint changes form: in the data center it usually binds as bandwidth, whereas on a microcontroller it binds first as capacity. Arranged along one physical continuum, these tiers run from warehouse-scale megawatts in data centers down to milliwatts on embedded microcontrollers (@fig-cloud-edge-TinyML-comparison).

[^fn-paradigm-deployment-tradeoff]: [offset=-12mm] **Deployment paradigm**\index{Deployment paradigm!operating regime}: A distinct operating regime defined by latency, power, memory, and connectivity constraints. The Cloud-to-TinyML spectrum changes which resources bind; optimizing within an infeasible regime cannot satisfy the application's deployment budget. Raising a cloud model's throughput by 5 percent, for example, cannot rescue an application whose 10 ms latency budget the network round trip alone exceeds.

title: Fifty Years of Microprocessor Trends
caption: **Fifty Years of Microprocessor Trends**: Transistor count, single-thread performance (SPECint benchmark score), clock frequency, typical power, and logical core count of microprocessors from 1971 to 2021 on a logarithmic axis. Transistor counts keep rising after the mid-2000s while frequency and typical power level off and single-thread performance slows; the gray band marks the end of Dennard scaling, after which added transistors went into more cores. Data from @rupp2022microprocessor.
alt: Scatter plot on a logarithmic vertical axis from 1970 to 2022 with five series: transistors in thousands rising steadily to about 10 to the 7.7, single-thread performance rising and then flattening after about 2005, frequency in megahertz flattening near 3,000 to 5,000 after 2005, typical power in watts leveling near 100, and logical cores staying at 1 until about 2005 and then rising. A gray vertical band near 2005 is labeled end of Dennard scaling.
context:
[^fn-dennard-scaling-origin]: **Dennard scaling**\index{Dennard scaling!origin and breakdown}: Named after Robert Dennard, whose IBM team described MOSFET scaling relationships under which shrinking devices could reduce voltage and current while keeping power density approximately controlled [@dennard1974]. As voltage scaling slowed and energy became a first-order architectural constraint, performance growth shifted toward parallelism and specialization: multi-core processors, GPUs, and TPUs [@hennessy2019; @esmaeilzadeh2011].

[^fn-tpu-hardware-specialization]: **Tensor processing unit (TPU)**\index{TPU!specialization trade-off}: An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) designed for operations common in ML, especially matrix multiplication. PFLOP/s-to-EFLOP/s figures describe aggregated TPU systems rather than one chip. Specialization trades general-purpose flexibility for workload-dependent efficiency; its advantage over a GPU depends on the model, numerical format, and systems being compared [@jouppi2023].

title: Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard
caption: **Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard**: Each bar is demand over supply, so the dashed line marks the point where a level is exactly saturated. The model occupies a small fraction of the ESP32-S3's 4 MB flash budget (Level 1: PASS), but its 101 ms latency (25 MFLOP of compute plus fixed overhead) is twice a tightened 50 ms budget for a responsive chime (Level 2: FAIL), even though it clears the scenario's canonical 200 ms budget.
alt: Horizontal bar chart of demand over supply with a dashed saturation line at 1.0. The latency (SLA) bar is red and extends to about twice the line. The memory (flash) bar is green and short, far below the line.
context:
```

A smart doorbell, a TinyML scenario that recurs through later chapters alongside the five lighthouses, applies the same always-on pattern to vision. A visual wake-word model [@chowdhery2019vww], a small classifier that answers only whether a person is in view, runs on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, the TinyML platform of @tbl-representative-systems. Its feasibility is screened in two levels, storage first and latency second. At level 1, the `{python} DoorbellScorecard.weight_mb_str` of 16-bit weights occupy `{python} DoorbellScorecard.flash_util_pct_str` of the `{python} DoorbellScorecard.flash_mb_str` flash. Passing this storage check does not establish complete memory fit, because intermediate results and runtime state must also fit in SRAM, the two-tier split that @sec-ml-systems-tinyml-advantages-operational-tradeoffs-2d40 develops. Level 2 applies the iron law. The model needs `{python} DoorbellScorecard.flops_str` per frame, and the microcontroller sustains about `{python} DoorbellScorecard.rate_str` at this precision, so compute takes `{python} DoorbellScorecard.compute_ms_str`; about `{python} DoorbellScorecard.overhead_ms_str` of fixed overhead brings the total to `{python} DoorbellScorecard.latency_ms_str`. That estimate clears the scenario's canonical `{python} DoorbellScorecard.canonical_sla_ms_str` budget; sensor acquisition and any data movement omitted by the estimate must still be checked. A more responsive chime with a `{python} DoorbellScorecard.strict_sla_ms_str` budget changes the verdict without changing the model, and @fig-doorbell-scorecard plots that tightened case. In the plot, flash stays far below the saturation line while latency reaches `{python} DoorbellScorecard.latency_util_pct_str` of its budget. Flash storage was not the binding constraint; latency is, and on-chip SRAM still has to be checked separately.

caption: **Cloud ML Constraint Map**: Centralized infrastructure solves the scale problem for compute-bound workloads, bandwidth-bound workloads, and capacity-bound workloads, but it introduces the distance, dependency, privacy, and cost constraints that determine when cloud ML stops being the right deployment target.
alt: Constraint map for cloud ML with four branches: binding constraint, system response, failure boundary, and workloads that fit. The map connects scale and relaxed latency budgets to pooled accelerators, sharding, speed-of-light latency, internet dependence, and cloud-scale workloads.
context:
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that cloud ML is "unlimited compute." In reality, the distance penalty $(\Latency)$ and the ingestion bottleneck $(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)$ are physics constraints that no software optimization can eliminate, setting a hard floor on response time for any workload whose data originates outside the data center.

:::

title: Cloud Data Center Scale
caption: **Cloud Data Center Scale**: Dedicated accelerator facilities aggregate thousands of specialized TPU chips in liquid-cooled racks to deliver exaFLOP-scale matrix throughput. This centralized infrastructure makes large-scale model training and high-throughput serving viable, but incurs megawatt-scale power consumption and speed-of-light network distance penalties. Source: [@pichai2023gemini].
alt: Perspective view down a central aisle between densely cabled server racks illuminated by blue and purple indicator lights.

title: Edge ML Constraint Map
caption: **Edge ML Constraint Map**: Moving computation near the data removes the network-latency term and reduces bandwidth pressure, but it replaces centralized scale with fixed local capacity, distributed security exposure, and operational complexity across many sites.
alt: Constraint map for edge ML with four branches: binding constraint, system response, failure boundary, and workloads that fit. The map connects sub-100 ms response, raw data rates, and on-premises data to nearby compute, local filtering, fixed capacity, distributed security, and edge workloads.
context:
:::

Real-time deadlines are not the only driver. Data sovereignty\index{Edge ML!data sovereignty} and privacy rules can restrict transmitting raw sensor streams across external networks, which places computation on local gateways, industrial PCs, and on-premises servers. Placing compute near sensors and filtering data locally helps meet sub-100 ms response budgets, while introducing failure boundaries in fixed node capacity and remote fleet management (@fig-edge-ml).

title: Mobile ML Constraint Map
caption: **Mobile ML Constraint Map**: On-device processing buys responsiveness, privacy, offline operation, and personalization, but the phone's shared battery and passive thermal envelope make sustained energy efficiency the binding design constraint.
alt: Constraint map for mobile ML with four branches: binding constraint, system response, failure boundary, and workloads that fit. The map connects battery, passive cooling, private sensor data, and mobility to on-device inference, NPUs, compression, thermal throttling, and mobile workloads.
context:
:::

Two boundaries define the mobile envelope, and together they push the design toward on-device NPU acceleration and model compression (@fig-mobile-ml). The first is the **battery tax**\index{Battery tax!definition}\index{Battery tax!always-on constraints}, the share of the phone's finite energy budget that an always-on ML feature spends before the rest of the system runs, because the battery limits total energy over time. Thermodynamics imposes the second boundary, which holds even for a plugged-in tablet: every watt becomes heat, and where a data center removes heat with active cooling, a thin mobile device relies on passive transfer through its chassis and surfaces. This creates the **thermal wall**\index{Thermal wall!definition}, the power wall's device-level form, which sets a hard ceiling on sustained power consumption independent of battery capacity.

title: TinyML Hardware Scale
caption: **TinyML Hardware Scale**: Microcontroller development boards integrate sensors, processing cores, and low-power radios onto a compact substrate, making constrained ML applications accessible for prototyping. Finished sensing devices must budget SRAM, sensor and radio power, inference cadence, and sleep energy to achieve multi-year battery life. Source: Figure 6 in @janapa_reddi2022, licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
alt: Composite image showing an Arduino Tiny Machine Learning Kit with its board, shield, camera module, and USB cable, and an annotated Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense board with callouts to its USB port, IMU, temperature-and-humidity sensor, microphone, processor, Bluetooth module, and TensorFlow Lite model.
context:
the deployment spectrum with low-cost, low-power ML on deeply constrained embedded devices [@warden2020tinyml; @janapa_reddi2022]. Devices costing under \$10 and averaging less than one milliwatt[^fn-milliwatt-power-threshold] of power when duty-cycled make ubiquitous[^fn-ubiquitous-computing-paradigm] sensing economically practical at large scale. MLPerf Tiny and MCUNet show how such constraints are evaluated and optimized in practice [@banbury2021mlperftiny; @lin2020mcunet]. Its first feasibility screen is memory capacity, because weights must fit in flash and working state in SRAM, but once a model fits, power is the limit that shapes the design. This is the domain of the power-bound archetype, where the optimization objective shifts from maximizing throughput to minimizing energy per inference. With duty-cycled execution, a keyword spotting model consuming about `{python} EnergyAnchors.e_kws_str` per inference on dedicated low-power audio silicon can operate for years on a coin-cell battery\index{Coin-cell battery!deployment longevity}, trading model capacity for operational longevity. A general-purpose microcontroller running the same model spends orders of magnitude more. On an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense development board (@fig-TinyML-example), on-board microphone, motion, and environmental sensors share a single substrate with a low-power microcontroller executing quantized TensorFlow Lite Micro models [@david2021tensorflow]. The board illustrates integration; its full power draw depends on the sensors, radio, and duty cycle.

[^fn-milliwatt-power-threshold]: **The 1 mW threshold**: Ambient energy harvesting\index{Energy harvesting!milliwatt threshold} can power a device indefinitely only when long-term harvested power exceeds the complete system's average load. Available power varies across sources and environments. Solar cells the size of a thumbnail may produce ~10 mW outdoors but ~10 µW indoors, thermoelectric generators on warm pipes ~100 µW, and RF energy from nearby transmitters ~10 µW. This crossover can transform the deployment model from "battery-limited lifetime" to "deploy and forget," but it depends on the source, environment, and workload.

title: TinyML Constraint Map
caption: **TinyML Constraint Map**: Milliwatt power and kilobyte memory make always-on sensing economically possible, but those same limits force the model, activations, runtime, and update path to fit a radically smaller engineering envelope.
alt: Constraint map for TinyML with four branches: binding constraint, system response, failure boundary, and workloads that fit. The map connects milliwatt power, kilobyte memory, always-on operation, and sparse connectivity to on-chip models, integer arithmetic, sleeping between detections, compression loss, firmware update risk, and tiny sensing workloads.
context:
This definition reframes the iron law of ML systems. In terms of @eq-bottleneck, TinyML imposes a physical memory-capacity precondition that execution time does not capture: the weight footprint $\WeightMemory$ and activation footprint $\ActivationMemory$ must stay within memory capacity $\DeviceMemoryCapacity$. When total memory is measured in kilobytes, model structure and runtime allocation determine feasibility before latency optimization begins, and every avoidable data movement spends part of the energy budget. The objective therefore shifts from raw throughput toward energy per inference and memory fit.

The same four-branch map applies at the bottom of the spectrum (@fig-tiny-ml). Milliwatt budgets and kilobyte memories favor low-precision execution and duty-cycled sleep, and they move the failure boundary away from latency toward compression-driven accuracy loss and risky firmware updates.

section: Four screening gates for choosing a tier {#sec-ml-systems-decision-framework-241f}
context:
:::

When this **complexity tax**\index{Complexity tax!definition}\index{Complexity tax!ML vs. heuristics} outweighs the operational value of improved statistical predictions, the ML deployment costs the system more than it returns. Once a learned system is justified, however, paradigm selection relies on a tiered decision framework\index{Decision framework!paradigm selection} ordered by how rapidly a constraint invalidates an architecture. The screening hierarchy evaluates four successive gates: regulatory privacy, physical latency, local compute capacity, and lifecycle economics. Privacy leads the order because a legal prohibition on moving data eliminates an option before anything is measured, whereas the latency and compute gates require numbers. Each gate passes only its survivors to the next, so the screening sequence acts as successive filters on a candidate set (@fig-mlsys-playbook-flowchart).

title: Hybrid System Interactions
caption: **Hybrid System Interactions**: Data flows upward from sensors through processing layers to cloud analytics, while trained models deploy downward to edge, mobile, and TinyML inference points. Five connection types (deploy, data, results, assist, and sync) establish a distributed architecture where each paradigm contributes unique capabilities.

section: How hybrid tiers communicate in production {#sec-ml-systems-production-system-integration-3bb3}
context:
### How hybrid tiers communicate in production {#sec-ml-systems-production-system-integration-3bb3}

If a phone's audio preprocessor updates its normalization constants while the cloud transcription model expects the old scaling, or if a smartwatch and phone disagree on which activity labels are active, the hybrid pipeline fails silently across the tier boundary. Keeping multiple execution tiers working as one system requires explicit communication pathways. Five interaction channels connect the tiers (@fig-hybrid). Compiled model artifacts deploy downward from cloud training clusters to edge, mobile, and TinyML inference engines. Raw sensor streams and filtered telemetry propagate upward toward cloud analytics. Peer-to-peer result forwarding, local assist handoffs, and state synchronization complete the set. State synchronization keeps feature definitions and model versions consistent across tiers.

These shared pillars in turn support unified requirements for performance optimization, operational monitoring, and trustworthy engineering.

context:
## What Every Tier Shares {#sec-ml-systems-hybrid-approaches-work-4bb8}

Although the four deployment tiers differ by orders of magnitude in available energy, memory capacity, and compute throughput, they rest on shared systems foundations. Every tier moves data through a pipeline, manages a fixed budget of compute, memory, energy, and network capacity, and binds models to hardware through a software architecture. On those three shared foundations rest the same cross-cutting concerns of efficiency, monitoring, and trustworthy engineering (@fig-ml-systems-convergence).

title: Simplified Lifecycle with Feedback
caption: **Simplified Lifecycle with Feedback**: The six core stages of ML engineering form a closed loop rather than a linear handoff. A primary feedback path from monitoring back to data collection supports investigation and adaptation as production distributions shift, model accuracy degrades, and operational constraints evolve.
alt: Six-stage flowchart across two rows, with each stage numbered 1 through 6: problem definition, data collection, model development, and evaluation run left to right along the top row; deployment and integration sits at the right of the bottom row with an arrow running left to monitoring and maintenance. Feedback loop arrow curves from monitoring back to data collection.
context:
That sequence is the **machine learning lifecycle**\index{Machine learning lifecycle}, a structured, iterative process[^fn-crisp-dm-lifecycle] that guides the development, evaluation, and improvement of ML systems [@amershi2019]. Numbered in the order a project first meets them, its six stages form a chain in which each stage produces the artifact the next one needs. Problem definition (1) turns a request into measurable targets and deployment constraints. These guide data collection and preparation (2), which turns raw observations into a versioned, validated dataset. Model development and training (3) then fits trained weights to that dataset, and evaluation and validation (4) tests those weights against the original targets and records the release evidence in a release manifest. Once the manifest clears the gate, deployment and integration (5) installs the approved model where it must run, while monitoring and maintenance (6) watches the live system and sends what it learns back to earlier stages, closing the loop drawn in @fig-lifecycle-overview.

[^fn-crisp-dm-lifecycle]: **CRISP-DM (cross-industry standard process for data mining)**\index{Cross-industry standard process for data mining!lifecycle influence}: CRISP-DM codified data-intensive system development as six interconnected, iterative phases rather than a linear waterfall [@chapman2000crisp]; its core design principle (moving back and forth between phases as results require) directly informs the modern ML lifecycle's structure.

title: Dual-Pipeline ML Development
caption: **Dual-Pipeline ML Development**: Machine learning engineering decouples into parallel data and model pipelines operating on different timescales. While the model pipeline executes rapid inner-loop training and evaluation, outer-loop feedback from production deployment and data validation continuously reshapes upstream collection and curation.
alt: Two parallel pipelines: a green data pipeline of six stages above a blue model pipeline of four stages. A deployment feedback arrow returns to data collection; curved arrows labeled Data fixes and Data needs loop back to earlier data stages.
context:
```

In practice, the stages between problem definition and deployment run as two pipelines on different clocks. @Fig-ml-lifecycle zooms into that work as ten finer-grained blocks. The upper data pipeline, the substance of stage 2, continuously transforms raw operational streams through ingestion, curation, annotation, and validation into versioned, ML-ready datasets. The lower model pipeline executes the inner development loop of stages 3 and 4: training architectures, computing evaluation metrics, validating system constraints, and packaging approved artifacts for deployment, with stage 4's release manifest drawn as an ML certificate. Outer-loop feedback arrows carry production telemetry and validation discoveries back to upstream data stages, the return path that stage 6 operates.

title: Retinal Hemorrhages in DR Screening
caption: **Retinal Hemorrhages in DR Screening**: Side-by-side fundus images illustrate the subtle visual features an ML screening system must detect. Identifying localized microvascular lesions (such as the indicated hemorrhage) requires preserving fine spatial resolution through the vision pipeline and establishing strict input-quality validation to handle lighting and camera variations in clinical field deployments. Source: [@peng2016deep].
alt: Two side-by-side retinal fundus images labeled A. HEALTHY and B. DISEASED. An arrow labeled Hemorrhages points to a small lesion in the diseased retina.
section: The running case: Diabetic retinopathy screening {#sec-ml-workflow-case-study-diabetic-retinopathy-screening-7d71}
context:
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a major cause of preventable vision loss.[^fn-dr-scale-screening] While early detection prevents severe vision loss, limited access to specialist ophthalmologists in rural regions motivates automated screening programs. Google built one of the best documented of these programs, a deep-learning model that performed at the level of ophthalmologists on curated retinal images [@gulshan2016] and that Google Health then deployed in clinics in Thailand [@beede2020human]. Detecting the pathology, however, requires identifying subtle microvascular features under variable capture conditions. @Fig-eye-dr contrasts a normal retina (Panel A) with one showing diabetic retinopathy (Panel B).

[^fn-dr-scale-screening]: **Diabetic retinopathy (DR)**\index{Diabetic retinopathy!deployment scale}: DR is a common complication of diabetes; early detection can prevent vision loss, but specialist access varies substantially across countries. This gap motivates scalable screening programs. In clinics with limited hardware or unreliable connectivity, model size, offline capability, latency, and workflow integration can become binding deployment constraints.

```
title: Feedback Paths Across Lifecycle Stages
caption: **Feedback Paths Across Lifecycle Stages**: Multi-stage feedback pathways show how downstream discoveries can require upstream corrections. Data-quality and distribution gaps detected during evaluation may prompt targeted collection or augmentation, while operational constraints and performance drift can motivate model, data, or pipeline changes after investigation.
alt: Diagram with six boxes: data collection, preparation, training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring. Labeled feedback arrows show data gaps, validation issues, performance insights, and deployment constraints flowing between stages.
context:
[^fn-rollback-ml-state]: **ML rollback complexity**\index{Rollback!ML state mismatch}: An ML model's validity is coupled to the data distribution on which it was trained, not just its code. Because the data environment keeps changing, rolling back to an older model binary cannot restore the past data distribution, so the older model may also misbehave on today's live inputs. Even a fast rollback is therefore a temporary containment step rather than a full restore.

Correlating production evidence with its causes sends work back upstream. @Fig-ml-lifecycle-feedback maps those return paths across stages 2 through 6, drawing data collection and data preparation as separate boxes and omitting problem definition, which sits upstream of every path shown. In the diabetic retinopathy deployment, when model evaluation uncovers accuracy drops on older fundus cameras, the *Data gaps* path triggers targeted image collection from those specific clinics. Similarly, when validation across patient cohorts reveals lower sensitivity for patients with cataracts, the *Validation Issues* path motivates retraining with synthetic lens-opacity augmentations. In production, runtime telemetry routes along the *Data Quality Issues* and *Performance Insights* paths back into data preparation and collection whenever clinic hardware upgrades change how images look.

title: The Four Pillars of Data Engineering
caption: **The Four Pillars of Data Engineering**: Quality, Reliability, Scalability, and Governance form the foundational framework for ML data systems. Each pillar contributes essential capabilities (solid arrows), while trade-offs between pillars (dashed lines) mark where strengthening one pillar stresses its neighbor.

context:
### Four foundational pillars {#sec-data-engineering-four-foundational-pillars-c119}

The ZIP-code failure crossed several concerns at once: the values were wrong (quality), the transform broke silently instead of rejecting the record (reliability), and no contract recorded what the field meant (governance). Preventing failures like it means balancing four competing operational priorities (@fig-four-pillars). Each feeds the ML data system, and each pulls against its neighbors: stricter validation costs throughput, stronger consistency limits distributed scale, privacy constraints cost performance, and bias mitigation can shrink the usable training set.

title: Keyword Spotting in Action
caption: **Keyword Spotting in Action**: An Amazon Echo Dot exchange shows the user saying “Alexa,” the device acknowledging the wake word, and the user issuing “dim the lights.” A lightweight, always-on wake-word detector listens continuously and triggers the main voice assistant only after the keyword is spoken.
alt: Amazon Echo Dot smart speaker on the left. On the right, three speech bubbles illustrate a short exchange: the user says 'Alexa...' (wake word), the device replies 'Hi, VJ!', and the user follows with 'dim the lights' as a command.
context:
A wake-word detector answers to two numbers at once. It must catch nearly every spoken wake word, and it must almost never wake for anything else, while listening continuously in tens of kilobytes of memory on a microcontroller or the low-power core of a phone or smart speaker. The chapter's illustrative smart speaker sets those numbers, and every later stage of the pipeline is measured against them.

In the wake-word interaction sequenced in @fig-keywords, an always-on detector traps "Alexa..." before the smart speaker acknowledges the utterance and opens the command channel for "dim the lights." Behind that brief exchange sits the data pipeline this chapter builds: the recordings the detector learned from, how they were labeled and checked, and how the result was verified before it shipped.

title: Shared Dataset Bias Propagation
caption: **Shared Dataset Bias Propagation**: Five models (A through E) all train on a single central dataset repository, reached by a path labeled shared training data. Beneath the models, five labeled arrows (bias propagation, shared limits, blind spots, common weaknesses, and systemic issues) converge on one box, limited real-world alignment. Shared training data can propagate correlated blind spots across models; their failures need not be independent.
alt: A central training dataset repository at the top connects downward to five model boxes labeled A through E, with one path labeled shared training data. Below the models, five labeled arrows reading bias propagation, shared limits, blind spots, common weaknesses, and systemic issues converge on a single box labeled limited real-world alignment. A dashed boundary around the models and that box is labeled potential issues.
context:
Whether an external dataset is safe to reuse depends on how well it is documented. Without records of sensor calibration, recording environments, and filtering rules, a team cannot reproduce an external dataset's conditions or check whether they match deployment [@pineau2021improving; @henderson2018]. Good documentation states how the data was collected, how each label was defined, and what baseline error rates were found, so another team can validate the corpus independently. Once ingestion reaches millions of examples from varied sources, hidden label errors also multiply past what humans can inspect by hand [@gudivada2017data], so the pipeline must run automated validation checks on every batch.

Reuse carries a less visible risk. Standard validation metrics can create an illusion of model readiness when the benchmark itself is unrepresentative, and when many teams train on the same repository, its blind spots do not average out across their models. They can recur across models, so five models trained on one dataset can share correlated failures (@fig-misalignment).

title: Data Source Noise
caption: **Data Source Noise**: A black-and-white photograph from 1914 shows early manually operated electric traffic signals, illustrating how historical images can appear in modern web scraping results for contemporary queries. Such anachronistic content requires systematic validation and filtering to prevent spurious correlations in training data. Source: [@stromberg2015traffic].
alt: Black-and-white photograph of a busy Cleveland intersection with streetcars, pedestrians, a roadside control booth, and handwritten arrows labeling red and green traffic signals.
context:
Web scraping reduces the cost of collecting raw examples at scale. Supervision remains a separate expense unless the source and task already supply usable labels or training targets. Foundational vision datasets such as ImageNet [@imagenet_website] and OpenImages [@kuznetsova2020] relied on automated scraping, while modern language models depend on multi-terabyte web crawls [@groeneveld2024]. Ingestion pipelines targeting domain-specific corpora, such as public code repositories [@chen2021evaluating], expand coverage at low per-sample acquisition costs. Scrapers are also fragile: page layouts change and break parsers, sites throttle crawlers, and dynamically rendered content goes missing. Raw web crawls also capture anachronistic or irrelevant samples that contaminate supervised targets.

The 1914 street scene in @fig-traffic-light captures this failure mode directly. An uncurated web query for "traffic light" returned a historical Cleveland intersection where streetcars and a roadside control booth surround early manually switched signals. If an autonomous driving model trained on such samples, it would learn spurious correlations with trolley tracks, period attire, and handwritten label annotations rather than modern LED traffic lights.

title: Training Data Approaching the Stock of Public Text
caption: **Training Data Approaching the Stock of Public Text**: Reported pre-training tokens for landmark language models from 2020 to 2025 on a logarithmic axis, with a least-squares fit, against the estimated stock of public human-generated text (shaded band, 90 percent interval; dotted line, median). The projection is a dated constraint scenario rather than a forecast, because data selection, synthetic generation, multimodal data, licensing, and filtering policy all change the usable supply. Stock estimate from @villalobos2024will; token counts from the model reports [@brown2020language; @rae2021scaling; @hoffmann2022chinchilla; @chowdhery2022palm; @touvron2023llama; @touvron2023llama2; @dubey2024llama; @qwen2024qwen25; @deepseek2025v3; @yang2025qwen3].
alt: Log-scale scatter plot of training tokens against release date from 2020 to 2028. Ten labeled points rise from GPT-3 and Gopher near 300 billion tokens in 2020 and 2021 to Qwen3 near 36 trillion in 2025, with a dashed fitted line that continues upward. An orange shaded band spans 100 trillion to 1 quadrillion tokens with a dotted median line near 300 trillion, and the fitted line enters the band around 2027.
context:
```

Even a well-governed crawl draws on a finite supply. Pretraining corpora for large language models grew at a fitted rate of about `{python} TrainingDataSupply.growth_mult_str` per year, from the `{python} TrainingDataSupply.first_tokens_str` tokens that trained GPT-3 in 2020 to the `{python} TrainingDataSupply.last_tokens_str` reported for Qwen3 in 2025 [@brown2020language; @yang2025qwen3]. @Fig-running-out-of-human-data sets that climb against the estimated stock of public human-generated text, roughly `{python} TrainingDataSupply.stock_median_str` tokens once quality and repetition are accounted for [@villalobos2024will], and at the fitted rate the largest corpora reach the middle of that estimate around `{python} TrainingDataSupply.crossing_year_str`. Once quality text runs short, acquiring more of it stops being a purchasing decision, and filtering, deduplication, and the selection methods of @sec-data-selection decide how much each additional token is worth. A wake-word model meets its own version of the limit far sooner. No crawl holds enough clean recordings of one phrase in every accent and acoustic setting, so the KWS pipeline has to commission the data it lacks.

title: End-to-End Data Pipeline
caption: **End-to-End Data Pipeline**: Heterogeneous raw sources (batch and streaming) normalize into unified storage before feeding downstream training and feature processing. The architecture decouples ingestion throughput from iterative transformation and labeling loops, all bounded by an overarching data-governance layer.
alt: Layered flow diagram with sources at top, then ingestion and a storage layer, then ML training and a processing layer side by side at the bottom, with labeling looping back to storage, all inside a data-governance boundary.
context:
## Ingestion and Validation {#sec-data-engineering-data-pipeline-architecture-b527}

A crowdsourced wake-word recording arrives as a stereo MP3, a synthetic one as a mono WAV file at a different sampling rate, and a clip from a consenting user's device as a compressed fragment stamped in the wrong time zone. The ingestion boundary turns this mix into one consistent record format and decides which records may enter at all. It is the front end of the **data pipeline**\index{Data pipeline!definition}\index{Data pipeline!architecture} in @fig-pipeline-flow, where records pass through ingestion and central storage before the transformation loops that feed training, inside a governance perimeter that controls what may be kept and who may read it. For keyword spotting, the boundary handles the recorded examples used to build and update the model; the detector's live audio on the device never passes through it.

title: ETL vs. ELT Architectural Paradigms
caption: **ETL vs. ELT Architectural Paradigms**: The two paradigms differ in where the transformation boundary sits relative to storage. ETL enforces schema validation and cleaning before loading to protect warehouse quality, whereas ELT loads raw data directly into scalable storage, trading warehouse compute and footprint for flexible, repeatable re-transformations.
alt: Side-by-side comparison showing ETL pipeline with extract, transform, then load sequence vs. ELT pipeline with extract, load, then transform sequence within the data warehouse.
context:
[^fn-etl-quality-first]: **Extract, transform, load (ETL)**\index{ETL!reprocessing cost}: Conventional ETL validates deterministic schema constraints, whereas ML ETL must additionally monitor distributional properties using the statistical drift tests developed in @sec-data-engineering-quality-validation-monitoring-498f. A detected shift prompts investigation and validation against labeled outcomes before concluding that model quality has degraded. When feature computation logic changes, reprocessing costs depend on replay scope, windowing, and execution plans rather than requiring an unconditional full-dataset pass.

[^fn-elt-flexibility-first]: **Extract, load, transform (ELT)**\index{ELT!iteration speed}: This approach stores raw data before transformation, allowing teams to revise a transformation query and rerun it over the stored input without re-ingesting from source systems. The iteration time still depends on data volume, query complexity, warehouse capacity, and materialization strategy.

title: Data Annotation Modalities
caption: **Data Annotation Modalities**: Four rows show classification, bounding-box, segmentation, and caption labels for one image; the fifth shows a transcript label for an audio input. The appropriate annotation representation depends on the input modality and task.
alt: Five-row figure. Four rows apply classification, bounding-box, segmentation, and caption labels to a dog-on-blanket image; the fifth maps a speaker icon to the transcript 'Once upon a time...'.
context:
Segmentation maps\index{Semantic segmentation!pixel-level labels} assign a class identifier to every pixel, producing dense 2D label matrices ($\ImageHeight\times \ImageWidth$). In autonomous driving and traffic monitoring, this entails tracing irregular boundaries for driveable road surfaces, vehicles, and pedestrians. These dense annotations multiply storage and ingestion bandwidth. A segmentation mask for a $1920{\times}1080$ image requires about `{python} SegmentationLabelScale.pixel_labels_m_str` labels (one per pixel), compared to perhaps `{python} SegmentationLabelScale.box_count_str` bounding boxes or a single classification label. If each box stores `{python} SegmentationLabelScale.box_coords_str` coordinates, that is roughly `{python} SegmentationLabelScale.label_entry_ratio_mult_str` more scalar label entries than `{python} SegmentationLabelScale.box_count_str` boxes before accounting for per-value encoding. The time manual segmentation takes per image (more than 1.5 hours for each Cityscapes image [@cordts2016cityscapes]) makes this approach suitable only when pixel-level precision is essential.

@Fig-labels arrays five annotation formats across vision and speech examples, demonstrating how labeling granularity ranges from coarse scene tags and captions to spatial bounding boxes, dense pixel-level masks, and audio transcripts. Classification can label an entire scene, while bounding boxes and segmentation maps localize objects or regions. Production datasets may combine formats: a single camera frame might carry a scene label, obstacle boxes, and path-region masks, with each label type serving a distinct downstream task.

Solid bars count errors confirmed by human reviewers; hatched bars (QuickDraw and Amazon Reviews) extrapolate from a reviewed sample. ImageNet uses the ILSVRC 2012 validation set. Data from @northcutt2021pervasive.

Image datasets are blue, text green, and audio orange, and each bar is labeled with its percentage and error count.

```

Benchmarks show how large that residue remains after careful curation. @Fig-test-set-label-errors reports the share of test-set labels that @northcutt2021pervasive found to be wrong in ten widely used datasets. About `{python} TestSetLabelErrors.imagenet_pct_str` of ImageNet validation labels are incorrect, CIFAR-100 carries a similar share, and the rate reaches `{python} TestSetLabelErrors.quickdraw_pct_str` for QuickDraw, whose labels came from a largely automated collection process. Audio fares better, but AudioSet still carries wrong labels, the same failure a crowdsourced wake-word corpus faces. These are the labels that rank published models, so an error rate of a few percent can reorder a leaderboard whose top entries differ by less than that.

title: Pervasive Label Errors
caption: **Pervasive Label Errors**: Confidently mislabeled examples from widely used benchmarks, each showing the given label against the corrected ground truth (MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256, ImageNet, QuickDraw). Fine-grained confusions, such as a crab labeled lobster or a black stork labeled white stork, show that even curated datasets carry systematic errors, motivating careful quality control and expert annotation. Source: [@northcutt2021pervasive].
alt: Six-panel grid of public-dataset label errors: MNIST digit (given 5, corrected 3); CIFAR-10 frog (given cat); CIFAR-100 crab (given lobster); Caltech-256 teapot (given ewer); ImageNet black stork (given white stork); QuickDraw eye (given tiger).
context:
:::

Labeling failures arise from two distinct sources requiring different engineering responses. Across the benchmark examples compiled in @fig-hard-labels, including an ImageNet black stork mislabeled as a white stork and a CIFAR-10 frog mislabeled as a cat, each panel contrasts the erroneous assigned label against the verified ground truth. Some examples reflect degraded or ambiguous inputs where the correct label is difficult to infer from the data alone; others are visually clear but require domain knowledge, dataset-specific semantics, or expert judgment to label correctly. These different failure modes drive architectural decisions about annotator qualification, task routing, and consensus mechanisms: quality-based errors call for upstream data filtering, while expertise-based errors call for tiered annotator routing. Wake-word clips show both. A clipped or whispered "Alexa" that no annotator can hear clearly is a quality problem, filtered before labeling, whereas a near-homophone such as "Alexis" is settled only by a rubric with canonical examples and a trained reviewer.

title: AI-Augmented Labeling Decision Hierarchy
caption: **AI-Augmented Labeling Decision Hierarchy**: A top-level question about obtaining labeled data branches into four paths: traditional supervision, semi-supervised learning, weak supervision, and transfer learning, with active learning as a cost-saving alternative. The branches distinguish where supervision comes from and what additional assumptions or pretrained artifacts the pipeline must validate. Adapted from @ratner2019weak.
alt: Hierarchical diagram with question about getting labeled data at top. Four branches: traditional supervision, semi supervised, weak supervision, and transfer learning. Active learning branches as cost-saving alternative.
context:
:::

[^fn-weak-supervision-cost]: **Weak supervision**\index{Weak supervision!cost trade-off}: A "data programming" paradigm that exchanges some manual annotation labor for the upfront effort of writing and validating programmatic labeling functions. Once written, a function can be applied cheaply at scale, but execution, conflict resolution, quality monitoring, and maintenance still incur cost; the useful comparison is workload-specific rather than literally zero marginal cost.

title: Multilingual Data Preparation
caption: **Multilingual Data Preparation**: Forced alignment and segmentation transform paired audio-text data into labeled one-second segments, creating a large-scale corpus for training keyword spotting models across `{python} KWSAutomatedLabelingScale.languages_count_str`. This automated process enables scalable development of KWS systems by efficiently generating training examples from readily available read-speech resources such as Common Voice. Source: [@mazumder2021tinyml].
alt: Flowchart illustrating multilingual speech data preparation: raw audio and text transcripts undergo forced alignment and word segmentation to produce labeled one-second audio clips for model training.
context:
At even 10 seconds per label, manual annotation of that many examples would require approximately `{python} KWSAutomatedLabelingScale.label_hours_str`, roughly `{python} KWSAutomatedLabelingScale.label_years_str` of full-time effort, which makes it impractical. Broad, documented sourcing can improve coverage, but language count alone does not guarantee representative speakers, accents, devices, or acoustic environments. The pipeline staged in @fig-mswc circumvents this manual annotation bottleneck, using forced alignment\index{Forced alignment!speech labeling}\index{Speech recognition!forced alignment} [@mcauliffe2017montreal] over paired sentence audio and transcriptions to estimate word boundaries before slicing individual one-second keyword windows for classifier training.

At this scale, quality control becomes a sampling and provenance problem rather than disappearing. The pipeline should report coverage by language, speaker, accent, device, and acoustic environment; retain the source recording, transcript version, aligner version, and boundary confidence for each extracted clip; and route low-confidence alignments and underrepresented slices to human review. Held-out evaluation must then measure the intended wake words across those slices. These controls distinguish a large corpus from a representative one and make extraction errors traceable when a downstream KWS model fails.

title: Shared Preprocessing State
caption: **Shared Preprocessing State**: Only the training split fits the preprocessing state. The resulting artifact supplies the same transformation code and frozen state to every application path; the model release carries that artifact with its weights.
alt: Training data feeds a fit operation and frozen state. A shared preprocessing artifact branches to training, validation and test, and serving. A parity test contrasts shared and independently fitted state.
context:
Preprocessing parameters fall under the same split-boundary rule as the data itself (@sec-data-engineering-data-engineering-dataset-compilation-0496). If the mean and variance, or a category vocabulary, are fitted on the entire dataset before it is split, statistics of the test examples flow into the transformation the model trains through, and the test score no longer measures generalization to unseen data. The pipeline therefore fits every transformation parameter on the training split alone and applies the frozen result to validation, test, and serving inputs.

The fit and apply paths in @fig-preprocessing-fitted-state separate learning a transformation from using it. This distinction keeps held-out data outside the fitting boundary while making the serving path reproducible.

title: Audio Feature Representations
caption: **Audio Feature Representations**: Three illustrative views show an audio waveform, its time-frequency spectrogram, and a compact MFCC approximation. The spectrogram encodes time, frequency, and signal power; the bottom panel arranges a smaller set of coefficients over time.
alt: Three stacked plots: a raw audio waveform (amplitude vs. time) at top, its spectrogram (frequency vs. time with power in dB as color) in the middle, and an MFCC approximation at bottom.
context:
Transforming audio data for KWS involves converting raw waveforms into formats suitable for ML models while maintaining training-serving consistency. Raw audio waveforms (sequences of amplitude values sampled thousands of times per second) are high-dimensional. KWS pipelines often transform them into compact representations that emphasize the frequencies and temporal patterns most relevant to speech. @Fig-spectrogram-example aligns three views of an audio sample across a two-second window: the raw amplitude waveform, the corresponding time-frequency spectrogram isolating high-power acoustic energy around 500 Hz, and a compact 13-coefficient MFCC approximation. These standardized feature representations, typically MFCCs or spectrograms,\index{Spectrogram!audio features}[^fn-spectrogram-audio-representation] emphasize speech-relevant characteristics while reducing noise and variability across different recording conditions. While a raw short-time Fourier transform (STFT) produces hundreds of linear frequency bins per time window, Mel-frequency analysis aggregates these bins through non-linear triangular filterbanks aligned with human auditory perception. A discrete cosine transform then compresses the signal into 13–40 decorrelated coefficients. For edge devices, this step collapses data volume by over an order of magnitude, allowing audio feature frames to fit inside the tight tens-of-kilobytes SRAM budgets of embedded coprocessors.

[^fn-spectrogram-audio-representation]: **Spectrogram**\index{Spectrogram!audio representation}: The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) computes this 2D representation by converting the one-dimensional waveform into a time-frequency image. This representation lets image-style ML models process audio, but it also creates a rigid dependency: a mismatch in STFT parameters (for example, a 25 ms vs. 30 ms window) changes the feature representation between training and serving and can degrade performance.
```
