```

That spread survived a long collapse in absolute price. @Fig-storage-price-trend traces the lowest recorded price per terabyte of each medium in constant 2020 dollars. Hard disk storage fell from about `{python} StoragePriceTrend.hdd_first_usd_str` per terabyte in `{python} StoragePriceTrend.hdd_first_year_str` to `{python} StoragePriceTrend.hdd_latest_usd_str` in `{python} StoragePriceTrend.latest_year_str`, roughly `{python} StoragePriceTrend.hdd_orders_str` orders of magnitude, yet in `{python} StoragePriceTrend.latest_year_str` DRAM still cost `{python} StoragePriceTrend.dram_over_ssd_mult_str` as much as solid-state storage per terabyte, and solid-state storage cost `{python} StoragePriceTrend.ssd_over_hdd_mult_str` as much as hard disk. Capacity became cheap, but since the 1980s the gaps between tiers have not closed, so the choice of tier, rather than raw capacity, sets the cost of keeping a training job fed.

title: The Dataloader Choke Point
caption: **The Dataloader Choke Point**: Training throughput (img/s) is plotted against DataLoader worker count, with storage and transfer provisioned above the required `{python} FeedingProblem.compressed_bw_mb_per_s_str` rate. The blue CPU-supply curve rises with worker count until it reaches the illustrative input-pipeline cap; the red dashed line marks accelerator consumption capacity. The lower curve is the bottleneck: the accelerator starves to the left of the crossing, while extra workers beyond the crossing do not increase accelerator throughput.
alt: Line chart of throughput vs. DataLoader workers. A blue CPU line with markers rises linearly, crosses a flat red dashed GPU-capacity line, then plateaus at the input-pipeline cap. The rising segment below the line is labeled starvation; the region past the crossing is labeled saturated.
context:
```

In computer vision, JPEG decode and augmentation on host CPUs represent the typical binding stage; in keyword spotting, MFCC extraction and audio augmentation load the same host threads. This host-side preparation executes within the framework's data loader (such as PyTorch's `DataLoader`), which decodes and transforms raw records across parallel worker processes before staging batches for device transfer. Input-pipeline frameworks such as tf.data treat this stage as a system in its own right, with operators for parallel transformation, prefetching, and caching [@murray2021]. To isolate CPU worker scaling, assume storage and bus transfers are provisioned to satisfy the `{python} FeedingProblem.compressed_bw_mb_per_s_str` compressed input requirement, which a SATA solid-state drive does (@sec-data-engineering-storage-bandwidth-budget-5d2a). When storage and interconnect are nonbinding, the training pipeline depends entirely on whether CPU workers can match the accelerator's sustained rate of `{python} DataloaderStats.gpu_limit_img_per_s_str`. If each worker process transforms `{python} DataloaderStats.worker_img_per_s_str`, `{python} DataloaderStats.resnet_worker_count_str` workers are required to reach the capacity crossing. Below this threshold the CPU input pipeline binds, and adding accelerators yields no speedup, which surprises teams that expect compute investments to scale linearly. Above the crossing, launching additional workers produces no gain because the accelerator binds. The worker count represents a capacity match rather than a hardware constant: actual ResNet-50\index{ResNet-50!data-loading requirements} requirements on a given accelerator shift with image transformations, host processor architecture, batch size, and runtime configuration. @Fig-dataloader-choke-point plots this capacity crossing, where the starved regime gives way to a compute-saturated plateau.

title: Data Pipeline Debugging Flowchart
caption: **Data Pipeline Debugging Flowchart**: Four sequential checks prioritize hypotheses involving drift, overfitting or data artifacts, training-serving skew, and subgroup coverage. Each side branch suggests a candidate cause to confirm before applying the indicated repair. Other hypotheses include model, code, and hardware faults.
alt: Vertical flowchart with four blue rectangular decision boxes and result boxes suggesting hypotheses involving data drift, overfitting or data artifacts, training-serving skew, and subgroup coverage. Downward arrows labeled continue lead through every check; a gray box at the bottom names model, code, and hardware as other hypotheses.
context:
### Debugging data pipelines {#sec-data-engineering-debugging-data-pipelines-2f26}

When data debt comes due, it surfaces as an unexplained accuracy drop, an ingestion crash, or a performance gap on a specific user slice. Debugging\index{Debugging!data pipelines}\index{Pipeline!failure diagnosis} draws on three earlier results: data cascades (@sec-data-engineering-data-cascades-systematic-foundations-matter-2efe) show that upstream ingestion flaws cause downstream model anomalies, training-serving skew (@sec-data-engineering-ensuring-trainingserving-consistency-c683) exposes mismatches between offline feature generation and online serving, and drift detection (@sec-data-engineering-detecting-responding-data-drift-509a) catches statistical shifts over time. @Fig-debug-flowchart arranges four symptom checks across temporal degradation, train-validation gaps, serving skew, and subgroup disparities. A "yes" at any branch points to a candidate cause, not the end of the investigation. Engineers should run through all four checks because multiple faults often occur together, then confirm each cause by comparing fixed artifacts before choosing a fix.

title: Traditional Programming Flow
caption: **Traditional Programming Flow**: Answers are the program's output, never its input. This input-output pattern formed the basis for early AI systems but lacks the adaptability needed for complex pattern recognition tasks.
alt: Flow diagram with four boxes: rules and data as inputs flowing into central traditional programming box, which outputs answers. Arrows show data flow direction from inputs to output.
context:
```

Writing explicit `if-else` rules to recognize a handwritten digit breaks as soon as a writer tilts a stroke, thickens a line, or leaves a loop open. Rule-based programming\index{Rule-based programming!limitations} requires developers to specify every procedure that maps inputs to outputs: in the classical flow of @fig-traditional, human-authored rules and input data enter the program together, and the program deterministically computes the answers.

title: HOG Method
caption: **HOG Method**: A local image patch is divided into cells, gradient orientations are accumulated into a histogram, and the resulting descriptor summarizes local shape while reducing sensitivity to illumination. Source: Figure 5 of @bakheet2021hog, licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
alt: Diagram of HOG extraction: an input image grid with one cell highlighted, a magnified cell containing gradient-direction arrows, an orientation guide, and an eight-bin histogram labeled HOG feature.
context:
The failures of rule-based systems suggested an alternative. Rather than encoding human knowledge as explicit rules, the system could discover patterns from data, and machine learning took that direction by replacing a rule for every situation with programs that identified patterns in examples. The success of these methods, however, still depended heavily on human insight to define which patterns to look for, a process known as feature engineering\index{Feature engineering!classical ML}\index{Classical machine learning!feature engineering}.

Feature engineering transformed raw data into representations that expose patterns to learning algorithms. The histogram of oriented gradients (HOG)[^fn-hog-feature-descriptor] [@dalal2005hog] exemplifies this approach. In @fig-hog, the feature-extraction pipeline divides an image into spatial cells and bins local pixel gradient directions into eight orientation histograms, turning raw pixels into shape descriptors that tolerate lighting changes and small shifts in position.

title: Data-Driven Rule Discovery
caption: **Data-Driven Rule Discovery**: The flow diagram inverts the traditional programming pattern: data and answers serve as inputs to the machine learning process, which produces a learned decision function as output. This shift replaces a hand-coded decision policy while leaving engineers responsible for the data, objective, architecture, and evaluation.
alt: Flow diagram with four boxes: answers and data as inputs flowing into central machine learning box, which outputs rules. Arrows show inverted flow compared to traditional programming, with rules as output rather than input.
context:
### Automatic pattern discovery {#sec-neural-computation-deep-learning-automatic-pattern-discovery-214d}

Neural networks remove that ceiling by discovering their own features\index{Deep learning!automatic feature learning}, learning representations directly from raw data instead of following explicit rules or human-designed extractors. Supervised learning inverts the traditional programming relationship. Engineers provide examples and target answers, and optimization produces the decision rules as output rather than taking them as input (@fig-deeplearning). Humans still shape the task through data, objectives, architectures, and evaluation.

title: Biological-to-Artificial Neuron Mapping
caption: **Biological-to-Artificial Neuron Mapping**: Each biological structure on the left has an arithmetic counterpart on the right. Read the mapping as an abstraction rather than a resemblance claim, since it keeps only what reduces to arithmetic and discards the electrochemistry that produced the behavior.
alt: Side-by-side comparison of biological neuron and artificial neuron. Left shows biological cell with dendrites, cell body, and axon. Right shows mathematical model with inputs x, including a constant input x0 equal to 1 whose edge carries the bias b, weights w, a linear-function node, an activation function, and output. A column of label pairs between the panels maps dendrites to inputs, synapses to weights, soma to the linear function, and axon firing to the activation.
context:
### One neuron {#sec-neural-computation-artificial-neuron-computing-primitive-45b4}

To test whether a $28{\times}28$ image contains a particular stroke, a single computing unit must weigh all 784 pixel intensities, sum the evidence, and decide how strongly to fire. That basic unit of neural computation, the **artificial neuron**\index{Artificial neuron!definition}\index{Artificial neuron!computing primitive}\index{Neural network!artificial neuron} (or node), began as a simplified mathematical model of nervous activity [@mcculloch1943] before digital implementations turned it into a standard arithmetic primitive. @Fig-bio-nn2ai-nn sets the biological cell and its mathematical counterpart side by side. The left panel draws a biological cell, with branching dendrites that receive signals, a cell body that holds the nucleus, and an axon that carries the output away. The right panel draws the mathematical model. Its inputs $\LayerInputComponent_1$, $\LayerInputComponent_2$, and onward, plus a constant input of one that carries the bias, flow along weighted edges into a node. The node first forms a linear sum $\NeuronPreactivation$ and then applies an activation function $\ActivationFunction$ to emit the output $\NetworkOutput$. The column of labels between the panels pairs each biological structure with its arithmetic counterpart: dendrites with inputs, synapses with weights, the soma (cell body) with the linear sum, and axon firing with the activation.

title: Perceptron Architecture
caption: **Perceptron Architecture**: Inputs enter on the left, each scaled by its own weight, and the weighted products plus a bias meet at the summation node before a single activation function produces the output. The multiplies and the accumulation along this path are the per-neuron unit of work that the chapter's layer-cost calculations multiply out.
alt: Perceptron diagram with inputs x1 through xn on left, each connected to weight circles w1j through wnj. Weights feed into red summation node, which receives bias bj from below. Output zj flows to blue activation function f box, producing output y-hat on right.
context:
The computational machinery within each dense layer is the **perceptron**\index{Perceptron!definition}\index{Perceptron!Rosenblatt}\index{Neural network!perceptron},[^fn-perceptron-rosenblatt-model] which Rosenblatt introduced as a learning form of the artificial neuron [@rosenblatt1958]. Its signal path (inputs, weights, bias, aggregation, activation) is the one @sec-neural-computation-artificial-neuron-computing-primitive-45b4 traced through its biological origins. What remains is to formalize that path mathematically, because this repeated operation becomes the layer-level kernel that hardware executes. In the MNIST network, a first-layer unit combines all 784 pixel intensities into one activation that may respond to a learned pattern, such as a vertical edge shared by "one" and "seven." Inside one unit (@fig-perceptron), input features $\LayerInputComponent_i$ travel along weighted channels $\NeuronConnectionWeight$ and accumulate into a scalar sum with bias $\NeuronBias_j$, and the resulting linear score $\NeuronPreactivation_j$ passes through an activation $\ActivationFunction$ to produce output $\PredictedOutputComponent$. Different neurons repeat the same structure with different learned weights, allowing one layer to test many patterns against the same input.

[^fn-perceptron-rosenblatt-model]: **Perceptron**\index{Perceptron!linear separability limit}: A machine built to execute a learning algorithm, directly linking hardware and software from the start. A single linear-threshold layer cannot represent nonlinearly separable functions such as XOR, regardless of additional input hardware [@minsky1969perceptrons]. Multilayer nonlinear networks expand the representable function class, but they also introduce the training and systems costs developed in this chapter.

title: Linear vs. Nonlinear Decision Boundaries
caption: **Linear vs. Nonlinear Decision Boundaries**: Two scatter plots compare the decision boundary a network draws on the same points with and without an activation function.
alt: Two scatter plots side by side. Left plot shows cyan and green points with straight red line failing to separate them, labeled NN without activation function. Right plot shows same points with curved red decision boundary successfully separating classes, labeled NN with activation function.
context:
$$ \PredictedOutputComponent_j = \ActivationFunction(\NeuronPreactivation_j) = \ActivationFunction\left(\sum_i (\LayerInputComponent_i \cdot \NeuronConnectionWeight) + \NeuronBias_j\right) $$ {#eq-perceptron}

In @fig-nonlinear, a network without activation functions is constrained to a straight decision boundary (left panel) that misclassifies overlapping point clusters, whereas nonlinear activations allow curved boundaries (right panel) that separate the two classes cleanly. The plot illustrates representational capacity rather than an optimization guarantee; training dynamics and sample coverage still govern whether optimization finds that boundary.

title: Common Activation Functions
caption: **Common Activation Functions**: Four panels plot nonlinear activation functions with their output ranges. Sigmoid maps inputs to $(0,1)$ with smooth gradients, tanh provides zero-centered outputs in $(-1,1)$, and ReLU outputs zero for negative inputs. Softmax (bottom-right) shows one component of a 3-element vector while the other two logits are fixed at 13 and 0. Its magnified y-axis (roughly $0$ to $0.05$) is not comparable to the other panels, and it shows only one component of a vector whose outputs are interdependent and sum to 1.
alt: Four plots arranged in 2x2 grid. Top-left: sigmoid S-curve from 0 to 1. Top-right: tanh S-curve from -1 to 1. Bottom-left: ReLU showing zero for negative inputs, linear for positive inputs. Bottom-right: one softmax component as its logit varies while the other two logits remain fixed at 13 and 0, shown on a magnified vertical axis spanning roughly 0 to 0.05.
context:
The choice of activation function therefore affects both learning and computational efficiency. ReLU[^fn-relu-hardware-efficiency] ($\max(0, \NeuronPreactivation)$) became a common hidden-layer activation for feed-forward networks because it is inexpensive, has local derivative one for positive inputs, and can produce sparse activations [@nair2010rectified; @glorot2011deep]. Earlier differentiable deep networks often used sigmoid or tanh. Their smooth S-curves saturate, a failure the sigmoid discussion below develops. That contrast is not a simple ranking: sigmoid remains appropriate for some binary outputs, tanh remains useful when bounded zero-centered activations are desired, and modern architectures use additional activation families. The relevant design question is which function supplies the required output semantics and gradient behavior at an acceptable execution cost. @Fig-activation-functions charts the response curves and output ranges of three standard element-wise nonlinearities alongside the vector-level softmax function, contrasting their saturation regimes.

[^fn-relu-hardware-efficiency]: **ReLU (rectified linear unit)**\index{ReLU!etymology}\index{ReLU!hardware efficiency}: ReLU's cheap comparison-and-select evaluation and its non-saturating positive branch made deep networks markedly faster to train; in the AlexNet paper, a four-layer convolutional network reached 25 percent training error on CIFAR-10 six times sooner with ReLU than with tanh [@krizhevsky2012imagenet].

title: Layered Network Architecture
caption: **Layered Network Architecture**: Deep neural networks transform data through successive layers, enabling the extraction of increasingly complex features and patterns. Each layer applies nonlinear transformations to the outputs of the previous layer, ultimately mapping raw inputs to desired outputs.
alt: Neural network diagram showing a four-node input layer on the left, four hidden layers of ten, eight, twelve, and eight nodes with an ellipsis indicating more, and a two-node output layer on the right. Arrows show data flow from left to right. A brace above the hidden columns is labeled Hidden layers, with Input layer and Output layer as plain labels at the top corners.
context:
Neurons run side by side in layers\index{Neural network!layers}\index{Layer!organization}, collections of units that execute in parallel across shared inputs, and the power of neural networks comes from that organization rather than from any single unit. An input layer\index{Layer!input} ingests raw feature tensors; one or more hidden layers\index{Layer!hidden} transform those representations through successive matrix multiplications and nonlinear activations; and an output layer\index{Layer!output} emits task-specific predictions or decision logits.

In the feedforward schematic of @fig-layers, the task fixes only the two ends. The input layer's width matches the four input features and the output layer's width matches the two predictions. The hidden layers between them can widen and narrow freely, which is why hidden width is a design decision rather than a property of the data. Each hidden layer applies a parameterized linear transformation followed by an element-wise nonlinearity, progressively constructing higher-level abstractions from raw input signals.

title: From Neuron to Machine
caption: **From Neuron to Machine**: One neuron is a dot product between an input row and a weight column. A layer applied to a batch stacks those dot products into one matrix multiply whose cost is the product of batch size, input width, and output width. On an accelerator, a tile of the weight matrix stays inside an array of multiply-accumulate units while input rows stream through, so the batch, not the neuron, sets how much arithmetic each fetched weight pays for.
alt: Three panels left to right. One neuron: a horizontal input bar of size 1 by n-in times a vertical weight bar of size n-in by 1, labeled a dot product of n-in MACs. One layer, one batch: matrix X of size B by n-in times W of size n-in by n-out equals Z of size B by n-out, labeled B times n-in times n-out MACs. On the machine: four input rows stream into a four-by-four grid of green multiply-accumulate cells holding a weight tile, producing Z on the right; caption says each weight is fetched once and reused by all B rows.
context:
As data flows through the network, it is transformed at each layer to extract meaningful patterns. Each layer applies the neuron's weighted sum and activation in parallel across all its neurons, and its outputs become the next layer's inputs. Simple features detected in early layers combine into increasingly complex patterns in deeper layers.

On the machine, a layer is one matrix multiplication over all of its neurons at once, and the boundary between layers is where data moves and waits. Each layer writes its output as an activation tensor that the next layer must read. Inference can discard that tensor once the next layer has consumed it, and training must keep it until the backward pass. The next layer cannot start until that tensor exists, which is the source of the latency floor that no amount of parallel hardware inside a layer removes. @Fig-neuron-to-machine traces that translation in three steps. One neuron is a dot product of $\LayerInputWidth$ MACs. Stacking a layer's neurons and a batch of $\BatchSize$ examples (inputs processed together in one pass) turns those dot products into one matrix multiply of $\BatchSize\cdot\PreviousLayerWidth\cdot\CurrentLayerWidth$ MACs (for the first MNIST layer at batch 32, $(32{\times}784)\cdot(784{\times}128)$). The hardware executes that multiply by holding a tile of weights in an array of multiply-accumulate units while rows of inputs stream past, so each weight fetched from memory serves every example in the batch. What each of those multiplications reads besides the activations is the layer's parameters.

title: Fully Connected Layers
caption: **Fully Connected Layers**: A two-layer network (three layers of units) connects every neuron to all neurons in the preceding layer. Labeled edges and nodes illustrate the organization of weights, biases, and activations; they are not a worked numerical forward pass.
alt: Network with three layers of units: three green input nodes, four blue hidden nodes, and two red output nodes. Labeled arrows show illustrative weight values on each connection. Input, hidden, and output nodes show illustrative values, and bias values are labeled at the hidden and output layers.
context:
The canonical case studied here connects each neuron in a layer to every neuron in the previous layer, forming a "dense" or "fully connected" layer\index{Fully-connected layer!dense connectivity}. This pattern allows each neuron to use all features from the previous layer. Fully connected layers establish the mathematical principles needed here, while alternative connectivity patterns exploit structure in the data and can reduce work or improve statistical efficiency.

@Fig-connections details this dense interconnect topology on a concrete two-layer network ($3 \to 4 \to 2$ units). Layer counts in this chapter count layers of weights, not layers of units, so this network has two and the MNIST network ($784 \to 128 \to 64 \to 10$) has three. The figure labels every scalar weight $\NeuronConnectionWeight$ and layer bias $\NeuronBias_j$ alongside intermediate node activations. Reading the incoming edges for any single destination neuron isolates one column of the weight matrix, while evaluating all destinations in parallel forms the complete matrix-vector multiplication. The numerical values illustrate parameter placement rather than an active inference pass; the essential systems property is the matrix dimension. For layers of widths $(\LayerWidth_0, \LayerWidth_1, \LayerWidth_2)$, with $\LayerWidth_0$ the input width, the weight matrices span $\WeightMatrix^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerWidth_0 \times \LayerWidth_1}$ and $\WeightMatrix^{(2)} \in \mathbb{R}^{\LayerWidth_1 \times \LayerWidth_2}$, requiring $\LayerWidth_0\LayerWidth_1+\LayerWidth_1\LayerWidth_2$ weights before biases.

title: MNIST Network Topology
caption: **MNIST Network Topology**: Both panels draw the same network; only the form of the input changes, from a two-dimensional image in panel (a) to the flattened vector the input layer actually receives in panel (b).
alt: Two panels showing MNIST digit recognition. Panel a: a digit 7 image labeled 28 px by 28 px beside a column of input-layer circles fully connected to 10 output nodes, one marked 1 and the rest marked 0. Panel b: the same network with the image flattened into a 784-element pixel vector that an arrow feeds into the input layer.
context:
```

Widening both hidden layers from 100 to 1000 neurons, comparing a $784 \to 100 \to 100 \to 10$ network with a $784 \to 1000 \to 1000 \to 10$ network, increases parameters from ~`{python} MnistScaleComparison.mnist_small_params_k_str` to ~`{python} MnistScaleComparison.mnist_large_params_m_str` (~`{python} MnistScaleComparison.mnist_small_mem_kb_str` vs. ~`{python} MnistScaleComparison.mnist_large_mem_mb_str` in FP32). Whether the wider network improves accuracy requires training and evaluation; the storage increase alone already matters for mobile deployment budgets.

title: Width Costs Quadratically, Depth Costs Linearly
caption: **Width Costs Quadratically, Depth Costs Linearly**: Forward multiply-accumulate operations (MACs) per example for fully connected networks on the MNIST input (784) and output (10) widths. Left: two hidden layers whose shared width sweeps from 64 to 4,096 on log-log axes; once the hidden-to-hidden matrix dominates, the curve follows the dashed slope-two guide, and the running 784-128-64-10 network sits near the narrow end. Right: hidden width fixed at 512 while depth sweeps from 1 to 32 hidden layers; MACs per example (left axis) and activations retained per example for training (right axis) both rise in a straight line.
alt: Two panels. Left: log-log plot of MACs per example against hidden width from 64 to 4096, a blue curve that steepens toward a dashed slope-two reference line, with a red marker for the MNIST 784-128-64-10 network near the left end. Right: linear plot against number of hidden layers from 1 to 32 at width 512, with a blue line of MACs per example in millions on the left axis and an orange dashed line of retained activation values per example in thousands on the right axis, both straight.
context:
$$ \Parameters = \sum_{\LayerIndex=1}^{\LayerCount} (\PreviousLayerWidth + 1)\,\CurrentLayerWidth, \qquad \Operations = 2\sum_{\LayerIndex=1}^{\LayerCount} \PreviousLayerWidth\,\CurrentLayerWidth, \qquad \ActivationMemory \propto \BatchSize \sum_{\LayerIndex=1}^{\LayerCount} \CurrentLayerWidth $$ {#eq-depth-width-cost}

When every hidden layer has the same width $\HiddenDimension$, the sums collapse. Parameters and operations grow as $\LayerCount\HiddenDimension^2$, linear in depth and quadratic in width, while retained activations grow as $\BatchSize\LayerCount\HiddenDimension$, linear in both. @Fig-depth-width-scaling plots the two sweeps on the running network's input and output widths. Holding the network at two hidden layers and doubling their width from `{python} DepthWidthCost.width_lo_str` to `{python} DepthWidthCost.width_hi_str` multiplies MACs per example by `{python} DepthWidthCost.width_double_mult_str`, short of four only because the input layer's share still grows linearly. Holding the width at `{python} DepthWidthCost.fixed_width_str` and doubling depth from `{python} DepthWidthCost.depth_lo_str` to `{python} DepthWidthCost.depth_hi_str` hidden layers multiplies MACs by `{python} DepthWidthCost.depth_double_mult_str` and retained activations by `{python} DepthWidthCost.retained_double_mult_str`.

title: Training Loop Architecture
caption: **Training Loop Architecture**: A prediction and true value meet at the loss function; backpropagation computes parameter gradients, and the optimizer turns those gradients into parameter updates for the next forward pass.
alt: Neural network training diagram. Input features x1, x2, through xn flow through blue, red, and green node layers via forward propagation. Prediction and true value feed the loss function. Backpropagation computes parameter gradients, which feed the optimizer; the optimizer updates weights and biases for the next forward pass. An orange arrow shows the backward-propagation direction.
context:
:::

Tracing dataflow along the red horizontal arrow in @fig-forward-propagation shows forward activations traversing the layers to evaluate loss, whereas the orange arrow running the opposite way carries gradients backward through the layers; the optimizer then turns those gradients into weight updates. This operational asymmetry creates a central memory obligation: training must retain intermediate forward activations in memory until the corresponding backward pass completes.

title: The Running Network on the Roofline
caption: **The Running Network on the Roofline**: Attainable FP32 throughput against arithmetic intensity for a desktop CPU and a data-center accelerator, with the running network's forward pass at batch 1 and batch 32 under the main-memory traffic model of the operation-count notebook. Both points sit left of both ridge points, so batching raises throughput by climbing the bandwidth slope, and at these intensities the accelerator's lead equals its memory-bandwidth advantage rather than its arithmetic advantage.
alt: Log-log roofline plot of attainable FP32 rate against arithmetic intensity. A solid blue roofline for a data-center accelerator and a dashed brown roofline for a desktop CPU both bend at a ridge near 20 FLOP per byte. Red markers on each sloped segment show the network at batch 1 near 0.5 FLOP per byte and batch 32 near 12 FLOP per byte: about 25 GFLOP/s and 595 GFLOP/s on the CPU, about 2 and 40 TFLOP/s on the accelerator.
context:
at batch 1 to ~`{python} MnistFlopsCalc.batch_arith_intensity_str` at batch 32, because one read of each weight now serves 32 images. Batching therefore trades memory for reuse. Memory capacity bounds how far that trade can go, while gradient noise and per-request latency bound it from other directions. Memory layout and optimized linear-algebra libraries decide how much of that reuse an implementation actually captures. This is why parallel processors\index{GPU!parallel computation}\index{Parallel processing!neural networks} that can be fed from on-chip storage run large dense matrix operations substantially faster than CPUs\index{CPU!neural network execution}\index{Central processing unit|see{CPU}}, and why specialized accelerators add reduced-precision arithmetic and dataflows tailored to these patterns. Energy follows the same logic\index{Energy consumption!hardware platforms}\index{Throughput!accelerator parallelism}. Power alone does not determine energy per inference; the relevant quantity is power integrated over execution time for the same workload and quality target, and memory hierarchy and data movement often explain most of the difference between platforms.

A roofline [@williams2009] plots a machine's attainable throughput against arithmetic intensity, with a sloped segment equal to bandwidth times intensity that meets a flat roof at peak compute. @Sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-3e1a develops that throughput bound in full. @Fig-mnist-roofline places those two intensities on the rooflines of two machines whose FP32 ridge points happen to sit near the same value. At both batch sizes the running network lies on the sloped, bandwidth-limited side of both machines, so its attainable rate is bandwidth times intensity. Batching therefore gains more than an order of magnitude by climbing that slope, and at these intensities the accelerator outruns the CPU because it moves bytes faster, not because it multiplies faster. The plot assumes that every operand streams from main memory, as the notebook's traffic model does; a model this small can instead stay in a CPU's cache, which raises the bandwidth that actually feeds it.

title: Cross-Entropy Compares a Distribution with a One-Hot Label
caption: **Cross-Entropy Compares a Distribution with a One-Hot Label**: Left: the network places 0.8 on the correct class and 0.1 each on digits 0 and 9, while the target places all of its mass on the correct class. Right: because the target is one-hot, the loss reduces to the negative log of the correct-class probability. A uniform guess over ten classes costs about 2.3, a confident correct prediction costs little, and the penalty grows without bound as the probability assigned to the truth approaches zero.
alt: Two panels. Left: bar chart over digit classes 0 to 9 with predicted probability 0.8 at digit 7 and 0.1 at digits 0 and 9, overlaid by a dashed outline of height 1 at digit 7 marking the one-hot true label. Right: the curve negative log p falling from above 5 near p equals 0 to 0 at p equals 1, with marked points for a uniform guess at p equals 0.1 (loss 2.30), p equals 0.8 (loss 0.22), and p equals 0.9 (loss 0.11).
context:
```

For example, suppose the network assigns the probabilities in the left panel of @fig-cross-entropy-loss to an image of a "seven." The prediction is a distribution over all ten digits, while the label is a single one at the correct class and zero everywhere else.

title: Gradient Descent on One Weight
caption: **Gradient Descent on One Weight**: An illustrative loss curve for a single weight, with each step moving the weight against the local slope by an amount proportional to the learning rate. Left: a well-chosen learning rate takes large steps where the slope is steep and smaller ones as the slope flattens near the minimum. Right: a learning rate close to the limit this curve tolerates overshoots the minimum on every step, so the weight oscillates from side to side and approaches the minimum only slowly; a slightly larger rate would diverge.
alt: Two panels plotting loss against a single weight w on the same U-shaped curve with its minimum at w equals 2. Left: green points from w equals minus 1.2 step down the curve with shrinking arrows and settle at the minimum. Right: red points jump back and forth across the minimum with long arrows, slowly descending. A dashed line marks the slope at the starting weight in both panels.
context:
where $\ModelParameters$ represents the collection of network parameters (weights and biases), $\LearningRate$ is the learning rate\index{Learning rate!update magnitude}\index{Hyperparameter!learning rate}, and $\nabla_{\ModelParameters}\LossFunction$ is the gradient of the loss with respect to those parameters, which backpropagation (@sec-neural-computation-gradient-computation-backpropagation-dacf) computes efficiently.

For the digit classifier, the update aims to reduce the chosen loss. If the network frequently confuses "seven"s with "one"s, the loss gradients from those examples guide the weight changes. The learning rate $\LearningRate$ controls adjustment magnitude. Values that are too large overshoot good parameters, values that are too small converge slowly, and the right value shifts with batch size, a coupling @sec-model-training-batch-size-parameter-updates-4d0b develops. @Fig-gradient-descent-steps shows the first failure on a single weight, where every step lands on the far side of the minimum.

@Fig-training-step-memory follows the same memory through one training step. ### Operational phase differences {#sec-neural-computation-operational-phase-differences-3f95}

The two phases differ first in what they execute and how long their state lives\index{Training vs. inference!operational differences}\index{Inference!forward pass only}. Inference executes only the forward pass, evaluating inputs against static parameters with batch sizes dictated by incoming traffic. Training couples that forward pass with backpropagation for gradient computation and parameter updates, selecting batch sizes to maximize accelerator occupancy and gradient stability. Unlike inference, training must retain intermediate activations, gradients, and optimizer state simultaneously, multiplying working memory demands. The underlying network weights are identical, but the execution graph changes. Training-only regularizers such as dropout are stripped away, while adjacent matrix operations and activations can be fused or quantized into specialized execution kernels. In @fig-training-vs-inference, training couples large-batch processing with a bidirectional loop in which output errors trigger a reverse gradient pass, whereas inference executes a strictly unidirectional forward pass over smaller, variable batch sizes without backward state retention.

### The document-recognition challenge {#sec-neural-computation-mail-sorting-challenge-ef8c}

In a physical postal sorter, envelopes move past optical scanners along mechanical belts at fixed speed, leaving only tens of milliseconds per item to capture the image, isolate the digits, evaluate the network, and trip the physical diverter gates. A misrouted envelope or misread check incurs costly manual re-handling or financial reconciliation. Yet raw accuracy on uncontrolled handwriting cannot reach 100 percent, so the pipeline must pair automated inference with an explicit rejection rule that routes ambiguous digits to human operators. The sample grid in @fig-usps-digit-examples shows this handwriting variation across real postal envelopes, where character segmentation and recognition must handle heavy cursive slant, uneven stroke widths, broken loops, and patterned envelope backgrounds across city names and five-digit ZIP codes.

Image acquisition and conventional preprocessing prepare handwritten digits for neural inference, and raw scores then pass through postprocessing to the final application output.
alt: Six-box linear pipeline: raw data and preprocessing in blue, a neural network in green, and raw output, postprocessing, and final output in purple.
context:
### Shared pipeline architecture {#sec-neural-computation-production-system-architecture-130f}

Feeding raw envelope scans straight into a digit classifier fails because the network expects isolated, size-normalized characters rather than full addresses on textured paper, and its raw scores still need a rejection rule before they can trip a sorting gate. The composite six-stage pipeline in @fig-usps-inference-pipeline separates the work shared by postal ZIP-code research and deployed bank-check readers (rather than reconstructing a single historical machine). Upstream preprocessing segments and normalizes the scanned digits. The neural network scores each candidate digit. Downstream postprocessing compares those scores against confidence thresholds, passing accepted digits to the sorter while routing ambiguous ones to human review.

title: Spatial Feature Extraction

alt: Diagram of a zebra image passing through three convolution-and-ReLU stages with pooling, stacked feature maps, a flatten layer, fully connected layers, and a softmax output labeled Horse, Zebra, and Dog.
context:
### Pattern processing needs {#sec-network-architectures-pattern-processing-needs-30b4}

In a photograph, neighboring pixels carry closely related brightness and color values that together form local edges, corners, and textures, whereas pixels on opposite sides of the frame have almost nothing in common on their own. Stacking local filters lets a network build larger features out of smaller ones: early layers combine nearby pixels into edges, middle layers combine edges into contours and surface textures, and deeper layers assemble those patches into object parts and whole objects. From stage to stage the spatial grid shrinks while the number of channels grows, so each later feature summarizes a wider patch of the image, until the features flatten into one vector for a dense classifier (@fig-cnn-spatial-processing).

title: Convolution Operation
caption: **Convolution Operation**: A $3{\times}3$ orange receptive field in a dashed $7{\times}7$ input maps to one cell of the violet $5{\times}5$ valid-convolution output. Applying a $3{\times}3$ filter to that receptive field requires 9 multiply-accumulate operations per input channel for each output value. Sharing the filter across positions encodes translation equivariance: the same edge detector works at any image location.
alt: A dashed 7-by-7 input grid contains one orange 3-by-3 receptive field. Blue lines connect that receptive field to one highlighted cell in a separate violet 5-by-5 output grid, as produced by valid stride-1 convolution.
context:
[^fn-receptive-field-growth]: **Receptive field**\index{Receptive field}: The input region influencing a particular output neuron. With $3{\times}3$ filters, receptive fields grow by 2 pixels per layer, so a neuron at layer 3 "sees" a $7{\times}7$ region. This growth rate constrains architecture depth: detecting objects spanning 100+ pixels in a $224{\times}224$ image requires either deep stacks of small filters (more layers, more memory for activations) or larger kernels (more parameters per layer), a fundamental depth-vs.-width trade-off in CNN design. \index{Receptive field!depth trade-off}

Convolutional layers typically use small spatial kernels ($3{\times}3$ or $5{\times}5$) to maintain compact parameter footprints while stacking layers to widen the effective receptive field. Each output activation depends on one small window of the input. In @fig-cnn, a $3{\times}3$ receptive field in a $7{\times}7$ input produces one value of the $5{\times}5$ output map, and sliding the same filter to every position fills in the rest. The interactive CNN Explainer tool [@wang2021] visualizes how these stacked sliding windows extract per-channel activation patterns across layers.

title: im2col Transformation
caption: **im2col Transformation**: Lowering converts convolution to GEMM by unfolding image patches into a dense matrix. The two $3{\times}3$ input feature maps produce four sliding-window positions, represented here as rows of a $4{\times}8$ matrix; the two $2{\times}2$ filter kernels stack into an $8{\times}1$ column. Their product, not drawn, yields the four output positions. Lowering can exploit optimized matrix kernels but expands memory by an amount that depends on kernel size, stride, padding, and implementation, so its performance benefit is workload dependent.
alt: Two 3-by-3 input feature maps and two 2-by-2 filters feed a matrix multiplication. Four unfolded input patches form the rows of a 4-by-8 matrix, and the stacked filter values form an 8-by-1 column. A multiplication sign joins the matrix and the column.
context:
Flattening the filter weights into a column vector $\FlattenedFilterWeights= [\FilterWeight_1, \FilterWeight_2, \FilterWeight_3, \FilterWeight_4]^T$, the entire convolution collapses into a single standard matrix product: $\UnfoldedConvolutionOutput= \UnfoldedPatchMatrix\FlattenedFilterWeights$. For batched multi-channel inputs, the unfolded matrix has shape $[(\BatchSize \cdot \OutputFeatureMapHeight \cdot \OutputFeatureMapWidth) \times (\KernelSize^2 \cdot \InputChannelCount)]$ and the filters reshape to $[(\KernelSize^2 \cdot \InputChannelCount) \times \OutputChannelCount]$. In $\UnfoldedPatchMatrix$, input element `5` appears in all four rows, and the miniature input expands from nine elements to sixteen, a storage ratio of $16/9$. For large stride-1 inputs, fully materialized unfolding approaches the kernel area as its expansion factor. The smaller ratio here reflects the borders of a valid convolution. Materializing the buffer trades this additional storage and traffic for access to wide matrix engines optimized for GEMM throughput. Implicit GEMM, described next, avoids allocating the duplicated buffer.

[^fn-im2col-lowering-transformation]: **im2col (image to column)**\index{im2col!memory trade-off}: Rather than being a new learning algorithm, im2col-style lowering is an implementation technique used by CNN frameworks and libraries such as Caffe and cuDNN [@chellapilla2006high; @jia2014; @chetlur2014cudnn]: it converts convolutions into standard GEMM calls by unfolding overlapping patches into matrix columns. The trade-off is memory: in a simple fully materialized stride-1 $\KernelSize{\times}\KernelSize$ transform, interior input elements can appear in up to $\KernelSize^2$ columns (9 times for $3{\times}3$ filters), though borders, stride, padding, tiling, and direct-convolution algorithms reduce the realized expansion. This memory-for-simplicity exchange explains why mobile frameworks (TFLite, NNAPI) prefer direct convolution, while data center GPUs with abundant HBM may use GEMM-oriented lowering when it improves throughput. \index{im2col!data center vs. mobile}

title: Spatial Filtering and Channel Mixing
caption: **Spatial Filtering and Channel Mixing**: At one output position, the standard layer combines spatial and channel sums separately for each output filter. The factorized layer first filters each input channel, then mixes the intermediate values into the same output shape. The lower panel uses one spatial filter per input channel, or depth multiplier one.
alt: Two panels show three input patches and two output channels. The upper panel connects all input channels to each output filter. The lower panel passes each channel through a separate spatial filter before a shared pointwise mixer.
context:
ResNet-50's compute-bound profile assumes abundant hardware resources, yet most inference runs on devices with power budgets three orders of magnitude smaller than a data center accelerator. Standard convolutions scale as $\mathcal{O}(\SpatialPositionCount\times \KernelSize^2 \times \InputChannelCount\times \OutputChannelCount)$, a compute volume that exceeds the strict energy budgets of always-on edge devices. To bridge this gap, efficient architectures like **depthwise separable CNNs (DS-CNN)**\index{Depthwise separable convolution}\index{Convolution!depthwise separable} decompose the standard convolution into two distinct operations. This factorization, introduced by Sifre in the context of feature extraction [@sifre2014rigid] and popularized by MobileNet [@howard2017mobilenets], decouples spatial filtering from cross-channel combination. The depthwise convolution\index{Convolution!depthwise} applies filters to each input channel independently ($\KernelSize\times \KernelSize\times \InputChannelCount$ parameters), while the pointwise convolution\index{Convolution!pointwise} uses a $1{\times}1$ convolution to project channels to the output dimension ($1 \times 1 \times \InputChannelCount\times \OutputChannelCount$ parameters). Per output position, a standard layer performs $\KernelSize^2 \InputChannelCount \OutputChannelCount$ multiply-accumulates, while the factorized pair performs $\KernelSize^2 \InputChannelCount+ \InputChannelCount \OutputChannelCount$. Dividing the two shows that the decomposition reduces parameter count and FLOPs to roughly $\frac{1}{\OutputChannelCount} + \frac{1}{\KernelSize^2}$ of standard convolution, a reduction factor approaching $\KernelSize^2$, or about 8--9$\times$ for $3{\times}3$ filters with large $\OutputChannelCount$. That reduction makes real-time execution feasible on resource-constrained microcontrollers.

The channel paths in @fig-depthwise-pointwise-channels show where the arithmetic reduction comes from. The depthwise stage produces one intermediate value per input channel at each output position, and the pointwise stage combines those values across channels.

title: Residual Connection Block (Original Post-Activation Form)
caption: **Residual Connection Block (Original Post-Activation Form)**: The original ResNet block [@he2016] implements $\ResidualBlockOutput = \text{ReLU}(\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector)$, where an identity shortcut bypasses the weight layers before a final ReLU activation. In later pre-activation variants [@he2016identity] and modern transformer blocks, the nonlinearity moves inside $\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector)$, making the addition a completely clean identity shortcut $\ResidualBlockOutput = \ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector$ that matches the unobstructed gradient flow in @eq-residual.
alt: Two blue weight layer blocks with ReLU between them. An input vector enters left, passes through the weight layers, then adds with an identity shortcut that bypasses both layers. Brown plus circle combines paths. Output shows the residual sum with final ReLU.

title: Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding
caption: **Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding**: The compact recurrent loop (left) unfolds into one copy of the cell per time step (right). Three weight matrices are shared across all steps: $\RecurrentInputWeights$ (input-to-hidden), $\RecurrentStateWeights$ (hidden-to-hidden), and $\RecurrentOutputWeights$ (hidden-to-output). These matrices are reused at every step, so the parameter count is independent of sequence length. For a 128-dimensional hidden state and a 100-dimensional input, each time step requires 16,384 MACs for recurrent connections plus 12,800 for input projection.

context:
### Pattern processing needs {#sec-network-architectures-pattern-processing-needs-4b64}

In "the trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big," the word "it" refers to "trophy," but if "big" changes to "small," "it" refers to "suitcase." The same positions, at the same distances, need different links depending on what the words mean. Neither a CNN's fixed spatial window nor an RNN's step-by-step hidden state can route information directly between arbitrary positions based on content. Dynamic sequence processing needs an operation that scores relationships from the tokens themselves, letting each word draw directly on the words that matter to it regardless of how far apart they sit (@fig-transformer-attention-visualized).

title: Query-Key-Value Attention Mechanism
caption: **Query-Key-Value Attention Mechanism**: For a 6-token sequence, queries (cyan) match against keys (red) to produce a $6{\times}6$ attention matrix with $\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)$ entries. The six tokens are the pieces a tokenizer cuts from \"Data visualization empowers users to,\" which is why \"empowers\" appears as \"em\" and \"powers.\" Cell color runs from blue to red across the grid as an illustrative gradient rather than as computed weights. Each output position aggregates information from all values (green) weighted by its own row of that matrix. The matrix structure reveals both the computational pattern (thirty-six similarity computations) and the naive memory bottleneck (storing $\SequenceLength^2$ attention weights). Adapted from Transformer Explainer [@cho2025].
alt: 6-by-6 attention matrix with an illustrative gradient coloring from blue to red across the grid. Cyan query vectors enter from left, red key vectors from top, green value vectors from below. Output vectors exit right, showing weighted aggregation pattern.
context:
:::

@Fig-attention traces this dataflow for a sequence of length $\SequenceLength= 6$: cyan query rows match against red key columns to populate the $6{\times}6$ similarity matrix, whose rows subsequently weight the green value vectors to produce the contextualized output vectors on the right. Each row of the resulting $\SequenceLength{\times}\SequenceLength$ matrix determines how strongly an individual token attends to every token in the sequence. In a trained model, the largest affinity values reflect strong contextual dependencies, while near-zero entries suppress irrelevant positions.

This single batched matrix multiplication, requiring $6{\times}768{\times}2304$ = `{python} QKVProjectionCosts.qkv_macs_str`, replaces three separate projection operations for efficiency. Adapted from Transformer Explainer [@cho2025].

title: Transformer Architecture (Encoder-Decoder)
caption: **Transformer Architecture (Encoder-Decoder)**: The encoder (left, repeated $\LayerCount$ times) consists of multi-head attention followed by feed-forward layers, each with residual connections (arrows bypassing blocks) and layer normalization. The decoder (right) adds masked attention to prevent attending to future tokens during training and autoregressive generation. Positional encodings (sine waves) inject sequence order information absent from the permutation-equivariant attention operation. This design enables training parallelism across all positions while the decoder maintains autoregressive causality during inference. Adapted from @vaswani2017.
alt: Encoder-decoder architecture. Encoder: multi-head attention, add-norm, feed-forward, add-norm, repeated N_L times. Decoder adds masked attention. Positional encoding sine waves at inputs. Skip connections bypass sublayers. Linear and softmax at top.
context:
Although individual attention heads often specialize in distinct syntactic or semantic patterns [@clark2019], adapting the effective connectivity graph to each input sequence, empirical analyses reveal substantial head redundancy and acute numerical sensitivity in reduced-precision formats. These hardware-relevant behaviors motivate structural pruning, low-rank factorization, sparse attention patterns, and specialized quantization strategies.

To build deep networks from these dynamic projections, the transformer places self-attention inside a repeating block (@fig-transformer). Each block wraps multi-head attention and position-wise feed-forward sublayers with residual connections\index{Residual connection!Transformer} and layer normalization\index{Layer normalization!Transformer}. Sinusoidal positional encodings combine with token embeddings at the base of both towers, feeding repeated multi-head attention and feed-forward stages before terminating in linear and softmax output heads. Because all positions can be processed in parallel rather than sequentially, the architecture trades recurrent state for large matrix operations that map well to accelerator training. A decoder-only model such as GPT-2 keeps only the right-hand tower of this figure, without the attention that reads an encoder's output. Tokens enter as embedding vectors, pass through the stack of blocks, and leave as a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token. The residual paths and normalization layers in this stack are shared building blocks rather than transformer inventions; @sec-network-architectures-evolution-dense-spatial-processing-2761 and @sec-network-architectures-normalization-layers-mathematical-foundations-0fb7 explain why they make deep stacks trainable and what each costs the machine.

title: Prefill and Decode
caption: **Prefill and Decode**: Prefill (left) runs the whole prompt through the model in one pass of matrix-matrix products, reusing every weight across all prompt tokens, and writes each prompt token's keys and values to the KV cache. Decode (right) then generates one token per step: each output becomes the next input, each step runs matrix-vector products that re-read every weight, and each step reads the whole cache and appends one entry. The first phase is usually compute-bound; the second is usually bandwidth-bound at small batch.
alt: Left panel labeled Prefill: four blue prompt tokens, The, cat, sat, on, feed one wide box labeled one pass over all prompt tokens (matrix-matrix products), which writes four orange KV cache cells. An arrow leads to the right panel labeled Decode: three narrow boxes labeled one token (matrix-vector), each taking a green token (the, mat, today) and producing the next (mat, today, end), with dashed arrows showing each output becoming the next input; each box reads the cache and adds one orange cell. Captions beneath read: weights reused across every prompt token, usually compute-bound; and every weight and the whole cache re-read for each new token, usually bandwidth-bound at small batch.
context:
The same mask is what lets training run in parallel. During next-token training the whole target sequence is already known, so shifting it right by one position pairs every input token with its successor (@fig-transformer), and the mask guarantees that position $\TimeStepIndex$ cannot see later tokens. An accelerator therefore evaluates every position at once with dense matrix multiplications instead of stepping through a serial time loop as an RNN must.

Generation splits into two phases with different machine profiles, drawn in @fig-prefill-decode. *Prefill*\index{Prefill} processes the whole prompt in one pass: every prompt token is known, so the model evaluates them in parallel, as in training, and stores each token's keys and values. *Decode*\index{Decode} then produces the remaining tokens one per step. Each step feeds a single token through the model, so its projections shrink from matrix-matrix to matrix-vector products, and its attention reads the stored keys and values of every earlier token instead of recomputing them. That store is the key-value (KV) cache, and @sec-network-architectures-inference-memory-bandwidth-wall-98d1 shows why decode, not prefill, usually sets a language model's serving cost.

title: Three Memory Regimes of a Long Context
caption: **Three Memory Regimes of a Long Context**: Memory against context length for a model with GPT-2 XL's shape (48 layers, width 1,600, 25 heads) in FP16, evaluated past its trained context to expose the scaling. The weights are fixed, the KV cache that serving keeps for one request grows linearly, and a single layer's materialized attention scores grow quadratically. The cache overtakes the weights near `{python} ContextMemoryCrossings.kv_crossing_tokens_str`, and one layer's scores alone would fill one accelerator's device memory near `{python} ContextMemoryCrossings.score_crossing_tokens_str`, which is why tiled attention avoids materializing them.
alt: Log-log plot of memory in gigabytes against context length from 512 to 128K tokens. A flat blue line marks FP16 weights near 3 GB. An orange line for one request's KV cache rises linearly and crosses the weights near 10K tokens. A dashed red line for one layer's materialized scores rises quadratically and crosses a dotted line for one accelerator's device memory near 41K tokens.
context:
```

For one model shape, the three memory regimes diverge sharply as context grows (@fig-context-memory). The weights do not grow with context at all, the KV cache grows linearly with every token a request keeps, and materialized attention scores grow with the square of the context. The cache overtakes the weights near `{python} ContextMemoryCrossings.kv_crossing_tokens_str`, and one layer's scores alone would fill an accelerator near `{python} ContextMemoryCrossings.score_crossing_tokens_str`, which is why serving systems size the cache per request and training kernels never materialize the scores.

title: DLRM Pipeline
caption: **DLRM Pipeline**: Dense features pass through a bottom MLP of small weight matrices, while each categorical ID selects one row of a large embedding table. The gathers are random reads with almost no arithmetic, and the tables can exceed one device's memory. An interaction stage takes pairwise dot products among the dense output and the gathered vectors, and a top MLP turns the result into a click probability.
alt: Two paths feed an interaction box. Left: dense features go up into a blue bottom MLP. Right: categorical IDs enter three tall orange embedding tables; one highlighted row from each is copied into a small vector. Labels note random reads with almost no arithmetic and tables of gigabytes to terabytes that may span devices. The interaction output feeds a top MLP that produces a click probability.
context:
The DLRM\index{DLRM} architecture [@naumov2019deep] organizes this computation into a four-stage pipeline split between dense and sparse paths. Continuous features such as user age or time of day first flow through a bottom MLP, a compute-intensive but memory-light stage dominated by dense matrix multiplications. In parallel, categorical IDs index into dedicated embedding tables\index{Embedding!table}, which is where the memory capacity wall appears.

For example, an embedding table for one billion users with 128-dimensional vectors requires $10^9 \times 128 \times 4$ bytes $\approx$ `{python} DLRMEmbedding.embed_table_gb_str` of memory. This stage is memory-intensive but compute-light because each lookup is a memory copy with zero arithmetic reuse. The interaction layer\index{DLRM!interaction layer} then combines the dense activations from the bottom MLP with the gathered sparse embedding vectors through pairwise dot products that capture user-item correlations. Finally, a top MLP processes the concatenated interaction representations through feedforward layers to predict a target probability such as click-through rate. Each of the four stages stresses a different part of the machine (@fig-dlrm-pipeline), and @sec-network-architectures-computational-mapping-b346 quantifies the capacity-bound profile that results.

title: Data Movement Primitives
caption: **Data Movement Primitives**: Four fundamental patterns govern information flow in neural network computation. Broadcast (top-left) replicates a single value to all destinations, used when sharing weights across batch elements. Scatter (top-right) distributes distinct elements to different destinations, enabling work partitioning. Gather (bottom-left) collects distributed values to a single location, as in attention pooling. Reduction (bottom-right) combines multiple values through aggregation (sum, max), appearing in gradient synchronization and attention scoring. Because moving data costs more than computing on it, these patterns are primary optimization targets.
alt: Four diagrams with nodes and arrows. Broadcast: one red square to four nodes. Scatter: four colored squares to four nodes. Gather: four nodes with colored squares to one. Reduction: four nodes labeled 1, 3, 5, and 7 combine into one node labeled 16.
context:
:::

The parallel-axis column determines how data must move among processing elements once the work is spread out. Four data movement patterns (broadcast, scatter, gather, and reduction; @fig-collective-comm) govern how tensors travel among processing elements, whether those are units on one chip or several accelerators in one server. Batch parallelism in MLPs, CNNs, and prefill broadcasts\index{Data movement!broadcast} stationary weight tiles to many units, each working on a different example or position, and compilers tile loops\index{Matrix tiling} to reuse each broadcast value as often as possible. Spatial and model partitioning scatter\index{Data movement!scatter} a tensor across tiles or devices. Mixture-of-experts models, which route each token to a few of many feedforward subnetworks, make the scatter input-dependent, so a popular expert can overload one accelerator while others idle. DLRM gathers\index{Data movement!gather} embedding rows from wherever the sharded tables live, and each attention query gathers keys and values from every position in its sequence. Reductions\index{Data movement!reduction} combine values through sums or maxima (softmax denominators, normalization statistics, and the summing of gradients across accelerators that each trained on a different slice of the batch). Tree-structured reduction hardware finishes a reduction over $\ReductionInputCount$ values in $\mathcal{O}(\log \ReductionInputCount)$ stages rather than $\mathcal{O}(\ReductionInputCount)$. The rows with a serial axis, RNNs and decode, are the rows these collectives cannot rescue, because no amount of broadcast or reduction bandwidth shortens a dependency chain.

title: Architecture Selection Decision Framework
caption: **Architecture Selection Decision Framework**: A systematic flowchart for choosing dense neural network architectures based on data characteristics and deployment constraints. The process begins by identifying the data type (text, sequences, images, or tabular features) to select initial candidates (transformers, RNNs, CNNs, or MLPs), then iteratively evaluates memory budget, computational cost, inference speed, accuracy targets, and hardware compatibility. High-cardinality recommendation workloads are handled separately by the sparse-embedding family, DLRM (@sec-network-architectures-sparse-architectures-recommendation-systems-5d19), then re-enter the same constraint checks.
alt: Flowchart from Define Problem, branching by data type to Transformers, RNNs, CNNs, MLPs. Diamonds check memory, compute, speed, accuracy, deployment. Each No loops back via Scale Down or Increase Capacity; each Yes passes to the next check, and the final Yes reaches Architecture Selected.
context:
:::

@Fig-dnn-fm-framework formalizes this selection pipeline as a multi-stage triage tree. Candidate architectures route first by input data structure (text, sequences, spatial grids, or tabular features) and then pass through sequential screening gates for memory capacity, compute budget, inference latency, accuracy targets, and hardware deployment readiness. High-cardinality recommendation workloads sit outside this dense flowchart and route to the sparse embedding family (@sec-network-architectures-sparse-architectures-recommendation-systems-5d19) before applying the same memory, compute, speed, accuracy, and deployment checks. If any constraint fails, the decision loop routes execution back to scale the model down, increase its capacity when accuracy falls short, or substitute an alternative architecture family.

title: Computational Library Evolution
caption: **Computational Library Evolution**: Numerical computing milestones from 1979 to 2018 show each era automating what the layer below exposed, from BLAS and LAPACK hardware routines to NumPy vectorized syntax and graph-based automatic differentiation in modern frameworks, trading low-level transparency for developer velocity.
alt: Horizontal timeline from 1979 to 2018 marking key milestones: 1979 BLAS introduced, 1992 LAPACK extends BLAS, 2006 NumPy becomes Python's numerical backbone, 2007 Theano introduces computational graphs, 2015 TensorFlow, 2016 PyTorch, 2018 JAX.
context:
[^fn-theano-framework-origin]: **Theano**\index{Theano!computational graph origin}: Developed at the Montreal Institute for Learning Algorithms (MILA) under Yoshua Bengio starting in 2007, Theano was an early and influential Python framework that compiled symbolic mathematical expressions into optimized CPU and GPU code via computational graphs [@bergstra2010; @al2016theano]. It demonstrated that a Python-defined computation graph could be compiled for GPU execution without requiring the researcher to write CUDA code. Mila ended active development of Theano in 2017 [@milaTheanoDevelopment].

Across that history (@fig-mlfm-timeline), the milestones run from BLAS and LAPACK routines through NumPy vectorization to symbolic graph capture in Theano and TensorFlow, dynamic graphs in PyTorch, and functional transformations in JAX. Each generation preserved the vendor-tuned kernel layer beneath it while raising the level of abstraction at which engineers express and differentiate models.

title: Simple Computational Graph
caption: **Simple Computational Graph**: Representing $\FunctionOutputVariable = \IllustrativeFunction(\FunctionInputVariable, \FunctionSecondInputVariable)$ as a directed acyclic graph decouples mathematical dependencies from physical execution order, providing the structural blueprint frameworks require to track gradients and schedule operations across devices.
alt: Simple directed graph with nodes x and y flowing into function f(x,y) which outputs z.
context:
If a runtime sees only one Python operation at a time and forgets it as soon as the kernel returns, it cannot know which intermediate tensors later gradient rules will need or which adjacent operations could share registers on the accelerator. To plan across operations, a framework represents the program the same way @sec-network-architectures represented model architectures, as a computational graph\index{Computational graph!definition (DAG)}: a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where nodes represent operations and edges represent data dependencies. The rest of this chapter follows that graph down toward the hardware. It is the same structure that backpropagation traverses in reverse, here serving as the framework's internal model of the computation for scheduling and optimization as well.

A graph decouples the mathematical operations from the order in which hardware evaluates them. In the minimal case (@fig-comp-graph), directed edges route input variables $\FunctionInputVariable$ and $\FunctionSecondInputVariable$ into the central transformation operator $\IllustrativeFunction(\FunctionInputVariable, \FunctionSecondInputVariable)$, which emits the output variable $\FunctionOutputVariable$.

title: Computation Graph with System Interactions
caption: **Computation Graph with System Interactions**: A neural network DAG (left) interfaces with framework runtime components (right). By maintaining an explicit graph representation independent of execution, the framework can analyze tensor lifetimes for memory reuse and assign operations to target accelerators before issuing arithmetic.
alt: Left side shows computational graph with six operation nodes connected by data flow edges. Right side shows system components box with memory management and device placement nodes that interact with the computational graph.
context:
:::

Real machine learning models require much more complex graph structures. @Fig-mlfm-comp-graph partitions this system interaction into two coupled domains: the left container isolates a six-node neural network DAG with explicit dataflow edges, while the right container houses the runtime components (memory management and device placement) that interface with it.

title: Dynamic Graph Execution Flow
caption: **Dynamic Graph Execution Flow**: In eager execution, each operation is issued as the program encounters it. Accelerator work may execute asynchronously after dispatch. This define-by-run model enables natural debugging and data-dependent control flow while limiting optimization across Python calls.
alt: Left-to-right flowchart with Start, Define Operation under Python Dispatch, Execute Operation under GPU Kernel, a More operations? decision, and End. A Yes branch loops back to Define Operation; a No branch continues to End.
section: The autograd tape exists NOW, built during execution
context:
:::

In eager execution frameworks, operations evaluate imperatively as host code encounters them. The define-by-run cycle is therefore a loop of one operation at a time (@fig-mlfm-dynamic-graph-flow). Python defines an operation, the runtime enqueues its device work, and control returns to Python for the next call while the device may execute asynchronously. When the runtime decides what to launch, it sees the current operation rather than a whole region of future calls.

title: Static Graph Execution Lifecycle
caption: **Static Graph Execution Lifecycle**: Separating symbolic graph definition (left) from concrete execution (right) provides global visibility over the computation, allowing compilers to apply ahead-of-time optimizations (such as kernel fusion, buffer reuse, and layout transforms) before any tensors are materialized.
alt: Flow diagram showing two phases. Definition phase: Define operations, declare variables, build graph. Execution phase: Load data, run graph, get results. Arrows connect boxes left to right.
context:
:::

In the definition phase, the program declares operations and variables and builds the symbolic DAG without allocating any tensor memory. Only in the execution phase do data load, concrete buffers materialize on the accelerator, and the captured graph run (@fig-mlfm-static-graph).

title: Eager Operator Surfaces versus Compiler Cores
caption: **Eager Operator Surfaces versus Compiler Cores**: Operators defined by the eager frameworks (PyTorch native-function schemas with overloads, and TensorFlow's registered operators) against the compiler-facing sets they lower to (PyTorch's Core ATen IR, XLA's HLO operations, the ONNX standard, and JAX's `lax` primitives) at each release, on a logarithmic axis. The eager surfaces grew past 1,500 and 2,600 entries while every compiler-facing set stayed between about 80 and 200. Counts mined from each project's repository at its release tags [@pytorch2025nativefunctions; @tensorflow2025opsregistry; @openxla2025hloopcodes; @onnx2026operators; @jax2025laxprimitives].
alt: Line chart on a logarithmic axis of operator counts against release date from 2017 to 2026. Two upper lines rise: PyTorch ATen schemas from about 1,064 in late 2018 to 2,658 in 2025, and TensorFlow operators from 594 in early 2017 to 1,563 in 2025. Four lower lines stay between about 80 and 200: XLA HLO operations from 84 to 123, ONNX operators from 95 to 203, Core ATen IR from 129 to 192, and JAX lax primitives from 111 to 135.
context:
grew from `{python} OperatorSurface.pt_first_str` schemas, overloads included, at version `{python} OperatorSurface.pt_first_release_str` in `{python} OperatorSurface.pt_first_year_str` to `{python} OperatorSurface.pt_latest_str` by version `{python} OperatorSurface.pt_latest_release_str` in `{python} OperatorSurface.pt_latest_year_str` [@pytorch2025nativefunctions]. TensorFlow's operator registry grew from `{python} OperatorSurface.tf_first_str` at version `{python} OperatorSurface.tf_first_release_str` in `{python} OperatorSurface.tf_first_year_str` to `{python} OperatorSurface.tf_latest_str` by version `{python} OperatorSurface.tf_latest_release_str` in `{python} OperatorSurface.tf_latest_year_str` [@tensorflow2025opsregistry]. Every one of those entries is something a backend must implement, or that the framework must first functionalize and decompose.

Compiler-facing representations work from far smaller sets, which grew by tens of operators while the eager surfaces grew by thousands. The Core ATen IR, the operator set that PyTorch's compiler and export paths lower to, holds `{python} OperatorSurface.core_aten_str` operators [@pytorch2025nativefunctions]. The XLA compiler that TensorFlow and JAX both target defines `{python} OperatorSurface.xla_str` high-level optimizer (HLO) operations [@openxla2025hloopcodes]. The Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) standard, which carries models between frameworks and runtimes, defines `{python} OperatorSurface.onnx_ops_str` [@onnx2026operators]. JAX starts on the compiler's side of this divide. Its user-facing operations reduce to about `{python} OperatorSurface.jax_prims_str` `lax` primitives [@jax2025laxprimitives], a set the size of the compiler cores, so a JAX program reaches XLA with little decomposition left to do. The `{python} OperatorSurface.gap_range_mult_str` gap between an eager surface and its compiler core (for TensorFlow, on its XLA path) is the work that decomposition performs. A new accelerator backend that implements a small core set can run models written against the full eager surface, which is why operator coverage, not peak throughput, often decides whether a model runs on a new device at all.

title: Python Dispatch Overhead
caption: **Python Dispatch Overhead**: Execution timelines illustrate how host dispatch latency ($\Latency$) starves the accelerator during fine-grained operations. Eager execution incurs per-operation host overhead for each kernel, whereas compilation and fusion collapse the sequence into a single launch (drawn in the overhead color as one direct device submission), eliminating intermediate dispatch gaps and intermediate global memory round-trips.
alt: Gantt chart of execution timeline. Eager mode shows alternating red Python dispatch and blue GPU kernel blocks. Compiled mode shows one red dispatch block followed by one fused blue compute block.
context:
```

Scaling this arithmetic to a sequence of `{python} PythonTaxTimeline.n_ops_str` small operations exposes the idle gaps on the accelerator timeline (@fig-python-tax). In eager execution, each `{python} PythonTaxTimeline.kernel_us_str` kernel waits on `{python} FusionSpeedup.python_dispatch_us_str` of Python dispatch, leaving the accelerator idle for about `{python} PythonTaxTimeline.eager_idle_pct_str` of the sequence. The figure isolates the Python share, and the per-kernel launch cost would widen each gap further. Compiling the sequence resolves both constraints. The framework submits the work in a single launch of `{python} FusionSpeedup.kernel_launch_only_us_str`, which eliminates all intermediate host dispatch gaps. Operator fusion keeps intermediate activations in registers or cache, so the entire sequence completes in `{python} PythonTaxTimeline.fused_compute_us_str` instead of the uncompiled `{python} PythonTaxTimeline.eager_compute_us_str`.

title: The Compilation Continuum
caption: **The Compilation Continuum**: An illustrative cost model shows how one-time compilation cost and per-execution cost create eager, JIT, and AOT crossover regions as production executions increase. The crossover locations depend on the assumed compilation costs and per-execution rates.
alt: Line graph with production executions on a logarithmic x-axis and total time in arbitrary units on the y-axis. Blue eager, orange JIT, and green AOT lines start at different offsets, stay nearly flat, then curve upward, with eager rising most steeply and AOT least. Dotted vertical lines mark the eager–JIT and JIT–AOT crossovers; labels identify the region where each strategy has the lowest total time.
context:
```

The cases form a continuum of increasing reuse (@fig-compilation-continuum). Each strategy's total time starts at its one-time compilation cost and grows at its per-execution cost. Eager therefore wins at low execution counts, JIT wins once its compilation is amortized, and AOT wins only at the largest counts, where its higher upfront cost is fully repaid. The figure's crossovers (near `{python} CompilationContinuumModel.eager_jit_cross_math` and `{python} CompilationContinuumModel.jit_aot_cross_math` executions) come from an illustrative cost model in arbitrary units, not from the ResNet-50 scenario, whose eager-to-compiled breakeven sits near `{python} CompilationBenchmark.resnet_breakeven_images_str`. What carries over is the order of the regions, not their positions.

title: Live and Cached Allocator Blocks
caption: **Live and Cached Allocator Blocks**: Equal widths represent equal amounts of a fixed virtual-address pool. Releasing a tensor makes its block reusable without reducing the reserved pool. After splitting a cached block and releasing another tensor, the remaining free regions cannot satisfy the larger contiguous request. The example permits no pool growth, compaction, or remapping.
alt: Three equal-width pool snapshots show tensors A, B, and C; then a hatched cached block in place of B; then cached regions separated by live tensors D and C. A dashed request spans more units than either free region.
section: Tensor lifetimes and the caching allocator {#sec-ml-frameworks-memory-management-gradient-computation-bb77}
context:
Allocation itself is also slow.
