The microcontroller's hardware limits (SRAM capacity, energy envelope, and real-time latency deadlines) dictate INT8 quantization and memory-efficient kernel compilation (Machine). Here every choice constrains the next, so a benchmark that measures only classification accuracy or only raw inference latency misses cross-stage interactions, where an engineering decision at any stage narrows the feasible design space downstream.

title: Benchmarking Granularity
caption: **Benchmarking Granularity**: Four-panel block diagram showing micro, macro, application, and end-to-end evaluation layers. Each panel maps a distinct scope of assessment, from isolated kernel operations through full-system deployment, enabling targeted optimization at every level of the ML stack.
alt: Block diagram showing four evaluation layers: micro (kernels), macro (models), application (compute logic), and end-to-end (full deployment), linked by dashed lines to show expanding scope.
section: │ Goal: Component-only vs end-to-end speedup under pipeline overhead.
context:
Optimization techniques operate across distinct granularities: kernel fusion targets micro-level execution, structured pruning alters macro-level parameter structures, and data curation\index{Data curation!end-to-end generalization} determines end-to-end generalization. System validation must align with these respective boundaries. An isolated micro-benchmark may show substantial kernel speedup, yet a macro-benchmark can reveal that increased activation memory footprints force smaller batch sizes that degrade overall throughput. Similarly, an end-to-end benchmark exposes storage or host deserialization stalls that remain invisible at the accelerator kernel level.

Measurement perimeters widen from left to right in @fig-granularity, and the figure inserts one tier between macro and end-to-end. Micro-benchmarks isolate kernel layers (ML Layers) and macro-benchmarks evaluate composed models (ML Model). An application benchmark then adds the supporting host compute around the model (AI Task), and the end-to-end benchmark adds the non-AI compute nodes the request also traverses. The three granularities in this section fold the application tier into end-to-end, but the four-tier view shows where bottlenecks migrate as the boundary widens: out of the accelerator and into the host systems around it.

title: Isolation vs. Representativeness
caption: **Isolation vs. Representativeness**: The core trade-off in benchmarking granularity. Micro-benchmarks provide high diagnostic precision but limited real-world relevance, while end-to-end benchmarks capture realistic system behavior but offer less precise component-level insights. Effective ML system evaluation requires strategic combination of all three levels.
alt: Scatter plot with three labeled points along a diagonal: micro-benchmarks at high isolation, macro-benchmarks, and end-to-end benchmarks at high representativeness.
context:
```

Selecting a single granularity level is rarely sufficient because benchmarking presents an inherent trade-off between diagnostic isolation and production fidelity. Along the descending diagonal in @fig-benchmark-tradeoffs, evaluation regimes trade diagnostic power for operational realism. Micro-benchmarks (the red point at the top left) isolate kernel-level memory bandwidth and warp occupancy at the expense of end-to-end context. Macro-benchmarks (the blue center point) capture composed model topologies. End-to-end benchmarks (the green point at the bottom right) encompass live production traffic but obscure the root causes of latency spikes. Effective evaluation requires strategically combining all three tiers to verify that kernel speedups survive full-system deployment.

title: ImageNet Error and GPU Adoption
caption: **ImageNet Error and GPU Adoption**: Sourced top-5 error rates are shown beside GPU use among challenge entries. The temporal association does not isolate hardware's causal contribution. Error-rate sources: [@russakovsky2015; @krizhevsky2012imagenet]. @gray2015ilsvrcgpu charts the per-year GPU entry counts.
alt: Dual-axis chart with a blue line showing top-5 error rate declining and green bars showing increased GPU use among ImageNet challenge entries from 2010 to 2014.
context:
:::

System benchmarks evaluate performance across scales, ranging from single-chip configurations to large distributed systems and covering both training and inference. The ImageNet challenge shows why separating the hardware's contribution from the model's is hard to do after the fact. Between 2010 and 2014, top-5 error (the blue line in @fig-imagenet-gpus) fell from 28.2 percent to 7.3 percent, with the steepest single drop at AlexNet's arrival in 2012. Over the same years, GPU-accelerated entries (the green bars) rose from zero to over 100 [@krizhevsky2012imagenet; @russakovsky2015; @gray2015ilsvrcgpu]. These paired series plot contemporaneous empirical trends, not a causal attribution of how much accuracy gain stemmed from hardware throughput versus algorithmic design, training schedules, or dataset expansion. A system benchmark avoids that ambiguity by construction: it fixes the model and quality target so that any change in the result belongs to the hardware-software stack.

title: MLPerf Training Progress
caption: **MLPerf Training Progress**: Workload lines report cumulative relative performance across benchmark versions against the plotted cumulative Moore's Law baseline. Every workload's latest point exceeds the baseline at the same date, and Mask R-CNN reaches the largest plotted gain at 48.8$\times$; the comparison captures combined hardware and software progress, not hardware scaling alone. Source: [@tschand2025].
alt: Line chart with nine model benchmarks from 2018 to 2024 showing relative performance gains. Every benchmark's latest point sits above the Moore's law baseline of 6.6×, and Mask R-CNN reaches the highest value at 48.8×.
context:
### Training benchmark motivation {#sec-benchmarking-training-benchmark-motivation-f365}

MLPerf Training\index{MLPerf Training!standardized framework} [@mattson2020mlperf; @mlperf_training_website] provides the standardized framework for this time-to-quality measurement. The longitudinal scaling curves in @fig-mlperf-training-improve track cumulative relative performance gains across nine model workloads between 2018 and 2024 against the orange Moore's Law baseline. Every workload curve outpaces cumulative transistor scaling (which reaches 6.6$\times$ by mid-2024), led by Mask R-CNN climbing to 48.8$\times$ and ResNet reaching 34$\times$ as distributed scaling and compiler optimizations compound hardware improvements [@tschand2025]. This trajectory documents improvements in the full hardware-software system beyond transistor scaling alone; the plotted results do not isolate the contribution of competitive pressure from other causes.

title: From Claimed to Delivered Speedup on the Edge Board
caption: **From Claimed to Delivered Speedup on the Edge Board**: MobileNetV2 latency per inference (left) and active energy per inference (right) on the camera trap's board. INT8 cuts the host CPU's isolated latency by `{python} MobileNetTradeoffCalc.latency_speedup_mult_str`, and the accelerator cuts it a further `{python} EdgeAccelSpeedupCalc.inference_speedup_mult_str` when only model compute is timed. Widening the boundary to include host preprocessing and the host-accelerator link (hatched) leaves a `{python} EdgeAccelSpeedupCalc.e2e_speedup_mult_str` end-to-end advantage, and the active-energy advantage is `{python} EdgeAccelSpeedupCalc.energy_ratio_mult_str` before idle and host power are counted. All values are the chapter's illustrative scenario, not measurements of a named product.
alt: Two bar panels. The left panel plots latency in milliseconds for two groups of bars. The isolated-compute group falls steeply from FP32 on the host CPU to INT8 on the host CPU to INT8 on the accelerator. The end-to-end group compares INT8 on the host CPU with INT8 on the accelerator, each bar split into a solid compute segment and a hatched segment for preprocessing and transfer. Ratio labels sit above arrows between bars. The right panel plots active energy per inference for the host CPU and the accelerator, with the accelerator bar shorter.
context:
The SingleStream result illustrates why benchmarking requires matching the MLPerf scenario to the deployment context: SingleStream emphasizes latency, while Offline benchmarks would optimize for bulk throughput rather than latency bounds.

:::

title: Power Consumption Differentials
caption: **Power Consumption Differentials**: Measured power spans about eight orders of magnitude across MLPerf divisions, from milliwatts for TinyML submissions through watts at the edge to kilowatts in data center inference and hundreds of kilowatts for training systems. Each pair marks the lowest and highest power among official MLPerf Power submissions in that division, after @tschand2025.
alt: Dumbbell chart on a logarithmic watts axis: Tiny 5.6 mW to 167 mW, Edge 3.9 W to 1.1 kW, Data center 267 W to 6.3 kW, Training 5.5 kW to 498 kW.
context:
:::

Measuring power differs from measuring execution time because power is not a single timestamped interval: instantaneous power (supply voltage times current) fluctuates continuously across microsecond execution phases and drifts over minutes as silicon heats up, increasing temperature-dependent leakage current. ML deployments also span a wide physical range. The dumbbell plot in @fig-power-differentials isolates this disparity on a logarithmic power scale. It plots minimum (blue) and maximum (red) envelopes across four deployment tiers: TinyML systems (5.6 mW to 167 mW), edge hardware (3.9 W to 1.1 kW), data center inference nodes (267 W to 6.3 kW), and large-scale training clusters (5.5 kW to 498 kW). Spanning about eight orders of magnitude from the TinyML floor to the training-cluster ceiling, this spectrum explains why no single efficiency metric serves all deployment contexts. A figure of merit optimized for multi-rack data center throughput becomes meaningless for a battery-powered keyword spotter governed by milliwatt budgets.

title: Power Measurement Boundaries
caption: **Power Measurement Boundaries**: MLPerf defines system boundaries for power measurement, ranging from single-chip devices to full data center nodes, to enable fair comparisons of energy efficiency across diverse hardware platforms. These boundaries delineate which components' power consumption is included in reported metrics, impacting the interpretation of performance results. Source: [@tschand2025].
alt: Four grouped system diagrams show power-measurement boundaries for a Tiny SoC, inference SoCs with off-chip DRAM, an inference node with accelerator memory, cooling, storage, host DRAM, and a NIC, and training racks. Solid enclosures mark measured boundaries, while red dashed boxes mark excluded remote storage, storage nodes, and data-center cooling components.
context:
### Power measurement boundaries {#sec-benchmarking-power-measurement-boundaries-982c}

Where an engineer draws the system boundary dictates what counts as efficient. If a benchmark measures only the accelerator core, it ignores the host CPU driving the PCIe bus, the off-chip DRAM holding weights, and the cooling fans dissipating heat. @Fig-power-diagram partitions these measurement perimeters across three deployment tiers (Tiny, Inference, and Training), where solid olive enclosures demarcate measured components and red dashed boxes isolate excluded infrastructure such as remote storage and data-center chillers [@tschand2025].

title: Data-Center Energy Efficiency Gains
caption: **Data-Center Energy Efficiency Gains**: Each series is normalized to its own first plotted version, so compare improvement within a workload rather than absolute efficiency across workloads. Source: [@tschand2025].
alt: Line chart of normalized energy efficiency across MLPerf Inference versions from 2021 to 2024. RetinaNet and ResNet rise to 3 times their initial values; BERT and GPT-J reach about 1.9 times, DLRM-v2 about 1.7 times, Llama 2 about 1.5 times, and RNN-T about 1.3 times.
context:
Standardizing the boundary prevents misleading comparisons across architectural families. By specifying instrumentation, measurement boundaries, matched logging windows, and the applicable workload constraints, MLPerf Power makes efficiency results interpretable within the tested scenario.

Over successive benchmark submission rounds from 2021 to 2024, standardized measurements capture how architectural improvements, compiler optimizations, and lower-precision arithmetic translate into production efficiency gains. Tracking normalized energy efficiency (samples per joule) across eight submission cycles from v1.0 to v4.1, @fig-power-trends charts diverging efficiency trajectories across seven distinct MLPerf Inference workloads.

title: Hardware-Dependent Latency–Accuracy Trade-offs
caption: **Hardware-Dependent Latency–Accuracy Trade-offs**: Each panel holds top-1 ImageNet accuracy on the vertical axis while using a target-specific latency scale horizontally. The arrow links MobileNetV3 Large at roughly equal accuracy on CPU float and DSP, exposing the hardware-dependent latency shift. Source: [@chu2021].
alt: Five scatter plots compare top-1 ImageNet accuracy with latency on Pixel 4 CPU float, CPU uint8, GPU, EdgeTPU, and DSP targets for eight model families. An arrow links approximately equal-accuracy points on the CPU-float and DSP panels.
context:
[^fn-hardware-lottery-hooker]: **Hardware lottery**\index{Hardware lottery!benchmark bias}: Coined by @hooker2021 to describe how algorithmic success depends on alignment with available hardware and software. Transformer workloads benefit from dense matrix operations that map efficiently to modern accelerators, while graph neural networks and sparse mixture-of-experts models can be harder to evaluate when available silicon and software stacks favor dense kernels. Hardware-specific leaderboards therefore favor architectures aligned with the measured platform and may obscure alternatives that would fare differently under other hardware assumptions.

Hardware compatibility dependence introduces systematic biases when evaluating models across heterogeneous execution targets. An architecture optimized for GPU execution may underperform on an embedded CPU, DSP, or custom edge accelerator with differing vector widths, cache hierarchies, and quantization support. Across five hardware targets on a Google Pixel 4, @fig-hw-lottery charts how the latency–accuracy Pareto frontier reshuffles between CPU float, CPU uint8, GPU, EdgeTPU, and DSP execution. The diagonal purple arrow links MobileNetV3 Large at roughly 75 percent top-1 accuracy, from approximately 20 ms on CPU float to 4.5 ms on the DSP. Multi-MAX reaches roughly 75 percent accuracy at 2.2 ms on EdgeTPU and 3.4 ms on DSP; its points at higher accuracy carry higher latency. Comparisons must therefore match both the model variant and the accuracy operating point. The shifted frontiers show why model selection requires measurements on the target execution path rather than a latency ranking inherited from another processor.

title: Performance Spectrum
caption: **Performance Spectrum**: Scientific and edge applications occupy widely separated operating points in data rate and available computation time, motivating benchmarks tied to each application's timing and data-movement constraints. Source: [@duarte2022fastml].
alt: Log-scale scatter plot of data rate vs. computation time for LHC sensors and triggers, scientific instruments and controls, Internet of Things systems, and mobile devices. Points and error bars span roughly 10^4 to 10^14 bytes per second and nanoseconds to fractions of a second, with a shaded Fast ML for Science benchmark region.
context:
Early deep learning benchmarks evaluated image classification and object detection on convolutional networks. As workloads expanded to large language models, recommendation systems, and generative AI\index{Generative AI!benchmark evolution}, those vision benchmarks failed to capture long-context attention, autoregressive decoding, and sparse expert routing, and community benchmarks moved to language understanding [@wang2018; @wang2019superglue] and foundation model capabilities [@liang2022helm]. How saturation erodes a static benchmark's discriminating power is a data question, taken up in @sec-benchmarking-data-benchmarking-22f9.

Benchmark evolution also expands the dimensions of measurement. While early benchmarks focused on throughput and accuracy, contemporary systems require multi-objective evaluation across energy efficiency, memory footprint, and tail latency under resource constraints. Scientific instruments provide a further constraint regime in @fig-sciml-graph. Its shaded "Fast ML for Science" envelope places high-throughput trigger pipelines outside typical mobile and IoT operating points [@duarte2022fastml]. The distance between these operating points is why a benchmark must match its application.

title: Development Paradigms
caption: **Development Paradigms**: Model-centric AI iterates on architecture while holding the dataset fixed, whereas data-centric AI iterates on annotations, diversity, and bias while holding the architecture fixed. The double arrow marks the approaches as complementary.
alt: Side-by-side diagrams: model-centric AI shows data cylinders feeding CPU with feedback loop to model, data-centric AI shows feedback loop to data instead. Double arrow indicates complementary approaches.
context:
:::

Distribution alignment challenges highlight a persistent tension in ML development between two paradigms: *fixing the data and iterating on models*, or *fixing the model and iterating on data*. The side-by-side schematics in @fig-model-vs-data isolate this divergence through the placement of the padlock and feedback path. In the model-centric panel\index{Model-centric AI!architectural innovation}, the dataset is locked while the feedback loop iteratively refines model parameters on the CPU. In the data-centric panel, the model architecture is locked while the loop routes back to enhance training data quality, diversity, and labeling. As the bidirectional red arrow emphasizes, the two paradigms are complementary engineering strategies rather than mutually exclusive philosophies.

title: Dataset Saturation
caption: **Dataset Saturation**: The zero line denotes reported human performance; each curve's crossing marks a capability for which the static benchmark has less remaining discriminating headroom. The crossings do not distinguish genuine capability gains from optimization to the evaluation set. Sources: [@perrault2024artificial; @kiela2021].
alt: Line chart showing five AI capabilities crossing human performance baseline from 1998 to 2020: handwriting, speech, image recognition, reading comprehension, and language understanding.
context:
#### Dataset saturation and dynamic benchmarks {.unnumbered}

Even when coverage, quality, and distribution alignment protocols are satisfied, static benchmarks encounter the problem of dataset saturation\index{Dataset saturation!performance capability illusion}. As models approach empirical upper bounds on fixed test suites, leaderboard deltas compress, making it difficult to distinguish genuine capability advances from over-optimization to benchmark-specific artifacts. The capability trajectories in @fig-dataset-saturation plot this exhaustion over two decades, showing AI scores rising from normalized baselines (-100) to cross the zero line marking human performance [@perrault2024artificial]. While handwriting and speech recognition required over a decade to reach human parity (the green shaded region), reading comprehension and language understanding surged across the threshold in under two years between 2016 and 2020, rapidly exhausting the discriminating headroom of static suites.

title: The Inference Pipeline
caption: **The Inference Pipeline**: ML serving systems transform raw inputs into final outputs through sequential stages: preprocessing, neural network computation, and postprocessing. The neural network represents just one component; preprocessing and postprocessing make end-to-end latency depend on more than neural-network execution.
alt: Left-to-right flow diagram of six connected boxes labeled Raw Data, Pre-processing, Neural Network, Raw Output, Post-processing, and Final Output. Outlined groups beneath the boxes identify Pre-processing, Deep Learning, and Post-processing.
context:
:::

[^fn-slo-sla-serving]: **SLOs in ML serving**\index{SLO!vs. SLA}\index{SLO!multidimensional targets}: An SLO is the internal target, as distinct from the contractual SLA. For ML serving, task quality and inference latency can both contribute to SLOs, creating multidimensional targets where improving one dimension (for example, deploying a larger model for accuracy) can violate another (latency).

title: Inference Server Anatomy
caption: **Inference Server Anatomy**: A modern inference server decouples network handling from accelerator execution through a staged pipeline. Each stage isolates a concern, from absorbing bursty traffic to forming efficient batches, so the hardware accelerator stays busy despite irregular arrival patterns.
alt: Flowchart showing a six-stage inference server pipeline: client to network ingress to request queue to dynamic batcher, then down to inference runner to accelerator. Arrows connect stages sequentially.
context:
If a web server invoked the accelerator synchronously every time a socket read completed, slow client uploads would stall the GPU and concurrent connections would contend for device memory. An inference server\index{Inference server!architecture}[^fn-inference-server-serving] (such as NVIDIA Triton or TensorFlow Serving) avoids this by acting as a specialized runtime scheduler that manages concurrency, device memory, and data movement between host CPUs and accelerator devices. Rather than running the model directly on the network thread, the server pipelines incoming requests through dedicated subsystems that isolate client network handling from accelerator compute. Every request traverses a six-stage runtime pipeline (@fig-server-anatomy) from network ingress and request-buffering queues through the dynamic batcher to the inference runner and hardware accelerator.

[^fn-inference-server-serving]: **Inference server**\index{Inference server!serving architecture}: Google's TensorFlow Serving\index{TensorFlow Serving!inference server} [@olston2017tensorflow] helped establish the separation of model logic from serving infrastructure; NVIDIA's Triton\index{Triton!inference server} [@nvidia_triton] extends this pattern across multiple model frameworks and backends. The critical design insight is that a scheduler and dynamic batcher turn irregular single-request traffic into accelerator-friendly execution, improving utilization when latency budgets allow batching. Exact utilization gains depend on model, hardware, arrival rate, and the configured batching window.

title: One Request on One Node
caption: **One Request on One Node**: The reference ResNet-50 request drawn on the three resources it crosses. JPEG decode, resize, and normalization occupy a host CPU core, the input crosses PCIe, and the forward pass occupies the accelerator; softmax and top-5 selection are drawn on the host. Durations follow @tbl-model-serving-resnet50-latency-budget, so the accelerator is busy for `{python} LatencyTableCalc.p_inf_prose_str` of the `{python} LatencyTableCalc.l_total_ms_str` request and idle while the host prepares the input. Network transfer, serialization, and batching delay lie outside this budget and are not drawn.
alt: Three horizontal lanes labeled host CPU, PCIe, and GPU along a millisecond axis from 0 to about 9. The CPU lane holds consecutive bars for JPEG decode, resize, and normalize. A short bar on the PCIe lane follows, then a long forward-pass bar on the GPU lane, then a very short postprocessing bar back on the CPU lane. A hatched band on the GPU lane covers the time before the forward pass and is labeled accelerator idle.
context:
:::

Laid on the node's hardware, the same budget occupies three resources in turn, and the accelerator is busy for less than half of the request (@fig-model-serving-request-timeline). While a host CPU core decompresses the JPEG, resizes the image, and normalizes pixel values before copying the tensor across PCIe, the GPU waits completely idle for work to arrive.

title: Request Pipelining
caption: **Request Pipelining**: Pipelining hides latency by overlapping independent operations across different hardware resources. In pipelined execution (B), the CPU processes the next request's data while the GPU executes the current request's inference. This can increase accelerator duty cycle and throughput without changing the model.
alt: Two timing diagrams. A (Serial): alternating CPU preprocessing, GPU inference, and idle blocks in sequence. B (Pipelined): two parallel rows where CPU preprocessing overlaps with GPU inference, eliminating idle time.
context:
#### Overlapping I/O and compute {#sec-model-serving-overlapping-io-compute-966c}

@Fig-serving-pipeline-timing sequences execution across CPU preprocessing and GPU inference to demonstrate how request pipelining recovers lost compute capacity. In serial execution (A), each request must complete its entire lifecycle (Network $\rightarrow$ CPU Preprocessing $\rightarrow$ GPU Inference $\rightarrow$ Postprocessing) before the next request begins, leaving the GPU idle for more than 50 percent of wall-clock time. Pipelining concurrent requests (B) overlaps CPU preprocessing of upcoming requests with active GPU inference on earlier inputs, eliminating the idle bubbles and maximizing accelerator duty cycle.

title: The Tail Latency Explosion
caption: **The Tail Latency Explosion**: Request latency vs. serving utilization $\ServingUtilization$. Mean latency (blue) and the p99 approximation (red) both grow nonlinearly as utilization approaches saturation; the 70 percent marker is an illustrative planning knee rather than a model-derived breakpoint. In an $\KendallMarkovianCode/\KendallMarkovianCode/1$ queue, the 99th percentile latency scales as $-\ln(0.01) \approx 4.6\times$ mean latency, illustrating why tail delays compound violently near saturation.
alt: Line plot of normalized request latency against serving utilization. A dashed blue mean-latency curve and a solid red p99 curve rise nonlinearly toward saturation, with the red curve remaining 4.6 times the blue curve. Green shading marks 0–50 percent as the Safe Zone, red shading marks 70–100 percent as the Danger Zone, and an arrow labels 70 percent ‘The Knee.’

title: The Throughput-Latency Knee
caption: **The Throughput-Latency Knee**: Batch size vs. throughput (blue) and latency (orange) for the reference ResNet-50 profile on the H100. Throughput rises nearly in proportion to batch size while fixed overhead dominates, then flattens toward its ceiling. Latency grows slowly at first and roughly in proportion to batch size beyond the marked planning knee, where it is twice the batch-one latency and throughput reaches half its ceiling. Each throughput value is batch size divided by the plotted formation-plus-service latency, for a single worker that waits out a 10 ms window and then serves each batch; pipelined serving sustains higher throughput. Values are modeled, not measured.
alt: Dual-axis line chart on a log batch-size axis. Blue line (throughput) rises steeply and then flattens. Orange line (latency) stays nearly flat through batch 32 and then climbs. A vertical dashed line labeled Planning Knee marks batch size near 400.
context: batching window requires a mean formation-plus-inference budget of approximately `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_budget_ms_str`. An arriving request waits on average half the window (`{python} BatchThroughputCalc.half_window_ms_str`, as derived in @sec-model-serving-queue-waiting-time-analysis-8d5c) and requires `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_inference_ms_str` of inference. If the service must meet a `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.slo_ms_str` SLO, the remaining `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_headroom_ms_str` provides headroom for worker backlog and auxiliary pipeline stages, while delivering `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.batch8_vs_batch1_mult_str` higher service throughput than batch 1 on identical hardware. On this accelerator the batching window, not the computation, is most of the batch-8 budget. Batch size cannot grow indefinitely, and @fig-throughput-latency-knee shows why by modeling this relationship across batch sizes on a logarithmic axis. To isolate the planning knee under worst-case scheduling conditions, the figure assumes a strictly serialized single worker that waits out the full batching window before executing each batch, without pipelined overlap ($\text{Latency} = \BatchingWindow + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)$). Under this unpipelined assumption, batch-1 throughput is `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.serial_b1_rps_str` rather than the `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.b1_rps_str` sustained when inference runs back to back. Throughput rises almost in proportion to batch size while the fixed overhead dominates each batch, because each added image costs only `{python} ResNetH100Profile.per_image_fp16_us_str` of device time. The planning knee sits where the batch's total per-image work equals the fixed part of its latency, the window plus the fixed cost, near batch `{python} BatchThroughputCalc.knee_batch_str`. There latency is twice that of batch one and throughput is half its ceiling. Beyond it, each doubling of the batch roughly doubles latency while throughput gains less and less. In this model throughput never declines; it saturates, so latency, not throughput, sets the largest useful batch.

title: Framework Interoperability
caption: **Framework Interoperability**: The inward spokes represent exports into the shared ONNX format, while the outward spokes represent loads into compatible tools and runtimes; portability requires support on both sides of that boundary.
alt: Hub diagram with ONNX at center. Left side (export): PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, Caffe2, MXNet, Microsoft CNTK with arrows pointing inward. Right side (load): ONNX Runtime plus the same six frameworks with arrows pointing outward.
context:
The development framework and deployment runtime need not be the same system, but they must exchange a representation both can interpret. The **ONNX**\index{ONNX!definition}\index{ONNX!cross-framework portability} format addresses this fragmentation by standardizing model exchange across runtimes [@bai2019onnx]. A pipeline can train an architecture in PyTorch, export the computation graph to an ONNX intermediate representation, and execute the serialized graph in ONNX Runtime or compile it for a target accelerator. In contrast, TensorFlow Lite relies on its own conversion path, translating TensorFlow SavedModels into FlatBuffers rather than routing through ONNX. Although standard interchange formats reduce manual model conversion between development and production environments, they do not eliminate compatibility testing, operator coverage gaps, or custom-kernel fallback overhead.

The exchange is hub-and-spoke\index{ONNX!hub-and-spoke interoperability} around the common ONNX intermediate representation (@fig-onnx). Training frameworks such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, Caffe2, MXNet, and CNTK export inward to the shared representation, and ONNX Runtime and other target frameworks load the serialized computation graph outward without reimplementing model code.

title: Prefill Admission and Decode Cadence
caption: **Prefill Admission and Decode Cadence**: A new prompt P shares one worker with an active decode stream. Admitting P whole leaves a long interval between that stream's tokens. Admitting P in chunks inserts a decode step at each iteration boundary; P finishes later in the schedule shown. Both paths process the same prompt. Bar widths and token spacing are schematic, not measured durations or a throughput prediction.
alt: Two schedules have a prompt P row and an active-stream row. In panel a, one continuous prefill bar lies between two decode-output markers. In panel b, four labeled prefill chunks alternate with decode steps, with an output marker after each step. A horizontal arrow points right toward later time beneath both schedules. Dashed lines mark prompt completion in each panel.
context:
Serving runtimes such as vLLM[^fn-vllm-page-table] and TensorRT-LLM improve throughput via two mechanisms: reclaiming wasted compute from completed sequences and shortening queue wait times for new arrivals [@kwon2023; @nvidiaTensorRtLlm]. However, admitting new requests dynamically creates a systems collision between prompt prefill and token decoding. Long-prompt prefill often exposes high arithmetic intensity and can occupy the GPU for tens of milliseconds. Low-batch decoding often has less weight reuse and is memory-bandwidth bound, advancing one token per active sequence at a time. When an engine executes a prefill in the same iteration as active decodes, the ongoing decode streams stall, causing severe spikes in inter-token latency. Sarathi-Serve resolves this interference through chunked prefill and stall-free batching [@agrawal2024sarathi]. By splitting long prompts into fixed-size chunks (e.g., 512 tokens) and co-scheduling a single chunk alongside active decode requests per step, the scheduler limits the prefill work admitted per iteration, reducing interference with active decodes. Measured iteration times determine the resulting token cadence.

The scheduling boundary determines when an existing stream can emit its next token. @Fig-serving-chunked-prefill compares admission of one complete prompt with admission of the same prompt in chunks, while keeping the active stream visible in both schedules.

title: Logical Pages and Physical KV Blocks
caption: **Logical Pages and Physical KV Blocks**: Request E's logical pages remain ordered even though its physical blocks are separated by other requests. Each table entry names one physical block; the partially filled last block remains allocated to E. After E completes and its pending accesses finish, its unshared blocks return to the free pool. C and D retain their blocks. The diagram assumes no prefix sharing and uses equal block sizes; paging changes placement, not the KV bytes per token.
alt: Four ordered logical pages of request E point downward to table entries 0, 1, 4, and 5. Elbow arrows connect those entries to blocks 0, 1, 4, and 5 in an eight-block physical pool. C occupies blocks 2 and 3, and D occupies blocks 6 and 7. Block 5 is partly filled and partly hatched. A second pool row shows E's four blocks marked free after release, while C and D remain in their original positions.
context:
**PagedAttention**\index{PagedAttention!memory fragmentation solution},[^fn-paged-attention-memory] introduced in vLLM, resolves this fragmentation by applying operating system virtual memory paging to accelerator memory [@kwon2023]. In static contiguous allocation, reserving maximum sequence length memory up front causes internal waste, while freed regions may be too small or poorly placed to satisfy a new contiguous reservation. Instead of allocating one contiguous region per sequence, PagedAttention divides the KV cache into fixed-size blocks mapped through a block table. A sequence's cache can therefore occupy noncontiguous physical blocks. When a sequence completes, its blocks return to a free pool for reuse. Rather than copying noncontiguous blocks into a temporary contiguous buffer before computing attention, a specialized PagedAttention CUDA kernel traverses the block table directly, staging noncontiguous blocks into on-chip SRAM during query-key multiplication. By eliminating external fragmentation and bounding internal waste to each sequence's last, partially filled block, PagedAttention reduced KV-cache waste below 4 percent in the reported evaluation and enabled substantially higher batch concurrency on the same accelerator hardware [@kwon2023]. Paging decides where cache blocks live, however. It does not reduce how many blocks each sequence needs, and that number grows with every generated token.

A block table separates a sequence's token order from its physical placement. @Fig-serving-paged-kv-mapping uses an eight-block pool: requests C and D occupy the middle pairs, leaving four free blocks in two separated runs. A request E that needs four blocks can use those scattered blocks without moving C or D.

title: The KV-Cache Explosion
caption: **The KV-Cache Explosion**: FP16 KV-cache usage vs. context length for a 70-billion-parameter-class model with GQA. On the modeled H100's 80 GB of HBM (85.9 GB decimal), 35.3 GB of INT4 weights leave 50.6 GB for KV cache before runtime overhead. Batch size 32 reaches that cache budget at roughly 4.8k tokens, forcing a trade-off between batch size and context length.
alt: Line chart of FP16 KV-cache size against context length for batch sizes 1, 4, 16, and 32. All four lines rise linearly, with steeper slopes for larger batches. A red dashed horizontal line marks the cache budget remaining after the INT4 weights on the modeled H100; batch size 32 crosses it near 4.8k tokens. The region above the budget line is shaded red and labeled Out of Memory (OOM) Zone.
context:
Once contexts grow, the cache rather than the weights sets how many conversations one accelerator can hold, and Llama 3 8B makes the budget concrete. Each token stores a key vector and a value vector in every layer for every key-value head. Storing 16-bit Key and Value tensors across $\LayerCount=32$ layers with $\KvHeadCount=8$ grouped-query attention heads of dimension $\AttentionHeadDimension=128$ requires $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 131{,}072\text{ bytes} \approx 131\text{ KB}$ per token per sequence. Grouped-query attention [@dubey2024llama] lets the model's `{python} KvBudget.heads_str` query heads share those key-value heads, which cuts the cache by `{python} KvBudget.mha_ratio_mult_str` relative to full multi-head attention. An `{python} KvBudget.context_tokens_str`-token conversation therefore holds `{python} KvBudget.kv_per_seq_gb_str`. With `{python} KvBudget.weights8_gb_str` of FP16 weights resident on an H100 whose `{python} KvBudget.capacity_gib_str` datasheet capacity is `{python} KvBudget.capacity_gb_str` in the decimal units used for tensor footprints, about `{python} KvBudget.free8_gb_str` remains for caches before runtime workspace, room for about `{python} KvBudget.n_seq_str` such conversations at once. The weights are a fixed cost; every additional conversation, and every additional thousand tokens of context, draws on the same remainder.

Larger models make the cache the binding constraint sooner. For a 70-billion-parameter-class model with grouped-query attention, 4-bit weights consume `{python} KvBudget.weights70_gb_str` of the same H100, leaving `{python} KvBudget.free70_gb_str` for FP16 cache before runtime workspace. A batch of `{python} KvBudget.batch_large_str` conversations exhausts that budget at roughly `{python} KvBudget.crossing70_str` tokens of context, so serving engines trade concurrent batch size against context length to avoid out-of-memory failures (@fig-kv-cache-growth).

title: Intelligence Deflation
caption: **Intelligence Deflation**: Representative public API input-token list prices per 1M tokens (\$) over time (Log Scale). Nine model-version list prices come from the launch and pricing announcements of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and DeepSeek between late 2022 and 2025; the dashed line is a log-linear fit through the price floor, the points that each set a new low. The series is intended as a market trend indicator, not a controlled or current-price comparison. API token-processing prices have collapsed by multiple orders of magnitude, transforming the economics of automated AI workflows.
alt: Log-scale scatter plot of nine public API input-token list prices from late 2022 to early 2025, ranging from 30 dollars to 0.075 dollars per million tokens. Blue points are labeled by model, and a red dashed trend line fitted through the cheapest price at each date slopes downward across the plot.
context:
:::

The same serving-economics pressure appears in public API prices. @Fig-intelligence-deflation tracks this cost collapse across representative public API list-price snapshots from 2023 through 2025 on a logarithmic scale. The steep downward trend line isolates how prompt token pricing fell by multiple orders of magnitude, from thirty dollars per million tokens for original GPT-4 down to several cents for Gemini 1.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3. Vendor prices change frequently, so these points should be read as historical provenance for the trend rather than as current purchasing guidance [@openai2023chatgptwhisper; @openai2023gpt4web; @openaiCommunity2024gpt4oApi; @openai2024gpt4oMini; @anthropic2024claude3family; @google2024gemini15flashPricing; @deepseek2024v3]. Each order-of-magnitude drop changes which applications are economically viable, and a provider can sustain such prices only if its serving stack extracts more completed requests from each accelerator-hour. Converting engineering efficiency into unit cost draws on the latency, batching, and memory mechanisms of the preceding sections.

title: Measured Accuracy Loss over Time
caption: **Measured Accuracy Loss over Time**: For six datasets, performance of the same trained model on held-out test data from its training period (blue) and on data from a later period (red), with error bars showing one standard deviation over three training seeds. The label gives each drop in percentage points. MIMIC mortality is scored by AUC; the others by accuracy. Data from @yao2022wildtime.
alt: Dumbbell chart with six rows sorted by drop size: Yearbook portraits accuracy falls from 98.0 to 79.5 percent, MIMIC mortality AUC from 90.9 to 72.9, MIMIC readmission accuracy from 73.0 to 61.3, HuffPost news from 79.4 to 70.4, arXiv papers from 53.8 to 45.9, and FMoW satellite from 58.1 to 54.1. Blue dots mark training-period performance and red dots later-period performance, each with error bars, and each row is labeled with its drop in points.
context:
```

The degradation is measurable. In the Wild-Time benchmark, @yao2022wildtime train a model on data from one period and test it both on held-out data from that period and on data from later years, across six real datasets that span yearbook portraits, satellite imagery, hospital records, news, and scientific papers. @Fig-temporal-shift shows the result. On every dataset the same model scores lower on the later data, by `{python} TemporalShiftDrop.min_drop_str` to `{python} TemporalShiftDrop.max_drop_str` points of accuracy or of area under the curve (AUC), although nothing about the model or its serving path changed. The loss comes entirely from the world moving away from the training data, and only monitoring that compares predictions against fresh outcomes can see it.

title: Iterative MLOps Loop
caption: **Iterative MLOps Loop**: Monitoring and triggering feed production evidence back into design and model development, turning requirements, engineering, testing, and deployment into a continuous operating cycle.
alt: Infinity-loop diagram with three phases. Design phase: requirements, use-case prioritization, data availability. Model development: data engineering, model engineering, testing. Operations: deployment, CI/CD pipeline, monitoring and triggering.
context:
:::

The loop has three stages (design, model development, and operations), but its defining feature is the return path. Runtime telemetry and retraining triggers carry live performance signals from operations back into requirements and data engineering, so deployment feeds the next design cycle instead of ending the project (@fig-mlops-diagram).

title: Hidden Infrastructure of ML Systems
caption: **Hidden Infrastructure of ML Systems**: ML code is one of ten components arranged around the ML system at the center, alongside data collection, data verification, feature extraction, configuration, machine resource management, serving infrastructure, monitoring, analysis tools, and process management tools. Modeling occupies one circle and the remaining nine identify the operational surface a deployment must also carry; circle counts do not measure code volume or maintenance cost. Source: [@sculley2015hidden].
alt: Hub-and-spoke diagram with the ML system at the center, connected by arrows to ten surrounding components: data collection, data verification, feature extraction, configuration, machine resource management, serving infrastructure, monitoring, analysis tools, process management tools, and ML code.
context:
:::

The debt is larger than manual retraining alone, because modeling code constitutes only a small fraction of a real-world deployment. Core modeling code is one peripheral component among ten around the ML system, alongside nine supporting subsystems spanning data verification, feature extraction, configuration, and machine resource management (@fig-technical-debt). Their presence broadens the maintenance surface; the diagram does not measure each component's cost.

title: Correction Cascades
caption: **Correction Cascades**: Each model is trained to correct the errors of the model before it, forming a chain of dependencies. Changing an upstream model can invalidate downstream corrections, turning one local fix into revalidation across the chain and potentially several retraining cycles.
alt: Four model boxes in a left-to-right chain labeled Model A through Model D, each trained to correct the previous one. A red change badge on Model A and red dashed arcs reaching Model B, C, and D show an upstream change propagating downstream, with must revalidate labels beneath the downstream models.
context:
When boundary erosion goes unaddressed, engineering fixes frequently trigger a **correction cascade**\index{Correction cascade!sequential dependencies}: patching a specific model defect with an auxiliary post-filter introduces secondary errors elsewhere, requiring further patches that destabilize the entire pipeline. In ML systems, these cascades are severe because changes propagate through statistical dependencies rather than deterministic code branches. Retraining a model to correct a specific false-positive cluster may degrade accuracy across previously stable cohorts. Adding an auxiliary model to override edge-case predictions introduces uncalibrated scores that confuse downstream consumers. Repeated dependent patches can demand coordinated revalidation, with maintenance costs that may exceed those of revising the base model.

@Fig-correction-cascades-flowchart traces this failure propagation along a four-stage dependency chain (Models A through D), where each downstream component compensates for the residual errors of its predecessor. When an upstream patch alters Model A, the dashed red arcs mark every downstream correction that requires revalidation and may need retraining.

title: MLOps Stack Layers
caption: **MLOps Stack Layers**: Five columns organize the ML system stack: ML Models/Applications, ML Frameworks/Platforms, Model Orchestration, Infrastructure, and Hardware. MLOps spans orchestration tasks from data management through model serving and infrastructure tasks from job scheduling through monitoring, supporting automation, reproducibility, and scalable deployment.
alt: Layered architecture diagram. Top row: ML models, frameworks, orchestration, infrastructure, hardware. MLOps section spans orchestration tasks (data management through model serving) and infrastructure tasks (job scheduling through monitoring).
context:
These operational components sit between the framework and the hardware and track what neither of them tracks, the data lineage and the cluster state. MLOps occupies the middle of the five-tier stack of @fig-ops-layers (ML models, frameworks, orchestration, infrastructure, and hardware). Model orchestration, which runs from data management to serving, and operational infrastructure, which runs from job scheduling to monitoring, together bridge mathematical frameworks and physical accelerator clusters and enforce the remediations of @tbl-mlops-infrastructure-debt. The tiers say *where* a component sits in the implementation stack, while the four layers of @tbl-mlops-layers say *who* owns an operational responsibility; the rest of the chapter reasons with the layers and the three interfaces.

Inside the orchestration and infrastructure tiers, four architectural mechanisms execute these operational responsibilities. At the data boundary, a feature storage and retrieval layer serves a unified schema across two disparate access patterns. Offline training uses high-throughput analytical scans over immutable columnar files, and online serving uses low-latency point lookups against key-value stores (@sec-ml-operations-feature-stores-c01c). To keep every transformation and checkpoint traceable, an artifact and lineage store records content-addressed hashes for dataset snapshots, code commits, container images, and model weights. Any live prediction can then be audited back to its exact training inputs (@sec-ml-operations-versioning-lineage-b1cf). Workflow orchestration then sequences the pipeline stages, from ingestion and validation through training and evaluation, as declared dependency graphs with retry semantics and automated triggers (@sec-ml-operations-cicd-pipelines-a9de). A compute runtime underneath schedules accelerator hardware, host memory, and processor cores across training jobs and serving endpoints under strict resource isolation (@sec-ml-operations-training-pipelines-2dcf). Specific frameworks implement pieces of this decomposition, but the underlying mechanisms and interface boundaries outlast any particular tool.

title: ML CI/CD Pipeline
caption: **ML CI/CD Pipeline**: Read the enclosed stages in execution order; the retraining trigger starts a new run, while connected repositories preserve the dataset, model, metadata, and artifacts needed to reproduce and govern it. Adapted from Google Cloud's MLOps continuous delivery and automation pipeline guidance [@googleCloudMlopsPipelines].
alt: Pipeline diagram labeled Continuous training pipeline. Seven stages connect dataset ingestion, data validation, data transformation, model training/tuning, model evaluation, model validation, and model registration. A dataset and feature repository connects on the left, a model repository on the right, an ML metadata and artifact repository above, and a retraining trigger above the pipeline. Three boxes below are labeled model processing engine, model training engine, and model evaluation engine.
context:
Without this automation, model deployment degrades into a manual, error-prone process in which an engineer retrains locally, copies artifacts to a staging server, and promotes to production with no guarantee that the data, code, or hyperparameters match what was validated. The cost of such ad hoc workflows compounds with team size and deployment frequency, producing configuration drift and silent regressions that surface only after the model has served incorrect predictions.

A continuous training pipeline runs seven sequential stages, from dataset ingestion, data validation, and data transformation through training, evaluation, validation, and registry promotion (@fig-ops-cicd). Driven by dedicated processing, training, and evaluation engines beneath the pipeline, the workflow coordinates with surrounding dataset, model, and metadata repositories whenever an external trigger initiates retraining.

title: Rollback Preserves a Compatible Version Bundle
caption: **Rollback Preserves a Compatible Version Bundle**: New requests switch to the previous model together with its feature schema and embedding namespace. Requests already admitted to the candidate retain their pinned bundle until completion or confirmed cancellation. Pairing old weights with the new namespace is invalid; reverting routing does not repair logs collected during the degraded interval.
alt: A routing box above two bundles, each containing matching weights, schema, and embedding-cache namespace. Solid and dashed arrows distinguish newly admitted and already admitted requests. A central dashed box marks an invalid cross-version pairing, and a separate lower box identifies degraded-window logs.
context:
ML systems vary in statefulness, which directly governs rollback complexity. For stateless workloads like tabular classification and static regression, rollback requires only swapping model weights or routing traffic back to the prior container, because individual inferences share no execution context. In contrast, stateful models (including sequential recommenders, session-based search rankers, and conversational systems) accumulate transient user state. Reverting such workloads can demand session resets, schema shims for cached context vectors, or explicit state migration. Capturing versioned checkpoints at deployment boundaries mitigates this friction, but clean restoration remains an architectural property that requires empirical validation rather than assumption. The ranking service is the stateful case. It precalculates dense user and item embeddings and holds them in low-latency caches, so if version 2 rotates the latent vector space or changes the embedding dimension, the cached vectors become meaningless to a rolled-back version 1. A stateful rollback must therefore orchestrate atomic cache invalidation or dual-version namespace switching alongside weight redeployment to prevent scoring queries against incompatible vector spaces. In systems with feedback loops, the most complex failure mode arises when bad predictions pollute downstream feature logs or clickstream training sets during the degraded window. Reverting the serving binary then leaves contaminated data in the retraining corpus, and that data must be expunged or quarantined before previous behavior is restored.

The compatible unit of rollback is larger than the weights. @Fig-rollback-compatible-bundles separates the bundle selected for a new request from the bundle retained by a request already in flight.

title: Data Drift Impact
caption: **Data Drift Impact**: In this illustrative scenario, incoming samples shift from predominantly online to increasingly offline sales while model accuracy declines over the same interval. Monitoring inputs and outcomes together helps determine whether the distribution shift is associated with the loss in accuracy.
alt: Three horizontally aligned panels over time. The top panel shows incoming samples as green and orange blocks. The middle panel shows the sales_channel feature distribution changing from a green Online store region to an expanding orange Offline store region. The bottom panel shows a green model-accuracy curve declining from left to right.
context:
Operations adds one distinction that the definitions alone do not make. **Model decay**\index{Model decay!definition} is the observed decline in prediction quality over time while the model code stays unchanged, and data drift is only one possible cause of it, alongside concept drift and changes in the surrounding pipeline. Monitoring model outputs alone can miss input drift or mistake a benign output change for quality loss, so operations also tracks the input feature statistics behind the divergence $\StatisticalDivergence$, using the distance measures of feature distribution monitoring (@sec-ml-operations-feature-distribution-monitoring-b8a0). These statistics can warn earlier than labeled performance because ground-truth feedback is often delayed.

The signature of data drift in live telemetry is a feature distribution that moves in step with a quality metric, and three synchronized telemetry tiers aligned over time expose how covariate shift erodes model performance (@fig-data-drift). Across the top panel, discrete request samples transition from predominantly green (online sales) to orange (in-store sales). The figure's "online store" and "offline store" labels name sales channels, not the feature-store tiers of @sec-ml-operations-feature-stores-c01c. The middle panel charts this shift as an expanding offline area in the sales_channel feature distribution, directly matching the steep decline of the model accuracy curve in the bottom panel. This temporal alignment motivates comparing input feature distributions with outcome metrics; their co-movement supplies a diagnostic hypothesis rather than establishing the cause by itself.

title: One Ranking Node's Day
caption: **One Ranking Node's Day**: Accelerator occupancy on an eight-accelerator H100 node over the day of a retraining run, under one schedule that keeps rollback immediate. The serving copy of the `{python} OpsRunningCases.dlrm_gb_str` tables holds `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` accelerators and the hot standby holds `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` more. The retraining run holds `{python} RetrainContention.retrain_accels_str` accelerators for `{python} RetrainContention.retrain_time_str`, so while it runs the standby is the only further copy of the tables that fits. After the run, the candidate it produces can go out as a canary on `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` of the freed accelerators. The schedule is illustrative and built from the chapter's worked numbers.
alt: Eight horizontal accelerator lanes across a 24-hour axis. The top two lanes hold the serving copy of the tables all day and the next two hold a hot standby all day. The bottom four lanes hold a retraining run for the first six hours. After the run, two of those lanes hold a canary copy and the last two are drawn as a dashed outline marked free.
context:
```

The run cost $\RetrainingRunCost$ bundles the four terms of @eq-retrain-cost, and on the ranking service the accelerator term is the smallest of them. In an illustrative scenario, a run that retrains on the logs gathered since the previous run occupies four H100s for six hours. Those twenty-four accelerator-hours cost `{python} RetrainContention.compute_cost_str` at the registry's training rate, about `{python} RetrainContention.compute_share_pct_str` of the `{python} RetrainContention.run_cost_str` run. Validation, deployment, and rollout risk make up the rest, which is why automating the validation path (@sec-ml-operations-model-validation-a891) shortens the economic interval more than faster training would. The accelerator-hours matter instead as contention. The serving copy of the tables already holds two accelerators. On an eight-accelerator node, a run that holds its own copy and training state on four more leaves room for exactly one further copy of the tables while it executes (@fig-ml-ops-dlrm-node-day). That copy can be a canary, a shadow, or the hot standby of @tbl-ml-ops-release-control-footprint, but not more than one of them. A team that releases and retrains on the same node must therefore schedule the two so that a retraining run never evicts the copy that makes rollback immediate.

title: The Rotting Asset Curve
caption: **The Rotting Asset Curve**: An illustrative exponential accuracy decay under two maintenance policies, both drawn as sawtooths. The scheduled policy resets every 90 days regardless of accuracy and dips below the drift threshold before each reset, while the triggered policy resets on crossing that threshold and holds a higher floor in this zero-delay model. Real response delays and update quality must be measured; neither cadence is universal.
alt: Line chart of model accuracy vs. days since deployment. An orange scheduled-retraining sawtooth resets every 90 days, a green trigger-based sawtooth resets when it crosses a red dashed drift-threshold line, and both begin at 0.94 accuracy, the ranking service at launch.
context:
### Scheduled versus triggered retraining {#sec-ml-operations-scheduled-triggered-retraining-b51e}

The interval derived in @eq-optimal-retrain fixes a calendar schedule from average drift, whereas the decision gate of @sec-ml-operations-retraining-decision-framework-e33d lets observed evidence decide when to run. Over a 365-day deployment on the ranking service, the two policies trace different sawtooths against a drift threshold of 0.88 accuracy (@fig-rotting-asset-curve)\index{Rotting asset curve!accuracy decay}. Under a scheduled policy (orange sawtooth), the model retrains at rigid 90-day intervals, repeatedly dipping below the quality floor before each reset. In contrast, a triggered policy (green sawtooth) initiates retraining the moment monitored accuracy touches the threshold, illustrating an idealized instantaneous reset; in practice the trigger is often a divergence or proxy signal calibrated against accuracy. Both curves are drawn from the temporal decay model of @eq-accuracy-decay. In deployment, sample collection, label arrival, training, validation, and rollout delays can carry accuracy below the trigger before recovery; the policy does not guarantee a performance floor.

title: The Business Cost Curve
caption: **The Business Cost Curve**: An equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold. Technical metrics like ROC curves hide the economic reality: errors have different costs. Here, a false negative (missed fraud) costs \$500, while a false positive (blocked user) costs \$100. The system flags a transaction as fraud when its score exceeds the threshold, so a lower threshold flags more transactions. Because missing fraud is $5\times$ more costly, the optimal threshold shifts left of center, making the system more aggressive at flagging suspicious transactions and accepting more false positives to minimize expensive misses. With equal costs the optimum would sit at threshold = 0.50; the asymmetry pulls it toward threshold $\approx 0.34$. A population expected cost would also weight each term by class prevalence. MLOps tunes thresholds as costs and prevalence change.
alt: Line chart showing an equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold from 0 to 1. Three curves are plotted: false positive cost index (dashed blue) decreasing sigmoidally from left to right, false negative cost index (dashed red) increasing sigmoidally from left to right, and total cost index (solid violet) as their sum forming a U-shape. The optimal threshold is marked with a green dot left of center where the total index is minimized.
context:
A frequent communication failure is the unconstrained request to "make the model more accurate." Model accuracy cannot be scaled independently of system costs. Boosting validation accuracy by two percentage points often requires moving to a significantly larger model architecture, incurring higher FLOP counts per sample, increasing memory bandwidth demands, and violating strict inference latency SLOs. Grounding improvement discussions in the Pareto frontier (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}) forces explicit decisions among model accuracy, inference latency budgets, training compute costs, and dataset acquisition expenses.

Translating statistical metrics into operational impact requires mapping errors to their consequences, which are rarely symmetric. Accuracy, ROC-AUC, and F1 treat errors symmetrically. The ranking service's errors differ in cost only mildly, so a separate illustrative case with a sharper asymmetry carries the argument. In an automated fraud detection pipeline, a false positive creates friction at checkout while a false negative allows unrecoverable theft. With missed fraud (\$500 per incident) five times as costly as a blocked legitimate user (\$100), the total cost across classification thresholds reaches its minimum near 0.34, well left of the symmetric 0.50 baseline (@fig-business-cost-curve).

title: Uptime Dependency Stack
caption: **Uptime Dependency Stack**: The waterline separates visible service uptime from data- and model-health failures that can remain hidden while the service stays available; the surrounding labels organize the monitoring surface into data, model, and service health.
alt: Iceberg diagram with uptime visible above waterline. Hidden below: model accuracy, data drift, concept drift, broken pipelines, schema changes, model bias, data outages, underperforming segments. Labels indicate data, model, and service health.
context:
The repeatable ranking service above already automates training and deployment, yet a change to its separately maintained feature SQL still requires manual validation. More frequent retraining would increase the manual validation burden without removing the mismatch risk. A versioned feature contract and matched-request parity tests address the failure boundary first; a shared feature store becomes useful when maintaining that contract across pipelines warrants the additional infrastructure. Maturity assessment therefore selects the next missing control for each system.

@Fig-uptime-iceberg provides a coverage map for that assessment. Service uptime is visible at the tip, while data- and model-health failures can remain hidden below the waterline. For each failure mode, the assessment must identify the evidence that exposes it and the action that contains it.

title: ClinAIOps Feedback Loops
caption: **ClinAIOps Feedback Loops**: The cyclical framework coordinates patients, clinicians, and AI developers to support continuous model improvement and safe clinical integration. Patients and clinicians use AI outputs in care workflows, while AI developers receive feedback from both groups to refine models and operations. Source: [@chen2023].
alt: Circular three-node diagram with Patient at top, Clinician at lower left, and AI developer at lower right. Paired arrows connect every stakeholder pair. Labels identify continuous monitoring data and health reports paired with alerts for clinician-approved therapy updates, therapy regimens paired with health challenges and goals, and therapy-modification alerts and monitoring summaries paired with limits and approvals for therapy regimens.
context:
#### Feedback loops {#sec-ml-operations-feedback-loops-3cdd}

Three interlocking feedback loops organize the proposed integration of machine learning into clinical practice; their effectiveness and safety require validation in the intended setting. @Fig-clinaiops models these three interlocking feedback loops as a triangular protocol among the patient, clinician, and AI developer. Each pair of actors exchanges different information in both directions. The patient streams wearable sensor telemetry and receives clinician-approved therapy alerts. The AI developer provides longitudinal monitoring summaries while accepting physician-defined dosing bounds. The clinician directly governs patient therapy regimens while establishing safety boundaries for algorithmic actuation. The outer cycle connecting all three nodes forms the overarching clinical governance framework.

title: Hypertension Management Loops
caption: **Hypertension Management Loops**: The three panels, labeled patient-AI, clinical-AI, and patient-clinical, each carry a two-way exchange. In this proposed workflow, the AI issues bounded dose recommendations within validated, authorized clinician-set limits and escalates severe readings, which leaves the patient-clinical panel for trend review, adverse-event checks, and treatment decisions. The developer feedback loop of ClinAIOps is not among them and is discussed in the prose. Source: [@chen2023].
alt: Three-panel diagram arranged with Patient-AI and Clinical-AI loops across the top and a Patient-clinical loop below. Each panel shows paired arrows between two icons and text boxes describing blood-pressure monitoring, dose recommendations, clinician limits, risk alerts, trend review, adverse-event checks, and lifestyle factors.
context:
##### Loop implementation {#sec-ml-operations-loop-implementation-2556}

The hypertension workflow labels each of its three panels by the two parties in the exchange (@fig-interactive-loop), so the panels do not line up one-to-one with the three loops of @fig-clinaiops. The patient-AI panel is the patient treatment loop, the clinical-AI panel is the clinician oversight loop, and the patient-clinical panel is the coordination those two loops produce together. The developer feedback loop operates out of band, as described in @sec-ml-operations-feedback-loops-3cdd, and does not appear. Across the top of the figure, the two AI-assisted loops operate concurrently. The patient-AI panel (upper left) captures continuous blood-pressure telemetry and issues recommendations for bounded dose titrations, while the clinical-AI panel (upper right) alerts the physician to severe hypertensive excursions and accepts updated titration boundaries. Below them, the patient-clinical panel captures the resulting clinical relationship, where routine telemetry offloaded to the AI loop frees consultation appointments for longitudinal trend review, adverse-event evaluation, and shared lifestyle goal setting.

title: The Responsible Engineering Lifecycle
caption: **The Responsible Engineering Lifecycle**: Four chained stages carry the credit service from requirement to production. Specify fixes the target, the named populations, and the oversight boundary; Measure turns them into release gates; Explain and document makes decisions and models legible; Operate watches the deployed model and feeds what it observes back into the next specification. Resource and Govern span every stage: each stage consumes accelerator-hours, energy, and money, and each must leave evidence that someone outside the team can audit. The machine cost under each stage names what the remedy consumes.
alt: Four boxes left to right labeled Specify, Measure, Explain and document, and Operate, joined by arrows, with a return arrow from Operate back to Specify labeled feedback and retraining. Under each box a short gray line names its machine cost: labeled evaluation data per named group and reviewer hours, per-slice evaluation and mitigation training, explanation compute on the serving path, and per-group telemetry and exploration traffic. Two long bars beneath all four boxes are labeled Resource: energy, carbon, and cost of every stage, and Govern: access control, privacy, lineage, and audit evidence for every stage.
context:
the care-management algorithm were both found to fail after the design options that could have addressed them were closed, so the lesson concerns timing more than vigilance. Each responsibility failure in this chapter has a point in the ML lifecycle before which it is cheap to prevent and after which it becomes expensive or impossible to repair, so responsible engineering\index{Responsible engineering!lifecycle methodology} is organized around that lifecycle rather than around a list of concerns.

Six stages follow from that premise, and the first four form a chain in which each stage depends on the output of the one before it. *Specify* comes first because a system cannot be tested against a requirement nobody wrote down. The target, the populations that matter, the evaluation data those populations demand, and the boundary of human oversight must all be fixed before training forecloses the alternatives. *Measure* turns those written requirements into release gates, evaluating each named population separately and quantifying the trade-offs among fairness criteria. Evidence that lives only in an engineer's notebook cannot be contested, audited, or reused, so *Explain and document* makes individual decisions legible to the people they affect and whole models legible to the teams that inherit them. The documented operating envelope then tells *Operate* what to watch after launch, when feedback loops and distribution shift erode a model that passed every gate. The last two stages span the whole lifecycle rather than following it, so each receives its own section, while the four chained stages structure the subsections of this one, each worked on the credit service. *Resource* accounts for the energy, carbon, and money that every stage consumes (@sec-responsible-engineering-environmental-cost-awareness-0f3e). *Govern* supplies the regulatory obligations and the data infrastructure of access control, privacy, lineage, and audit that make each earlier stage provable to someone outside the team that built it (@sec-responsible-engineering-data-governance-compliance-bd1a). The four chained stages and the two that span them form one loop (@fig-responsible-lifecycle).

title: Threshold Effects on Subgroup Outcomes
caption: **Threshold Effects on Subgroup Outcomes**: Two candidate classification thresholds intersect different score distributions for Subgroups A and B. Circles mark positive outcomes (loan repayment), plus markers mark negative outcomes (default), and color distinguishes subgroup; each boundary approves the markers to its left. Each dashed line carries the overall accuracy that boundary achieves, not a score cutoff. Moving to the higher-accuracy boundary lifts overall accuracy from 75 percent to 81.25 percent, but the whole gain falls in Subgroup A, which becomes perfectly separated, while Subgroup B goes from one misclassification to three.
alt: Two horizontal rows labeled Subgroup A and Subgroup B contain colored circle and plus markers at different positions. Dashed vertical lines labeled 75 percent and 81.25 percent cross both rows. Circles denote positive outcomes, plus signs denote negative outcomes, and color identifies subgroup.
section: Compare groups and flag disparities exceeding threshold
context:
: **Fairness Metrics Summary**: In the constructed credit-service scenario, approval rate and true positive rate differ across groups, while false positive rates match; the table establishes disparity but not its cause. {#tbl-fairness-metrics-summary tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}

Shared classification thresholds applied to differing score distributions illustrate how aggregate performance masks severe subgroup divergence [@barocas2016]. Shifting between the two candidate decision boundaries (@fig-fairness-threshold) lifts overall accuracy from 75 percent to 81.25 percent by achieving perfect separation in Subgroup A, yet simultaneously triples the misclassifications in Subgroup B. Because the two subgroups' scores are distributed differently, one shared boundary cannot sit at the best point for both. The move that raises the global metric does so by trading away Subgroup B's outcomes. Aggregate accuracy alone cannot determine whether those outcomes are equitable for either cohort.

title: An Illustrative Fairness-Accuracy Pareto Frontier
caption: **An Illustrative Fairness-Accuracy Pareto Frontier**: A hypothetical relationship between model accuracy and demographic disparity. The x-axis is inverted so lower disparity lies to the right. Points A, B, and C illustrate three possible operating choices along this constructed frontier; B's label of 3.6 times fairer means its disparity (0.05) is 3.6 times smaller than A's (0.18). The curve is not an empirical or universal law.
alt: Hypothetical curve relating accuracy and disparity, with three labeled operating points A, B, and C. The x-axis is inverted so lower disparity lies to the right.
context:
#### Quantifying the fairness-accuracy trade-off {#sec-responsible-engineering-quantifying-fairnessaccuracy-tradeoff-ce4a}

The worked example showed that fairness criteria can conflict. A separate question is how a chosen engineering constraint changes predictive utility. The Pareto frontier (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}) collects the configurations for which one plotted objective cannot improve without degrading another. @Fig-fairness-frontier plots a hypothetical fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier\index{Pareto frontier!fairness-accuracy trade-off}\index{Fairness!accuracy trade-off} against demographic disparity. Disparity is measured as the difference between two groups' positive-prediction (approval) rates, the demographic parity gap defined in @sec-responsible-engineering-worked-example-fairness-analysis-loan-approval-2c72. The disparity axis is inverted so that fairer configurations lie to the right. The figure contrasts an unconstrained maximum-accuracy operating point (A) against a balanced compromise (B) and a steep accuracy collapse under strict demographic equality (C). These annotated configurations illustrate candidate policy choices along the frontier; they do not imply that unconstrained training always maximizes accuracy at high disparity, that zero disparity must reduce accuracy, or that every application has a sweet spot.

title: Model Interpretability Spectrum
caption: **Model Interpretability Spectrum**: A horizontal continuum groups decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression as intrinsically interpretable, while random forests, neural networks, and CNNs/transformers require post-hoc explanation. The grouping is schematic: interpretability depends on model size and feature semantics, and any attribution method requires fidelity validation. It frames an auditability trade-off rather than a universal ranking of model quality.
alt: Horizontal green-to-red spectrum labeled More Interpretable on the left and Less Interpretable on the right. Six positions are labeled Decision Trees, Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Neural Network, and CNN/Transformer. Braces group the first three as intrinsically interpretable and the last three as requiring post-hoc explanation; notes below say to inspect decision logic directly on the left and evaluate LIME or SHAP fidelity on the right.
context:
```

Whatever the requirement, the candidate models lie along a gradient continuum from intrinsic interpretability to post-hoc explanation (@fig-interpretability-spectrum). On the left, small trees and sparse linear or logistic models with meaningful features can expose decision logic to human inspection. Large trees or opaque engineered features can defeat that advantage. On the right, high-capacity representations, such as random forests, deep neural networks, and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or transformers, often need supplementary explanation methods. LIME and SHAP require fidelity checks; attention maps alone do not establish faithful explanations. The spectrum organizes candidate approaches, not a categorical guarantee for any model family.

title: Decisions Select the Labels Available for Retraining
caption: **Decisions Select the Labels Available for Retraining**: Routine repayment labels come from approved loans, so the current policy selects the evidence used by its successor. A denied loan supplies no repayment outcome. The separate intervention samples eligible marginal applicants, issues loans, and follows their actual repayment; recording the selection policy preserves the basis for later analysis. Sampling supplies evidence but does not guarantee fairness.
alt: Applicants pass through an approval policy to repayment labels and retraining, with a return arrow to the policy. A denial branch ends at a box marked repayment unobserved, not a negative label. A separate dashed path samples applicants, approves loans, and follows repayment before adding observed labels to retraining.
context:
