alt: Two stacked grids of four slots by eight iterations. Top: static batching, where requests R1 to R4 end at iterations 3, 8, 5, and 4, and every later cell in the finished slots is hatched as idle; a note reads 20 of 32 slots busy. Bottom: continuous batching, where requests R5, R6, and R7 enter the freed slots with a dark prefill cell and continue decoding, leaving no idle cells; a note reads 32 of 32 slots busy. Final-token cells are green.
section: Continuous batching for large language model (LLM) inference {#sec-inference-scale-continuous-batching-llm-inference-f8e6}
context:
```

Admitting, completing, and refilling slots on every iteration lets waiting work use capacity released before the longest sequence finishes. The illustrated preemption path adds HBM-to-CPU-DRAM transfers under memory pressure, so recovered capacity must repay both scheduling and state-movement costs. Counted in slot-iterations (@fig-continuous-batching-comparison), fixed membership leaves only 20 of 32 productive, while continuous admission fills all 32 under the illustrated arrival and capacity assumptions. Prefill and decode cells do not necessarily take equal time. Slot occupancy therefore measures the opportunity; the realized throughput gain depends on how much longer the inserted prefill cells take than the decode steps they share an iteration with.

title: Feature-Parallel Batching Pipeline
caption: **Feature-Parallel Batching Pipeline**: Requests are batched by feature type (Users, Items, Context) and dispatched to specialized embedding servers in parallel. The retrieved embeddings are then concatenated and processed by the dense ranking head. This architecture enables scaling to trillions of parameters by decoupling embedding storage from dense compute.
alt: Left to right: a request enters a feature split box, by type, which fans out to three embedding tables labeled user, item, and context embeddings. Each table is drawn as rows split across two side-by-side shards, shard 0 and shard 1, with the one looked-up row filled solid: the user row in shard 0, the item row in shard 1, and the context row in shard 0. Amber lines labeled gather, concatenate carry the three rows into one stacked vector of segments U, I, and C. The vector feeds a ranking head, dense MLP, drawn as three narrowing layers, which produces a ranked output drawn as four green bars of decreasing length.
context:
A single recommendation request may issue thousands of sparse lookups across embedding tables holding billions of entries before the dense ranking head can score a candidate. Grouping requests solely at the dense MLP therefore leaves the service bottlenecked on scattered memory reads and cross-server transfers. While fixed-shape vision inputs allow simple request grouping and autoregressive generation pairs iteration-level admission with KV-cache management (and with prefill-decode scheduling in @sec-inference-scale-prefill-decode), recommendation systems must also batch around the placement of sparse state. *Sparse embedding lookups* can dominate memory access and communication in an embedding-heavy workload even when *dense matrix multiplications* account for much of the arithmetic. Grouping those accesses by feature type and destination—feature-parallel batching\index{Feature-parallel batching}—improves lookup locality at each shard, complementing request batching in the dense stages.

Recommendation batching starts by grouping work around embedding locality rather than request shape. An incoming request splits across user, item, and context feature types to query sharded embedding tables concurrently, after which a gather barrier concatenates the retrieved representations for the dense MLP ranking head (@fig-feature-parallel-pipeline).

title: The KV Cache Wall
caption: **The KV Cache Wall**: Total GPU memory usage for a 4-bit quantized 70B model (`{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` weights) on an `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str` H100. While the model fits easily at small context lengths, the KV cache (sloped lines) eventually consumes all remaining HBM. At 128K context, a batch size of 2 is physically impossible on a single GPU (`{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` + `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.batch_example_kv_gb_str` exceeds `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str`), forcing the system to either reduce batch size, change the state representation, or distribute the state across devices.
alt: Memory usage plot against sequence length. A red dashed line at 80 GB marks HBM capacity, with the region above it shaded red. A light blue band at the bottom is the 35 GB of model weights. Sloped lines for batch 1, 2, 4, and 8 rise from the weights line; batches 8, 4, and 2 stop at open circles where they meet the capacity line, batch 8 earliest at about 17K tokens, while batch 1 stays below the line out to 128K tokens.
context:
```

Even when a 4-bit quantized 70B model occupies only `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` of an `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str` H100, admitting a second 128K-token request pushes the combined weight and KV-cache footprint past `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str` and exhausts HBM before execution resources saturate. Increasing batch size in LLM serving therefore hits the KV cache wall\index{KV cache!capacity wall} long before compute binds. @Fig-kv-cache-wall leaves the reference replica to show the wall on a single H100. It combines an idealized `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` weight payload for a quantized 70B model with its full-attention, eight-KV-head GQA state. The budget is a conservative decimal capacity that matches the nameplate label, unlike the registered byte capacity of the node estimator below. A batch of `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.batch_largest_str` reaches the memory boundary at roughly `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.batch_largest_wall_k_str`K tokens per sequence; quantization metadata, runtime buffers, and other allocations make the plotted boundary an optimistic sizing limit.

title: KV Cache Fragmentation and the PagedAttention Solution
caption: **KV Cache Fragmentation and the PagedAttention Solution**: The panels replay the eight-slot example from the text. (a) Contiguous reservation holds the maximum length of four slots per sequence, so the slots Seq A and Seq B never fill sit idle (internal fragmentation). (b) After sequences finish, four slots are free but the largest contiguous gap is two, so Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, cannot be admitted (external fragmentation). (c) PagedAttention maps Seq E's logical pages through a block table onto any free physical blocks, so the same memory now holds it; only the unfilled tail of its final block remains unused.
alt: Three panels built from eight memory slots. Panel a: Seq A uses two of its four reserved slots and Seq B uses three of four; the unused reserved slots are hatched. Panel b: slots 2 and 3 hold Seq C and slots 6 and 7 hold Seq D, leaving two 2-slot gaps; four dashed red cells for Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, do not fit. Panel c: Seq E's logical pages 0 to 3 pass through a block table mapping them to physical slots 0, 1, 4 and 5 among the C and D slots; page 3's slot is only partly filled. A legend identifies in-use entries, reserved but unused slots, free slots and other sequences.
context:
:::

PagedAttention [@kwon2023], introduced in vLLM\index{vLLM!PagedAttention integration}\index{vLLM!paged KV cache}, applies virtual memory concepts to KV cache management\index{Paged memory management}\index{KV cache!paged memory allocation}. Instead of contiguous allocation, the KV cache is divided into fixed-size pages, using 16-token blocks in the original paper's default configuration, and sequences are allocated pages on demand. Whereas contiguous reservation strands non-adjacent free slots when earlier sequences finish, PagedAttention uses a per-sequence block table to map logical token pages to scattered physical HBM slots on demand (@fig-paged-attention). The block size\index{PagedAttention!block size trade-off} fixes how many tokens each page holds, so a sequence's pages need not form one contiguous allocation run.

title: Prefix Caching via Block Sharing
caption: **Prefix Caching via Block Sharing**: PagedAttention enables efficient prefix caching by allowing multiple sequences' block tables to point to the same physical blocks for shared content. In this example, the system prompt is stored in blocks 0--5. Request A and Request B map their first six logical pages to these same physical blocks, storing only their unique suffixes in new blocks. Sharing reduces KV memory and repeated prefill computation for workloads with a common context.
alt: Three rows. Request A logical pages at top and Request B logical pages at bottom each begin with green shared-prefix pages P0, P1, P2, and P5, separated by an ellipsis, and green arrows from both rows point to the same green physical blocks B0 to B5 in the GPU HBM panel in the middle. Request A's gray suffix pages P6 and P7 point to private blocks B10 and B11, and Request B's gray suffix pages P6 to P8 point to private blocks B12 to B14.
context:
### Prefix caching {#sec-inference-scale-prefix-caching-8e8b}

Recomputing the same 2,000-token system prompt, few-shot example block, or shared document on every arriving request burns prefill compute and fills HBM with identical copies of the same key-value tensors. Because many LLM workloads prepend those shared prefixes\index{Prefix caching!prompt sharing} across thousands of concurrent queries, prefix caching stores the prefix's KV-cache blocks once and shares them across compatible requests. Reuse requires the same token prefix and the same model computation, including any task-specific weight adapter and other inputs that affect the cached state. The cache key must distinguish those conditions, and the service must restrict sharing to the permitted users or tenants; matching visible text alone is insufficient. In valid block-level sharing (@fig-prefix-caching), logical tables for independent requests map common prefix tokens to physical blocks B0–B5, skipping their repeated prefill work while storing request-specific suffix state separately.

title: Speculative Decoding Process
caption: **Speculative Decoding Process**: Instead of generating tokens sequentially with the large target model, a small draft model proposes a sequence of $\SpeculativeDraftLength$ tokens. The target model verifies all $\SpeculativeDraftLength$ tokens in a single parallel forward pass. Drafted tokens that pass the acceptance test are emitted together; the first rejected token triggers a corrected sample and discards the remaining draft.
alt: Two timelines above a shared time axis. Top lane, standard decoding: four equal-width target passes in sequence, each emitting one green token, T1 to T4, at its end. Bottom lane, speculative decoding: four narrow gray draft steps labeled T1 to T4 followed by one target pass that verifies T1 to T4. Beneath the verify pass, green tokens T1 to T3 are marked accepted, draft T4 is crossed out in red and marked rejected, and a resampled token T4 prime sits below it. Dashed guides and ticks on the time axis, labeled speculative and standard, mark where each lane has four tokens, and a green double arrow between them marks the time saved for the same four tokens.
context:
When a lightly loaded replica serves one or a few interactive streams, batching has no other requests to share each weight read with, so every generated token pays the full latency of streaming the target model's weights from HBM. While KV compression and GQA shrink the state each decode step reads, speculative decoding raises the useful work each step performs within a single request. A small draft model\index{Speculative decoding!draft model} proposes $\SpeculativeDraftLength$ tokens, and the target model verifies\index{Speculative decoding!verification step} all of them in one parallel forward pass [@leviathan2023speculative; @chen2023accelerating]. That pass streams the target's weights once, as a single decode step does, so it processes $\SpeculativeDraftLength$ candidate positions for roughly the weight traffic of one token. This is the reuse that batching buys, drawn from one request's future tokens instead of from other requests, and it moves the decode operating point up the bandwidth slope toward the ridge\index{Speculative decoding!bandwidth optimization}.

On a shared time axis (@fig-speculative-decoding), standard decoding uses four target passes to emit four tokens. In the speculative round, the draft model proposes $\DraftedToken_1$ through $\DraftedToken_4$ sequentially and the target evaluates those positions in one pass; three drafts are accepted, and the first rejected token, $\DraftedToken_4$, is replaced by $\ResampledReplacementToken$ sampled from the target. The shorter timeline holds only when drafting, verification, and correction together cost less than the target passes they replace. If too many drafts are rejected, the target streams its weights and keeps little of the work; if the draft model is too expensive, its own sequential passes consume the time that one-pass verification saved.

title: Chunked Prefill Trades One Prompt's TTFT for Every Stream's TBT
caption: **Chunked Prefill Trades One Prompt's TTFT for Every Stream's TBT**: Three streams decode while a long prompt P arrives; the timing is illustrative. (a) A monolithic prefill runs P's whole prompt in one pass, and every active stream stalls for its full duration. (b) Chunked prefill gives P one chunk per hybrid iteration beside the streams' decode tokens, so each stream's gap shrinks to one hybrid iteration, and P's first token arrives later. Chunking changes when the prefill work runs, not how much of it there is.
alt: Two timelines on a shared time axis, each with rows for streams A, B, and C and a row for prompt P. Panel a, monolithic prefill: streams A to C decode two steps, then all three rows are hatched red as stalled while P's row shows one long dark block labeled prefill, whole prompt; afterward the streams resume and P decodes in green cells. A red double arrow under the panel marks that the stream gap spans the whole prefill. Panel b, chunked prefill: after two decode steps, P's row shows four dark blocks labeled chunk 1 to chunk 4, each beside wider decode cells for A, B, and C, and P begins decoding only after chunk 4. A gray double arrow marks one hybrid step as the stream gap, and a second gray double arrow marks that P's first token arrives later than in panel a. A key identifies decode steps, prefill work, P decoding, and stalled streams.
context:
To limit this interference, chunked prefill (definition \ref{dfn-inference-chunked-prefill}, used by Sarathi-Serve\index{Sarathi-Serve!chunked prefill} [@agrawal2024sarathi]) partitions prompts into chunks of at most $\PrefillChunkSize$ tokens. A candidate range such as $256\text{--}512$ tokens must be tested against the model, hardware, and streaming deadline rather than treated as a universal setting. A prompt of length $\PromptLength$ requires at least $\lceil \PromptLength/ \PrefillChunkSize\rceil$ scheduling iterations; a smaller residual token budget can require more.

The two schedules in @fig-chunked-prefill hand the same long prompt to the same worker. Run whole, its prefill sits between two decode steps of every active stream, so each stream's token gap stretches to the full prefill time. Split into chunks, the prompt advances one chunk per hybrid iteration beside the streams' decode tokens, so each stream waits at most one hybrid iteration, while the prompt's own first token arrives later than it would have under the monolithic schedule.

title: Disaggregated Serving Architecture
caption: **Disaggregated Serving Architecture**: A long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime separates compute-bound prefill instances from memory-bandwidth-bound decode instances, mediated by RDMA KV-cache transfer. Because prefill sets time to first token and decode sets time per output token, each pool is sized for its own token rate. Other batch and context sizes can change the binding resources.
alt: Left to right: a prompt enters a prefill pool labeled compute-bound, sets TTFT, and sized for prompt tokens per second. Each of its three workers, Prefill 0 to 2, shows its work as two wide solid blocks, each a whole-prompt pass. An amber arrow carrying four small KV-cache page tiles, labeled KV cache transfer (RDMA), crosses to a decode pool labeled bandwidth-bound, sets TPOT, and sized for output tokens per second. Each of its three workers, Decode 0 to 2, shows its work as a row of eight narrow cells, each a one-token decode step. The decode pool emits a token stream. A key below names the wide block a whole-prompt pass and the narrow cell a one-token decode step.
context:
Even with chunked prefill, every hybrid step still forces active decode streams to wait while prompt chunks execute on the same GPU, and a single worker pool must compromise between prefill's compute-heavy parallelism and decode's bandwidth- and capacity-heavy layout. Disaggregation removes that compromise by giving each phase its own hardware pool, while the KV-cache sizing of @sec-inference-scale-kv-cache-wall sets the price of separating them. The cache that prefill builds is the exact payload that the network must hand off to the decode pool.

Disaggregation partitions the serving pipeline into specialized physical tiers (@fig-disaggregated-serving). In the illustrated long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime, the compute-bound prefill pool and the bandwidth-bound decode pool are joined by a remote direct memory access (RDMA) KV-cache transfer [@zhong2024distserve]. This keeps the phases from competing on one accelerator and permits independent parallelism and capacity plans. The phase asymmetry tells each pool what to buy. The prefill pool wants arithmetic throughput for its compute-bound GEMMs, while the decode pool wants memory bandwidth and capacity for weight streaming and KV cache, which also makes it the natural home for aggressive weight quantization. The transfer and queueing at each pool still add to request latency, and other batch or context sizes can change which resources bind.

title: Block-Wise versus Per-Tensor Quantization
caption: **Block-Wise versus Per-Tensor Quantization**: Under per-tensor scaling (left), one outlier weight sets the scale for the whole tensor, so six of the seven small weights round to zero and the seventh rounds to one. Under block-wise quantization (right), each group of weights gets its own scale: the block without the outlier keeps full INT8 resolution, while the small weights that share the outlier's block are still crushed. Smaller blocks confine the damage further at the cost of more scale metadata.
alt: Two side-by-side panels quantize the same eight FP16 weights, one of which is an outlier of 58.7. Left, per-tensor: a single scale of about 0.462 maps six weights to 0, one to 1, and the outlier to 127, with the collapsed cells shaded red. Right, block-wise with blocks of four outlined by dashed boxes: the first block's scale of about 0.00165 maps its weights to 73, -48, 127, and -91, shaded green, while the second block, containing the outlier, maps to 127, 0, 1, and 0.
context:
:::

The metadata price stays small across formats\index{Block-wise quantization!storage overhead}. An INT8 scheme with one FP32 scale per 128 weights adds $32/128 = 0.25$ bits per weight, about 3 percent of its payload. Block-wise scaling therefore isolates outliers without the bandwidth penalty of a higher-precision format, which keeps the decode traffic saving of a low-bit format intact. @Fig-block-quantization isolates this dynamic-range protection across an eight-weight sample containing a single outlier ($58.7$). Under per-tensor scaling (left), the outlier dictates a coarse scale factor ($\QuantizationScale\approx 0.462$) that forces six of the seven small weights to round to zero. Partitioning the tensor into four-element blocks (right) confines that coarse scale to the second block, allowing the uncorrupted first block to adopt a fine scale ($\QuantizationScale_1 \approx 0.00165$) that preserves full INT8 resolution.

title: Tensor Parallelism for Inference
caption: **Tensor Parallelism for Inference**: Computation is distributed across devices by splitting tensor operations. Attention heads are partitioned across GPUs, requiring an AllReduce operation to synchronize results. Feed-forward networks use a column-row splitting strategy that requires only one AllReduce synchronization per block. This partition can reduce latency when saved compute exceeds communication cost, which is why the two collectives run over a fast local interconnect.
alt: Two columns labeled GPU 0 and GPU 1, separated by a dashed divider. In the attention stage, each GPU shows eight head tiles: GPU 0 holds the first four as solid tiles and draws the other four dashed, and GPU 1 holds the second four. From the bottom of each GPU's solid head tiles, labeled first or second half of heads, an amber arrow carries a partial output down into an AllReduce over NVLink bar. In the feed-forward stage, each GPU draws the matrix W1 split down the middle into columns, with its own column slice solid and the other dashed, labeled column slice of W1 plus activation. The matrix W2 is split across the middle into rows, with GPU 0 holding the top rows and GPU 1 the bottom rows, labeled row slice of W2 partial sum; on each GPU a blue arrow marked no communication runs from its column slice of W1 to the row slice of W2 it holds, GPU 1's arrow routing around the dashed top rows to enter its bottom rows from the side. Both partial sums feed a second AllReduce bar that leads to the next layer. A key reads held on this GPU for solid tiles and held on the other GPU for dashed tiles.
context:
Cross-device reuse requires compatible cache content and placement. Matching tensor-parallel configurations can align the head partitions, but the receiver must also use the same model state, prefix inputs, cache representation, and logical token positions. A different partition requires redistribution rather than direct shard reuse. Equal parallelism degree alone does not establish cache validity.

Each device applies its shard of the attention output projection to its local heads, and an AllReduce\index{AllReduce!tensor parallelism synchronization} sums the projected partial outputs; its latency includes collective startup and coordination as well as payload transfer. @Fig-tensor-parallel-flow traces the resulting two synchronization points per layer across two GPU ranks.

title: Pipeline Parallelism Bubbles
caption: **Pipeline Parallelism Bubbles**: (a) An 80-layer model split into four stages passes one request's activations from stage to stage, so splitting the layers alone does not shorten its sequential computation; it must still traverse all four stages. (b) With many requests in flight, later stages idle during the fill bubble, and from slot t4 onward every stage is busy and one request leaves the pipeline per slot. Pipeline parallelism therefore suits throughput-oriented serving better than latency-critical interactive serving.
alt: Two panels. Top: a request box, four stage boxes labeled GPU 0 to GPU 3 with layer ranges 1 to 20, 21 to 40, 41 to 60, and 61 to 80, and an output box, joined by activation arrows. Bottom: a grid of four GPU rows and seven time slots in which requests R1 to R7 enter GPU 0 one slot apart and shift one GPU down per slot. Hatched fill-bubble cells precede the first request on GPUs 1 to 3, and a dashed line at slot t4 marks the pipeline as full.
context:
Splitting an 80-layer model sequentially across four GPU stages leaves three accelerators idle during an isolated request and does nothing to shorten its forward pass. Pipeline parallelism distributes layers across devices so each stage runs a contiguous subset of layers and passes activations to the next stage without intra-layer synchronization.

For inference, pipeline parallelism creates bubbles\index{Pipeline parallelism!bubble overhead} differently than in training. Executing an isolated request serially across four GPU stages leaves three accelerators idle at every step, whereas maintaining multiple in-flight requests fills the pipeline and amortizes the initial bubble across steady-state token delivery (@fig-pipeline-bubbles).

title: Horizontal Scaling with Shard Groups
caption: **Horizontal Scaling with Shard Groups**: The load balancer treats each shard group as a single logical inference server and chooses among groups by round-robin, two-choice, or session-affinity routing. Within a group, eight GPUs hold the tensor-parallel weight shards and join partial results with an NVLink AllReduce inside every layer, which the router never sees. Adding ready groups raises aggregate capacity; the group's internal parallelism affects per-request latency.
alt: Requests 1, 2, through N feed a violet Load balancer box listing round-robin, two-choice, or session affinity. One arrow per group fans out to Shard group 0, drawn in full detail, and to lighter dashed outlines for Shard groups 1 through N. Shard group 0, labeled one replica, TP = 8, one node, shows eight numbered GPU tiles, each attached by a short link to an amber ring labeled NVLink AllReduce every layer; the other groups repeat the same ring in miniature. Beneath group 0 a note reads TP inside the group sets latency, and an arrow beneath the other groups reads add groups: more aggregate throughput.
context:
### Request routing for sharded models {#sec-inference-scale-request-routing-sharded-models-6432}

Treating individual GPUs inside a sharded model as independent routing targets breaks execution: a tensor-parallel group must run every layer in lockstep across all its ranks, and a pipeline group can admit new requests only at its first stage. A sharded replica is therefore one routing destination even though several devices execute the request. A tensor-parallel group presents one destination whose latency already includes its per-layer collectives (@fig-tensor-parallel-flow). A pipeline group admits requests at its first stage (@fig-pipeline-bubbles), so the router must account for the group's service capacity rather than treat each stage as a replica. In expert-parallel architectures, the gating network (@sec-inference-scale-moe-parallelism) routes tokens across internal expert destinations after the external router has chosen the replica, so expert imbalance and replica imbalance require different controls. The result is a two-tier topology (@fig-shard-group-scaling) in which the external load balancer sees each shard group as one destination and the group's NVLink collectives stay inside it.

title: Circuit Breaker States
caption: **Circuit Breaker States**: The circuit breaker protects the system from cascading failure. Closed: normal operation. Open: error threshold exceeded; all requests fail fast to prevent resource exhaustion. Half-open: after a timeout, a limited number of requests are allowed through to probe the dependency's health. Success resets to closed; failure returns to open.
alt: State diagram with three rectangular state blocks, each dominated by a switch drawn as a thick hinged blade between two ring terminals, on a wire from the caller to a dependency box. The green closed state, normal traffic, shows the blade closed across both terminals, with two requests arriving and a third crossing the blade toward the dependency. It transitions to the red open state, requests fail fast, when an error, timeout, or latency threshold is exceeded; the open state shows the blade raised, an x mark in the gap, and a single arriving request turned straight back by a red arrow toward the caller, with nothing queued and nothing reaching the dependency. After a timeout, open transitions to the gray half-open state, limited probes, whose blade is closed but whose wire carries a probe limit bar: two requests wait behind the bar while a single probe crosses the switch toward the dependency. Half-open returns to closed when the probe succeeds or to open when the probe fails. A key identifies the dot as a request, the bar as the probe limit, and the small box as the dependency.
context:
When a GPU inference server slows down, routing more requests to it can turn a local problem into a fleet-wide failure. Consider an illustrative rise in service time from 50 ms to 500 ms. Queues accumulate, client timeouts generate retries, and rerouted work consumes neighboring replicas' headroom. The cause might be a stalled dependency, device degradation, or resource contention. The load balancer needs a policy for withdrawing an unhealthy replica while controlling the displaced load.

The circuit breaker pattern\index{Circuit breaker!circuit breaker pattern} [@nygard2007releaseit] limits repeated work sent to an unhealthy destination. In the closed state, the server receives normal traffic. When the configured error, timeout, or latency threshold is exceeded, the breaker opens and requests fail fast or become candidates for rerouting. After a recovery interval, a half-open state admits limited probes, closing on recovery or reopening on failure (@fig-circuit-breaker). Opening a breaker does not create replacement capacity, so rerouting must respect admission limits and retry budgets or it can overload the surviving replicas.

title: Bulkhead Isolation Patterns
caption: **Bulkhead Isolation Patterns**: To prevent cascading failures in multi-tenant systems, bulkheads isolate resources. Deployment-level bulkheads (shown) assign dedicated physical replicas to high-priority tenants, separating their compute and memory pools. Request-level bulkheads enforce strict concurrency limits within shared processes. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane dependencies remain possible paths for interference.
alt: Two side-by-side compartments, standard tier on the left and gold tier on the right, separated by a thick dark wall labeled bulkhead and both standing on a shared floor band divided into network, storage, and control plane segments. Each tier's traffic enters from above through its own load balancer. Every replica is drawn as a node of four GPU tiles above a memory pool bar. The standard tier has three replicas; the one against the bulkhead is red, crossed out, receives only a dashed line, and is labeled engine crash, and a pale red dashed region marking its blast radius ends flush at the bulkhead wall. The gold tier's two replicas are unaffected and labeled keeps serving. A red dashed line labeled interference path runs from the crashed replica down into the shared floor, passes under the bulkhead, and rises into a gold replica. A key identifies the GPU tile, the memory pool bar, and the blast radius shading.
context:
[^fn-bulkhead-service-isolation]: [offset=-30mm] **Bulkhead limits**\index{Bulkhead pattern!isolation}: A divider isolates failure only if it closes the relevant boundary. The Titanic's incomplete bulkheads allowed water to cascade between compartments; similarly, a soft quota cannot isolate shared memory or bandwidth that remains globally exhaustible.

Dedicated replicas separate more resources than request limits inside one process. @Fig-bulkhead-patterns assigns distinct compute and memory pools to tenant groups, so an engine crash or exhausted local allocation in the standard tier need not stop the gold-tier engines. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane services can still carry interference across that boundary.

title: Predictive vs. Reactive Scaling
caption: **Predictive vs. Reactive Scaling**: Reactive scaling (gray line) responds to traffic spikes after they occur, leaving a capacity deficit (red region) during cold start in this scenario. Predictive scaling (green line) anticipates traffic and begins provisioning before the spike peaks, shrinking that deficit to a brief, small shortfall at onset in the illustrated forecast. Its early ramp does not eliminate every interval when demand exceeds capacity.
alt: Two time-series panels stacked on a shared time axis and a shared vertical axis of normalized demand or capacity, each showing the same dashed demand curve that rises to a spike and falls back. Panel (a), reactive scaling: a gray capacity line stays flat until near the peak, where a dotted marker labeled scale-up begins sits, then ramps up after demand has already risen; the large region where demand exceeds this capacity is shaded red and labeled capacity deficit. Panel (b), predictive scaling: a green capacity line is marked scale-up begins early in the rise and climbs ahead of demand toward the peak; only a thin red sliver at the onset, labeled brief, small shortfall, shows demand briefly above capacity before the ramp overtakes it.
context:
:::

Example \ref{exmp-inference-predictive-scaling-traffic} shows how capacity can be prepared before demand arrives. @Fig-predictive-reactive-scaling depicts a forecast that anticipates the surge, while the reactive curve starts later and temporarily lacks capacity. Whether that deficit produces queueing, rejection, or missed deadlines depends on admission and existing headroom. The predictive curve illustrates a successful forecast, not a guarantee that future demand or startup time will match it.

title: Spot-Aware Traffic Distribution
caption: **Spot-Aware Traffic Distribution**: The gateway classifies requests by SLO and routes 70 percent of traffic, the SLO-critical share, to on-demand replicas that face no spot reclamation, and 30 percent, the best-effort share, to discounted spot replicas that can be preempted. When a spot worker receives an eviction notice, the gateway stops routing to it while it drains, and best-effort requests tolerate occasional retries. The traffic split is illustrative; cost savings depend on provisioned capacity, discounts, retries, and idle headroom.
alt: A Requests box, tagged with an SLO class, feeds a violet Spot-aware gateway box that classifies SLO, watches preemption, and drains. Below it, traffic leaves the gateway as pale gray lanes, each from its own exit point along the gateway's lower edge and ending in an arrowhead at a worker, with combined width proportional to each share. Three wider lanes labeled SLO-critical (70%) fan out to the three on-demand workers, 0 to 2, of an On-demand pool with no spot reclamation. Two thinner lanes labeled best-effort (30%) reach spot workers 3 and 4 of a dashed Spot pool, discounted and preemptible; Worker 5, drawn red and dashed and marked draining, receives no lane. A red dashed arrow labeled eviction notice runs from Worker 5 back to the gateway.
context:
:::

Replica-level draining protects in-flight requests only if the upstream router avoids placing strict-SLO traffic on interruptible capacity in the first place. The gateway in @fig-spot-aware-routing separates traffic by its tolerance for capacity revocation, and an eviction notice triggers draining when time permits; requests that cannot finish need a permitted retry, reconstruction, or rejection path.

title: Serving Deployment Stack
caption: **Serving Deployment Stack**: A cache miss crosses three tiers before reaching a model replica. Tier 1 edge points of presence (PoPs) enforce authorization and reuse eligibility before answering repeated requests from cache; a miss passes to Tier 2, where the gateway applies rate limits and authentication and the router picks a destination; Tier 3 GPU workers run prefill and decode while an autoscaler sizes the fleet from queue depth and KV cache use. Tokens stream back up through the tiers to the client. The per-tier latency budgets on the right, drawn on a log scale, are illustrative.
alt: Three pale stacked bands labeled Tier 1 edge cache, Tier 2 gateway and router, and Tier 3 model serving, with a client bar above them. A thick blue path traces one request: from the client into authorize, then into an Edge PoP, where it is marked cache miss and drops into Tier 2 through rate limit, auth, and router, then is marked dispatch and drops into a GPU worker in Tier 3, through prefill to decode. A thick green line labeled token stream rises from decode straight back up through all three tiers to the client. Supporting elements are drawn lighter: two dashed sibling PoPs in Tier 1, a telemetry card in Tier 2, and in Tier 3 two dashed sibling workers fed by a dashed arrow from an autoscaler card driven by queue depth and KV use. On the right, a latency budget column draws one bar per tier on a log scale, labeled under 10 ms, under 50 ms, and under 2 s, so the Tier 3 bar is longest.
context:
## Global Inference Infrastructure {#sec-inference-scale-global-inference-infrastructure-df52}

A fleet confined to one region can batch, shard, route, isolate, and autoscale well, yet a user in Sydney still pays roughly a 200 ms round trip to a US-East deployment before any of that machinery acts. A regional outage also removes every replica at once. Extending resource isolation and failure boundaries beyond one data center introduces placement decisions at geographic scale. Distance, regional failures, and data-placement requirements can motivate regional replicas, caches, or a centralized service with an explicit network budget. @Fig-serving-deployment-stack illustrates three tiers: edge points of presence for reusable responses, regional gateways for authentication and routing, and GPU clusters for model execution. Its 10 ms, 50 ms, and 2 s budgets are scenario targets, not measured performance or universal deadlines. The application must define whether its execution budget governs first response, individual tokens, or completion of the entire request.

title: Global Load Balancing across Inference Regions
caption: **Global Load Balancing across Inference Regions**: A global load balancer routes each user to an eligible region with suitable latency and ready capacity (@tbl-rtt-by-user-location gives the round-trip times this avoids). Each region (US-East, EU-West, Asia-Pacific) runs independent replicas of the same model, and EU requests can stay in the EU to meet data-residency rules. A shared model registry supplies versioned weights to every region. If a region fails, the load balancer reroutes its users only to destinations that still satisfy placement, readiness, and capacity requirements.
alt: Three user populations across the top, users in North America, users in the EU, and users in Asia and Oceania, each drawn as a row of dots, send arrows down into a wide violet Global load balancer bar that routes each user to an eligible, ready region. Arrows continue straight down to three region frames, US-East, EU-West, and Asia-Pacific, each with a one-line role and two replicas, each drawn as a server of four GPU tiles. A pale indigo column labeled EU data-residency zone runs behind the EU users, their heavier blue path through the shared load balancer, and the EU-West region, whose role reads EU data stays in region. Below, a wide Model registry box, versioned weights for every region, sends dashed green sync arrows up to each region.
section: Global load balancing with regional replicas {#sec-inference-scale-pattern-1-global-load-balancing-regional-replicas-b7ac}
context:
### Global load balancing with regional replicas {#sec-inference-scale-pattern-1-global-load-balancing-regional-replicas-b7ac}

Deploying replicas in multiple regions cuts wide-area latency only if the global router avoids sending users to a nearby region whose GPU queues are already saturated or whose data-residency rules forbid the request. In @fig-global-inference-multiregion, a global load balancer\index{Global load balancing!regional replicas} selects among regions that satisfy placement policy, readiness, and capacity requirements. Measured network latency helps choose among those eligible destinations, because geographic proximity alone does not determine completion time, while a shared registry supplies versioned artifacts to the independent regional replicas.

title: Cache Hit and Cache Miss Paths at the Edge
caption: **Cache Hit and Cache Miss Paths at the Edge**: A query first reaches the nearest edge point of presence (PoP). After enforcing authorization and reuse eligibility, the edge targets a cache-hit response in under 10 ms without touching a GPU. On a miss, the request passes through the regional gateway to the central GPU cluster, which runs prefill and decode. Generated tokens stream back to the user, and a response eligible for reuse can be stored at the edge for later queries. The saving depends on the rate of requests eligible for reuse; open-ended generation may offer few such requests.
alt: Four boxes in a row joined by arrows: User, Edge PoP with authorize then cache, Regional gateway for auth and rate limiting, and GPU cluster for prefill and decode. The arrows are labeled query, miss, and forward. A green path above the row returns from the Edge PoP to the User, labeled cache hit, returned from edge in under 10 ms. A navy path below the row returns from the GPU cluster to the User, labeled cache miss, generated tokens stream back. A dashed green branch from that path goes up into the Edge PoP, labeled store response.
context:
### Edge caching with central inference {#sec-inference-scale-pattern-2-edge-caching-central-inference-f08e}

Standing up a full GPU cluster in every continent is an expensive way to reduce round-trip latency when a large fraction of distant requests ask repeated FAQ or autocomplete questions. Caching responses at the edge\index{Edge caching!central inference} avoids both the wide-area round trip and repeated central inference whenever a stored response remains valid for the incoming request. Before returning a hit, the edge must enforce authorization and match the relevant model version, conversation or retrieval context, generation policy, and freshness requirements. Identical visible queries do not necessarily permit the same answer, and fresh-sample semantics may prohibit reuse. A hit returns within an illustrative 10 ms budget, while a miss reaches the central cluster (@fig-edge-cache-routing); only responses eligible for reuse should enter the edge store.

title: Ranking Cascade Architecture
caption: **Ranking Cascade Architecture**: To optimize latency and cost, search and recommendation systems use a cascade of increasingly complex models. Early stages (Retrieval) filter millions of candidates down to thousands using fast, cheap heuristics. Later stages use expensive, high-precision models only on the most promising candidates.
alt: A funnel of four stacked trapezoid bands that narrow from top to bottom and deepen in blue, with band widths proportional to the logarithm of the candidate count. Retrieval, using lexical and ANN embeddings, cuts 1,000,000 candidates to 10,000; first-stage ranking, using two-tower models and GBDTs, cuts 10,000 to 1,000; second-stage scoring, using deep MLPs and DLRM, cuts 1,000 to 100; and final re-ranking, using a cross-attention transformer, cuts 100 to 10. A separate column of horizontal bars, with length proportional to the latency budget, grows downward as the funnel shrinks: at most 10 ms, about 20 ms, about 50 ms, and about 100 ms.

title: On-Device Prediction Strategies
caption: **On-Device Prediction Strategies**: Gboard performs next-word prediction and Smart Compose rescoring locally at inference time. These request-time mechanisms use local context without sending each keystroke to a central server; asynchronous federated training is the separate process that improves shared model parameters from eligible on-device updates. Source: [@xu2023federated].
alt: Mobile keyboard interface showing two prediction modes: next-word suggestions above keys and Smart Compose autocomplete in the text field, both using local context to produce suggestions.
context:
[^fn-gboard-federated-scale]: **Gboard (2017)**\index{Gboard!definition}: One of the first widely reported commercial federated learning deployments at mobile scale. Published reports showed that keyboard models could improve from aggregated on-device updates while raw typed text remained local. The systems consequence is durable. Compressed updates and privacy mechanisms make cross-fleet learning possible over constrained mobile networks without centralizing raw keystrokes.

The same keyboard also runs two interactive prediction strategies at inference time\index{On-device prediction!inference strategies} (@fig-ondevice-gboard). Next-word prediction ranks discrete candidate tokens ("favorite," "address," "schedule") in the suggestion bar, whereas Smart Compose generates multi-word inline ghost text ("ail address") through on-the-fly rescoring directly inside the input buffer. Both mechanisms personalize the immediate interaction through local context; longer-lived model improvement occurs separately when federated training aggregates eligible on-device updates.

title: Local-Only, Centralized-Cloud, and Federated Learning
caption: **Local-Only, Centralized-Cloud, and Federated Learning**: The panels compare three architectures by what crosses the device boundary (dashed line), rather than imply a required evolution. (A) Local-only learning trains on the device and sends nothing. (B) Centralized-cloud learning uploads raw data to a cloud trainer. (C) Federated learning keeps data on the device, downloads the global model $\ModelParameters$, and uploads only model updates $\FiniteChange\ModelParameters$ to a federated averaging (FedAvg) coordinator. Data locality in (C) still requires separate privacy controls for updates and metadata.
alt: Three panels separated by a dashed device boundary line. Each device box holds a small grid of green data records. Panel A, local only: one device with a self-loop arrow labeled train and an empty dashed box labeled no server. Panel B, centralized cloud: three devices send amber arrows carrying green record tiles up to a cloud trainer that holds a pooled grid of all the records. Panel C, federated: three devices keep their records, send amber delta theta arrows up to a FedAvg coordinator holding global theta, and receive gray theta arrows down. Footers read nothing leaves the device, raw data leaves the device, and only model updates leave.
context:
Local-only adaptation specializes a model to its user's observations, which are often non-IID[^fn-noniid-federated-distribution] and noisy, so sharing that specialization requires an explicit boundary between personal state and the parameters intended to improve the population model. Federated coordination adds population learning by periodically aggregating updates to shared parameters. A deployment must specify which parameters enter the aggregate and which remain personal; averaging every local adaptation would erase that distinction. Data locality limits raw-data transfer, while separate privacy controls govern the updates that leave each device. The three architectures therefore differ in what crosses the device boundary, not in how advanced they are (@fig-centralized-vs-decentralized): local-only learning sends nothing, centralized training sends raw examples, and federated learning sends only model updates $\FiniteChange\ModelParameters$ while receiving the shared weights $\ModelParameters$.

[^fn-noniid-federated-distribution]: **Non-IID (not independent and identically distributed)**\index{Non-IID data!definition}: Samples may be dependent or drawn from different distributions; in a device fleet, user-specific label and feature distributions can make local updates conflict. Such distributions can degrade federated averaging relative to independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) baselines [@zhao2018federated]. The observed failure determines whether to change local work, aggregation, or personalization rather than prescribing one remedy for every non-IID population.

(b) On a log axis, inference and training totals keep the same ratio from 1M to 100M parameters. The configuration is illustrative (activations assumed at 5$\times$ the weights), producing a representative 9$\times$ amplification.

title: Adaptation Memory Budget
caption: **Adaptation Memory Budget**: Working memory must hold the resident weights $\ResidentWeightMemory$, the trainable state $\TrainableStateMemory$, and the peak of live activations plus workspace; together these form $\AdaptationPeakMemory$, which must fit under the device limit once the runtime and foreground application are reserved. Frozen weights kept in nonvolatile flash count toward storage, not working memory, until they are staged, and staging buffers belong to the workspace term. Segment heights are schematic, not to scale.
alt: Lower left: a green nonvolatile flash box holding frozen weights, with a dashed stage arrow up into the bottom of a working-memory stack. The stack, from bottom, holds resident weights M weights,resident in gray, trainable state M train in light blue, and max over t of M activations of t plus M workspace of t in blue; a bracket labels these three as M peak. Above them a dashed block M reserve, held for the runtime and app, reaches a red dashed line labeled M device. Right: a curve of activations plus workspace over time rises through the forward pass to a peak and falls through the backward pass; a dotted line carries the peak level across to the top of the activations segment.
section: │ Context: Peak memory usage — smartphone RAM envelope.
context:
$$ {#eq-edge-adaptation-peak-memory}

Admission then requires $\AdaptationPeakMemory+ \ReservedDeviceMemory\le \DeviceMemoryCapacity$, where $\ReservedDeviceMemory$ holds the runtime, the operating system, and the foreground application; for a background task, $\DeviceMemoryCapacity- \ReservedDeviceMemory$ is the allowance just described. Weights stored in nonvolatile memory still consume deployment storage, and any staging buffers belong in $\OperatorWorkspaceMemory(\TimeInstant)$. The maximum must follow the actual execution schedule because activation and workspace peaks need not coincide. Each term is a separate lever, and the adaptation strategies of @sec-edge-intelligence-model-adaptation-6a82 differ in which term they shrink. Freezing weights removes their gradients and optimizer state from $\TrainableStateMemory$, but it does not make the frozen base or every backward dependency disappear.

The hollow A13 point is derived from Apple's stated speedups rather than a stated figure. Apple does not state the rating precision, so the 2023 step may partly reflect a change in the rating's number format rather than in the hardware alone. These inference-oriented peak ratings do not establish training throughput or backward-operator support. Ratings from @apple2017iphonex, @apple2018iphonexs, @apple2020a14, @apple2021iphone13pro, @apple2022iphone14pro, and @apple2023iphone15pro.
