title: The TCO Iceberg
caption: **The TCO Iceberg**: The analysis separates visible infrastructure costs from operational costs that are easier to omit. In this illustrative budget, the hidden operational costs (engineering labor, pipeline maintenance, retraining, monitoring, incident response, and compliance) together constitute half of total cost.
alt: A ten-by-ten grid of square cells, each 1 percent of total cost of ownership, filled row by row from the top. Each category is a rectangular block labeled inside with its name and share, the label sitting on a solid strip of merged cells centered in the block, six cells wide in full-row blocks and three in half-row blocks. All cells are equal squares; blocks are separated by wider white gutters added between cells, and color encodes only visible versus hidden. The top five rows are pale blue: four rows of GPU cloud compute, 40 percent, and one row of object storage, 10 percent, together labeled visible infrastructure, 50 percent of TCO. A dashed waterline separates them from the bottom five rows, all in a darker gray: two rows of engineering labor, 20 percent, one row of data pipeline maintenance, 10 percent, and two rows split in half among retraining, monitoring, incidents, and compliance, 5 percent each, together labeled hidden operational costs, 50 percent of TCO.
context:
Here, $\TrainingCost$ is the initial training and evaluation cost, $\InferenceCost$ is recurring serving cost, $\TotalDataCost$ covers data acquisition, storage, cleaning, and governance, and $\IterationCost$ captures subsequent experimentation and maintenance. The categories require a common accounting horizon and an explicit allocation rule. If retraining compute is charged to $\TrainingCost$, it must be excluded from $\IterationCost$; shared hardware depreciation and energy likewise enter these workload costs once rather than being added again as a separate fleet bill.

In the illustrative budget of @fig-tco-iceberg, engineering labor (20 percent), pipeline maintenance (10 percent), continuous retraining, monitoring, incident response, and governance together equal the visible infrastructure spend. The example shows what an incomplete budget can miss; its proportions are not universal cost shares. Each organization must measure these obligations within the same accounting horizon as its infrastructure costs.

title: Organizational Patterns for ML
caption: **Organizational Patterns for ML**: (A) A centralized platform team gives every model team the same infrastructure, but all requests pass through one shared queue, which can become the bottleneck. (B) Embedded teams each build their own tooling, which is fast locally but duplicates infrastructure and lets stacks diverge. (C) A hybrid keeps a core platform and places ML engineers (MLE) inside model teams as liaisons, balancing standardization with responsiveness.
alt: Three panels of the same three blue team boxes. Panel A, centralized: each team sends an arrow up into a red-outlined shared request queue drawn as a row of slots, five filled and one empty, whose single red exit arrow leads into one violet platform team box. Panel B, embedded: a dashed gray outline labeled no shared platform sits where the platform would be; each team box sits under an own tooling label and contains its own stack of violet bars, with bar lengths differing from team to team. Panel C, hybrid: one violet core platform box sends an arrow down into each team box, where it ends at a violet MLE chip inside the team.
context:
### Centralized platform team {#sec-ml-operations-scale-centralized-platform-team-16fc}

When eight product teams each build their own deployment scripts, feature pipelines, and alert dashboards, the same stale-feature or rollback outage repeats across the company. A centralized ML platform team\index{Organizational pattern!centralized platform} eliminates that duplication by building and maintaining shared infrastructure while model teams own model development and behavior. Three organizational patterns trade consistency against local responsiveness (@fig-ml-org-models). A shared request queue (Panel A) centralizes prioritization but can become a bottleneck; uniform standards depend on enforced contracts, not the queue itself. Embedded tooling (Panel B) favors local responsiveness while risking duplication. The hybrid pattern (Panel C) places dedicated ML engineers near product teams while retaining a common platform. Self-service interfaces can preserve central standards without routing every routine action through a human queue.

title: ML System Attack Surface
caption: **ML System Attack Surface**: Red arrows mark where an adversary enters the system: the training data, the training job and its dependencies, the stored weights, the serving API, and the infrastructure beneath all three layers. Each entry point calls for a different control, so defense spans data collection, training and weights, the serving interface, and the provenance of firmware and hardware.
alt: Pipeline of training data, training job, weights, and serving API in data, model, and interface layer frames, with clients exchanging queries with the API. Training data is a grid of sample tiles with two red poisoned tiles; the training job holds three imported package chips, one red; the weights are a shaded parameter matrix. An infrastructure layer below shows accelerator hosts, network fabric, firmware and drivers, and schedulers and keys. Red arrows enter from above at poisoning and backdoor triggers, tampered packages and frameworks, artifact theft and unsafe loading, and extraction, adversarial inputs, and membership inference, and from below at hardware Trojans, co-tenant leakage, firmware tampering, and side channels.
context:
Learned-information exposure follows from the difference between *transient processing* and *persistent learning*. Many applications process sensitive data without encoding it into learned parameters; machine learning systems can preserve patterns from training data in their model parameters. Sensitive information may then remain in a model after the original processing has ended and become accessible through outputs or systematic interrogation. Queries to a healthcare model may expose memorized patient information, while queries to a proprietary model may reveal enough behavior to train a substitute. The first threatens training-data privacy (@sec-security-privacy-leakage-authorized-outputs); the second threatens model confidentiality.

Architectural complexity compounds these challenges. A contemporary ML deployment spans data ingestion pipelines, distributed training infrastructure, model serving systems, and continuous monitoring frameworks, each introducing distinct vulnerabilities as @fig-attack-surface maps across the ML lifecycle. Continuous adaptation at edge nodes and federated coordination protocols add further entry points, each with its own trust assumptions.

title: Stuxnet and the ML Supply Chain
caption: **Stuxnet and the ML Supply Chain**: The top row traces the Stuxnet chain from removable media through Windows hosts and Siemens Step7 software to altered PLC logic, which damaged centrifuges while operators saw normal readings. The bottom row places the ML analog under each stage: a compromised public artifact passes through trusted build and training steps into a model whose misbehavior monitoring does not reveal.
alt: Two aligned rows of four stage boxes. Top row, Stuxnet 2010: USB media, Windows hosts, Siemens Step7, PLC logic. Bottom row, ML supply chain: public artifact, build host, training job, model artifact. A red dot inside every stage box marks the hidden payload, and red arrows carry it from box to box. A dashed vertical line between the first and second stages is labeled air gap and trust boundary. Each row ends in a displayed-versus-actual pair: a dashed gray monitor view with a flat line, tapped from the last stage, reads operators see normal or health checks pass, while the red payload arrow enters a red box with a jagged trace reading centrifuges damaged or model misbehaves.
context:
[^fn-air-gapped-isolation]: **Air-gapped**\index{Air-gapped!isolation}: Physical network separation does not eliminate transfer paths through removable media or authorized personnel. An isolated ML training cluster still needs a controlled process for admitting frameworks, datasets, and pretrained weights; each transfer must preserve the intended trust boundary.

ML supply chains that ingest public packages, datasets, model weights, or firmware face four analogous vectors: compromised dependencies (malicious packages in PyPI and conda repositories), poisoned datasets on public platforms, backdoored model weights in model repositories, and tampered accelerator firmware. Each can introduce behavior through an artifact the pipeline accepts. Because a model's behavior depends on every contributor to its data, code, weights, and hardware, the model can be trusted only as far as a verifiable record of those contributors extends. That statement is the provenance bound on trust (principle \ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}), and it carries the Stuxnet lesson to every artifact an ML pipeline admits. Artifact signatures and immutable provenance logs establish origin and integrity evidence; controlled dependency admission limits which artifacts enter the pipeline. Behavioral testing addresses a different question, because an authentic, unchanged artifact can still contain a backdoor. Each stage of the Stuxnet attack chain has a counterpart in the ML supply chain (@fig-stuxnet).

title: Threat Prioritization Matrix
caption: **Threat Prioritization Matrix**: Likelihood and impact place each example threat in a quadrant, and the quadrant sets the response. Likely, damaging threats such as federated data poisoning warrant automated defenses; rare but severe threats such as hardware side channels justify preparation in high-value deployments; likely but lower-impact extraction calls for API limits; and membership inference through a public API is monitored and reassessed when the training data is sensitive. Dashed arrows show how deployment assumptions move a threat to another quadrant.
alt: Likelihood and impact plane split into four quadrants, with the high-likelihood, high-impact quadrant shaded red. Each quadrant names a response and holds one example threat as a dot: automate defenses for data poisoning in federated training, prepare where value is high for hardware side channels on cloud-hosted models, limit and shape the API for model extraction via a public API, and monitor and reassess for membership inference via a public API. Two dashed arrows move threats to new positions: side channels shift right toward higher likelihood with sensitive co-tenants or exposed edge hardware, and membership inference shifts up toward higher impact with sensitive training data.
context:
The lower-likelihood quadrants receive different treatment. Low-likelihood/high-impact\index{Threat prioritization!low-likelihood high-impact} hardware side-channel attacks describe a deployment in which obtaining the necessary observations is difficult but a successful attack could reveal valuable secrets. The required access depends on the channel; some attacks use a physical probe, while others exploit shared resources or remotely observable timing. In the public API scenario used for this matrix, membership inference attacks, which test whether a particular record was part of the training set (@sec-security-privacy-membership-inference), may sit in a lower-likelihood/lower-impact quadrant than direct integrity failures. That placement must be reassessed when the training data is sensitive or the exposed outputs make membership easier to infer. The matrix records those deployment assumptions rather than assigning a permanent rank to each attack family.

The framework guides resource allocation, as @fig-threat-matrix summarizes. The example prioritizes accessible model and data threats before more specialized hardware attacks. A deployment with sensitive co-tenants or exposed edge hardware may require a different order. The allocation decision depends on the expected harm, the control's effectiveness, and its engineering cost, not on the attack category alone.

title: ML Lifecycle Threats
caption: **ML Lifecycle Threats**: Poisoning, backdoor insertion, model theft, and adversarial inputs enter at different lifecycle stages (red arrows), and each stage has its own first control (green gates). Dashed lines show a training-time compromise that passes its gate persisting into every later stage, so a control placed at a different stage cannot intercept the threat before it takes effect.
alt: A left-to-right pipeline of four stage boxes: data collection, training, deployment, inference. Above each stage a red arrow labeled with its threat strikes a green gate box naming that stage's first control: poisoned samples and flipped labels hit data validation and provenance, backdoor insertion hits a secure training environment, model theft by artifact or API hits access control and API design, and adversarial inputs hit input validation. Below the pipeline, two dashed red lines, the first marked if missed, leave the data collection and training boxes, run beneath every later stage, and end under inference at a red bracket labeled compromised model.
context:
These entry points sit at different stages of the ML lifecycle (@fig-ml-lifecycle-threats). Upstream, an attacker may inject samples or alter labels in a data source the pipeline accepts. A backdoor can then remain inactive on ordinary evaluation inputs and activate on a chosen trigger. Downstream, deployed files expose an artifact-access boundary, while prediction APIs expose a query boundary. An adversarial input crosses the latter without requiring the attacker to alter the training pipeline.

Controls must act at the relevant entry point and preserve their assumptions through later stages. Data validation limits what enters training, artifact controls authenticate what deployment loads, and serving controls constrain requests and returned information. None establishes behavioral correctness by itself; the threat model determines which attack each control must withstand.

title: Model Theft Strategies
caption: **Model Theft Strategies**: Exact artifact theft (left) obtains the model file, checkpoint, registry entry, or device artifact and reconstructs the original model. Approximate behavioral theft (right) uses black-box API queries, output signals, and surrogate training or distillation to clone the model's behavior without direct access to weights.
alt: Two panels. Left, exact artifact theft: a registry, bucket, or device frame holds a shaded weight grid; a red arrow labeled access the file, extract weights leads to a red exact-copy box with an identical grid, captioned same weights, no training cost paid. Right, approximate behavioral theft: a table of recorded x and y pairs sends queries to a dark deployed-API box and receives labels, logits, and scores; a red arrow labeled train surrogate leads to a red behavioral-clone box with a differently shaded grid, captioned different weights, similar outputs.
context:
[^fn-model-serialization-pickle]: **Model serialization**\index{Model serialization!security}: Python's pickle format, common in PyTorch checkpoint workflows, can execute arbitrary code during deserialization, so loading an untrusted checkpoint is equivalent to running untrusted code. Formats such as SafeTensors store only tensor data and remove that execution path [@huggingface_safetensors].

Model theft pursues two distinct objectives, and each requires different controls (@fig-model-theft-types). **Exact artifact theft**\index{Exact artifact theft!definition} obtains the model file or deployment artifact through storage, registry, or device access. The attacker can reuse the recovered weights without repeating their training. **Approximate behavioral theft**\index{Approximate behavioral theft!definition} uses API responses, such as labels, logits, embeddings, or confidence scores, to train a surrogate. It can exploit permitted queries without breaking authentication. The literature names this query-based branch in several ways. *Model extraction* and *model stealing* are synonyms for the attack, while *knockoff modeling* and *model distillation* name its usual training step, in which a surrogate learns from the victim's outputs. Its usual product is a behavioral surrogate, but the same query access can also recover selected internal parameters, a third outcome that the OpenAI results below demonstrate. Encryption, access control, and protected deployment paths restrict artifact access; signatures separately authenticate artifact integrity. Output limits, query budgets, auditing, and pricing constrain behavioral extraction, while watermarking can support attribution after copying.\index{Model theft!strategies}

title: Diffusion Model Memorization
caption: **Diffusion Model Memorization**: A training-set photograph (left) and a diffusion model's near-identical generation (right) under the extraction protocol of @carlini2023diffusion. Memorization is not confined to language models, so a model trained on sensitive images can return one of them through an authorized output.
alt: Side-by-side comparison of two nearly identical portrait photographs of a woman in professional attire. Left shows original training image, right shows diffusion model output with matching pose, lighting, and details.
context:
#### Memorization and training-data extraction {#sec-security-privacy-memorization-extraction}

**Memorization**\index{Model memorization!definition} is the strongest form of the leak, in which a model retains enough of a specific training record to reproduce it. It is not confined to language models. Under one published extraction protocol, a diffusion model reproduced a training-set photograph almost exactly [@carlini2023diffusion]; @fig-diffusion-model-example pairs the original with the reconstruction. Evidence of extraction concerns that specific training instance; a similar-looking output of the same subject would not establish memorization. The exposure matters most for assistants trained or adapted on user logs, where the memorized strings are the users' own messages.

title: Data Poisoning as Bilevel Optimization
caption: **Data Poisoning as Bilevel Optimization**: The attacker (outer loop) chooses poisoning data $\PoisoningDataset$ to raise the trained model's loss on a test set, the untargeted form drawn here, or, for a targeted attack, to lower its loss on the attacker's chosen label. The system (inner loop) attempts to minimize its training loss on the combined dataset $\CleanTrainingDataset \cup \PoisoningDataset$. The nested attack objective can require repeated training evaluations or approximations. It does not imply that every poisoning defense must simulate full training.
alt: A red attacker box at top holds the outer objective, maximizing test loss over the poison set subject to a size budget. A red arrow labeled inject leads to a grid of training tiles in which three red poisoned tiles sit among clean tiles, labeled S union S poison. A blue arrow leads to the inner-loop training box with the arg-min training equation and a chain of SGD steps ending at theta star. A theta-star arrow feeds an evaluation box that computes the target test loss, and a red feedback arrow returns the target loss along the right edge to the attacker.
context:
$$ {#eq-targeted-poisoning}

In the training system, the nested objectives become two coupled loops (@fig-data-poisoning-loop). The outer loop is the attacker's proposal step, which optimizes the attack objective, either raising loss on the test set (@eq-untargeted-poisoning) or, for a targeted attack, lowering loss on the chosen label $\ExampleLabel_t$ (@eq-targeted-poisoning). The inner loop is the defender's training process, which minimizes loss on the combined data. The attacker evaluates or approximates this inner effect on training, and uses the resulting target loss to refine the proposal. An attacker without access to the defender's training process must instead rely on a surrogate or other available feedback.

title: Data Poisoning Impact
caption: **Data Poisoning Impact**: A nominal pipeline (top) and a poisoned pipeline (bottom) pass through the same four stages. In the illustrated successful attack, a poisoned record admitted at ingestion contaminates the training corpus, pulls the optimizer's gradients toward the attacker's trigger, and yields a backdoored model whose clean accuracy can remain intact, so aggregate validation alone can miss it.
alt: Two rows of four panels under the headings ingestion, training corpus, optimization, and trained model, joined by arrows. In the nominal row, three green clean records arrive, the corpus is a grid of green record tiles, a gray step descends into the minimum of a set of loss contours, and a straight decision boundary separates hollow and filled points. In the poisoned row, the middle arriving record is red, one tile of the corpus grid is red, a red step bends away from the contour minimum toward a red trigger diamond while a dashed gray path shows the clean direction, and the same decision boundary now has a small red dashed pocket around a trigger diamond on the filled side, labeled backdoor pocket and clean accuracy intact. The arrows in the poisoned row are red.
context:
Data poisoning attacks differ in their objective and scope [@biggio2012poisoning]. Availability attacks\index{Data poisoning!availability attack} seek broad degradation of useful performance. Targeted attacks\index{Data poisoning!targeted attack} seek errors on selected inputs or classes and may leave aggregate accuracy largely unchanged [@shafahi2018poison]. Backdoor attacks\index{Backdoor attack!trigger patterns}\index{Data poisoning!backdoor attack}\index{Backdoor attack!BadNets} associate an attacker-chosen trigger with unwanted behavior; the trigger can be visible, as in a sticker, even when its significance is hidden [@gu2017badnets]. Subpopulation attacks\index{Data poisoning!subpopulation attack} instead target a group defined by shared features [@jagielski2021subpopulation]. These categories can overlap. Their objectives guide which evaluations are needed beyond aggregate accuracy, including targeted, trigger-specific, and subgroup tests.

The objective classes say what an attacker wants; the attack *mechanism* depends on the attacker's access to the system and knowledge of the data pipeline. Every mechanism shares the shape traced in @fig-poisoning-impact, in which a poisoned record enters the training pipeline alongside clean data and attempts to alter the resulting model's behavior. The most direct mechanism is label modification, where an attacker selects a subset of training samples and alters their labels, flipping $\ExampleLabel= 1$ to $\ExampleLabel= 0$ or reassigning categories in multi-class settings. Even small-scale label corruption can shift decision boundaries. At web scale the same mechanism mislabels multimodal pretraining pairs, as in the dirty-label sample of @fig-dirty-label-example, which pairs cat images with misleading "dog" captions to induce false associations.

title: Dirty-Label Data Poisoning
caption: **Dirty-Label Data Poisoning**: Mismatched image-text pairs represent a dirty-label poisoning attack where cat images are paired with misleading 'dog' captions in training data. Incorporating these corrupted pairs can cause models to learn incorrect multimodal associations. Source: [@shan2024].
alt: Three panels labeled 'Dirty-label poison data', each showing a cat image paired with a misleading text caption that calls the image a dog: 'A dog on the grass', 'Animal art dog pencil drawings', and 'Dog digital art...'.

title: Concept Poisoning Dose-Response
caption: **Concept Poisoning Dose-Response**: Stable Diffusion XL outputs across four poison doses (clean, 50, 100, 300 samples) and eight source prompts (dog, car, handbag, hat, fantasy art, cubism, cartoon, concept art). As the dose grows, outputs morph from the intended source concept toward the attacker's destination concept, demonstrating Nightshade-style concept poisoning of a pretrained model. Source: [@shan2024].
alt: 4x8 grid of Stable Diffusion XL outputs. Rows are poison doses (clean, 50, 100, 300); columns are source prompts (Dog, Car, Handbag, Hat, Fantasy art, Cubism, Cartoon, Concept Art). Outputs morph toward destination concepts as dose grows.
context:
Clean-label poisoning is not always malicious in intent; researchers have begun exploring it as a defensive tool, particularly for protecting creative work from unauthorized use by generative AI models. Nightshade, developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, aims to deter unauthorized training by poisoning images that a scraper may collect [@shan2024]. It does not block scraping itself. Its perturbations preserve the apparent image content while changing how a model learns from it; the reported experiments show targeted concept corruption when the modified images enter the tested training pipelines.

The dose-response matrix in @fig-poisoning charts this progressive corruption across four poison doses (0 to 300 samples) and eight prompt concepts. As the dose increases, Stable Diffusion XL outputs morph away from source concepts (generating cows for "car" or cats for "dog") under the tested training conditions. These outputs demonstrate changed behavior without, by themselves, identifying the internal representation that caused it. The experiment demonstrates concept poisoning\index{Data poisoning!concept poisoning}, in which poisoned samples distort a model's semantic associations.

title: Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation
caption: **Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation**: In a collaborative learning setting, multiple clients each train on local data and contribute model updates to a central server that aggregates them into a shared global model. A single malicious participant can inject poisoned updates that the server folds into the aggregated model, so the corruption spreads to every client without any one obvious anomaly. This attack surface differs from adversarial examples because it targets the model during *training* rather than at *inference*.
alt: A violet aggregation server box at the top shows the weighted mean w t plus 1 equals w t plus the sum over k of n k over n times delta w k, and an inset plot of update vectors drawn from the point w t: three amber honest updates point steeply upward in a narrow fan, one red update delta w 2 points nearly sideways, and a thicker violet aggregate arrow sits between them, tilted away from the honest fan. A row of clients sits below: client 1, a red malicious client 2, client 3, an ellipsis, and client N, each holding a row of small green data tiles, with two red tiles in client 2. Each benign client sends an amber update arrow, delta w 1, delta w 3, and delta w N, up to the server, while client 2 sends a red update delta w 2 marked poisoned. Dashed red arrows labeled w t plus 1 run from the server down to each client.
context:
[^fn-dual-use-ml]: **Dual-use dilemma**\index{Dual-use dilemma!ML security}: The structural tension that defensive ML capabilities (adversarial training, data poisoning tools, red-teaming frameworks) are simultaneously offensive capabilities. This creates an arms race where defensive research publications become attack playbooks. For ML systems engineering, the consequence is architectural: robustness mechanisms must assume attacker knowledge of the defense, ruling out security-through-obscurity and motivating formal guarantees where feasible and adaptive empirical evaluation within the remaining threat model.

Whether crafted examples become poisoning depends on the data boundary. Web scraping, social media feeds, crowdsourced annotation, and untrusted user submissions all allow poisoned records to enter upstream and pass through weak cleaning checks in a "trusted" form. Physical systems add a second path. A sticker on a road sign is an inference-time adversarial attack when the car sees it, but an image of it harvested into a training corpus becomes a poisoning path only if the contribution serves an attack on the learner. Correctly labeled examples of such inputs can instead help train resistance to them. Online learning systems tighten the feedback loop further, allowing an attacker to introduce small increments of malicious data until model behavior drifts without a single obvious anomaly. In collaborative training the same boundary sits at aggregation, where one malicious client's update reaches every participant (@fig-poisoning-attack-example). @Sec-security-privacy-gradient-sync-integrity examines the same exposure among the workers of a synchronous data-parallel job.

title: Threat Mitigation Flow
caption: **Threat Mitigation Flow**: Threats, assessment evidence, and candidate controls have different roles. Dashed lines link each piece of evidence to every control it can inform, so a signal does not uniquely select a defense, and the listed controls require a stated threat model and validation.
alt: Four threat rows, each with red-dot threat, blue assessment-evidence chips, and green candidate-control chips, with a solid line from each threat to its evidence chips and dashed lines from every evidence chip to every control chip in the row. Model extraction: query telemetry to access and query limits and output restrictions. Data poisoning: provenance audit and targeted evaluations, crossing to intake controls and quarantine and retraining. Adversarial input: adaptive attack tests to adversarial training and input validation. Membership inference: privacy attack audit and privacy accounting to an accounted DP mechanism.
section: Availability abuse and denial of wallet {#sec-security-privacy-availability-denial-wallet}
context:
: **Threat Landscape**: Machine learning systems face diverse threats throughout their lifecycle, ranging from data manipulation during training to model theft postdeployment. The table categorizes these threats by lifecycle stage and attack vector, clarifying how vulnerabilities manifest and enabling targeted mitigation strategies. {#tbl-threats-models-summary}

The appropriate defense depends on the attack vector, lifecycle stage, and available evidence. For each threat, assessment evidence and candidate controls play different roles (@fig-threat-mitigation-flow). Monitoring can reveal suspicious querying, while watermarking can support attribution after extraction; neither establishes that theft was prevented. Privacy audits measure attack success under tested conditions, whereas an accounted DP mechanism provides a formal bound under its stated assumptions. Each row identifies a design starting point, not a guaranteed detection-to-defense pipeline, and this distinction between training-time and inference-time attacks is easiest to verify in a concrete deployment scenario.

title: Attestation Before Recovery Admission
caption: **Attestation Before Recovery Admission**: A restarted node answers a fresh verifier challenge with authenticated measurements. Under the illustrated admission policy, the verifier authorizes the key service only after appraisal succeeds. Protected key delivery permits checkpoint restoration; the node rejoins the collective afterward. Stale or rejected evidence stops this sequence before authorization. The diagram shows ordering rather than elapsed time and assumes the platform protects key delivery and custody.
alt: Four vertical lifelines labeled restarted node, verifier, key service, and collective. In descending order, arrows show a fresh challenge, signed evidence, policy approval, and checkpoint-key delivery. A restore box on the node precedes a rejoin arrow to the collective.
section: Attestation and key custody at fleet scale {#sec-security-privacy-fleet-attestation}
context:
When `{python} ReferenceClusterAttackSurface.node_count_str` cluster nodes restart and update independently, releasing the decryption key for a `{python} ReferenceClusterAttackSurface.ckpt_total_tb_str` checkpoint to a node whose boot firmware was silently modified exposes the entire model. Remote attestation\index{Remote attestation!fleet admission} lets a verifier appraise authenticated hardware claims about each node against an admission policy before delivering keys or data. The central claim is a set of measurements, cryptographic hashes of the firmware and software the node loaded, recorded and signed by the node's hardware so that compromised software cannot rewrite them. Before releasing the key for the `{python} ReferenceClusterAttackSurface.ckpt_total_tb_str` checkpoint, the service can require fresh evidence covering the relevant firmware and workload measurements. Coverage depends on the platform; a valid measurement does not prove that approved code is free of vulnerabilities or that every runtime update is correct. The provenance bound on trust (principle \ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}) links this evidence to the release path. Confidential computing\index{Confidential computing!hardware isolation} adds runtime protection for code and data placed inside a hardware-enforced boundary, under the platform's stated adversary model. @Sec-security-privacy-hardware-security-foundations-f5e8 develops those mechanisms and their limits.

The recovery sequence in @fig-attestation-key-release places key delivery between fresh appraisal and checkpoint restoration.

title: Fault Injection Attack
caption: **Fault Injection Attack**: A timed laser pulse that skips the unconditional jump at line 6 forces a positive ReLU activation through the zeroing block at lines 7–10. The fault changes executed control flow without changing the stored model parameters.
alt: Eleven-line ReLU assembly listing with line 6, jmp end, highlighted in red. A dashed arrow from line 6 to line 11 marks the intended jump and is crossed out. Brackets label lines 2 to 3 as positive input with branch not taken, lines 4 to 5 as copying the activation, line 6 as the laser fault skipping the jump, lines 7 to 10 as falling through to zeroing, and line 11 as the intended jump target.
context:
The ML-specific risk is that a small computation fault can become a semantic failure. An embedded classifier running on a microcontroller may misclassify a safety-important input, while a fault in memory or control logic may expose proprietary weights or architecture details. Unlike ordinary random faults, adversarially timed faults are chosen to land on computations the model or security protocol depends on.

The experiments of @breier2018 targeted activation-function implementations on a microcontroller with timed laser faults.\index{Laser fault injection} @Fig-injection identifies the vulnerable instruction in the observed ReLU implementation. For a positive accumulator, the copy instructions assign the activation to the output, and the following `jmp end` normally skips the zeroing block. A laser pulse timed to suppress that jump makes execution fall through into the clear instructions, overwriting the positive output with zero and forcing the neuron inactive. The conditional `brge` instruction is not the skipped instruction in this example, and the fault changes executed control flow rather than any stored model weight.\index{Fault injection attack!activation manipulation}

title: Side-Channel Attack Vulnerability
caption: **Side-Channel Attack Vulnerability**: Power consumption patterns reveal information about a password comparison; consistent power usage indicates correct password bytes, while abrupt changes signal incorrect input and halted processing. Even without knowing the password, an attacker can infer it by analyzing the device's power usage during authentication attempts. Source: Colin O'Flynn.
alt: Oscilloscope trace showing red serial data line and blue power line. Power remains stable through first three correct bytes, then jumps sharply at fourth incorrect byte, revealing partial password match through timing.
context:
Studies of Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)\index{AES!side-channel vulnerability} implementations showed that an implementation can leak information about a key without an attacker breaking the cipher's mathematical construction. The same distinction between an algorithm and its implementation applies to the ReLU activations, softmax normalizations, and weight-load sequences that constitute a forward pass.

Power analysis of a password check shows the mechanism in its simplest form [@kocher2011]. A device that compares a 5-byte password one byte at a time draws a stable power profile while the bytes match,\index{Side-channel attack!power profile} and @fig-encryption2 shows the trace jump at the first wrong byte, where the device halts the comparison.\index{Side-channel attack!power signature divergence}\index{Side-channel attack!power consumption jump}

title: Power Traces
caption: **Power Traces**: Cryptographic computations reveal subtle, data-dependent variations in power consumption that reflect internal states during specific operations. The traces are schematic: amplitudes are illustrative and follow the Hamming-weight ordering rather than a measured capture.
alt: Two line graphs. Left shows three overlapping power traces over six clock cycles in one orange hue, dotted, dashed, and solid; a gray band, outlined as the region magnified on the right, marks the S-box window where the traces peak. Right zooms into that window, where the peaks separate by weight; labels to the right at each peak's height, each led by a short swatch in its trace's line style, read 1111 wt 4, 0101 wt 2, and 0000 wt 0, and a double arrow marks the amplitude gap delta P between 0000 and 1111.
context:
Machine learning also changes the attacker's side of this analysis. Extracting a key from noisy power traces requires finding signal patterns associated with secret-dependent computations, and a convolutional neural network can learn those patterns from labeled traces, turning part of the analysis into a learned classification task. The attacker still needs suitable measurements and training data, but can reuse the trained model across repeated attempts under compatible conditions. The SCAAML framework (Side-Channel Attacks Assisted with Machine Learning), developed by researchers at Google, is a widely studied and reproducible demonstration of this learned pipeline [@bursztein2024; @burszteindc27].

Power drawn during an AES S-box substitution depends on the data being processed (@fig-side-channel-curves). The left panel places a possible leakage interval within a longer trace; the right panel magnifies a schematic difference between processed values. Hamming weight counts the ones in a binary value: 1111 has weight 4, 0101 has weight 2, and 0000 has weight 0. The drawing orders amplitudes by that weight to illustrate a leakage model, not a measured law of CMOS switching. Actual leakage depends on circuit structure, state transitions, noise, and countermeasures. A classifier must learn a reproducible relationship in measured traces before these differences can support key recovery.\index{Power traces}

title: Hardware Supply Chain Attack Surface
caption: **Hardware Supply Chain Attack Surface**: Each lifecycle stage admits its own compromise (red arrows) and needs its own assurance evidence (green gates); no single check covers the chain, and dashed lines carry each missed compromise forward to deployment. Unlike software, which can be patched remotely, a compromise that survives to deployment often requires physical replacement.
alt: A left-to-right pipeline of five stage boxes: design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, deployment. Above each stage a red arrow labeled with its compromise strikes a green gate box naming its assurance check: design flaws or malicious IP hit design review and verification, hardware Trojans hit die inspection by micrography, substituted components hit X-ray screening, cloned or relabeled parts hit provenance and functional tests, and probing and fault injection hit secure boot and attestation. Below the pipeline, dashed red lines marked if missed leave the first four stage boxes and run to deployment, where they end at a red bracket labeled physical replacement.
context:
A component's life runs through design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, and deployment (@fig-hw-supply-chain), and each stage presents opportunities for tampering or substitution. Recycled electronic waste can be relabeled as new, distributors can mix cloned parts into legitimate shipments, and insiders at manufacturing facilities can embed hardware trojans that routine functional tests may miss. Micrography, X-ray screening, and functional testing provide different evidence, with coverage and cost determined by the suspected modification. Procurement therefore needs risk-based provenance controls as well as inspection; passing a functional test does not establish a component's origin or exclude dormant malicious behavior.

Fleet procurement changes the shape of this risk. A training cluster is bought in bulk from a small number of part numbers, so each of the `{python} ReferenceClusterAttackSurface.node_count_str` nodes of the reference cluster carries the same accelerators, network adapters, management controller, and firmware images as every other. A compromised shared design, firmware release, or production batch can therefore affect many nodes at once. Replication does not remove a vulnerability shared by the replicas, although one compromised unit is evidence about its part number, not proof that every unit carrying it is affected. The provenance bound on trust (principle \ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}) applies to silicon and firmware as much as to data. Supplier, batch, and firmware records help identify the affected population; supplier concentration increases common dependencies even when those records are complete.

title: Layered Defense Stack
caption: **Layered Defense Stack**: Controls are grouped by the layer they protect, from the silicon root of trust through platform isolation and model safeguards to data privacy. A compromised component can undermine controls that rely on its execution or stored state. These runtime dependencies must be checked against each control’s threat model; a correctly released differentially private artifact retains its release-level guarantee.
alt: Four stacked tiers of four controls each. From top: data (encryption at rest, provenance tracking, secure aggregation, differential privacy), model (adversarial training, input validation, output monitoring, rate limits), platform (container isolation, network segmentation, access control, runtime telemetry), and hardware (trusted execution, secure boot, HSM key custody, PUF device identity). A red dot on the platform tier marked compromised host sends a dashed red arrow up to the differential privacy block, labeled alters it before release, while a green arrow from differential privacy leads to a separate green released-artifact box.
context:
mechanisms include trusted execution environments, secure boot, HSM key custody, and physical unclonable function (PUF) device identities. Platform controls include container isolation, network segmentation, access control, and runtime telemetry. The model layer includes adversarial training, input validation, output monitoring, and rate limiting, while data-layer controls include differential privacy, encryption at rest, provenance tracking, and secure aggregation. These tiers partition defenses by the layer they protect, which differs from the data, model, interface, and infrastructure layers of @sec-security-privacy-attack-surface-analysis-b10b that partition where an adversary enters. The two maps line up except at the interface. Interface controls such as rate limiting, input validation, and output monitoring guard the model's query boundary, so the stack files them with the model tier. The serving platform beneath enforces them, which is why the runtime-monitoring discussion below treats them as platform mechanisms. Infrastructure threats fall to the hardware and platform tiers. The dependency arrow highlights the runtime support that many controls require. A compromised host can expose raw records or alter a privacy mechanism before release, but it does not retroactively invalidate the differential privacy guarantee of an artifact already produced by a correctly implemented mechanism. The dependency analysis must identify the protected asset and release, not assume that every control fails together.

Layered defense\index{Defense in depth!layered architecture} (also known as defense in depth) makes these dependencies explicit. Differential privacy bounds what a specified release reveals about an individual's contribution; it does not protect a separate copy of raw training records from theft. Federated learning changes where training data reside but does not, by itself, bound what updates reveal. Hardware isolation can protect execution within its threat model without establishing that an application follows the intended data policy. Combining these mechanisms requires stating each guarantee and checking which assumptions the other layers preserve.

title: Secure Enclave Architecture
caption: **Secure Enclave Architecture**: The Secure Enclave is an isolated region of the system on chip with its own processor, random-number generator, public-key accelerator, AES engine, and root keys. The application processor reaches it only through a mailbox, enclave memory in DRAM passes through a memory protection engine, and storage keys go directly to the inline AES engine, so a compromised application processor never holds them. Source: Apple.
alt: Block diagram. A system-on-chip frame holds an application processor and a Secure Enclave region containing an enclave processor, TRNG, memory protection engine, PKA, AES engine, and root keys. Arrows connect the application processor to DRAM and to the enclave through a mailbox, the memory protection engine to an encrypted enclave region of DRAM, the enclave to secure storage over I2C, and the root keys to a storage AES engine that writes encrypted data to NAND flash.
context:
[^fn-trustzone-hardware-security]: **ARM TrustZone**\index{ARM TrustZone!adoption}: Introduced in 2004, TrustZone partitions an ARM processor into secure and normal "worlds" with hardware-enforced isolation. Its presence on a device does not by itself protect an ML deployment: the model, keys, and data path must actually be placed inside the secure world, which depends on whether the device vendor exposes secure-world applications beyond key storage.

Apple's system-on-chip (SoC) Secure Enclave shows these boundaries in silicon (@fig-enclave). Its dedicated processor, true random number generator (TRNG), public key accelerator (PKA), and cryptographic engines operate separately from the application processor, which communicates through a mailbox interface. A memory protection engine encrypts and authenticates the enclave's external memory, while protected key paths support storage encryption [@apple2024secureenclave]. On consumer devices, Apple's Face ID applies this architecture by binding its biometric templates and comparison logic to the Secure Enclave rather than treating them as ordinary application data [@apple2024facialmatching]. This example demonstrates isolation of designated security operations and state; it does not imply that arbitrary application model weights or activations reside inside the Secure Enclave, because their protection depends on the execution and data paths the platform supports.\index{Secure Enclave!architecture}

title: Secure Boot Sequence
caption: **Secure Boot Sequence**: Each trusted stage authenticates the next component before use. Extending the chain to a verified model loader permits model-artifact authentication; generic boot verification does not provide that extension automatically. Measured boot records evidence, whereas verification enforces the loading decision.
alt: Horizontal chain of four stages: 1, immutable boot root; 2, verified bootloader; 3, verified OS or loader; 4, authorized ML workload. Green diamonds between stages authenticate the bootloader, the kernel and startup policy, and the manifest and artifact digest; each diamond sends a red fail arrow up to a shared box labeled halt and reject the component. Below, a measurement log row records bootloader hash, kernel hash, and model digest under stages 2 to 4, and a bracket under the last gate and stage reads extension to the model. A dashed after-boot arrow leads to a dashed box reading runtime controls still required.
context:
For machine learning systems, secure boot authenticates the components included in its verification chain. Model artifacts receive this protection only when a verified loader checks their signatures or a signed manifest before loading them; boot verification alone does not authenticate weights read later from storage. Secure update flows must extend the same verification policy to replacement firmware, runtimes, and model artifacts.

Secure boot frequently operates in tandem with hardware-based TEEs to establish an unbroken chain of trust prior to code execution. The chain is a stepped verification handshake that pairs each trusted execution stage with an explicit cryptographic authentication gate [@nist2018sp800193], as @fig-secure-boot traces. Execution proceeds from an immutable boot root through a verified bootloader and operating system, halting and rejecting the component if any signature check fails. For machine learning pipelines, Stage 3 extends this chain beyond conventional system software: the verified OS or loader authenticates the model manifest and artifact digest before launching the authorized ML workload. The terminal stage emphasizes that while boot-time authentication blocks unauthorized or tampered binaries, dynamic runtime controls remain necessary to guard against post-boot attacks and data-dependent exploits.\index{Secure boot!sequence}

title: Physical Unclonable Functions
caption: **Physical Unclonable Functions**: Each panel turns uncontrolled manufacturing variation into a device-specific response. Two chips of the same design answer the same challenge differently (A); a laser challenge scattered by a random token yields a speckle response (B); a challenge sets each arbiter stage straight or crossed, and the faster of two racing edges sets the response bit (C); and threshold-voltage mismatch decides the value a cross-coupled SRAM cell settles to at power-up (D).
alt: Four panels. A: two chip squares with different dot patterns produce response R1 and response R2, marked not equal. B: a tilted laser sends a beam at a marked angle into a token filled with scattered particles, and diverging rays reach a speckle image. C: two signal paths pass through switch stages C1, C2, and Ck, crossing in one stage, into an arbiter that outputs bit r. D: two cross-coupled inverters between nodes A and B, one drawn heavier and labeled threshold-voltage mismatch, with node A settling to 0 and node B to 1.
context:
For ML fleets, a PUF can reduce the need to inject and persistently store a unique secret in each device. The phone-class devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) and the cameras and drones of edge deployments still need enrollment: the verifier must associate a device with trusted authentication evidence and manage its admission and revocation. A PUF-derived key can encrypt the on-device model at rest, so copying the stored file does not yield the device-bound key that decrypts it. Authentication can use enrolled challenge-response information or a credential backed by a derived key, depending on the design. Both protections have limits. Plaintext weights extracted during execution expose the shared model regardless of how the storage key was generated, and successful authentication establishes which device is speaking, not that its runtime software is uncompromised.

Four PUF architectures draw on different physical sources of variation [@gao2020], as the panels of @fig-puf show. In each, two devices of the same design answer challenge $\PufChallenge$ with different responses ($\PufResponse_1 \ne \PufResponse_2$), whether the response is an optical speckle pattern, an arbiter's response bit $\PufResponseBit$ set by racing signal paths, or the startup state of an SRAM cell. These responses are not perfectly repeatable under every operating condition, which motivates the error correction and calibration discussed next.\index{Physical unclonable function!arbiter PUF}\index{Physical unclonable function!SRAM PUF}

title: Adversarial Prompt Evasion
caption: **Adversarial Prompt Evasion**: Implicitly adversarial prompts bypass typical content filters by triggering unintended generations, revealing limitations of solely relying on pregeneration safety checks. These examples show the need for post-hoc content analysis as a complementary defense layer for robust generative AI systems. Source: [@quaye2024].
alt: Three deliberately blurred images generated by a text-to-image model, each showing graphic red content resembling blood or injury.
context:
Prompt filtering alone is nonetheless insufficient. Text-to-image systems can be manipulated through implicitly adversarial prompts, queries that appear benign but lead to policy-violating outputs, as the Adversarial Nibbler red-teaming project demonstrated on models such as Stable Diffusion [@quaye2024; @parrish2023adversarial]. Such prompts bypass filters because the risk arises from model behavior during generation rather than from lexical cues in the prompt.

Prompts that pass a filter can still yield graphic outputs, such as the three blurred generations in @fig-adversarial-nibbler, so an output needs assessment against the application's policy even when the prompt appears acceptable. Diagnosing how a prompt bypassed a filter requires prompt, model, and filter records alongside the outputs, and the output classifiers that catch these cases need their own errors evaluated.\index{Adversarial attack!prompt evasion}

title: Differential Privacy and Output Distributions
caption: **Differential Privacy and Output Distributions**: These illustrative densities show how outputs can overlap without having identical likelihoods. Differential privacy bounds how much the output distribution can change between adjacent datasets $\NeighboringDataset$ and $\AdjacentNeighboringDataset$. The privacy parameters limit, rather than eliminate, the information an observer can gain about any one individual's inclusion.
alt: Two overlapping bell curves over the mechanism output space, blue for the mechanism on dataset X and orange for the mechanism on adjacent dataset X prime, each labeled directly. A gray region marks their overlap, and a vertical double arrow at outcome o marks the difference between the two density values there.
context:
central model of differential privacy. Each person supplies a bounded salary to a trusted analyst; the analyst computes the sum, adds one Laplace draw calibrated to the sum's global sensitivity, and divides by the fixed, public group size. The example protects a salary replacement within a public roster. If participation itself is private, adjacency must be add/remove, meaning adjacent datasets differ by the presence or absence of one person's records rather than by a change to one value. Under that relation the count becomes data dependent and needs its own privacy treatment, so division by that count is not automatically safe post-processing. This differs from local differential privacy, in which each person randomizes a value before submission and the analyst aggregates the randomized reports. Both models compare output distributions on adjacent inputs, but their mechanisms, trust assumptions, and utility are not interchangeable.

A randomized mechanism $\RandomizedMechanism$ run on adjacent datasets $\NeighboringDataset$ and $\AdjacentNeighboringDataset$ produces two output densities that overlap without coinciding (@fig-differential-privacy, blue and orange curves). Overlap means that either dataset can produce outcomes in the same region; it does not make the distributions identical. For a discrete outcome $\MechanismOutcome$ in $\text{Range}(\RandomizedMechanism)$, relative likelihood can be expressed as $\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset)=\MechanismOutcome] / \Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)=\MechanismOutcome]$ when the denominator is positive. Continuous curves instead depict densities, whose ratio is not their vertical difference. The $(\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)$ guarantee applies to probabilities of measurable output sets: it bounds one probability by $e^{\PrivacyBudget}$ times the other plus $\PrivacyAdditiveSlack$. For a continuous output, those probabilities are areas under the curves over the selected set. The definition therefore constrains distributional change across all such sets, rather than declaring an overlapping region private or treating additive slack as a pointwise density-ratio allowance.

title: Published Privacy-Utility Results
caption: **Published Privacy-Utility Results**: Accuracy at selected privacy budgets from [@abadi2016deep; @bu2020gaussian; @de2022dp]. MNIST stays comparatively accurate under single-digit epsilon budgets in these experiments, while CIFAR-10 trained from scratch without extra data remains harder, with De et al. reporting 81.4 percent at $\PrivacyBudget = 8$. Comparisons require the full mechanism, accountant, adjacency relation, training regime, and data rather than epsilon alone.
alt: Test accuracy versus privacy budget epsilon on a log axis. A blue line of MNIST results from Bu 2020 rises from 95 to 98 percent, blue triangles mark MNIST results from Abadi 2016, and orange markers at epsilon 8 mark CIFAR-10 results from Abadi 2016 at 73.0 percent and De 2022 at 81.4 percent. Dashed lines mark the nonprivate baselines, 98.3 percent for MNIST and 93.0 percent for CIFAR-10, each labeled directly. A double arrow at epsilon 8 spans from the CIFAR-10 baseline down to the lower result and is labeled roughly 12 to 20 points below its baseline.
context:
Tightening differential privacy to single-digit $\PrivacyBudget$ keeps MNIST within about 3.5 percentage points of its 98.3 percent nonprivate baseline, yet drops CIFAR-10 trained from scratch by 12 to 20 percentage points even at $\PrivacyBudget = 8$ [@abadi2016deep; @bu2020gaussian; @de2022dp]. That gap shows how strongly the utility cost of differential privacy depends on task complexity, architecture, privacy accountant, pretraining, and whether extra public data are allowed.

@Fig-privacy-utility-frontier collects those published MNIST and CIFAR-10 results on a logarithmic axis [@abadi2016deep; @bu2020gaussian; @de2022dp]. These comparisons show setting-specific utility costs; differences in architectures and training procedures prevent isolating task complexity alone. The plotted MNIST results stay within about 3.5 percentage points of the 98.3 percent nonprivate baseline at budgets in the range $\PrivacyBudget\in [1, 2]$. For CIFAR-10 without extra data, the plotted results reach 73.0 percent in @abadi2016deep and 81.4 percent in @de2022dp at $\PrivacyBudget= 8$, roughly 12 to 20 points below the displayed 93.0 percent nonprivate reference. These CIFAR-10 settings therefore pay several times the MNIST accuracy cost at a budget four times looser. That reference is a comparison point, not a ceiling on achievable accuracy. Selecting a budget therefore requires the full training regime, adjacency relation, additive slack, accountant, and utility requirements rather than the horizontal coordinate alone.

title: Clean Predictions and Perturbation Robustness
caption: **Clean Predictions and Perturbation Robustness**: Two illustrative two-dimensional classifiers demonstrate the distinction between clean-data accuracy and certified robustness. Both decision boundaries correctly separate the labeled clean inputs. Dashed circles delimit identical perturbation neighborhoods around each point. Boundary A maintains separation outside both circles, whereas boundary B intersects them, allowing a small adversarial perturbation to change the classification. Agreement on clean inputs does not establish resilience under attack.
alt: Two panels show the same negative and positive inputs surrounded by dashed circles. A vertical decision boundary in panel A lies outside the circles. A sloped boundary in panel B crosses both circles. The same arrow moves the positive input within its circle, crossing only boundary B.
context:
:::

Two models can agree on every clean input and still differ in how far an input can move before its label flips. In @fig-clean-vs-robust-classification, each labeled point is surrounded by the same perturbation radius, the largest input change the evaluation allows. Vertical boundary A keeps every allowed change on the correct side, while oblique boundary B cuts through the neighborhood around $\PositiveClassInput$, so a small displacement $\AdversarialPerturbation$ flips the predicted class. The adversarial defenses of @sec-robust-ai-input-attack-detection-defense-19d3 turn that distance into a measured quantity and, under stated assumptions, a certified one.

title: The Robustness Taxonomy
caption: **The Robustness Taxonomy**: Environmental shifts, input-level attacks, and system-level faults decomposed into concrete failure subtypes (dark), each paired with its principal defense (green). Each pillar descends onto a defense wall at the point where it enters the ML pipeline, the data stream, the model's inputs and training data, or the weights and accelerators. Software and pipeline defects originate in the system layer, but they are drawn as the cross-cutting pipeline rail on which all three walls sit because their symptoms can amplify or imitate any of the pillars.
alt: Three side-by-side pillar columns sit above one horizontal dashed pipeline band that runs left to right from data in to output and is labeled software and pipeline defects, cross-cutting; inside the band, a labeled icon sits centered under each column. Each column holds four white failure chips, each naming a failure in dark text and its defense in green. A red arrow from each column's chips ends on a solid green wall bar resting on the pipeline band, directly above the component that pillar strikes: a data stream of sample dots under environmental shifts, a grid of input and training data tiles under input-level attacks, and an accelerator chip holding weight cells under system-level faults. Environmental shifts: covariate shift to importance weighting, concept drift to retraining on fresh labels, label shift to prior re-estimation and recalibration, domain shift to domain adaptation and fine-tuning. Input-level attacks: evasion (FGSM, PGD) to adversarial training, C and W and boundary attacks to certified defenses, data and backdoor poisoning to provenance and spectral filtering, physical perturbations to transformation-robust training. System-level faults: silent data corruption to redundant execution and fleet screening, memory and weight bit flips to ECC and weight range checks, underflow overflow and NaN to loss scaling and NaN guards, distributed training desync to checkpoint rollback and watchdogs.
section: The three pillars of robust AI {#sec-robust-ai-three-pillars-robust-ai-2626}
context:
### The three pillars of robust AI {#sec-robust-ai-three-pillars-robust-ai-2626}

When a model's error rate climbs without a service outage, an engineer must determine whether customer behavior shifted, an attacker perturbed the inputs, or an accelerator corrupted a weight before choosing a defense. Each of the three pillars named at the start of the chapter decomposes into concrete failure subtypes, and each subtype pairs with the defense that targets it (@fig-robustness-taxonomy).

title: Types of Distribution Shift
caption: **Types of Distribution Shift**: (a) Under covariate shift, deployment inputs move to a new region of feature space while the labeling rule, and so the correct boundary, stays fixed. (b) Under label shift, class frequencies change while each class's inputs look the same; the bar heights are illustrative. (c) Under concept drift, the same inputs acquire new labels, so points between the old and new boundaries become errors. Covariate shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$ fixed, label shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput \mid \ExampleLabel)$ fixed, and concept drift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$; the distinction determines whether reweighting, recalibration, or model adaptation is appropriate.
alt: Three panels with a shared key for class 0 (filled) and class 1 (open) points and red label-changed points. Panel a, covariate shift: blue training points labeled train, of two classes, sit on either side of a dashed boundary, and an arrow points to amber deployment points labeled deploy, of the same two classes in a new region, still on the correct sides of the unchanged boundary. Panel b, label shift: paired blue train and amber deploy bars for y equals 0 and y equals 1; training bars are equal, and the deployment bar for y equals 1 is much taller than for y equals 0. Panel c, concept drift: the same points with a dashed boundary labeled old and a solid green boundary labeled new crossing it; points between the two boundaries are red to mark changed labels.
context:
Consider a medical diagnosis model trained on X-ray images from one hospital and deployed in a clinic with different imaging equipment\index{Distribution shift!clinical imaging}. Even for the same medical conditions, acquisition settings can change the image characteristics. This difference between training and deployment populations is **distribution shift**\index{Distribution shift!definition}; whether it reduces diagnostic accuracy requires evaluation on the clinic's data. A move to a different source altogether, such as a new hospital, sensor, or region, is often called domain shift\index{Domain shift}, and it can combine several of the shift types distinguished below.

Distribution shift takes three geometric and statistical forms (@fig-shift-types). Inputs can migrate to an unfamiliar region of feature space (panel a), label priors can skew (panel b), or the underlying mapping itself can invert (panel c). Here, $\ModelInput$ denotes an input and $\ExampleLabel$ its outcome label. Input-only monitors can detect changes in $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)$; distinguishing changes in label frequencies or in $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel\mid \ModelInput)$ generally requires outcome evidence or additional assumptions.

title: Accuracy on a Fresh Test Set from the Same Recipe
caption: **Accuracy on a Fresh Test Set from the Same Recipe**: Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-V2, a test set rebuilt by following the original ImageNet collection protocol, against accuracy on the original ImageNet validation set, for testbed models that reach at least 55 percent on the original. Every point lies below the dashed line of equal accuracy, and the red least-squares line shows that the loss tracks accuracy almost linearly. ImageNet-V2 is from @recht2019imagenet; model evaluations from the testbed of @taori2020measuring.
alt: Scatter plot of ImageNet-V2 top-1 accuracy from about 43 to 81 percent against original ImageNet accuracy from about 56 to 88 percent. A dashed diagonal marks equal accuracy; all points lie 7 to 14 points below it. A red fitted line runs through the points. AlexNet near 56.5 and 43, VGG-16 near 72 and 59, ResNet-50 near 76 and 63, and EfficientNet-L2 Noisy Student near 88 and 81 are labeled.
context:
```

Even a shift that was designed to be no shift at all costs accuracy. @recht2019imagenet rebuilt the ImageNet validation set a decade after the original by following the original collection and labeling protocol, then evaluated existing models on the new images. In the larger testbed of @taori2020measuring, every one of the `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.model_count_str` models that reach at least `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.val_floor_str` percent on the original set scores lower on the new one, by `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.gap_min_str` to `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.gap_max_str` points with a median of `{python} ImageNetV2Shift.gap_median_str` (@fig-imagenet-v2-shift). The loss follows a nearly straight line, so a model that is better on the original set is better on the new one, yet no architecture, training recipe, or amount of extra data closes the gap. Whatever separates the two sets is not an obvious visual change, yet it is costly to every model. For a fleet, accuracy measured on held-out data from the training distribution is therefore an optimistic estimate of accuracy on the next population of inputs, not a prediction of it.

title: A Calibrated Distribution-Shift Workflow
caption: **A Calibrated Distribution-Shift Workflow**: In this synthetic service, PSI enters the warning zone as user behavior shifts and crosses the service's escalation threshold at week 32. Following investigation and validation of the changed operating population, the service versions a new input reference at week 41. Values on either side of that reference change use different comparison populations; the drop is not evidence of model recovery.
alt: Line plot of weekly PSI over 52 weeks with service-calibrated green, orange, and red alert zones labeled stable, warning, and major shift. Drift crosses the escalation threshold at week 32. A gray band from week 32 to week 41 is labeled investigation and validation, and a discontinuity at week 41 is labeled approved reference change, after which PSI uses the new reference.
context:
The fleet convention bands of @sec-ml-operations-scale-drift-detection-793f map PSI values to negligible, moderate, and major shift. They are monitoring conventions, especially common in credit-scoring practice, rather than universal statistical guarantees, so a service validates them against its own binning, baseline, sample size, predictive features, and response cost, and reads PSI together with feature importance and downstream model-performance metrics [@yurdakul2020].

Binning and the treatment of empty bins change what PSI can see, so the bin boundaries chosen on the reference sample must be reused for the comparison population. An empty bin is handled with a smoothing constant\index{Population stability index!smoothing constant} $\PopulationStabilitySmoothingConstant$ and renormalization; because that choice can materially change PSI on sparse bins, the monitoring configuration records it alongside the reference. Monitoring population stability index over time as plotted in @fig-distribution-shift-detector reveals when the input population moves from the stable band into the warning band and then the major-shift band. That movement triggers an escalation path that may lead to retraining after performance correlation. At week 41, the service approves and versions a new input reference after validating the changed operating population. The lower PSI thereafter compares traffic with that new reference, not the original one. Changing model weights alone would not reduce input PSI against a fixed reference, and the discontinuity does not establish improved predictions.

title: Per-Request Competence Routing
caption: **Per-Request Competence Routing**: An acceptance gate compares each request's score with threshold $\ResponseThreshold$ and sends it to one of three paths. Accepted requests are answered from the model's prediction; the rest are routed to a stronger model or reviewer or receive a validated safe default. Raising $\ResponseThreshold$ moves the operating point down the risk-coverage curve, lowering selective risk only if the score orders errors well, and every point of coverage given up becomes fallback load that those paths must serve within the latency budget. The curve's shape is illustrative.
alt: Left to right: a request box labeled input x feeds a model box listing prediction f of x, calibrated confidence, and OOD score, which feeds a violet acceptance gate labeled score s of x versus tau. Three arrows leave the gate: green to an Answer box reading s of x at least tau, act on f of x; violet to a Route box reading stronger model or reviewer; red to an Abstain box reading validated safe default. A bracket groups Route and Abstain above the label fallback load, one minus coverage times arrival rate, served within the latency budget. Lower left, an inset plots selective risk rising with coverage, with a dot marking tau and an arrow labeled raise tau pointing toward lower coverage.
context:
$$

Sweeping $\ResponseThreshold$ produces a risk-coverage curve\index{Selective prediction!risk-coverage curve} rather than one accuracy number. Raising the threshold reduces coverage, but lowers accepted-request risk only when the score orders requests by error risk well enough. That relationship must be measured on the deployment population, and the rejected traffic does not disappear. The fallback path needs enough queue, reviewer, or secondary-model capacity to absorb the abstention rate within the original latency and safety budget. If labels arrive days later, the system can monitor scores and fallback load immediately but cannot confirm selective risk until outcomes return. During that delay, rate limits and conservative thresholds can limit exposure, while the default response still requires validation against the application's hazards.

title: Imperceptible Misclassification in GoogLeNet
caption: **Imperceptible Misclassification in GoogLeNet**: Adding a perturbation of $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget = 0.007$ in the sign direction of the loss gradient changes GoogLeNet's prediction from panda (57.7 percent confidence) to gibbon (99.3 percent confidence), although the two images look identical to a person. The attack does not merely flip the label; it leaves the model more confident in the wrong answer than it was in the right one. Source: [@goodfellow2015explaining].
alt: Three-panel demonstration: a panda photograph labeled panda, plus a faint noise pattern scaled by 0.007, equals a visually identical photograph that GoogLeNet labels gibbon.
context:
:::

Adversarial attack categories encode access and cost. A white-box attacker can use gradients directly, a black-box attacker uses surrogate transfer or queries to the target, and a physical attacker must survive cameras, lighting, and distance. With gradient access, a change no person can see is enough to fool an image classifier. A perturbation that follows the sign of the loss gradient ($\AdversarialPerturbationBudget = 0.007$), the fast gradient sign method defined below, flips GoogLeNet's prediction (@fig-adversarial-googlenet) from panda (57.7 percent confidence) to gibbon (99.3 percent confidence). The classifier is left paradoxically more confident in the erroneous label than in the ground truth.

title: Gradient-Based Attack Geometry
caption: **Gradient-Based Attack Geometry**: Around a correctly classified input $\ModelInput$, the dashed square marks every perturbation allowed by the $\ell_\infty$ budget $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$. FGSM moves each coordinate by the full budget in the sign direction of the loss gradient $\nabla_\ModelInput \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$, which lands $\AdversarialExample$ on a corner of that square, the allowed point that maximizes the first-order increase in loss. A step no larger than $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ in any coordinate therefore carries the input across the decision boundary. The class labels are illustrative.
alt: Two-dimensional input space divided by a solid diagonal decision boundary into a true-class region and an other-class region. A clean input x sits inside a dashed square labeled allowed set. A short blue arrow labeled gradient of L points up and to the left from x; a longer red arrow runs from x to the square's upper-left corner, marked x adv equals x plus epsilon times sign of the gradient, which lies across the boundary. A bracket under the square marks its half-width epsilon adv.
context:
In this formulation, $\ModelInput$ denotes the original input, $\AdversarialExample$ is the generated adversarial example, and $\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$ represents the prediction loss evaluated at model parameters $\ModelParameters$ and true label $\ExampleLabel$. The gradient term $\nabla_\ModelInput\LossFunction$ describes local loss sensitivity, $\text{sign}(\cdot)$ extracts each component's sign to maximize the linearized loss within the coordinate-wise budget, and the scalar $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ bounds the maximum allowable perturbation magnitude under the $\ell_\infty$ norm. This single step need not maximize the nonlinear loss or cause misclassification. Image implementations also clip the perturbed input to its valid pixel range. The subscript distinguishes this adversarial radius from other uses of $\Glyph{\epsilon}$ in the book, such as the differential-privacy budget.

Geometrically, moving along the sign vector of $\nabla_\ModelInput\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$ carries input $\ModelInput$ to a corner of the bounding cube defined by the $\ell_\infty$ budget $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$, producing $\AdversarialExample$. In the illustration of @fig-gradient-attack, that corner lies across the decision boundary in the adjacent class region. A different boundary or gradient need not produce a successful attack within the same budget.

title: Adversarial Stickers on Stop Signs
caption: **Adversarial Stickers on Stop Signs**: In the cited study, the modified signs achieved targeted misclassification on all tested laboratory images and 84.8 percent of moving-vehicle field-test frames. The gap between those conditions shows why physical attacks must be evaluated across the actual sensing path. Source: [@eykholt2018].
alt: Photo of stop signs with small black and white stickers applied. The signs remain recognizable as stop signs to a person but cause the evaluated classifier to predict a targeted speed-limit class.

title: Standardized Robustness Evaluation of Published Defenses
caption: **Standardized Robustness Evaluation of Published Defenses**: Clean accuracy (gray) and accuracy under AutoAttack (red) for CIFAR-10 defenses on the RobustBench leaderboard by publication year, at a perturbation budget of 8/255 in the $\ell_\infty$ norm. Filled red points trained only on CIFAR-10; hollow points used additional data. The line tracks the best robust accuracy published by each year. Points near zero are defenses that do not withstand the standardized attack. Data from @croce2021robustbench.
alt: Scatter plot of CIFAR-10 accuracy from 0 to 100 percent against publication years 2018 to 2024. Gray clean-accuracy points cluster between about 80 and 95 percent. Red robust-accuracy points spread lower, between about 30 and 75 percent, with a stepped line for the best so far rising from 44 percent in 2018 to about 66 percent in 2020 and 75 percent in 2024. Four red points sit near zero in 2019 and 2020.
context:
```
