From the core Development Team outward through the Organization, Industry, and Government/Society, each surrounding layer enforces norms the inner layers cannot self-impose. External anchors, including ISO AI management standards, fairness testing, model cards, red-teaming, impact assessments, GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific law, bind these layers to practice [@isoiec420012023ai; @gdpr2016; @euaiact2024].
alt: Four nested rectangles around a central AI system box, from outer to inner: government and society, industry, organization, and development team. The tint deepens from the pale outer layer to the inner layer, and the AI system at the center is a dark filled box. Each layer's anchor is written into a gap in its own top boundary, so the norm forms part of the wall: GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific law; ISO standards and external audits; impact assessments and ethical review boards; and fairness testing, model cards, and red-teaming.
context:
:::

The responsibility for ethical system behavior is distributed across multiple constituencies, including industry, academia, civil society, and government. The resulting governance hierarchy surrounds the AI system with four concentric tiers (@fig-human-centered-ai). The development team executes technical controls (fairness testing, model cards, red-teaming). The organization governs operational processes (impact assessments, ethical review boards). Industry establishes consensus baselines (ISO standards, external audits). Government and society enforce legal boundaries (GDPR, the EU AI Act, sector-specific statutes) [@shneiderman2022human; @shneiderman2020]. Within organizations, this distribution must be mirrored by mechanisms that connect technical design with strategic oversight and operational control. Without these linkages, responsibility becomes diffuse, and well-intentioned efforts may be undermined by systemic misalignment.

title: A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop
caption: **A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop**: In the conversational arrangement (A), the model answers and the developer runs every tool and carries each error back by hand. In the agentic arrangement (B), the runtime assembles context, receives the model's proposal, and dispatches only actions it grants; the model holds no authority, and verifier evidence returns to the runtime rather than to the model's own report.
alt: Two panels with the same layout and a dashed line separating the proposing tier above from the acting tier below. Panel A, A person closes the loop: a model endpoint labeled answers only sits above the line; a developer labeled carries everything sits below it, sends prompt plus error up to the endpoint and receives a patch, runs commands in a local terminal, and receives the error back. Panel B, A runtime closes the loop: a foundation model labeled holds no authority sits above the line; an agent runtime labeled grants each action sits below it, sends context up and receives a proposal, dispatches to an isolated sandbox along a violet arrow and receives an observation, and the sandbox feeds verifiers labeled tests, linters, whose evidence returns to the runtime.
section: From a Useful Proposal to an Accepted Task {#sec-vol3-intro-existence-moment}
context:
An agentic system comes into existence when software closes this interaction loop. Rather than relying on an engineer to copy prompts and error traces back and forth, the surrounding software feeds the foundation model an objective alongside fresh environmental observations and captures the model's proposed action. It then dispatches that action and returns structured execution feedback to guide the next decision.

The surrounding software, the **runtime**\index{Runtime (agent)!definition}, enforces the boundary between what the model proposes and what the environment executes. All execution authority resides with the runtime. Because a model outputs only text or token streams, generating an operation's name confers no permission to run it. The runtime parses the proposed action, checks that it complies with current access policies, and dispatches the call through a designated tool. A **tool**\index{Tool!definition} provides a structured interface to an environmental action, such as reading file contents, editing source code, running a shell command, or running a test suite. The part of the runtime that drives this loop is often called the agent harness, and @sec-vol3-agent-harness develops it as a component of the runtime rather than a separate system. @Fig-vol3-open-vs-closed-loop-control sets the two arrangements side by side. In panel A a developer carries every command and every error by hand; in panel B the runtime dispatches only the actions it grants and routes verifier evidence back to itself rather than trusting the model's account of what happened.

title: The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map
caption: **The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map**: The agent stack structured around traditional computing layers (marked with ≈). The live execution loop (top) executes one task trajectory turn by turn. The across-task loop (bottom) compiles evaluated trajectories into updated model policies and coordinates multi-agent scale. While the architectural analogy provides intuition, the chapters develop each subsystem through its own rigorous systems mechanisms.
alt: Map in two bands. The live loop band, one trajectory turn by turn, holds the model, Part I, approximately a processor; agent memory, Part II, approximately a memory hierarchy; the agent runtime, Part IV, approximately an operating system, spanning the band between them; and tool use, Part III, approximately input and output, connected to a dashed environment box. Every arrow passes through the runtime: proposal and context between model and runtime, stored state and record between memory and runtime, validated call and observation between runtime and tools, and effect and result between tools and environment. Below, an across-tasks band holds learning from trajectories, Part V, approximately recompiling, fed by evaluated trajectories and sending updated weights back to the model along a dashed perimeter arrow, and agents at scale, Part VI, approximately scale-out, drawn as a stack of cards fed by many trajectories at once.
context:
The **stochastic computer**\index{Stochastic computer!definition} names that map (@fig-vol3-stochastic-computer-map).[^fn-stored-program-map] Its upper band is the live execution loop of a single task, and its lower band acts across tasks. In the live band, the foundation model plays the processor. Context and external stores play the memory hierarchy, from the active context window to long-term retrieval indices. Tools play input and output. The agent runtime plays the operating system, scheduling model calls, mediating every privileged operation, and enforcing access control. Across tasks, learning from recorded runs plays the role of recompiling a program from measurements of its earlier executions, refining the model's policy without changing the runtime's safety boundaries. Coordinating many agents mirrors scale-out across a network, where agents divide one workload and contend for shared state and resource limits.

[^fn-stored-program-map]: **The Stored-Program Organization**: Von Neumann's 1945 draft report on the EDVAC partitioned a computer into central arithmetic, central control, memory, and input/output organs [@vonneumann1945edvac]. In von Neumann's architecture, central control holds the absolute authority to fetch and execute instructions. In an agentic system, that authority is deliberately inverted: authority resides strictly within the surrounding runtime, while the learned model only proposes actions. Trust is decided outside the processor. \index{Von Neumann architecture!stochastic computer map}

title: The H·S·A Exposure Space
caption: **The H·S·A Exposure Space**: Horizon ($\TurnHorizon$, turns), carried state ($\StateExposureLevel_0$ to $\StateExposureLevel_3$), and authority ($\AuthorityExposureLevel_0$ to $\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$) map the operational departures of an agent from an isolated model call. Plotted positions represent illustrative task configurations rather than intrinsic properties of each workload class. The formal task contract and failure consequences dictate necessary runtime controls. System closure represents the engineering response to these exposures rather than an independent coordinate axis.
alt: Three-axis diagram. Authority runs up the vertical axis in four bands, A0 read only, A1 workspace, A2 compensable, and A3 irreversible, with the A3 band tinted red. Horizon in turns runs along a logarithmic horizontal axis marked 1, 10, 100, and 1,000, with the origin labeled one model call. State runs along a diagonal depth axis from the origin with ticks S0 stateless, S1 context, S2 working copy, and S3 durable. Four workloads are plotted as markers at their horizon and authority, each with a diagonal tail whose length in ticks equals its state level: the support agent (H at most 3, S1, A0), the remediation agent in red (H about 20, S3, A3), the repair agent (H about 100, S2, A1), and the research agent (H at least 1,000, S3, A0).
context:
[^fn-least-privilege-mediation]: **Least Privilege and Complete Mediation**: Saltzer and Schroeder's protection principles state that every program should run with the smallest set of privileges needed to complete its task (least privilege), and that every access to every object should be checked for authority (complete mediation) [@saltzer1975]. Checking capability grants on every tool call applies both principles to a non-deterministic model whose proposals cannot be trusted on their own. Restricting the task's initial capability grant remains the most dependable way to limit damage when runtime verification checks fail to catch an unsafe request. \index{Least privilege!task grant}

The coordinate space in @fig-vol3-hsa-taxonomy maps agentic workloads across three operational exposure axes: horizon ($\TurnHorizon$, turns along the horizontal), authority ($\AuthorityExposureLevel_0$ to $\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$ on the vertical), and carried state ($\StateExposureLevel_0$ to $\StateExposureLevel_3$ on the depth axis). This space serves as an analytical lens rather than a rigid taxonomy: two workloads occupying the same cell may still demand different runtime controls if their data sensitivity, tool reliability, or failure thresholds differ. Changing the execution environment can shift a task into a completely different cell even when its foundation model and turn horizon remain identical, as shown in example \ref{exmp-01-hsa-incident}. The four workloads plotted in the space are the book's lighthouse workloads, described in @sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses.

title: The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle
caption: **The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle**: Each phase marks a change in which component is responsible, not a mandated scheduler. The runtime assembles context, authorizes requests, records outcomes, and assesses progress; the model only proposes, and only an authorized request reaches a tool. A timed-out tool leaves its outcome unknown, and acceptance requires evidence independent of the model's own report, so exhausted limits end in an unresolved outcome or escalation rather than success.
alt: Six phase boxes arranged in a U, each colored and labeled by the component responsible. Top row, left to right: 1 context assembly, runtime; 2 model invocation, model; 3 validate and authorize, runtime, joined by context and proposal arrows. A bold violet authorized arrow descends from phase 3 to the bottom row, which runs right to left: 4 tool execution, tool; 5 observation and evidence, runtime; 6 assess against contract, runtime, joined by outcome and evidence arrows, with a dotted note under the outcome arrow reading unknown if timed out. A dashed red rejected, no execution arrow runs from phase 3 to phase 5 without touching phase 4. Dashed arrows labeled needs approval from phase 3 and wait from phase 6 lead to a dashed wait box labeled resumes, not an exit. A next-turn arrow returns from phase 6 to phase 1, and phase 6 also leads to a green accept deliverable box, evidence meets contract, and a red stop without acceptance box, unresolved or escalate.
section: The six phases of a turn {#sec-vol3-intro-execution-lifecycle}
context:
6. **Assess against contract**: The runtime checks the updated task state against the contract's completion criteria. Depending on the result, it can start another turn, wait on background jobs, ask the user for clarification, stop the trajectory as unresolved, or accept the deliverable. That decision rests on external evidence and remaining budgets rather than the model's own report.

These six phases mark boundaries of responsibility rather than a rigid synchronous schedule. In production, authorized tools may run asynchronously against remote services, and a model call may propose a final answer instead of a tool call. Implementations can overlap independent work, but causality fixes the order of decisions: a runtime cannot authorize an action from observations that arrive after dispatch, and it cannot tell whether an external effect succeeded from the proposal alone. @Fig-vol3-ch01-execution-lifecycle draws the phases as a U in which only an authorized request drops from validation to the tool. Its dashed paths carry the exceptions. A rejected request returns to the observation history as error feedback without touching any tool, approvals and background jobs pause the turn, and assessment at the end of the turn either starts the next turn, accepts the deliverable, or stops without acceptance.

title: The Model Call Surface
caption: **The Model Call Surface**: The request carries messages, tool definitions, and limits into a model with frozen weights, which returns a proposal with a stop reason and usage counts. Every arrow out of the response lands in the agent runtime. The runtime validates and authorizes a tool call before anything runs, returns the result as a new message for the next call, sends a finished answer to verification, and quarantines output cut off at its limit.
alt: Diagram. A request card lists tools and limits above a stack of message slabs labeled system, user, assistant, and tool, the tool slab dashed. An arrow leads to a model box showing tokens y1, y2, y3 drawn one per step with frozen weights, and an arrow leads to a response card with rows for text, tool calls, usage, and a highlighted stop reason row. From the stop reason an arrow drops into an agent runtime region to a route on stop reason box. Its tool call branch goes to validate, authorize, then run in sandbox, and from the sandbox an arrow returns up to the tool slab of the request. Its end of turn branch goes to verify, and its output limit branch goes to a red quarantine box.
context:
Here, `kind` tells the runtime parser how to read the payload. The normalized `status` confirms that transport and generation finished under the adapter's contract, while `stop_reason` records the **stop reason**\index{Stop reason!definition} reported by the serving engine: whether the model emitted a tool-call marker, hit an end-of-sequence token, or stopped at the token limit. The `usage` block counts $\SequenceLength$ input tokens read and $\OutputLength$ output tokens generated. Bare $\SequenceLength$ is sequence length throughout this book, here the prompt a call reads; the State levels $\Glyph{S}_0$ to $\Glyph{S}_3$ always carry their subscript. Tracking usage across calls prevents context-window overflow and feeds cost accounting; if a provider omits token counts, the runtime records usage as missing rather than zero.

Every path out of the response ends in the runtime, and the stop reason chooses the path (@fig-vol3-model-call-surface). A tool call goes to validation and authorization before anything runs, a finished answer goes to verification, and output cut off at its limit goes to quarantine, where it is kept for diagnosis and never executed (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-status-envelope states the rule).

title: One Keyword, Two Token Sequences
caption: **One Keyword, Two Token Sequences**: The same Python line, unindented and indented by four spaces, drawn on one character grid, with a compiler lexer's tokens above the characters and a byte-pair tokenizer's tokens below. The lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword and identifier for both lines. The tokenizer absorbs the fourth space into the keyword, so the indented line opens with two tokens that do not appear in the unindented one; only the four tokens after the keyword are shared. Identifiers are from the `cl100k_base` vocabulary.
alt: Two stacked blocks, unindented and indented by four spaces. Each block shows a row of character cells for the line def get_user_id():, with lexer tokens above and byte-pair tokens below, each token spanning the characters it covers. Lexer tokens are def, get_user_id, open parenthesis, close parenthesis, and colon; the indented line adds a dashed indent token over the four spaces. Byte-pair tokens for the unindented line are def 755, space get 636, _user 3398, _id 851, and parentheses colon 4658, labeled 5 tokens. For the indented line they are three spaces 262, space def 711, and the same four tokens, labeled 6 tokens. Tokens 755, 262, and 711 are filled dark; a dashed line marks where the lexer splits the indent from def, which the 711 token straddles. Brackets below mark the two leading tokens, where the fourth space joins the keyword, and the four tokens shared by both lines.
context:
[^fn-bpe-compression-origin]: **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)**: The algorithm began as a data-compression scheme that repeatedly replaces the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes with an unused symbol [@gage1994bpe]; @sennrich2016subword repurposed the same merge rule to build open vocabularies for neural translation. Because the merges are learned from the training corpus's frequencies, the token cost of a string reflects how common it was in that corpus, so an unusual identifier or path can split into more tokens than a common word of the same length, and the runtime must count rather than estimate. \index{Byte-pair encoding!compression origin}

Indentation alone alters the resulting sequence. Under one widely used byte-pair vocabulary, `cl100k_base`, for example, the unindented line `def get_user_id():` encodes as five tokens beginning with `def` (identifier 755). Indenting that exact line by four spaces yields six tokens: three leading spaces (262), followed by ` def` with the fourth space fused to the keyword (711), and finally the remaining four tokens. A compiler lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword token at both levels; the model instead receives a different opening sequence of integer identifiers, with only the four tokens after the keyword shared (@fig-vol3-token-ast-mismatch).

The runtime outcomes on the left hold regardless of the service; the service outcomes on the right hold only if the service receives and honors the cancel request.

Consider a call with an output allowance of `{python} StreamCancel.k_cap_str` tokens whose stream validator detects a schema violation at step $\RejectionDecodeStep =$ `{python} StreamCancel.k_cut_str`. The runtime's part of the response finishes at once. It records the rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The service's part depends on whether that request is honored (@fig-vol3-streaming-cancellation).

title: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
caption: **Grammar-Constrained Decoding**: A tool schema compiles once into an automaton whose states each carry a token mask. At every step the mask sets illegal tokens to $-\infty$ before normalization, so only a legal continuation can be drawn, and the drawn token advances the automaton. The logit values are illustrative: a fluent but illegal continuation can outscore the legal one and still receive zero probability. A precomputed per-state mask suits a finite-state constraint; nested structures need additional parser state. The strip along the bottom lists what the mask leaves unchecked.
alt: Diagram. Top: a tool schema with query and limit fields compiles into an automaton with states q0, q1, q2, and final state qF, joined by edges labeled opening brace and query. Above each state sits a strip of mask bits; the strips for q0 and q1 show a few legal bits filled, and q0 is highlighted as the current state. A lookup arrow runs from q0 to an operator plus M of q0 between two bar charts. The left chart, logits z_t, shows illustrative scores SELECT +14.2, I think +18.5, opening brace +8.1, and Sure +12.0. The right chart, masked z prime t, shows SELECT, I think, and Sure as dashed outlines marked minus infinity and only the opening brace bar solid at +8.1. The sampled token y_t, an opening brace, feeds an arrow back up to state q1, labeled advance to q1. A dashed strip at the bottom reads not checked by the mask: table exists, values right, call authorized.
context:
Setting the logits of invalid tokens to $-\infty$ forces their sampling probabilities to zero, renormalizing the distribution entirely across viable continuations. Once the sampler draws a token from this restricted set, the engine consumes that token's characters and advances the parser to state $\DecodingConstraintState_{t+1}$. This formulation assumes that $\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$ remains nonempty and that the sampling configuration respects the mask. The engine applies the mask before top-$\TopTokenSampleCount$ or nucleus truncation so that these filters select among legal continuations. If an implementation instead truncates first and no retained token belongs to $\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$, the serving runtime must raise an explicit constraint-satisfaction error rather than silently disabling the mask. Positive finite temperature rescales the remaining probabilities without removing their support.

Recomputing $\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$ from scratch at every step would cost a scan of the whole vocabulary per token. Engines therefore compile the tool schema once into an automaton whose states each carry a precomputed mask $\LogitMask(\DecodingConstraintState_t)$, so that each step is a lookup followed by a state transition [@willard2023outlines]. Incremental parsing of this kind yields syntactically valid output even for a language as structured as SQL [@scholak2021picard]. The automaton in @fig-vol3-grammar-constrained-fsm is compiled for a query tool with two fields, `query` and `limit`, rather than for `read_file`; the mechanism is identical.

title: First-Token Accounting
caption: **First-Token Accounting**: A schematic timeline separates server prefill from client time to first token. Here K is the total number of output tokens. Prefill supplies the initial logits; only the remaining output tokens require subsequent generation passes. The later tokens arrive together in an illustrative buffered chunk, so client arrivals do not identify individual service steps. Distances are not measured durations.
alt: Service boxes show queueing, prompt prefill, first-token sampling, and later generation passes. Paths connect the service to the first client token and a later chunk. Separate brackets mark client TTFT and server prefill.
section: Where a call spends its time {#sec-vol3-foundation-model-call-latency-decomposition}
context:
When TTFT includes sampling and delivering the first token, the remaining decode interval covers only the next $\OutputLength-1$ tokens in a completion of length $\OutputLength$. For a streamed reply, adding client-measured TTFT, the $\OutputLength-1$ inter-token intervals, and final deserialization gives the full call latency without double-counting the first token. Client-measured TTFT is larger than server prefill time because it also includes network transit and queueing, and because servers and networks often batch several streamed tokens into one network chunk, chunk arrival times on the client do not always match per-token step times on the accelerator.

The first-token boundary separates these two measurements in @fig-vol3-first-token-accounting. The service produces the initial logits during prefill, but the client must still wait for sampling and delivery before its TTFT interval ends.

title: Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It
caption: **Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It**: Both paths start from the same connection-pool failure. On the left, generation builds on the timeout explanation without any observation that separates it from a missed notification, so the patch can hide the symptom while the defect remains. On the right, a targeted test orders a waiting worker and a returning connection, and its observation contradicts the timeout explanation before any edit. The revised candidate passes the reproducer, which still falls short of task acceptance.
alt: Two lanes below a box reading observed failure, request waits after a connection frees. The left lane, labeled commit first, holds H1 timeout too short with H2 missed notification drawn faded and dashed, then generate on H1 with no new evidence, then a timeout patch applied unchecked, ending in a red box reading symptom masked, notification defect remains. The right lane, labeled check first, holds both H1 and H2, then an amber targeted test observing the waiter still blocked after return, then the hypotheses again with H1 struck through and marked contradicted, then a notify on return patch, the revised candidate from H2, ending in a green box reading reproducer passes, acceptance still pending. A dashed horizontal line labeled first edit crosses both lanes: the left lane reaches it with no check, the right lane only after the test.
context:
This division marks the boundary between model computation and runtime observation. Extra model computation re-evaluates information already present in the prompt. Within a single generation, a model can backtrack and revise an earlier analytical misstep even as the previous tokens remain frozen in its prefix. Pure computation, however, cannot create new empirical facts. Only an executed test reports how the running process behaves, and its conclusions hold only for the conditions and thread schedules that the test harness exercised.

Suppose the targeted test forces an interleaving where one worker thread waits while another returns a connection. The trace shows that the connection enters the pool, yet the waiting worker stays blocked past the notification point. That observation rules out the timeout hypothesis immediately and points the agent toward the signaling path. The agent can then write a patch that repairs the notification logic and test it against the failing reproducer. Passing a targeted reproducer still does not establish full task acceptance, because narrow tests can miss edge cases, and neither an unchecked hypothesis nor an isolated micro-test is enough to ship code to production. Even so, the two paths part ways before any file changes (@fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree). Acting on the first guess hides the symptom and keeps the defect, whereas checking first spends one short test to learn which hypothesis survives.

title: Proxy and Reference Scores under Selection
caption: **Proxy and Reference Scores under Selection**: A qualitative sketch of the measured best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ pattern. The proxy score of the selected candidate keeps rising as $\CandidatePoolSize$ grows, while a held-out reference score rises and then declines. The widening gap illustrates proxy optimism under selection; the declining reference score is an empirical pattern, not a necessary consequence of growing scoring error. The axes carry no values, and the point where the reference score turns down depends on the task.
alt: Line sketch with candidates selected from, N, on a log-scale horizontal axis and score of the selected candidate on the vertical axis, without tick values. A dashed blue curve labeled proxy score rises and flattens. A solid green curve labeled held-out reference follows it at first, peaks near the middle at a marked dot, and then declines. The region between the curves is shaded, a red double-headed arrow at the right labels the gap scoring error of the winner, and a dashed line below the green peak notes that where the decline begins depends on the task.
context:
[^fn-gumbel-tail-growth]: **Extreme-Value Asymptotics**: The form $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation\sqrt{2\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$ is only the leading term of the Gaussian maximum, and convergence is slow, which is why the chapter computes the exact expectation beside it. The Gaussian is also a favorable case. Scoring errors with heavier tails, such as a learned judge that occasionally misjudges badly, push the selected error up faster than $\sqrt{\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$, so the drift in a real pool can exceed this estimate. \index{Extreme value!argmax selection}

A rising scoring error on the winner does not by itself mean that true utility is falling. In Exercise 8(b), independent Gaussian utility and noise make both the winner's expected utility and its expected scoring error rise with pool size. Empirical studies of best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling under learned reward models show a sharper divergence: the proxy score keeps climbing while a held-out reference score rises, flattens, and then drops [@gao2023scaling]. That downturn comes from tail miscalibration or exploitable gaps in the proxy, not from @eq-vol3-argmax-noise alone. @Fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence sketches the pattern, with the winner's proxy score rising (dashed blue curve) while the held-out reference score peaks and turns down (solid green curve).

title: Invalidation and Scoped Regeneration
caption: **Invalidation and Scoped Regeneration**: In (A), the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis. Following the recorded dependency edges marks the patch and check selection for review, while the recorded inputs and the separately derived API notes keep their support. In (B), a new request supplies that supported frontier and regenerates only the diagnosis, patch, and check selection. The graph records candidate artifacts, not executed operations, and each replacement must still pass its own checks. The test inventory that also feeds check selection is omitted.
alt: Two stacked panels with the same dependency graph. Inputs on the left are source excerpt, failure observation, waiter-return test, and API declaration. In panel A, source excerpt and failure observation feed a red diagnosis marked timeout too short, which feeds a patch candidate and then a check selection; source excerpt also feeds the patch candidate. The patch candidate and check selection are drawn with dashed red borders, labeled needs review, inside a dashed region labeled Desc of diagnosis. The waiter-return test points to the diagnosis with a dashed red arrow labeled contradicts. The API declaration feeds API notes labeled support kept. In panel B, a dashed blue region labeled regenerated contains diagnosis prime labeled missed notification, patch candidate prime labeled notify on return, and check selection prime labeled ordering test; the same inputs, now including the waiter-return test, feed diagnosis prime, and API notes are labeled retained.
context:
When an input changes or a premise fails, the runtime marks that node unsupported and walks the directed edges to find every downstream artifact that needs review. If node $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ loses support, the invalidated set is its reachable descendants in the graph: $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode) = \{\ReachableArtifactNode \mid \InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode\}$, where $\InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode$ means a directed path runs from $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ to $\ReachableArtifactNode$. Breadth-first search finds $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ in time linear in the vertices and edges.[^fn-make-rebuild-dependencies] Every node outside $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ keeps its support, including separate subgraphs such as the API compatibility notes. Walking a candidate graph of dozens or hundreds of nodes, like the one in @tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies, takes a negligible fraction of the illustrative `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` needed to decode a single token. The real engineering work is therefore recording the dependency edges accurately rather than traversing them. In the connection-pool repair, the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis, and graph traversal marks its descendants (the patch and check selection) for review. The next call regenerates only the diagnosis and that branch from the retained inputs (@fig-vol3-plan-revision).

[^fn-make-rebuild-dependencies]: **Dependency-Driven Rebuilding**: Build tools solved the same problem for files. Make rebuilds a target only when one of its declared prerequisites is newer than the target [@feldman1979make], and its characteristic failure is the one described here, in which an undeclared dependency leaves a stale target that looks up to date. The saving is only as sound as the recorded edges. \index{Make!dependency tracking}

title: Choosing the Revision Scope
caption: **Choosing the Revision Scope**: Two questions about the new evidence select among three responses. If the artifact's dependents still have what they need, a local repair replaces it alone. If they do not but the task's premises hold, subgraph resynthesis replaces the artifact and its descendants. If a premise has failed, deliberation stops and the task is reported unresolved or escalated. The tiers classify responses by how much support the evidence removes rather than establishing an unconditional preference for minimal edits.
alt: Flowchart. An amber box reading new evidence removes support from an artifact leads to a diamond asking whether dependents' needs are still met. Yes leads down to a card labeled local repair. No leads right to a second diamond asking whether task premises still hold. Yes leads down to a card labeled subgraph resynthesis. No leads by a red arrow to a red card labeled stop deliberation. Each card draws the same small dependency graph, a premise square feeding a chain of three artifact nodes and one side node. In local repair only the first chain node is filled and outlined as replaced, with the caption replace one artifact. In subgraph resynthesis the whole chain is filled and outlined, with the caption replace artifact plus descendants. In stop deliberation the premise square is red and every node is dashed, with the caption report unresolved or escalate. An arrow along the bottom runs from less support removed to more support removed.
section: Choosing how much of a plan to regenerate {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-revision-mechanics}
context:
1. A **local repair**\index{Local repair!definition} replaces a single node while keeping its interface and contracts unchanged so that its dependents stay valid, such as fixing a malformed shell flag in a test command without changing what the test checks.
2. A **subgraph resynthesis**\index{Subgraph resynthesis!definition} replaces a node and all of its descendants, feeding the model the intact upstream frontier and asking it to rebuild the path to the goal. In the connection-pool repair, this replaces the diagnosis, patch, and test selection while keeping the source excerpt and API compatibility notes.
3. **Stopping deliberation**\index{Stopping deliberation!definition} applies when new evidence refutes a premise of the task itself, such as a missing host library or credentials without write access. No plan revision can fix a broken task premise, so the runtime stops deliberating and escalates or reports the task unresolved instead of spending more tokens.

title: Where Each Search Structure Prunes
caption: **Where Each Search Structure Prunes**: Best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ generates complete candidates independently and discards all but the selected one only at the end. Beam search generates the beam width times the extensions per candidate at each step, scores them, and keeps the beam width. Tree search expands the leaf its selection rule favors, evaluates it, and updates visit counts and value estimates along the path to the root. The drawings show structure only; the pool size, beam width, and depth are illustrative.

Beam: a prompt node branches into two nodes, each of which generates two children; a dashed line labeled score, keep 2 marks two children pruned, the two survivors each generate two more, and a second dashed line labeled keep 2 marks two retained and two pruned. title: Stopping Precedence
caption: **Stopping Precedence**: Before admitting more work, the runtime tests three conditions in a fixed order. A hard ceiling on tokens, calls, depth, or time stops new admissions, preserving any already acceptable candidate for the acceptance decision. Within the ceilings, a candidate that meets the acceptance criteria ends search and goes to the acceptance decision, which stopping does not itself make. Only then does the marginal rule compare the gain per unit cost with $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$. A stop without an acceptable candidate is reported as incomplete or escalated, never returned as accepted.
alt: Flowchart. A box reading before admitting more work leads to three diamonds in sequence: 1, hard ceiling reached; 2, acceptance criteria met; 3, gain per cost below epsilon stop. A no from the first two passes to the next diamond. A no from the third leads up to a box reading admit next work, which loops back to the start. Each yes leads down to an outcome card: stop new work, listing tokens, calls, depth, and time and reading keep acceptable candidate, else incomplete or escalate; stop search, reading return the candidate for the acceptance decision; and stop early, reading further work not worth its cost, report incomplete or escalate.
context:
The numerator measures the gain in the estimated chance of a verified pass, not the number of new candidates or a rise in a heuristic score. The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) explains why, since generating more candidates and obtaining a verified solution are distinct events. A search whose calibrated chance of passing stays flat is burning budget without making progress, no matter how many tokens it emits. The threshold $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$ is an economic choice set by the value of an automated fix relative to human escalation, net of checker error and delay; high failure costs never justify searching longer against an untrustworthy check.

For satisficing workloads, the runtime applies these three stopping checks in a fixed order before admitting any new work (@fig-vol3-stopping-boundaries). First, hard ceilings on tokens, calls, depth, or wall-clock time stop new admissions unconditionally; if an acceptable candidate is already in hand it goes to the acceptance gate, and otherwise the runtime abstains or escalates. Second, within the ceilings, any candidate that meets the acceptance criteria stops the search and goes to the acceptance gate. Third, when the ceilings still have room and no candidate has passed yet, the marginal stopping rule (@eq-vol3-marginal-stopping) stops the search early if the next round's expected gain per dollar falls below $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$. Reversing this order would either let an optimistic gain estimate breach a hard ceiling or let a diminishing-returns check discard a candidate that already passed. Whichever condition ends the search, the runtime settles all open reservations and separates verified passes from unverified attempts.

title: Selection Protects the State Budget
caption: **Selection Protects the State Budget**: Each bar is one serialized request, stacked by the four terms of @eq-vol3-context-budget-partition beneath the input limit $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$, with the output reserve $\OutputLimit$ hatched above it. Appending every tool result (A) lets $\ObservationTokenCount$ grow until it displaces the task state the next decision needs. Selection (B) keeps each term's share by moving older results into retained records outside the request, where a handle can reach them if a later decision needs them. Segment heights are schematic, not measured token counts.
alt: Two panels of stacked vertical bars for turns t, t plus 1, and t plus 2, on a shared scale with a dashed input limit S max minus K max and a hatched output reserve up to S max. Each bar stacks gray system and tools segments, a green state segment, and amber observation slices, one slice per tool result. In panel A, append every result, the bars hold two, four, and six slices and the state segment shrinks until it turns red at turn t plus 2, labeled state squeezed. In panel B, select for the next step, all three bars hold two slices and an unchanged state segment, labeled state keeps its share; an arrow moves older slices into a violet retained-records stack of four slices outside the bars, and a dashed arrow labeled retrieve by handle returns to the last bar.
context:
[^fn-react-appended-observations]: **Interleaved Observations**: ReAct prompting interleaves reasoning traces, tool actions, and observation payloads within an ever-expanding prompt transcript [@yao2023react]. While keeping full execution history visible simplifies early prototyping, it carries a steep cost, because the unchecked growth of $\ObservationTokenCount$ consumes prompt capacity and raises input token costs on every subsequent call. \index{ReAct!appended observations}

@Eq-vol3-context-budget-partition is a planning budget rather than an exact identity, because sub-word tokenization across joined strings does not equal the sum of separately tokenized parts. The runtime must therefore check the assembled wire request against the provider's limit, and when the request runs over, the budget partition tells the runtime which share (usually the observation buffer or older history) to trim or compact first. Prompt staging (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging) then orders these same four components by how often they change so the serving engine can reuse their cached prefix.

title: Reuse Ends at the First Changed Token
caption: **Reuse Ends at the First Changed Token**: Three consecutive requests follow the root, trunk, and leaf order of @tbl-vol3-context-zone-stratification, with the output reserve $\OutputLimit$ beyond the input limit $\ContextWindow-\OutputLimit$. A new observation changes only the leaf, so the root and trunk remain a reusable prefix. Refreshing the trunk to r18 moves the first changed token to the end of the root, and every later token is processed again. The figure assumes compatible cached state on the serving side; an identical prefix alone does not guarantee reuse.
alt: Three horizontal request bars labeled call n cold start, call n plus 1 new observation, and call n plus 2 trunk refreshed. Each bar has root, trunk, and leaf segments with tick marks for token positions, followed by a hatched output reserve past a dotted line labeled S max minus K max. In call n every segment is marked processed. In call n plus 1 the root and the trunk at r17 are marked prefix reused, and a red dashed line labeled first changed token sits at the leaf boundary, with the first leaf token outlined in red. In call n plus 2 only the root is reused, the trunk is at r18, and the red dashed line and outlined token sit at the root boundary. Headers name the zones above an arrow running from changes rarely to changes every call.
context:
Because causal self-attention computes each token's keys and values from all preceding tokens, a single changed token near the beginning of a request invalidates the cached key-value (KV) attention state for every later position, even when thousands of trailing tokens are identical. Serving engines equipped with prefix caching[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse] skip redundant prefill computation only across an identical leading token sequence, because attention state is derived from the token prefix (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}). Ordering the zones by change rate is what turns this rule into savings. A call that changes only the leaf reuses the root and trunk, whereas a compaction that rewrites the trunk ends reuse at the root boundary and forces recomputation of every later token (@fig-vol3-context-zones).

[^fn-automatic-prefix-reuse]: **Automatic Prefix Reuse**: Serving systems such as SGLang index cached attention state by token prefix within a radix tree, allowing an incoming request that shares an existing token prefix to reuse cached KV blocks transparently [@zheng2024sglang]. Because radix tree lookups evaluate exact token equality rather than semantic equivalence, two requests that diverge on an early timestamp share zero cache entries past that offset. Layout discipline directly determines cache hit rates. \index{Prefix cache!radix tree}

title: Invalidation Follows Recorded Dependencies
caption: **Invalidation Follows Recorded Dependencies**: Each staged observation carries the binding $\ObservationBinding(\TrajectoryObservation_{t})$ of @eq-vol3-observation-binding, and each derived entry holds an edge to the observations it depends on. When the patch writes src/pool.py from r17 to r18, propagation marks the source excerpt and the controlled test run historical and flags the missed-notification hypothesis for reassessment. The documentation excerpt and the note derived from it keep their status because nothing they depend on changed. A historical observation remains evidence about r17; the marking removes only its support for claims about r18.

Middle, staged observations bound by lambda of o: o1 source excerpt at pool.py r17 and o2 controlled test run at r17, both marked historical, and o3 documentation excerpt at pool.md r17 marked unchanged. Right, derived entries: missed-notification hypothesis marked reassess with a red border, and API usage note marked unchanged. Red arrows run from src/pool.py to o1 and o2 and from o1 and o2 to the hypothesis; gray arrows connect tests/test_pool.py to o2 and the documentation chain. The historical observations and the reassess hypothesis are drawn unfilled with colored borders, while the unchanged documentation excerpt and note keep their amber and green tints. A dashed red L-shaped region labeled reached by the write encloses src/pool.py, o1, o2, and the hypothesis, leaving tests/test_pool.py and the documentation row outside.
context:
where $\ObservationBinding(\TrajectoryObservation_{t})$ records the artifact identifier, its kind (source file, test run, daemon process, or build output), the revision observed, the byte range or symbol read, and a cryptographic hash of the content. Derived entries (working hypotheses and test summaries) hold directed edges to each supporting observation, forming the in-memory dependency graph.[^fn-truth-maintenance-system] Propagation follows the plan-graph traversal with one difference made possible by the binding: a tool write marks its directly bound observations historical rather than unsupported, and only the conclusions downstream of them are flagged for reassessment. Running this propagation when the patch writes `r18` produces the right-hand column of @tbl-vol3-context-tracking-schemas, while an excerpt of `docs/pool.md` and the API usage note built from it keep their status because nothing they depend on changed (@fig-vol3-invalidation-graph).

[^fn-truth-maintenance-system]: **Invalidation Is Not Retraction**: A truth maintenance system [@doyle1979truth] retracts a belief when its premise fails, which suits a candidate plan whose refuted diagnosis should simply disappear. An executed observation is different, because the `r17` failure stays true of `r17`. The runtime graph therefore marks an affected observation historical, removing only its support for current-state claims, and reserves retraction for derived conclusions such as a hypothesis. \index{Truth maintenance system!invalidation}

The worked estimate uses a representative configuration: the Llama 3 70B model geometry, with `{python} KvGeometry.params_str` parameters, and a DGX H100 node containing `{python} KvGeometry.n_acc_str` accelerators. While specific hardware platforms and checkpoint dimensions vary, the underlying capacity arithmetic remains unchanged. Unlike the single-device, 8-bit illustration in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-per-call-work-estimate, both weights and KV cache tensors use 16-bit storage here, with the model weights sharded across the node's accelerators by tensor parallelism. The aggregate high-bandwidth memory remaining after provisioning model weights and a runtime reserve constitutes the **KV pool**\index{KV pool!definition}. The number of active sequences whose KV payloads can reside simultaneously within this pool defines the **resident-fit bound**\index{Resident-fit bound!definition}. This aggregate derivation assumes perfectly balanced shards without redundant weight replication; in production, memory limits must be satisfied on every individual accelerator device. None of the r18 context's internal structure survives into this accounting. System prompt, tool schemas, workspace state, turn history, and latest observation all become key and value tensors at every layer, so the whole `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str`-token context costs `{python} KvGeometry.kv_agent_str` whatever its zones contain (@fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy). The figure's zones follow the change-rate order of context staging. Its shared invariant prefix is the root of instructions and tool schemas together with the slow-changing workspace description, its growing trajectory state is the rest of the trunk, and its active turn is the leaf.
