title: The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log
caption: **The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log**: The record in runtime memory (top) is lost on a crash; the durable, append-only log (bottom) is not. Folding the logged events through a deterministic reducer, starting from the initial record $\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0$, rebuilds the recorded projection $\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_j$ at boundary $\LogPositionIndex$ without calling the model or any tool. Because the log ends at the test's recorded intent with no recorded result, the reconstructed record keeps the admission and reservation and marks the test unresolved rather than inventing its outcome.
alt: Two regions. Top region, runtime memory lost on a crash, drawn with a dashed border: an initial record R zero with rows for task, grants, limits and no admitted operations; a deterministic reducer applying apply of R and e with no model or tool call; and a reconstructed record R j with rows admission held, reservation held, and a dashed red row test r18 unresolved. Bottom region, the durable append-only trajectory log, drawn as a contiguous tape of cells labeled e1 TaskStarted, e2 ContextBuilt, e3 ModelReplied, e4 Authorized and BudgetReserved, and e j ToolIntent test r18, then a vertical line labeled boundary j and a dashed cell for a ToolResult that was not recorded. An arrow labeled fold, in log order runs up from the log to the reducer, and a red dotted line links the unrecorded ToolResult to the unresolved row.
context:
In this formulation, $\LogPositionIndex$ indexes the durable log sequence boundary rather than the interaction turn $\TurnIndex$. Given deterministic reducer semantics and complete event payloads, folding reconstructs the precise control state without invoking the foundation model or re-executing external tools. This architecture embodies the classic **event sourcing**\index{Event sourcing!definition} pattern [@kleppmann2017designing]: historical decisions serve as deterministic inputs to state reconstruction, while unrecorded events remain explicitly unknown. If the latest durable log entry indicates that a test execution was authorized and dispatched, but contains no corresponding completion event, the reconstructed state marks that operation as unresolved (@fig-vol3-event-sourcing). For the worksheet crash, the fold keeps the held reservation and the dispatched `test_r18` intent, and it invents no outcome for the test.

[^fn-append-log-lineage]: **Append-Only Log as Primary Record**: Rosenblum and Ousterhout's log-structured file system treated the sequential log as the primary on-disk data structure, boosting write throughput and simplifying crash recovery [@rosenblum1992lfs]. A trajectory log inherits these exact advantages: append operations never overwrite historical evidence required by future recovery passes, so a recovering worker can reconstruct state by streaming an ordered log rather than untangling conflicting in-place updates. \index{Log-structured file system!append-only trajectory log}

title: Intent Before Dispatch
caption: **Intent Before Dispatch**: The runtime validates a proposal, admits it with a reservation, and waits for the intent's acknowledgment under the declared failure domain before dispatch carries the request past the durability barrier. Where a crash falls determines the recovery state of @tbl-vol3-durable-recovery-states. Before the worker receives the acknowledgment, dispatch is withheld, but the intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. An absent intent establishes non-dispatch only when the authoritative prefix is complete. Between the acknowledgment and adequate recorded evidence, including a crash before dispatch, the operation is in doubt; a pending or timeout observation leaves it there. After correlated outcome evidence is recorded, the outcome is established within the endpoint's contract.
alt: A row of five ordered event boxes: e prop, proposal; e auth, admission; e flush, intent ack; a ext, dispatch, in amber; and e obs, evidence. A dashed vertical line labeled durability barrier separates e flush from a ext, with runtime can still withhold on its left and request may have left on its right. Below, a time axis is marked at e flush and e obs, and three bands show the recovery state if the crash falls there: a gray band before e flush, not dispatched, intent may be durable; a red band from e flush to e obs, in doubt, withhold dependent work, which the barrier line crosses; and a green band after e obs, established, per endpoint contract.
context:
$$ {#eq-vol3-wal-ordering}

In @eq-vol3-wal-ordering, $\ValidatedProposalEvent$ is the validated complete proposal, $\AdmissionDecisionEvent$ is the admitted authorization and reservation decision, and $\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent$ acknowledges its recoverable `ToolIntent` and required preceding records under the declared failure domain. The action $\ExternalDispatchAction$ is dispatch, not endpoint completion. The event $\EvidenceRecordEvent$ is the later durable recording of received evidence, whose status may still be pending, partial, or unknown. The ordering constrains the events that occur; an attempt can stop before dispatch or never produce evidence. Its payoff is that the position of a crash in this sequence determines what recovery may conclude (@fig-vol3-intent-before-dispatch). A crash before the worker receives $\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent$ means the attempt was never dispatched, but an intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. Recovery must inspect the complete authoritative prefix to determine whether that intent survived. A crash after $\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent$ but before adequate outcome evidence becomes durable leaves an **in-doubt action**\index{In-doubt action!definition}, an admitted operation whose outcome the surviving evidence cannot settle. This includes a crash before dispatch or after a pending or timeout observation. It is the tool layer's uncertain outcome (definition \ref{dfn-uncertain-outcome}) seen from the recovery side, and it is what the fold of @sec-vol3-durable-execution-log-evidence marked unresolved. Only recorded, correlated evidence establishes an outcome.

title: A Recoverable Checkpoint Cut
caption: **A Recoverable Checkpoint Cut**: The record and workspace on the left refer to the same committed boundary. Payload durability precedes manifest publication; restoration then folds the recorded suffix while preserving unresolved operations and their reservations. The right-hand pair is invalid because the newer record refers to bytes absent from the older workspace. Recovery must reject that pair and use a compatible published checkpoint with an available suffix.
alt: On the left, record and workspace snapshots join at durable payload storage, followed by manifest publication, suffix folding, and a retained pending test and reservation. On the right, a newer record and older workspace lead to a rejected recovery pair.
context:
Snapshot publication must strictly follow data availability. The runtime first captures the consistent state and flushes all underlying bytes to durable storage within the failure domain. Only after those bytes are durable does the runtime commit the manifest or append a `Checkpoint` event to the authoritative log, marking the snapshot eligible for recovery. If a host crashes during capture, the recovery supervisor ignores the incomplete snapshot and falls back to the previous published checkpoint and its subsequent log suffix. Background cleanup can safely reclaim unreferenced staging files, provided garbage collection protects any artifacts still referenced by active recovery paths. Operating systems and storage engines frequently offer copy-on-write snapshots (file-system subvolume snapshots or process-level memory forks) to freeze point-in-time state with near-zero latency; however, serializing and offloading those blocks to independent durable storage remains a necessary second phase.

The publication order in @fig-vol3-checkpoint-consistent-cut makes the recovery boundary explicit. A compatible pair becomes eligible only after its payload bytes are durable and its manifest has entered the authoritative history.

title: Live Execution vs. Replay
caption: **Live Execution vs. Replay**: In live execution (top), each turn samples the model, passes its proposal through the authorization gate, dispatches the tool, and appends every step to the log. In replay (bottom), the model client is stubbed and tool dispatch is disconnected, so recorded replies and results stream into the harness and any request the log does not account for stops the replay. Folding those events reconstructs the recorded projection, and running harness logic against them is regression replay. A counterfactual branch differs from both, because after restoring its starting state it obtains new observations from compatible fixtures or isolated execution.
alt: Two panels with the same row of boxes: harness, model, authorization gate, and tools. Top panel, live execution: solid arrows run harness to model to gate to tools, a loop labeled next turn returns to the harness, and downward arrows from every box append ContextBuilt, ModelReplied, Authorized, ToolIntent, and ToolResult cells to a trajectory log tape. Bottom panel, replay: the model, labeled stubbed, and the tools, labeled disconnected, are dashed gray boxes; the link from the gate to the tools ends in a red bar labeled unlogged request: stop; and the same log cells feed a line that streams up into the replaying harness.
context:
: **Three uses of a recorded trajectory**: Reconstructing history, testing code, and exploring alternative execution paths answer distinct engineering questions. None establishes an unobserved external outcome. {#tbl-vol3-replay-comparison}

The first two modes make the same change to live execution. Where a live turn samples the model, passes the authorization gate, and dispatches the tool, replay disconnects the model and the tools and streams recorded replies and observations from the log into the harness (@fig-vol3-replay-mode). They differ in what runs on those recorded inputs.

title: Registration Before Dispatch, Release After Evidence
caption: **Registration Before Dispatch, Release After Evidence**: The forward lane records the cleanup obligation before `provision_test_env_r18` is sent, and binds `env_r18_01` only when correlated evidence arrives; a lost reply leaves the obligation open with an owner instead of guessing a target. The dashed link shows the binding supplying the target of the registered cleanup. In the cleanup lane, `release_test_env_r18` waits for its predecessors, and its own outcome either closes the obligation or remains owned, so no path ends in an assumed clean state.
alt: Two stacked panels. The top panel, forward operation, shows three boxes left to right: register obligation, target unbound; dispatch provision_test_env_r18; and bind on evidence, env_r18_01. A red arrow labeled reply lost leads from dispatch to a dotted box, outcome unknown, obligation open, owned. The lower panel, registered cleanup, receives two purple links into a release box for release_test_env_r18: a solid link labeled registers from register obligation, and a dashed link labeled binds target from bind on evidence. Test ended or cancel confirmed and artifacts preserved outside the environment both feed the release box, while a separate scratch removal box has no dependency and no connections. Release branches by a green arrow to obligation closed, postcondition shown, and by a red arrow to a dotted box, retained, owned, release unconfirmed.
context:
signifies that compensating operation $\SagaCompensatingStep_j$ must establish its declared settlement conditions before $\SagaCompensatingStep_k$ is permitted to dispatch. Declared cleanup dependencies must form a directed acyclic graph (DAG); cyclical dependencies represent contradictory recovery requirements that demand explicit operator intervention rather than an arbitrary stack ordering.

In our temporary environment scenario, an active integration test may still be executing when a failure is detected. Confirming that the test process has stopped, or canceling it and verifying that it stopped, must precede `release_test_env_r18`. Similarly, extracting and preserving diagnostic test artifacts outside the sandbox must occur before deprovisioning the virtual machine. By contrast, removing an unrelated local scratch directory can proceed independently, provided no active test or pending evidence collection depends on it. The cleanup graph answers what must happen first, settlement rules determine what has been empirically verified, and admission control determines which operations may run next. The graph cannot be sequenced until provisioning evidence has bound its target, which is why @fig-vol3-saga-flow draws the release ordering beneath the registration step it depends on.

title: Recovery Decision Order
caption: **Recovery Decision Order**: Evidence class comes first, because an unknown outcome admits only a retry of the same operation under its repeat contract (a result-recovery probe or a wait gathers evidence that moves the outcome out of this branch rather than acting on it), while a rejected proposal or an established effect opens new proposals, repair, and compensation. Admissibility then removes candidates that lack authority, allowance with the finalization reserve intact, or time; if none remain, the runtime holds or escalates. Expected cost at a matched endpoint chooses only among the admissible survivors, and applies separately to seconds and dollars.
alt: Top-to-bottom flowchart drawn as three stacked horizontal gates crossed by vertical lanes. A box labeled failure evidence recorded leads to gate 1, evidence class, what is known about the effect. Gate 1 feeds two dashed groups: outcome unknown, which covers one lane, and rejected or established, which covers three lanes. All four lanes pass down through gate 2, admissibility, listing authority, allowance with finalization reserve, and deadline; below it the lanes turn dashed and are labeled survivors only. They continue through gate 3, expected cost at a matched endpoint, repair first when p exceeds C repair over C fallback, per axis in seconds and dollars, and the lanes leaving it are labeled ranked by cost. The lanes end in four boxes: retry same operation under outcome unknown, and new proposal, repair using feedback, and compensate under rejected or established. A red arrow labeled none admissible leaves gate 2 on the right and runs down to a fifth box, hold or escalate.
context:
$$\RepairSuccessProbability > \RepairSuccessProbability^* = \frac{\RepairAttemptCost}{\FallbackCost}.$$ {#eq-vol3-repair-breakeven}

Engineers must evaluate this comparison independently for latency (in seconds) and monetary expense (in model dollars), as their respective break-even thresholds $\RepairSuccessProbability^*$ often diverge. If $\RepairAttemptCost \ge \FallbackCost$, no success probability below one can make repair cheaper on that resource axis. Furthermore, if a failed repair alters residual side effects, extends resource holding times, or increases fallback complexity, the term $(1-\RepairSuccessProbability)\FallbackCost$ must be replaced by the corresponding conditional fallback cost. Expected cost is the last of three gates, not the first. Evidence class decides which candidates exist at all, admissibility removes those that authority, allowance, or the deadline forbids, and only then does @eq-vol3-repair-breakeven rank the survivors; @fig-vol3-recovery-decision-tree lays out that order.

title: From Recurrence to Guarded Response
caption: **From Recurrence to Guarded Response**: Four observations of the repair alternate between two versions of the same change with the same test failure, so $\CurrentStateDigest = \OscillationPriorStateDigest$ and @eq-vol3-state-recurrence reports period $\StateRecurrencePeriod = 2$. Equal digests establish equality of the captured projection only, and a deliberate backtrack can produce the same pattern. title: Scoped Breaker Transitions
caption: **Scoped Breaker Transitions**: The breaker trips from `CLOSED` to `OPEN` only when the window holds at least $\BreakerMinimumSampleCount$ classified outcomes and their failure fraction reaches $\BreakerTripThreshold$, as in @eq-vol3-breaker-trip. After the cooldown, one probe slot is claimed atomically; only a result from the current generation may close the breaker, while a failed probe reopens it, advances `breaker_generation`, and lengthens the cooldown up to its cap. A late result from an older generation settles its own operation in the operation table and changes no breaker state. Thresholds and cooldowns are policy parameters.
alt: State diagram inside a dashed boundary labeled one dependency scope. Three state boxes: CLOSED, ordinary guards; OPEN, new calls withheld; HALF_OPEN, one probe slot. A red arrow from CLOSED to OPEN is labeled W size at least n min and r at least r trip. An amber arrow from OPEN to HALF_OPEN is labeled T cool elapsed, slot claimed atomically. A green arrow from HALF_OPEN to CLOSED is labeled current-generation probe succeeds. A red arrow from HALF_OPEN back to OPEN is labeled probe fails or times out, advance breaker_generation, lengthen cooldown. Below the boundary, a dotted box, late probe result from an older generation, has a dashed arrow to a box labeled operation table, settles, no transition. Beside it, the update T cool becomes the minimum of twice T cool and T cool max sits above five same-color horizontal bars, labeled per failed probe, with a downward arrow marking successive failed probes; the bars double in length and then stop at a dashed line labeled cap.
context:
ensuring that an uncooperative or persistently degraded dependency receives geometrically fewer probe attempts up to the ceiling $\MaximumBreakerCooldownInterval$. If a delayed response from an earlier probe generation eventually succeeds, that late arrival can settle its own operation record and its charges, but the generation guard prevents it from closing the newly reopened breaker or usurping a newer trial's slot.

A probe is a concrete network operation, not a cost-free diagnostic abstraction. It must pass normal admission checks and follow a safe operational contract. A supported read-only status query serves well as a probe; issuing a resource-creation request under the label of a health probe risks creating orphaned remote state. Moreover, because a successful probe proves only that the service handled a single isolated request, the gateway must restore regular traffic gradually under rate-limiting and concurrency constraints. @Fig-vol3-circuit-breakers illustrates transitions across the three breaker states (`CLOSED`, `OPEN`, `HALF_OPEN`). Failure rates trip the breaker, atomic probe slots govern trial execution, generation counters fence out late responses, and consecutive probe failures double the cooldown interval ($\BreakerCooldownInterval$) up to its maximum ceiling.

```
title: Trial Sandbox and Grading Boundary
caption: **Trial Sandbox and Grading Boundary**: The agent under test edits and runs checks inside a single-use fixture whose base image is shared read-only and whose writes land in a per-trial copy-on-write layer; external egress is blocked, and service fixtures stand in for the dependencies the task declares. context:

A robust grading architecture must enforce two distinct security boundaries: the live agent's access during task execution and the submitted artifact's execution reach during evaluation. In @fig-vol3-eval-gym-architecture, an external trusted controller manages evaluation logic, holds the private test suites, and commits results to a secure database, while candidate code executes inside a strictly sandboxed runner. The controller orchestrates testing over a narrow, well-defined remote procedure call (RPC) interface and strictly enforces a patch-admission policy specifying which repository files the candidate was permitted to touch. It treats all candidate-generated stdout, stderr, and exit codes as untrusted observations.
```

title: Verdict-Aware Trace Selection
caption: **Verdict-Aware Trace Selection**: Trace bodies pass a fallible minimization boundary into a bounded buffer that holds them until task verdicts, which can arrive late, reach the selector. Selection applies a declared precedence among the classes of @tbl-vol3-tail-sampling-policies, keeps inclusion probabilities with retained traces, and discards unselected bodies. Every admitted trial also enters the accounting record directly, together with recorded drops, evictions, and truncation, so the denominator does not depend on which bodies survived. Assigning high retention priority protects failure traces under moderate load, though severe buffer saturation can still force evictions before verdicts arrive.
alt: Left-to-right flow diagram. An admitted-trials box sends traces through a dashed amber capture boundary, labeled minimize, redact, into a green bounded buffer drawn as a row of eight slots, some shaded red for failures, some dashed for pending verdicts, one gray, the rest plain, held until verdict. One plain slot drops below the buffer, labeled evicted. The buffer feeds a selection precedence ladder that also receives late task verdicts from above. Its four numbered rungs are failed or violation, shaded red; pending or unknown, dashed; accepted, slow or costly, gray; and ordinary accepted, plain, matching the slot styles. The ladder sends selected traces to a violet trace store that keeps inclusion probability and, from its bottom edge, unselected traces to a dashed discarded box. Along the bottom, a violet evaluation accounting record spans the width, receiving an arrow labeled every trial straight from admitted trials and a red dashed arrow from the evicted slot labeled drops, evictions, truncation.
context:
:::

Physical buffer limits inevitably govern this architecture. Buffer managers must enforce four concurrent bounds: active trace count, aggregate byte volume, individual trace size limits, and maximum staging age. Sizing from averages, such as mean concurrent traces multiplied by mean trace size, is a frequent engineering trap, because cascading failures typically produce bursts of unusually long, tool-heavy trajectories that quickly exhaust buffer memory. Telemetry systems must expose real-time metrics for head-dropped records, buffer evictions, and span truncations broken down by cohort and selection class. Without this visibility, correlated loss during incidents will silently purge the exact failure traces engineers need to diagnose system outages. Furthermore, while deferred tail selection curtails long-term downstream storage, it does not reduce the network ingress and memory needed to buffer traces prior to selection, and strict privacy restrictions apply to these staging buffers as well. The accounting record therefore sits outside the buffer (@fig-vol3-tail-sampling-pipeline). Every admitted trial enters it directly, together with every recorded drop, eviction, and truncation, so the denominator survives whatever the buffer loses.

title: Staged Release and Its Hold Path
caption: **Staged Release and Its Hold Path**: Each stage applies its own criterion: the lower bound of the paired acceptance interval against the declared margin offline, a divergence measure of tool-call drift in shadow execution, and a sequential likelihood-ratio monitor with hard tripwires in the canary. The symbols in the stage boxes are defined in the subsections that follow. A wider release requires every criterion of the declared release gate (@eq-vol3-eval-release-gate). An unmet or inconclusive offline result, a drift review that finds a problem, or a canary alarm leads to the same hold. The hold stops new candidate admission; outstanding candidate operations keep their identities and owners, and recovery, not rollback, settles their effects.
alt: Four stage cards in a row joined by arrows labeled met, beneath a strip showing the live tasks assigned to the candidate at each stage: none for offline trials, copies only for shadow execution, a small amber fraction rho for the canary, and a larger scoped share for the release decision. Stage 1, offline trials, holds L sub delta greater than minus delta sub tol, a paired interval. Stage 2, shadow execution, holds script D sub JS of p sub b and p sub c, tool-call drift. Stage 3, canary, holds Lambda sub n versus b sub low and u, a sequential monitor, with red text for hard tripwires. Stage 4, release decision, holds 1 sub ship equals 1, every gate criterion, scoped next step. Red arrows from stages 1, 2, and 3, labeled not met or inconclusive, problem found, and alarm or tripwire, lead down to one red-outlined hold band, candidate routing stops, containing two boxes: stop new candidate admission, enforced at admission boundaries; and outstanding candidate work, which keeps owners and is settled by recovery, not rollback.
context:
Staging separates evidence available before live execution from evidence that requires it. Offline trials compare configurations on declared fixtures. **Shadow execution**\index{Shadow execution!definition} tests a candidate against authorized copies of current inputs without assigning it the live task. After that, a **canary**\index{Canary release!definition}[^fn-canary-release-origin] assigns a bounded portion of eligible live tasks to the candidate under an explicit release policy. The canary is the ramped online controlled experiment of web services, applied to agent configurations [@kohavi2008]. Each stage answers its own question, and causal and statistical release evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence})\index{Principle!causal and statistical release evidence} supports a scoped decision at each step. Failure at any stage routes to the same enforced admission hold (@fig-vol3-canary-deployment-pipeline), which stops new candidate work while recovery settles the work already in flight. The subsections that follow develop the criterion each stage applies.

[^fn-canary-release-origin]: **Canary Release**: The name borrows from coal miners, who carried canaries underground as an early warning of toxic gas. The analogy holds in one respect and misleads in another: a canary detects a hazard by meeting it first, so a small allocation warns early but does not protect the tasks it exposes. \index{Canary release!etymology}

title: Probes Before Weights
caption: **Probes Before Weights**: Under the default diagnostic route, counterfactual probes evaluate a measured failure in ascending ladder order. A failure that disappears under a probe routes to an immediate systems repair, modifying versioned artifacts that revert cleanly as configuration. Only failures that survive every lower-rung probe reach the weight modification stages, where supervised fine-tuning precedes reinforcement learning. Engineering cost rises and operational reversibility falls from top to bottom.
alt: Flowchart running down a left column from a red measured failure box, recorded failing trace, through three probe boxes: context probe, missing fact supplied; schema probe, rerun with corrected tool description; and runtime probe, clean sandbox, raised limits. Red arrows labeled persists link the probes. From each probe an arrow labeled disappears leads right to a repair box under the heading repair below the weights: repair context, retrieval or assembly; repair tool or schema, schema, docs, or adapter; and repair runtime, bounds, sandbox pool, recovery. A red arrow labeled survives every probe crosses a dashed horizontal boundary to a red residual failure box, plausibly behavioral, which leads on evidence to supervised fine-tuning, curated residual corpus, and then down to reinforcement learning, rollouts, protected reward check, under the heading change the weights. A gray wedge on the far left widens from top to bottom, labeled cheap, reversible at the top and costly, global at the bottom.
context:
The end-to-end argument [@saltzer1984endtoend] yields the same conclusion for tool interfaces: a function belongs where it can be implemented completely and correctly. A typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}) provides enforceable guarantees across any model version placed behind it. By contrast, fine-tuning a model to guess fields omitted by an API schema teaches brittle habits that break as soon as the interface changes. An integration test on an observation adapter can verify directly that truncated outputs return explicit pagination markers, resolving the ambiguity at the interface layer without asking downstream models to guess what was cut.

Empirical evidence, rather than administrative habit, decides when a failure climbs the ladder. Engineers test each lower rung with a **counterfactual probe**\index{Counterfactual probe!definition}, a controlled re-execution of the recorded failure trace with that rung's suspected defect removed. A context probe begins by injecting the missing fact directly into the prompt. An interface probe resumes matched saved prefixes with corrected tool descriptions or schemas and samples fresh continuations under the controlled conditions of @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor (since replaying a fixed proposal would test only the validation or adapter boundary, not whether the model chooses a different action). If both checks leave the failure intact, a runtime probe runs the identical tool payload inside an isolated sandbox with relaxed resource limits. Whenever a failure disappears under one of these probes, the result supports a repair at that rung under the probed conditions without ruling out other contributing causes. Probing in ladder order routes each resolved defect to an immediate, reversible repair, so only the failures that survive all three probes reach the weights (@fig-vol3-failure-diagnostic-tree). Even then, checkpoints trained on this residual must pass the evaluation protocol of @sec-vol3-evaluation-rigor rather than ship merely because model weights were the last hypothesis left.

title: One Admission Route
caption: **One Admission Route**: A collection record meets the five predicates in execution order and is admitted to the route only if every one passes. The first result other than a pass stops that route's checks. A failure rejects the record for this route without deleting it, and a pending or unknown result goes to an unresolved hold instead of counting as a pass. Other routes evaluate the same record under their own conditions.
alt: Grid with five columns headed R record adequacy, U permitted use, P process, O outcome, and T target suitability, and three rows for record A, record B, and record C. Record A passes all five predicates and an arrow leads to a box labeled admitted for this route. Record B passes R, U, and P, fails O, and its T cell is marked not run; a red line from the fail cell leads to a box labeled rejected, record kept. Record C passes R, is pending at U, and its P, O, and T cells are marked not run; a gray line from the pending cell leads to a dotted box labeled unresolved hold, evidence missing.
context:
A preference route adds the shared-context and justified-ordering conditions that define a preference comparison (@sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-learning-artifacts) to its outcome and target predicates. Until paired with a matching winning rollout, a failed attempt remains only an unassigned comparison candidate. For reinforcement learning pipelines, curation delivers versioned task definitions, resettable environment fixtures, and automated grading harnesses for fresh rollouts rather than static records of past failures. While these downstream consumers share the same requirements for permitted use ($\text{chk}_{\text{use}}$) and record adequacy ($\text{chk}_{\text{record}}$), they differ in how they check outcomes ($\text{chk}_{\text{out}}$) and assign target labels ($\text{chk}_{\text{target}}$).

Each predicate returns one of four canonical states (`pass`, `fail`, `pending`, or `unknown`), following the four-verdict rule of @sec-vol3-evaluation-contract-verdicts. A `fail` stops evaluation along that route at once and retains the record for diagnosis or another route (@fig-vol3-verifier-cascade). A missing or timed-out check never defaults to a pass; unverified candidates move to an unresolved holding queue, tagged with the missing evidence needed to finish the check. Curation telemetry counts evaluated, admitted, rejected, and unresolved records per route so that traces redirected to diagnostic pools never inflate the reported yield of demonstrations, and so that outcome checks themselves are guarded against manipulation by the candidate code.

```
The source trace preserves the original task prompt, tool definitions, intermediate observations, and evaluation logs intact, while target selection marks only the policy tokens inside events `e3`, `e4`, and `e6`. The refused proposal (`e2`) and test summary (`e5`) stay in the sequence as conditioning context, supplying the history that makes the schema lookup and corrected edit make sense. Passing the overall task does not make every intermediate action a training target; each selected step must be a sound decision given what the agent knew at that turn. Placed beside the other two record roles, the recovery record sits between a direct success, whose supported responses can all be targets, and a hard negative, whose deficient response is never one (@fig-vol3-trajectory-typology).

title: A Derived Record and Its Lineage
caption: **A Derived Record and Its Lineage**: Redaction produces a new record version instead of editing the source. The derived record carries its parent reference, the fields its transformation changed or omitted, and the source's split group, but its assessment is pending until revalidation decides what the new view still supports. The source keeps a reverse reference, so a later correction or withdrawal can reach every derived version.

An arrow from the source passes through a redaction box, versioned policy, to a derived record card labeled trace_r19_01_redacted_v1 listing parent reference, changed fields and omissions, same split group, and a dotted row reading assessment: pending. From the pending assessment row an arrow leads to a revalidate box reading what the view supports, then down to an admission box reading declared use, or withheld.
context:
### Derived records {#sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-derived-records}

Scrubbing a private file path or API token from a recorded trace in place can sever the causal link that justified the agent's next command while erasing the only copy of what actually ran. At the same time, the data minimization and disclosure boundaries established in @sec-vol3-evaluation-budgets-disclosure must be enforced before trajectory content enters an ingestion queue, a model-assisted curation worker, or a training store. To resolve that tension, a **derived record**\index{Derived record!definition} is always created as a new version rather than an in-place modification. The derived record binds a reference to its parent trace, the versioned redaction policy and implementation, the explicit set of altered or excised fields, and any intentionally withheld content. Lineage references do not grant read authorization to restricted raw data, and systems must store original raw bytes only where retention policies explicitly permit them. When source records reach their retention expiration limit and are purged, the lineage envelope documents that boundary directly; retaining a cryptographic hash is not the same as retaining the source data. The source also keeps a reverse reference to each derived version, so that a later correction or withdrawal at the source reaches every artifact derived from it (@fig-vol3-provenance-envelope).

caption: **Observation Loss Masking**: The mask over a simplified view of the serialized repair example that omits the schema request (selected) and its returned schema (context). title: Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples
```
caption: **Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples**: Two independent examples share one buffer. Under an ordinary causal mask (a), every query in the second example scores keys in the first, so the second example can use context it will not have when served. The block-diagonal mask (b) keeps causal scores only inside each example and sets every cross-example entry to $-\infty$ before the softmax, as in @eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention. The boundary offsets define the blocks; whether a kernel also skips the masked blocks is an implementation property.
alt: Two eight-by-eight attention grids, queries down the side and keys across the top, each split into example 1 with five positions and example 2 with three. In panel a, the lower triangle within each example is shaded as a score, the remaining upper cells are gray minus infinity, and the block where example 2 queries meet example 1 keys is shaded red and labeled leak. In panel b, the same lower triangles are shaded, the whole cross-example block is gray and labeled minus infinity, and the key axis carries the boundary offsets 0, s 1, and s 1 plus s 2. A legend defines the score, minus infinity before softmax, and cross-example score.
context:
Under an ordinary causal mask, every query in a later example can score keys in an earlier one. The block-diagonal mask sets each of those cross-example entries to $-\infty$ before the softmax, and excludes trailing padding keys the same way (@fig-vol3-block-diagonal-mask). Variable-length attention kernels [@dao2023flashattention2] enforce this without materializing a dense $-\infty$ matrix. The loader hands the kernel the example boundaries as cumulative offsets, $0$, $\PackedExampleLength_1$, $\PackedExampleLength_1+\PackedExampleLength_2$, and so on through the buffer's total length ($\BatchSize+1$ entries for $\BatchSize$ examples), so that example $\PackedExampleIndex$ occupies one contiguous interval of positions. The kernel then computes scores only for query and key pairs that fall inside the same interval. Whether a given kernel also skips the computation for cross-example blocks of the score matrix, and how much time that saves, is an implementation property to measure on the target accelerator. The mask is the correctness requirement; skipped work is a throughput bonus that must be shown, not assumed.

[^fn-packing-cross-contamination]: **Cross-Contamination**: @krell2021efficient used the term for attention and label leakage between sequences packed into one buffer, and showed that masks, position resets, and per-sequence loss handling make a packed model mathematically equivalent to the unpacked one. The equivalence is the property to test: a packed loader that trains faster but lets examples read one another has changed the learning problem, and no loss curve will show it.

title: Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling
caption: **Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling**: Training only on recorded reference states (a) leaves any state the learner reaches after a deviation without a recorded correction, and the applicable bound, @eq-vol3-quadratic-derivation, grows with $\TurnHorizon^2\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate$. Each labeling round (b) runs the current policy, mixed with the reference at probability $\ReferenceMixingProbability_k$, labels the states it visits, keeps a label only if the sandbox continuation passes the verifier, aggregates, and retrains. A fault-injected record masks the injected error and selects the diagnosis and corrective call. The bound in @eq-vol3-linear-regret-bound applies only when error is measured on learner states and each deviation's disadvantage is bounded by $\DeviationDisadvantage$; aggregation broadens coverage but does not by itself make the training and learner distributions equal.

title: Three Ways to Connect a Terminal Outcome to Earlier Turns
caption: **Three Ways to Connect a Terminal Outcome to Earlier Turns**: The same trajectory runs a debugger, makes a faulty edit, and fails the terminal check. (a) With only the terminal check, every remaining return equals the one outcome, so the check alone does not separate the useful turn from the faulty one. (b) Learned step scores supply intermediate feedback by adding a criterion to the objective, one the policy can learn to satisfy without progress on the task. (c) Continuation sampling restores each fork condition and averages the returns of its continuations; the difference between the two means estimates how much the debugger turn raised the chance of passing the declared check, with sampling error and without establishing cause.
alt: Three stacked panels, each showing the same chain of interaction histories h0, h1, h2, and hH, with action a0 labeled run debugger, action a1 labeled faulty edit in red, and a red terminal check box reading R equals 0. In panel a, one rail from the terminal check feeds identical chips, one under each action and tied to it by a dashed line, each reading that its reward-to-go equals R. In panel b, a separate learned scorer box feeds a step score chip under each action along the same kind of rail. In panel c, twenty continuations fan out from h0 and from h1, each ending in a dot that is filled green for a pass and hollow for a fail: 1 of 20 pass from h0 and 12 of 20 pass from h1, labeled K equals 20 per fork. Boxes below read V hat of h0 equals 0.05 and V hat of h1 equals 0.60, and both feed a box reading estimated difference 0.55, standard error at most 0.11 per estimate.
section: Scope: The hypothetical fork pair above; the two-bound rule of Exercise 5.
context:
```

A hypothetical fork makes this estimate concrete. Out of `{python} MCValueDifference.k_str` continuations launched from the initial bug report, `{python} MCValueDifference.passes_before_str` passes, giving a sampled value of `{python} MCValueDifference.v_before_str`. In the primary trajectory, the policy then runs a debugger, producing an observation that contains the failing line. Forking `{python} MCValueDifference.k_str` continuations from this updated history yields `{python} MCValueDifference.passes_after_str` passes, corresponding to a sampled value of `{python} MCValueDifference.v_after_str`. The estimated value difference for the debugger turn is `{python} MCValueDifference.delta_str`, even if the primary trajectory later fails on a subsequent edit. Each sample mean carries a standard error of at most `{python} MCValueDifference.se_str`. Because the two fork estimates are independent, their variances add, so the difference has a standard error of at most $\sqrt2/(2\sqrt \ContinuationCount)$, or `{python} MCDifferenceResolution.se_diff_str`. Treating a difference as resolved only when it is at least twice that bound, here `{python} MCDifferenceResolution.resolve_str`, the observed `{python} MCValueDifference.delta_str` clears the threshold, so the gain is unlikely to be sampling noise. Resolution against noise does not make $\FiniteChange \EstimatedRemainingReturn$ an exact advantage, however; it remains an empirical estimate at two particular fork conditions. Of the three ways to connect the terminal failure to earlier turns (@fig-vol3-credit-assignment), only the forks separate the debugger turn from the faulty edit on this trajectory. They do it by paying for extra rollouts rather than by adding a criterion the policy could learn to satisfy.

title: Group Barriers and Version-Checked Admission
caption: **Group Barriers and Version-Checked Admission**: (a) In the hypothetical group of four, the barrier holds every slot until the `{python} Straggler.barrier_str` member finishes, leaving `{python} Straggler.idle_str` of reserved slot time idle. (b) Asynchronous collection releases slots early, so the trainer's version advances while rollouts run. Each record carries the version that sampled it, and its lag $\FiniteChange\text{ver}$ at admission grows with its duration; the long rollout exceeds the illustrative bound and is excluded with its reason recorded. (c) A record leaves verification with a pass, a fail, or an unavailable verdict, waits in a bounded group buffer, and reaches the trainer only if its lag is within the bound. While this admission check enforces a strict bound on version lag, it cannot prevent distribution drift when individual gradient updates make large steps in parameter space.
alt: Three stacked panels. Panel a is a to-scale timeline of four rollouts lasting 0.2, 2.1, 4.2, and 16.8 seconds, with hatched idle regions after the first three up to a red dashed barrier, and a trainer row that waits until the barrier before an update; a note reads 65 percent of reserved slot time idle. Panel b shows trainer versions ver through ver plus 4 as consecutive columns above three rollout bars, with a dark tick on each bar wherever it crosses a version boundary, so the number of ticks equals the lag. Rollout A, from ver, crosses one boundary and is admitted at lag 1; rollout B, from ver plus 1, crosses two and is admitted at lag 2; rollout C, from ver, crosses four, ends in a red mark, and is excluded at lag 4; in the lag column a red dashed line labeled delta ver max separates the two admitted lags from the excluded one. Panel c is a flow from a rollout pool sampled at ver b, to verification with pass, fail, or unavailable, to a group buffer drawn as six slots with four filled, to a decision diamond testing whether delta ver is at most delta ver max; the yes branch reaches the trainer, which advances ver t to ver t plus 1, and the no branch leads to a box reading excluded, reason and cost recorded. A return path carries new weights at ver t back to the rollout pool.
context:
where $\RolloutAdmissionAge$ is the wall-clock time elapsed from sampling the first prompt token to admission into the training batch, and $\PolicyUpdateStepTime$ is the training step latency. This relationship enables system designers to calibrate staleness bounds directly from rollout duration. Long agent rollouts are precisely the trajectories most prone to severe staleness. Bounded staleness has a long lineage in distributed training architectures, where worker parameter reads are constrained to a fixed step horizon [@ho2013more], and asynchronous actor-learner algorithms tolerate bounded lag in exchange for high actor utilization [@mnih2016asynchronous]. Applied at admission (@fig-vol3-asynchronous-freshness-pipeline, panels b and c), the check admits the two short rollouts and excludes the long one, recording why it was dropped. These are record-level lag decisions, not a complete group-admission rule. Under an objective that requires the planned cohort, every member must also have a resolved reward and satisfy that bound before the group enters an update.

[^fn-vtrace-truncation-rlvr]: **V-trace**: IMPALA's correction weights each step by the ratio of learner to actor probabilities, truncated at a ceiling, accepting some bias to keep the variance of long products of ratios in check [@espeholt2018impala]. Truncation matters more for agent rollouts than for short episodes, because a product of per-token ratios over thousands of tokens is otherwise dominated by a few extreme values. \index{V-trace!off-policy correction}

title: Four Coordination Arrangements
caption: **Four Coordination Arrangements**: Each panel shows where work crosses a boundary. A supervisor sends envelopes down and collects receipts, a pipeline passes artifacts through bounded queues, a blackboard mediates claims and versioned publications through a shared store, and actors exchange addressed messages through mailboxes. One supervisor round costs $2\WorkerCount$ deliveries and a full mesh round $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)$. Each topology imposes specific runtime obligations for bounding queues, isolating concurrent state, and verifying result correctness.
alt: Four panels. Panel a: a wide supervisor box above three worker boxes, each worker with a downward solid envelope arrow and an upward dashed receipt arrow, labeled 2N per round. Panel b: stage 1, stage 2, and stage 3 in a row, separated by two bounded queues drawn as three slots each, partly occupied, with artifacts passing through them. Panel c: three worker boxes sending claim and publish arrows to a shared store holding task 2 claimed and artifact versions 2 and 3, with dashed read arrows back. Panel d: four actor boxes, each with a small mailbox of slots, joined by faint dashed links of the possible full mesh, labeled N times N minus 1, with three solid addressed messages drawn on it.
context:
Message counts scale with the communication graph and its interaction protocol. If each of $\WorkerCount$ participants transmits an update to every other participant during an execution round, the network must handle $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)$ directed deliveries. With an average payload size of $\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength$ tokens per delivery, that single round consumes $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength$ tokens across the system. In contrast, a supervisor managing $\WorkerCount$ workers requires only $2\WorkerCount$ deliveries per round (one dispatch envelope and one receipt per worker), consuming $2\WorkerCount{}\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength$ tokens. The full mesh thus scales quadratically, transmitting $(\WorkerCount-1)/2$ times more messages per round than the centralized coordinator.

Raw transmission volume measures network traffic, not what the receiving models must ingest. In a fully connected mesh where each agent appends every incoming peer message to its prompt history, ingested tokens per round grow as $\mathcal{O}(\WorkerCount^2)$. The append-only re-send of @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend compounds that growth across rounds, because each later prompt carries every earlier delivery. Even in a centralized topology, verbose receipts, iterative deliberation rounds, or frequent status polling against a blackboard store can exhaust context windows and inflate inference budgets. Across the four arrangements of @fig-vol3-multi-agent-topologies, the supervisor's round costs $2\WorkerCount$ deliveries and the actor mesh up to $\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)$, while the pipeline and blackboard replace direct deliveries with bounded queues and versioned claims that the runtime must police. An arrangement therefore keeps context windows bounded only when each handoff carries the specific inputs and checks a subtask requires, and deciding when those handoffs may fire belongs to the dependency graph.

title: Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree
caption: **Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree**: Under the one-for-one policy (a), only the failed worker restarts, as a newly admitted attempt with its own reservation, while its siblings continue. Under the one-for-all policy (b), the supervisor stops the coupled siblings through the cancellation protocol and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs, because the caller's partial work has lost its meaning. Either supervisor that exceeds its declared restart intensity stops restarting and escalates the failure to its parent.
alt: A parent supervisor box above two cards. Card a, one_for_one: a supervisor with three worker children; the middle worker is marked failed and is the only node inside a dashed red blast radius, with an arrow labeled restart to a new attempt box with its own reservation, while the other two workers are marked continues. Card b, one_for_all: a supervisor with interface, caller, and test children all inside one dashed red blast radius; caller is marked failed, interface and test are marked stopped, and arrows from all three lead to one box labeled group restarts, new attempts from recorded inputs. A dashed red arrow from supervisor b to the parent is labeled restart intensity exceeded, escalate.
context:
[^fn-erlang-supervisor-trees]: **Erlang Supervision Trees**\index{Supervision tree!Erlang/OTP}: Erlang emerged from a telephone-switching research program initiated in 1981, established on the design principle that systems should allow failing processes to crash cleanly while a designated supervisor restores known-good state, rather than attempting defensive error handling locally [@armstrong2003making]. In agentic systems, this principle is even more vital: allowing a confused agent trajectory to attempt local recovery within a contaminated context window frequently compounds its errors, whereas a supervisor restart provisions a clean execution context from recorded inputs.

The two policies differ in blast radius (@fig-vol3-supervisor-tree-isolation): one failure under `one_for_one` costs a single fresh attempt and its reservation, whereas under `one_for_all` it discards the progress of every coupled sibling and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs. To prevent degenerate retry storms under either policy, supervision trees enforce a **restart intensity**\index{Restart intensity!definition} bound, the maximum number of restarts permitted within a sliding time window. When a child agent repeatedly fails and breaches this threshold, the supervisor ceases local restarts, aborts its remaining subordinates, and escalates the failure upward to its own parent supervisor. In an agentic system, a restart must never continue from the failed worker's corrupted or circular context window. Instead, the runtime treats each restart as a freshly admitted attempt. It provisions a clean context initialized from recorded input artifacts and acquires a fresh budget reservation. Whenever it aborts sibling processes under `one_for_all` or escalation, it also invokes the structured cancellation and cleanup protocols of @sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure.

title: Private Workspaces and Guarded Publication
caption: **Private Workspaces and Guarded Publication**: Linked worktrees (a) give each worker its own files, index, and HEAD while sharing repository storage; the sandbox around each one, not the worktree, scopes its writes. The caller edits files the interface change never touched (b), so the staged merge is textually clean even though the caller relies on the interface as of $\WorkerBaseCommitHash$. Publication (c) therefore revalidates dependencies at the captured head, checks the exact integration candidate, and advances the target only if the head is unchanged and the publication guard holds. A moved head returns the attempt to validation, and every other exit returns an explicit status.

Panel b: a commit graph in which h base has an interface-change arrow to h head and a caller-edits arrow to h worker; a dashed red arrow labeled stale dependency points from h worker back to h base; h head and h worker both lead to h candidate, the worker by a staged merge. Panel c: four numbered steps in a row, 1 revalidate h base vs. h head, 2 build candidate makes h candidate, 3 checks on h candidate, and 4 atomic update expects h head and the guard, ending in published with evidence; each step has a red exit, request revision, request reconciliation, reject, and reconcile outcome, and a dashed arrow labeled head moved returns from step 4 to step 1.

title: Majority Review Under an Assumed Error Mixture
caption: **Majority Review Under an Assumed Error Mixture**: Every reviewer has the same false-approval rate, $\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=0.20$. With independent errors (a), majority false approval at five reviewers (open markers) is `{python} ReviewCorrelation.independent_majority_str` and keeps falling as reviewers are added. Under the beta mixture with $\CorrelationCoefficient=0.40$ it is `{python} ReviewCorrelation.mixture_majority_str` and levels off toward the floor $\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)$ of `{python} ReviewFloor.floor_str`. At five reviewers (b), the mixture shifts probability toward the extremes, so a candidate is either approved by no one or approved by a majority far more often than independence predicts. The curves follow from an assumed beta mixture, not a measured law of model ensembles.
alt: Two panels. Panel a: line chart of majority false approval, 0 to 25 percent, against odd reviewer counts 1 to 15. The solid gray independent-errors line falls from 20 percent toward zero; the dashed red beta-mixture line, rho 0.40, falls only slightly and flattens just above a dotted red floor line near 15 percent labeled Pr of Q greater than one half. The five-reviewer points are open markers. Panel b: grouped bars for 0 to 5 reviewers approving an invalid candidate among five, solid gray for independent errors and red hatched for the beta mixture, with the region for 3 or more shaded as majority approves. The mixture's bar at 0 is the tallest, near 57 percent, and its bars at 3, 4, and 5 exceed the independent ones.
context:
The mixture model also bounds what ensemble scaling can achieve. Conditional on a candidate's propensity $\FalseApprovalPropensity$, the weak law of large numbers implies that the fraction of reviewers falsely approving converges to $\FalseApprovalPropensity$ as the ensemble grows. Consequently, an arbitrarily large majority vote falsely approves precisely those candidates with $\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2$. Rather than decaying toward zero, majority false approval approaches a nonzero asymptotic floor at $\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)$.

Under the parameters modeled in the notebook, that floor is `{python} ReviewFloor.floor_str`. At `{python} ReviewFloor.large_ensemble_str` reviewers, independent errors would reduce majority false approvals to `{python} ReviewFloor.independent_large_str`, whereas the beta mixture leaves the error rate stalled at `{python} ReviewFloor.mixture_large_str`. In @fig-vol3-correlated-ensemble-failure the independent curve keeps falling toward zero while the mixture curve flattens just above the floor. At five reviewers the mixture moves probability to the extremes, so a candidate is approved by no one or by a majority far more often than independence predicts. Tripling the committee from five to `{python} ReviewFloor.large_ensemble_str` reviewers of the same kind triples review spend yet lowers majority false approval only from `{python} ReviewCorrelation.mixture_majority_str` to `{python} ReviewFloor.mixture_large_str`, because the remaining errors concentrate on candidates that every such model finds difficult.
```

title: Faster Model Calls, a Barely Shorter Episode
caption: **Faster Model Calls, a Barely Shorter Episode**: The serial repair episode of @tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path drawn to scale, each bar partitioned into disjoint category sums rather than a chronological trace. Required tests and sandbox lifecycle form a non-model floor that no model acceleration crosses. A `{python} CriticalPath.model_speedup_mult_str` model speedup and a `{python} SpecComposition.s_high_mult_str` speculative decode speedup under the negligible-nondecode approximation each shorten the episode by less than a tenth, and even instant model calls stop at the floor. The runtime-status interval is too short to draw at this scale.
alt: Four horizontal stacked bars on a shared elapsed-time axis, each labeled above. Every bar has a long required-tests segment and a hatched sandbox segment, which end at a dashed red line marking the non-model floor, followed by a model-calls segment with the end time and speedup labeled at the right. The model segment is widest in the baseline bar, narrower for model calls four times faster and for speculative decoding, and absent for instant model calls; a dashed outline marks the model time each faster variant removes, and a dashed gray line marks the baseline end.
context:
On the critical path, speculative decoding shortens only the decode portion of each model call; prefill, queueing, and other call overhead join the non-model spans in the fixed part of the trajectory. Its trajectory-level effect follows from substituting the decode-stream speedup $\SpeculativeDecodingSpeedup$ for the acceleration factor $\AcceleratorGain$ in the Amdahl bound of notebook \ref{nbk-18-critical-path-investment}. Here $\ModelTimeFraction$ is the decode share of baseline elapsed time, so the trajectory-level speedup stays below $1/(1-\ModelTimeFraction)$. The estimate below treats the model intervals of the serial episode as pure decode, which makes it an optimistic bound.

Consider a concrete deployment scenario where the draft model proposes `{python} SpecComposition.gamma_str` tokens per round at a relative cost of `{python} SpecComposition.r_str` per token. The break-even threshold requires the mean accepted draft count to exceed `{python} SpecComposition.breakeven_str` draft tokens per round. If the draft model aligns well with the agent's prompt distribution and achieves `{python} SpecComposition.m_high_str` accepted tokens per round, @eq-vol3-spec-speedup yields a decode-stream speedup of `{python} SpecComposition.s_high_mult_str`. Applying this factor to the decode subtotal under the zero-nondecode approximation within the serial episode of @tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path reduces total elapsed time from `{python} CriticalPath.total_str` to `{python} SpecComposition.t_high_str`, a modest `{python} SpecComposition.traj_high_mult_str` speedup for the overall episode. Conversely, if a complex reasoning task drops acceptance to `{python} SpecComposition.m_low_str` tokens per round, the system drops below break-even. Decode-stream performance then degrades to `{python} SpecComposition.s_low_mult_str` of baseline speed, expanding total episode duration to `{python} SpecComposition.t_low_str`. Drawn to scale, required tests and sandbox lifecycle operations form a non-model floor that no model acceleration crosses, so even instantaneous inference shortens this episode by less than a tenth (@fig-vol3-critical-path-waterfall).

```
## From Prediction to Action {#sec-boundary-prediction-to-action}

The acting line begins with feedback. Wiener's cybernetics described animals and machines alike as systems that measure the result of their own action and use it to correct the next one [@wiener1948cybernetics], and control theory soon learned to estimate a moving system's state from noisy measurements [@kalman1960new]. The first industrial robots needed little of this at the level of the task. In 1961 a Unimate arm began stacking hot die-cast parts at General Motors by replaying step-by-step commands stored on a magnetic drum [@chm1961unimate]. Nothing in that program could notice a person in the arm's path, so protecting people meant keeping them out of its reach. The machine acted, but it did not perceive, and nothing in it was learned. The two lines this section follows, robotics and control learning to act and machine learning mastering prediction, run as the upper and lower lanes of @fig-01-evolution until they merge.
```

**Systems insight**: The learned model's backbone accounts for `{python} StoppingBudget.t_backbone_str` of the delay, or `{python} StoppingBudget.d_backbone_str` of travel; the chunk lease alone costs `{python} StoppingBudget.d_lease_str`. Each added millisecond of delay anywhere in the chain costs `{python} StoppingBudget.d_per_ms_str` at this speed, so a slower but more accurate model is a distance cost the budget must absorb. The spare is not yet a safety margin. @Sec-enforcement-composite-budget adds the localization bound, a protective margin, tracking error, and the longer stop of a jerk-limited brake (one that limits jerk, the rate of change of deceleration, by ramping its braking up instead of stepping it). Together they exceed the clear distance at the drive limit, which is why the card sets the aisle speed at `{python} StoppingBudget.v_aisle_str`.

:::

title: Three machine classes
caption: **Three machine classes**: Each class is named for the constraint that dominates it and the margin it spends: (a) mass-dominated mobility (Class 1) spends stopping clearance, set by momentum and braking; (b) contact-dominated manipulation (Class 2) spends force and deformation margin, set by contact stiffness and the strength of the object and mechanism; and (c) energy- and thermal-dominated operation (Class 3) spends heat and supply margin, set by Joule heating, thermal capacitance, and power delivery.
alt: Three panels. Class 1, mass-dominated mobility: a wheeled base moving at speed v toward a rack end, with the clear distance D clear marked in red, above the relation d stop equals v tau delay plus v squared over 2 a brake. Class 2, contact-dominated manipulation: an arm whose gripper presses a spring of stiffness k contact into a stiff fixture, deformation delta x and force F in red, above F approximately equals k contact delta x. Class 3, energy- and thermal-dominated: power P in entering a winding of thermal capacitance C th, heat P out leaving, and a temperature bar T wind below a red T limit line, above d T wind over d t equals P in minus P out over C th. Each panel names the margin it spends: stopping clearance, force and deformation margin, heat and supply margin.
context:
**Contact-dominated manipulation** (Class 2) spends force and deformation margin. When an articulated arm presses against a stiff fixture, minute position displacements can generate destructive contact forces over fractions of a millimeter. Physical contact is both the means of task success (seating a part or opening a latch requires deliberate force) and the immediate hazard. The engineering task is to supply the wrenches (the combined forces and torques) needed to complete the assembly while guaranteeing that contact forces never exceed the mechanical yield limits of the payload or the manipulator.

**Energy- and thermal-dominated operation** (Class 3) spends heat and electrical supply margins. Supporting a heavy load or resisting gravity demands sustained motor current, driving continuous Joule heating in actuator windings even when joints remain stationary. Concurrent peak current draws from drive inverters, compute accelerators, and sensor payloads can induce voltage sag across a shared DC bus. The system must sustain these thermal and electrical loads across the entire operational profile while reserving sufficient energy and thermal headroom to execute a safe protective abort.

title: The physical AI scope test
caption: **The physical AI scope test**: Physical AI combines a learned component, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority to let learned outputs reach actuation without human approval. An independent veto belongs inside this intersection because accepted proposals can still move the plant. The pairwise overlaps locate advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control.
alt: Three-set Venn diagram defining physical AI at the intersection of learned models, physical feedback, and delegated authority. The pairwise overlaps show advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control.
context:
Together, these three criteria delineate the domain of physical AI. The three-set Venn diagram in @fig-01-scope-venn formalizes this boundary, locating physical AI at the central intersection where a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority converge. Each pairwise overlap holds systems that meet only two of the three criteria. Advisory systems place a learned model inside a physical process, as when a technician inspects learned toolpaths before loading them onto a mill, but a person still approves each action. Digital autonomy executes learned outputs without human approval, as in an automated trading engine, but its actions land in software rather than in physics. Classical control closes a physical feedback loop automatically, as in a PID speed governor, but relies on an analytical control law rather than a learned model. Excluding these pairwise overlaps restricts the design problem to systems where statistical uncertainty collides directly with physical irreversibility.

[^fn-sysid-scope-test]: **System Identification**: The control-engineering practice of fitting low-order dynamic models to measured input-output time series. When this fitting establishes bounded parameter uncertainty under stated modeling assumptions, control engineers can use those bounds to prove stability guarantees before deploying the controller. Modern high-dimensional neural networks lack tractable closed-form uncertainty bounds and therefore require empirical verification across explicitly specified operating domains. \index{System identification!scope test}

```
title: Tempe test vehicle sensor locations
caption: **Tempe test vehicle sensor locations**: The NTSB diagram identifies the developmental ADS vehicle's lidar, camera, radar, computing, and telecommunications locations. (Source: NTSB, public domain).
alt: NTSB side-view diagram of the Volvo test vehicle with colored outlines marking lidar, cameras, radar, ADS computing and data storage, and GPS equipment.
context:
On a March night in 2018, a modified Volvo XC90 operating Uber Advanced Technologies Group's developmental automated driving system (ADS) struck and fatally injured a pedestrian pushing a bicycle across a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation] The vehicle carried a roof-mounted lidar, forward and side radars, surround cameras, and GPS antennas, all routed to ADS compute and data-storage racks in the cargo bay (@fig-01-tempe-vehicle). The ADS first detected the pedestrian `{python} IncidentRecord.t_detect_str` before impact, but detection alone did not provide a correct path prediction [@ntsb2019uber]. The failure ran through perception and path prediction, a response rule that withheld braking, and a human operator the design relied on as its last countermeasure.

[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation]: **Reading the Tempe Record**\index{2018 Tempe Autonomous Collision!NTSB report}: Times in this section count backward from impact at $\Time$, as the event table of NTSB/HAR-19/03 does, and speeds are those the ADS itself recorded [@ntsb2019uber]. The report also cautions that communication delay leaves unclear exactly when the planned slowdown began. Reading each time as an interval before impact, rather than as a clock time, is what lets it be converted into distance traveled at the recorded speed, the conversion this section applies.

title: The spine of the book
caption: **The spine of the book**: Each part is led by one law, and each chapter of Parts I to IV except The Cognitive Brain (Chapter 3) produces a record that a later one consumes. What the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do run as one strand, what the proposer proposes now as another, and the two meet at the permission decision.
alt: Flow diagram of sixteen record boxes, each labeled with its chapter number, on shaded bands for the four parts. In the Part I band, labeled Irreversibility, the limit record of Chapter 2 feeds the handoff record of Chapter 4, and a dashed arrow labeled Chapter 3, proposer limits, also enters the handoff record. The handoff record forks into two rows. The upper row, in the Part II band labeled Endogenous data, runs provenance record 5, policy manifest 6, and evaluation record 7. The lower row, in the Part III band labeled Proposal is not permission, runs observation contract 8, belief record 9, intent lease 10, and trajectory record 11. Both rows converge on the enforcement record of Chapter 12, which feeds the placement record of Chapter 13. An arrow then runs down to a lower row in the Part IV band, labeled Permission must be earned: authority record 14, fault record 15, release manifest 16, and approval record 17, which feeds the residual-claims register of Chapter 18 outside the bands. A separate arrow runs from the evaluation record around the top and right edges to the release manifest.
context:
system of records illustrated in @fig-01-spine formalizes this progression, capturing operating assumptions and empirical evidence so that downstream runtime decisions can inspect and rely on them. Conceptually, these records trace two converging pipelines. One strand establishes offline physical limits and verified competence; the second processes online sensor observations and real-time candidate actions. Both pipelines converge at the permission decision, where the system admits or rejects a proposed trajectory. In @sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis, this architecture synthesizes both strands to resolve the book's central challenge of engineering dependable, high-performance physical systems out of unverified learned models and unforgiving mechanical hardware.

A record is a machine-checkable artifact that downstream safety and runtime decisions can verify and trust. The initial stopping calculation (notebook \ref{nbk-boundary-stopping-budget}) already sketches the first record in the chain: a limit record, with the six elements the reader guide introduces (nominal value, operating conditions, uncertainty, margin, runtime detector, and provenance). Its nominal value is the derived stopping distance under stated operating conditions of loaded payload mass, dry concrete, a stationary obstacle, and constant approach speed. Because those inputs are illustrative scalars rather than calibrated distributions, however, its uncertainty remains unquantified. The apparent buffer between the obstacle and the machine is therefore only an arithmetic difference between provisional figures rather than a verified safety margin. The calculation also lacks a runtime detector—no sensor yet monitors whether floor traction drops or cargo shifts outside the assumed envelope (@sec-body-limit-record-schema)—and its provenance rests on baseline assumptions rather than calibrated hardware logs. An ungrounded calculation becomes operational engineering evidence only when all six fields are populated and backed by empirical data. Every numbered box across the four part bands in @fig-01-spine establishes a machine-checkable record of this rigor for a distinct architectural decision.
```
