title: Stopping distance of the warehouse mobile manipulator
caption: **Stopping distance of the warehouse mobile manipulator**: Each bar splits the stop into blind travel during the pre-brake delay, braking travel under the credible deceleration, and the fixed overhead of the localization bound and protective clearance, against the `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance. Case 1 counts only the terms the body owns at the `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit and stops within `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_body_str`. Case 2 charges the full `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.tau_full_str` pre-brake delay of the elementary stopping budget (the kinematic roofline); at `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_full_str` it still fits, although later chapters add a stop profile and a tracking bound. Case 3 raises speed to a hypothetical `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.v_fast_str`, above the drive limit, with the same delay; braking travel grows by `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.brake_growth_pct_str` and the stop, at `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_fast_str`, breaches the clear distance.
alt: Horizontal stacked bars for three cases, each split into blind travel, braking travel, and fixed overhead, against a dashed vertical line marking the rack-end clear distance. The first two bars end inside the line with the remaining margin shaded green; the third bar extends past the line into a hatched red breach.
context:
:::

Three cases on the running machine show how the terms trade against one another (@fig-02-stopping-distance). With only the terms the body owns, the stop needs `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_body_str`. Charging the full `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.tau_full_str` pre-brake delay of the elementary stopping budget (@sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline), whose terms later chapters measure one by one, gives that elementary stop plus the `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.overhead_str` fixed overhead, or `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_full_str`. That stop still fits the `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance. Raising speed above the drive limit with that same delay pushes the stop to `{python} BodyStoppingBudget.case_fast_str`, past the rack end, because speed enters the blind travel linearly and the braking travel quadratically. Notebook \ref{nbk-body-stopping-distance-budgeting-high-tail-compute} works the first case term by term.

title: Strain wave gear set
caption: **Strain wave gear set**: The three parts of a Harmonic Drive strain wave gear, disassembled: the elliptical wave generator with its thin-race ball bearing (top left), the flexspline cup with external teeth on its open rim (top right), and the rigid circular spline ring with internal teeth (bottom). The wave generator bends the flexspline so that its teeth mesh with the circular spline at two opposite zones; because the flexspline carries slightly fewer teeth, each turn of the wave generator advances it by only that difference, which gives a high reduction with little backlash. (Credit: Pieceofmetalwork, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)
alt: Photograph of three machined steel parts on a white surface: a round ball bearing assembly at top left, a cylindrical cup with fine teeth around its rim at top right, and a flat ring with fine internal teeth and bolt holes at the bottom.
section: Transmission compliance, contact impedance, and tooth fracture {#sec-body-transmission-compliance}
context:
[^fn-strain-wave-origin]: **Strain Wave Gearing**\index{Strain wave gearing!origin}: @musser1959strain patented the mechanism, now sold as the Harmonic Drive: an elliptical wave generator flexes a thin toothed cup inside a rigid ring that carries two more teeth, so a single stage yields a high ratio with near-zero backlash. The flexing that makes the ratio possible is also the joint's torsional compliance, which makes the link elastic.

[^fn-limit-cycle-backlash]: **Limit Cycle**\index{Limit cycle!backlash}: A self-sustained oscillation of fixed amplitude that a nonlinear feedback loop settles into, here excited by the backlash deadband as the motor crosses the gap, the teeth strike, and the controller corrects back across it. Unlike an instability, it does not grow, so it can run unnoticed through a shift while every cycle adds a tooth impact to the fatigue count.

title: Broken gear tooth
caption: **Broken gear tooth**: A spur gear from gear research at the NASA Lewis (now Glenn) Research Center, photographed in 1974, with one tooth broken away at its root and the fragment lying in the gap. The root is where a tooth's bending stress concentrates, so repeated or impulsive loading that the transmission passes to the teeth ends here. (Credit: Martin Brown, NASA Glenn Research Center, via the U.S. National Archives, NARA 17417956, public domain.)
alt: Black-and-white close-up of the edge of a spur gear showing several teeth; the middle tooth has broken off at its base, and the broken piece sits in the gap next to a curved fragment of the root.
section: Transmission compliance, contact impedance, and tooth fracture {#sec-body-transmission-compliance}
context:
:::

The strain wave gear of @fig-02-real-strain-wave-gear packs a high reduction into a compact joint by deforming its flexspline continuously, and that elasticity has a cost. This intentional compliance decouples rotor position from link position under dynamic loading: while the motor encoder registers smooth rotation, the flexspline winds up like a torsion spring, introducing unmeasured end-effector deflection.

title: Motor stator damaged by overheating
caption: **Motor stator damaged by overheating**: The opened stator of an electric motor that failed from overheating, showing the copper phase windings bound with tape at left, the insulating slot liners where the windings leave the laminated iron core, and the end bell with its bearing seat at right. The windings are where resistive heat ($\WindingLossPower = \TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \EffectiveLossResistance$) is generated, and the insulation between them is what accumulated heat ages. (Credit: K. Kudelina, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.)
alt: Color photograph looking into an opened electric motor stator: dark copper wire windings bound with fabric tape on the left, pale insulation paper protruding from slots in a laminated steel core that recedes toward the right, and a round end bell with a bearing seat at the far right.
context:
Reducing motor current to shed heat also reduces holding torque. A loaded arm therefore needs a response that preserves support, such as transferring the load to a mechanical brake, rather than assuming that thermal derating leaves the task unchanged. Excess winding temperature can damage electrical insulation, while excess rotor temperature can permanently reduce magnet strength. Those material limits bound the allowable temperature trajectory.

The winding and housing respond on different timescales. Copper heats rapidly under current, while the larger core and housing absorb and reject heat more slowly. A case temperature measurement can therefore lag the winding hotspot during a torque burst. The stator in @fig-02-real-burnt-motor-stator failed from overheating, and its damage sits where this model puts the heat: in the copper windings and the insulation between them.

title: Torque, speed, and time on one joint motor
caption: **Torque, speed, and time on one joint motor**: (a) The TQ-RoboDrive ILM 70x18 of the arm's stand-in joint on its `{python} TorqueSpeedEnvelope.v_bus_str` supply. Continuous duty $\Glyph{S_1}$ extends up to the `{python} TorqueSpeedEnvelope.tau_rated_str` rated torque; intermittent duty $\Glyph{S_3}$ extends to the `{python} TorqueSpeedEnvelope.tau_peak_str` peak. Both end where back-EMF plus the resistive drop uses up the supply, from the `{python} TorqueSpeedEnvelope.n0_str` no-load speed down to `{python} TorqueSpeedEnvelope.n_peak_str` at peak torque; winding inductance, neglected here, pulls that boundary lower. (b) The winding temperature of the threefold-current burst of notebook \ref{nbk-body-thermal-burst-limits}, a first-order rise toward `{python} ThermalBurst.t_inf_str` with $\ThermalTimeConstant =$ `{python} ThermalBurst.tau_str`. From ambient the burst reaches the `{python} ThermalBurst.t_limit_str` insulation class after `{python} ThermalBurst.t_cold_str`; from the continuous-duty equilibrium it gets there after `{python} ThermalBurst.t_hot_str`. The thermal values are illustrative, because the data sheet leaves them to the installation.
alt: Two stacked panels. Top panel (a): torque against speed in revolutions per minute. A gray region below 1.25 newton meters is labeled S1 continuous, and an amber band from 1.25 to 4.05 newton meters is labeled S3 intermittent. A sloping line labeled voltage limit bounds both regions on the right, running from 2,110 revolutions per minute at zero torque down to about 1,570 at 4.05 newton meters. Bottom panel (b): winding temperature against time from 0 to 100 seconds. Two rising curves that bend over, one starting at 40 degrees Celsius and one at about 96 degrees, cross a red horizontal line at 155 degrees at about 78 and 43 seconds, marked with dots. A dashed gray line marks 140 degrees.
context:
```

The burst calculation limits duration, while the back-EMF relation in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants limits torque at speed. A feasible maneuver must satisfy both. At low speed, the drive can supply the current needed for a burst, but the winding temperature limits how long it may do so. At higher speed, back-EMF consumes voltage headroom and can prevent that current from appearing at all. On the arm's stand-in joint motor, voltage headroom and thermal history bound the usable torque-speed region simultaneously (@fig-02-motor-torque-speed-envelope). Back-EMF pulls its voltage limit from `{python} TorqueSpeedEnvelope.n0_str` at no load down to `{python} TorqueSpeedEnvelope.n_peak_str` at peak torque, and the burst that a cold winding sustains for `{python} ThermalBurst.t_cold_str` reaches the insulation class in only `{python} ThermalBurst.t_hot_str` from continuous-duty equilibrium.

caption: **An instrumented propulsion test stand**: An electric motor with its propeller, speed controller, and wiring secured at the top of the Airvolt test stand at the NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center in 2016, instrumented to collect data on the propulsion system under load. A stand like this measures what a data sheet only asserts, on the assembled drive under stated conditions. (Credit: Lauren Hughes, NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center, AFRC2016-0100-05, public domain.)
alt: Photograph against a blue sky of a white angled pylon carrying a mounting plate at its top, with a two-blade propeller, an electric motor, a finned electronics box, and bundled orange and red wiring.
context:
- **Backdrive friction and impact dynamics**: By driving the actuator output shaft with the dynamometer load motor, the testbed measures the torque needed to backdrive the joint across speed, load, and temperature:
  $$\ExternalJointTorque = \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia \JointAcceleration + \JointFrictionTorque$$
  The measured response establishes whether the transmission can yield under the intended external load and maps the friction term that @sec-body-actuation-regimes shows is not a constant. Contact qualification must additionally exercise the relevant compliance and impact conditions. The backdrive model alone does not predict tooth failure.

title: Two-speed brain architecture
caption: **Two-speed brain architecture**: Above the proposal boundary, two learned proposers run at their own rates, an intent model at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_intent_str` and a chunk policy renewing at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_chunk_str`. Below it, the permission path checks each proposal against measured state on a `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick, and the drives close their own current and velocity loops. A proposal carries no authority until it is admitted; a refusal returns the proposers to a plan from measured state.
alt: Two regions separated by a dashed vertical line labeled proposal boundary. Left region, Brain learned proposers: observations feed an intent model at 2 hertz and 336 milliseconds per evaluation, which passes a goal to a chunk policy at 20 hertz renewal and 40 milliseconds inference; a state resynchronization box below feeds the chunk policy. Right region, Nervous System and Body: encoders and scanner feed a permission path at a 1 kilohertz tick, which sends an admitted command to drives with current and velocity loops, which move the physical plant; the plant feeds back to the encoders. A dashed proposal arrow crosses from the chunk policy to the permission path, and a dashed refusal arrow returns from the permission path to state resynchronization.
context:
```

The machine card of @sec-boundary-running-machine already commits the running machine to one answer, the **two-speed brain architecture**\index{Two-speed brain architecture!hybrid control}: a slow intent model revised at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_intent_str` above a fast chunk policy renewed at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_chunk_str`. Both propose to a permission path that checks measured state on a `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick (@fig-two-speed-brain). The card states these rates; this chapter prices and checks that design. The slow intent model names a target. The fast chunk policy emits an action chunk, the short sequence of future setpoints from one inference that @sec-boundary-prediction-to-action introduced, so the drives below have motion to track between evaluations [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. The sections that follow test the three claims that govern this split. Because no single large model can renew its proposal fast enough to supply the arm, the fast policy must emit multi-step chunks, yet a chunk keeps the arm supplied without keeping the evidence behind it fresh. Consequently, the permission path can evaluate and refuse the slow model's intent alongside the fast model's candidate motion only when that intent arrives as a target checkable against independent depth measurements and time. Such a target is a metric pose stamped with the capture time of the frame that generated it (@sec-brain-proposer-interface).

title: Cadence regimes on the machine's processor
caption: **Cadence regimes on the machine's processor**: The weight-streaming ceiling $\ProposerEvaluationRate \le \SustainedMemoryBandwidth/\WeightMemory$ on the mobile manipulator's application processor for FP16 and INT4 weights (16-bit floating-point and 4-bit integer representations, @sec-brain-quantization) plotted against model parameter counts, alongside the operating points for the machine's intent model and chunk policy. This ceiling establishes an upper bound on throughput rather than an achieved operating frequency, because input token prefill, vision encoding, and autoregressive generation consume execution cycles beyond raw DRAM weight traffic (@sec-brain-memory-wall).
alt: Log-log plot of update rate against parameter count. Two parallel descending lines show the FP16 and INT4 weight-streaming ceilings. The chunk policy at 80 million parameters and 20 hertz and the intent model at 7 billion parameters and 2 hertz both sit below their ceilings. Shaded bands mark the permission-loop, chunk, and intent rate ranges.
context:
A learned proposer earns its place in an embodied system when training distribution coverage generalizes beyond preprogrammed edge cases. In the conveyor pick task, this capability translates into interpreting natural language instructions, recognizing the target mug amid visual clutter, and proposing reachable grasp affordances. However, high-level semantic identification alone cannot direct a robot arm; the system must project proposed grasp regions into metric Cartesian space using calibrated depth sensing and forward kinematics. Furthermore, environmental challenges such as specular reflections, dynamic shadows, and transient occlusions inevitably induce perceptual errors. Whatever algorithmic sophistication a proposer introduces, its execution demands must conform to the throughput, memory bandwidth, and thermal dissipation envelope of the onboard processor.

A first estimate shows why one model cannot do both jobs. If every fresh evaluation must stream all of a model's weights from off-chip memory, its renewal rate can be no higher than the sustained bandwidth divided by the bytes of weights, a ceiling that falls in proportion to parameter count (@fig-cadence-gap). The intent model stores its weights as 4-bit integers (INT4, priced in @sec-brain-quantization) rather than 16-bit floating point (FP16), which raises its ceiling fourfold. Both of the machine's proposers still sit below their ceilings, because reading the input tokens in one pass through the model (the *prefill*) and then decoding the output add work that weight streaming alone ignores. Neither approaches the kilohertz rate at which the permission path and the servo loops run. The design problem is therefore deciding which computation can finish before the observation it started from goes stale. @Sec-brain-memory-wall derives the ceiling and the work above it; the figure is a preview of where the derivation lands.

title: Unstructured search-and-rescue robot
caption: **Unstructured search-and-rescue robot**: A four-wheeled rescue robot carrying cameras and a laser scanner on a pan-tilt mast works through a test arena of tilted ramps and narrow openings, with a victim dummy placed on a high shelf. In such unmapped environments, preauthored geometric models and rigid state machines can lose coverage; learned policies may help infer spatial affordances and traversability from sensory streams. (Credit: Hector, Technische Universität Darmstadt, at the 2010 RoboCup German Open; photo by Mike1024, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RoboCup_Rescue_robot_Hector_from_Darmstadt_at_2010_German_open.jpg), public domain.)
alt: Four-wheeled robot with a sensor mast on tilted plywood ramps in a rescue test arena, seen through a round cutout, with a doll on a shelf in the background.
context:
[^fn-lyapunov-stability-certificate]: **Lyapunov Stability**\index{Lyapunov stability!energy-like certificate}: Aleksandr Lyapunov's 1892 method establishes stability near an equilibrium using a positive-definite, energy-like function whose derivative along the modeled dynamics is nonpositive; asymptotic convergence requires stronger decrease or invariance conditions [@slotine1991applied]. Applying the method requires a justified closed-loop dynamics model and verified certificate conditions; a learned proposer does not acquire such a certificate merely from training. The barrier certificates of @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission reuse the idea to keep the machine inside a safe set rather than at a point.

When an embodied machine steps outside the structured factory cage into unstructured, open-world environments, however, this analytical paradigm hits the **classical wall** [@brooks1991intelligence; @levine2018learning]. Physical reality defies closed-form geometric modeling: real objects deform under contact, ambient illumination shifts unpredictably, and scenes present near-infinite visual and mechanical variety. A rescue test arena of tilted ramps and a victim dummy on a high shelf (@fig-unstructured-rescue) has none of the fixtures that made the welding cell analyzable: no part arrives at a known pose, and no template describes the terrain. In such unmapped, irregular settings, preauthored geometric templates and rigid state machines lose state coverage and fail to generalize.

title: Bimanual teleoperation workcell
caption: **Bimanual teleoperation workcell**: Dual-arm teleoperation setup featuring two six-degree-of-freedom follower arms, two leader arms for kinesthetic teleoperation, multi-view cameras (overhead and wrist-mounted), and parallel grippers mounted to an extruded aluminum frame. The physical AI policy ingests synchronized multi-camera streams to predict continuous end-effector trajectories, and the permission path must refuse any proposal that would cause self-collision or motor over-torquing during closed-loop execution. (Credit: ALOHA 2 Team, ALOHA 2: An Enhanced Low-Cost Hardware for Bimanual Teleoperation, arXiv:2405.02292, CC BY 4.0.)
alt: Dual-arm robotic teleoperation workstation with leader and follower arms, overhead cameras, and grippers mounted on an aluminum frame.
context:
whose contacts and structural deformations resist analytic kinematic modeling. In a bimanual teleoperation workcell (@fig-aloha-manipulator), an operator moves low-cost leader arms while follower arms with parallel grippers reproduce the motion, and overhead and wrist cameras record what the followers saw. Those recordings become the training data for policies that later act alone [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. The running machine's chunk policy takes its size from ACT, which was trained on exactly such recordings. What such a policy learns from them is the action chunk itself, a short stretch of the operator's motion predicted from one view. How demonstrations become a policy belongs to @sec-training; this chapter prices what the trained policy costs to run. Although learned representations tolerate sensory variations captured across training distributions, executing any proposed motion safely still demands calibrated spatial geometry and strict physical boundary enforcement. Empirical task success demonstrates capability over tested operating envelopes, but out-of-distribution shifts in illumination, surface friction, or payload dynamics can quickly induce behavioral drift or outright failure.

The computational cost of this capability depends directly on the model's underlying representation. A transformer does not read pixels or words directly; it reads *tokens*\index{Token!embedding of an input slice}, embedding vectors that each represent one slice of input, such as an image patch, a word fragment, or a joint angle. Across a VLA model, that token sequence flows from camera patches and prompt embeddings through self-attention to candidate action chunks (@fig-vla-architecture). Multi-view camera frames consume significant memory bandwidth during ingestion, historical context expands key-value (KV) cache footprints in memory, and the inference engine must produce subsequent actions before the physical state diverges from the initial observation. Evaluating an embodied learned model alongside a classical perception-planning pipeline requires assessing both task generalization and the end-to-end latency required to refresh action proposals.

title: Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture
caption: **Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture**: A representative dataflow. (1) Camera patches receive 2D image-position and camera identifiers alongside language and robot-state tokens; metric depth still requires calibrated evidence. (2) Self-attention mixes the combined token sequence; the colored grid illustrates internal attention weights, not a verified affordance or grasp pose. (3) Autoregressive token decoders emit tokens sequentially, whereas one-pass chunk heads and iterative action experts generate candidate multi-step chunks ($\PolicyActionWindow$) in one pass or over several refinement steps. (4) An independent permission path checks candidate motion against sensed state and modeled limits before actuation. (Synthesized from Brohan et al. [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2], Kim et al. [@kim2024openvla], and Octo Model Team [@octo_2023]).

title: Topological vision-language navigation
caption: **Topological vision-language navigation**: Embodied navigation architecture executing natural-language spatial instructions. Panoramic visual observations are encoded into perceptual tokens, matched against prompt embeddings, and cross-referenced with a dynamically updated topological navigation graph. The action decoder prunes unreachable nodes and emits metric waypoint offsets $(\FiniteChange \GroundPlaneAbscissa, \FiniteChange \GroundPlaneOrdinate)$ and heading setpoints to guide the chassis along traversable semantic frontiers without requiring an exact geometric prior map. (Adapted from @an2023etpnav, arXiv:2304.03047, CC BY 4.0.)
alt: Schematic of topological vision-language navigation showing panoramic observation tokens, topological graph matching, and decoded waypoint offsets and heading setpoints.
context:
[^fn-affordance-grasp-planning]: **Affordance**: Gibson's term for the action possibilities an environment offers an agent, defined jointly by object properties and agent physical capabilities [@gibson1979ecological]. A handle affords a grasp only when its physical dimensions and clearance accommodate the robot's gripper geometry and kinematics. While self-attention weights across image patches highlight semantically relevant features such as a handle, they do not certify mechanical grasp stability or kinematic reachability, the failure mode @sec-brain-semantic-hallucinations analyzes. \index{Affordances!grasp geometry}

[^fn-flow-matching-steps]: **Flow Matching**: A method that trains a neural network to predict a continuous velocity field carrying samples from Gaussian noise to the target data distribution along nearly straight paths [@lipman2022flow]. Because those paths are straight, numerical solvers can generate samples in a handful of Euler steps, whereas older denoising diffusion models needed hundreds of sequential steps [@ho2020denoising]. On an embedded robot processor, the step count directly sets latency because each solver step rereads the action expert's weights and cached visual context from off-chip memory. \index{Flow matching!integration steps}

title: Illustrative embodied roofline
caption: **Illustrative embodied roofline**: Arithmetic intensity (operations per byte moved from off-chip memory, @eq-brain-arithmetic-intensity) against attainable throughput using the application processor's dense FP16 GPU ceiling and rounded peak memory bandwidth. Single-token weight streaming sits deep in the memory-bound region, while the intent model's prefill, which reuses each fetched weight across all of its input tokens, lies past the ridge, the intensity at which the bandwidth roof meets the compute roof, where compute binds. Chunk length alone does not determine arithmetic intensity; chunked workloads require measured operations and memory traffic. A separate real-time loop executes accepted waypoints between fresh model updates.
alt: Illustrative roofline diagram plotting arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput, with a single-token weight-streaming point on the sloped memory-bound roof, an intent-model prefill point on the flat compute-bound roof, and a ridge separating the two bounds.
context:
For the dense weight projections of single-token decoding at batch size 1, each a matrix-vector product $\LayerOutputVector = \WeightMatrix\LayerInputVector$, counting weight traffic alone gives an optimistic estimate, because activation and context traffic add further bytes. In FP16 each weight occupies 2 bytes and participates in exactly one multiply-accumulate operation (2 FLOPs), so
$$\HalfPrecisionGemvIntensity = \frac{2\,\text{FLOPs}}{2\,\text{Bytes}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
The roofline model [@williams2009roofline] turns that ratio into a bound (@fig-patterson-roofline). It plots attainable throughput against arithmetic intensity as two roofs. Below a crossover, the ridge point, throughput is capped by a sloped roof equal to bandwidth times the intensity; above it, by a flat roof equal to the processor's peak arithmetic rate. It is read the same way as the stopping-budget plot of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline, where delay travel and braking travel trade dominance at a crossover speed. Both plots show two regimes and the point at which one gives way to the other.

On one clock, the schedule looks like @fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon. With direct replacement, each chunk is in force for only `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str` before its successor replaces it, so motion computed from that capture ends when the capture is `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str` old, inside the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str` evidence horizon. Temporal ensembling instead retains contributions from older chunks. A blend must exclude contributions whose evidence has expired and carry the oldest capture time among the contributions it retains; the direct-replacement timing strip does not bound the age of that blend. If the chunk policy overruns its inference target, the notebook's assumption no longer holds, and if renewal stops altogether, a further setpoint remains eligible only while both its evidence and the active chunk lease remain valid. title: The two-processor implementation
caption: **The two-processor implementation**: The application processor runs the learned proposers and has no access to the drive registers. Proposals cross a black-channel board link as framed packets into a double buffer in the microcontroller's own memory. The receive DMA fills a private receive buffer, and the receive interrupt copies each checked frame into the seqlock-guarded mailbox slot, so the processors share no memory. The permission tick reads the latest proposal, checks it against measured state, freshness, and the lease, and sends only an admitted command to the drives, which close their own current and velocity loops. Measured state returns to the application processor as telemetry over the same link.
alt: Three horizontal tiers. Top, application processor: perception feeds an intent model at 2 hertz, which passes a goal to a chunk policy at 20 hertz renewal. Middle band: a dashed black-channel board link, a serial peripheral interface (SPI) bus or a Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate (CAN FD) bus, framed packets with CRC and sequence number, no shared memory. A dashed proposal arrow runs from the chunk policy through the link into a double buffer with seqlock, filled by receive DMA in MCU-local SRAM, inside the safety MCU. The buffer feeds a permission tick at 1 kilohertz that checks freshness, lease, and limits. Bottom: the tick sends an admitted command to drives with current and velocity loops, which move the physical plant; the plant feeds back to encoders and scanner, which feed the permission tick and send telemetry up through the link to perception.

title: Integrated motor-driver silicon
caption: **Integrated motor-driver silicon**: A Trinamic TMC2209 stepper-motor driver in a quad flat no-lead (QFN) package, with a low-value current-sense resistor (marked R110) beside it on the board. The chip carries its own power transistors and current regulation, so the winding current is measured and switched next to the motor it drives rather than by the host processor. A photograph shows the placement; the timing of the current loop is a property of the silicon that the datasheet and measurement must establish. (Photo: Phiarc, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Trinamic_TMC2209_stepper_motor_controller_chip.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0).
alt: Macro photograph of a square QFN integrated circuit marked TMC2209-LA on a black printed circuit board, with a larger surface-mount resistor marked R110 at upper left and small capacitors and copper traces around it.
context:
Closing those loops in the drive is a hardware arrangement rather than merely a firmware setting. The fastest loop sits beside its sensor and its switch, so phase current is measured and switched next to the winding with no host processor in the loop. Dedicated PWM timers in the same silicon enforce the gap between complementary switch transitions that keeps the power bridge from shorting.[^fn-hw-epwm-deadtime] The running machine's brushless hub drives follow this arrangement at a larger scale; the small stepper-motor driver of @fig-real-motor-controller shows it on one chip.

[^fn-hw-epwm-deadtime]: **Dead-Time Delay**\index{Dead-time delay}: The interval in which both switches of a half-bridge leg are off, so the leg never shorts the DC bus, is the inverter dead time introduced in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants. Dedicated pulse-width modulation timers insert it in hardware ($100\text{--}500\text{ ns}$) on every transition, and drive firmware applies online volt-second compensation for the voltage error it introduces.

title: Multi-rate cadence and the mailbox exchange
caption: **Multi-rate cadence and the mailbox exchange**: (a) The running machine's clocks during a proposer stall, to scale. The chunk policy renews every `{python} MultirateStall.t_renew_str` and needs `{python} MultirateStall.t_infer_str`; the admitted chunk supplies a setpoint every `{python} MultirateStall.t_step_str`. When the third renewal never completes, the tick keeps executing the admitted chunk only until the `{python} MultirateStall.t_lease_str` lease from the last admission lapses; the tick, bus, and brake onset then put the fallback stop `{python} MultirateStall.renewal_to_onset_str` after that admission. (b) The single-slot seqlock in the microcontroller's own memory, in event order. The receive interrupt makes the counter odd, copies a checked frame, and makes it even; the tick accepts a copy only when it reads the same even value before and after. A tick that preempts a write reads an odd value and keeps its last validated chunk, and a stalled application processor leaves the slot unchanged while the lease runs.

Tick preempts a write: the counter reads 9 during a paused write, the reader rejects, then after the counter becomes 10 the reader accepts. For an integrated mobile manipulator, the core architectural question is whether cyclic actuator commands and feedback fit within the allocated bus period while preserving sufficient margin for MCU control loop execution and motor drive processing. High-bandwidth perception streams (such as camera and LiDAR data) and asynchronous supervisory middleware require separate networks or prioritized channels to prevent unmodeled queuing delays from invading the motor command path. Industrial controllers build that separation into the hardware (@fig-industrial-ethercat-controller), with ports that serve only the deterministic drive network and local I/O attached through terminals on the controller itself rather than through host software. The running machine does not use this controller; the photograph shows the pattern its own permission path follows.

context:
Actuator commands also demand strict temporal freshness. Even when delivered comfortably within a deterministic transport window, a setpoint computed from stale perception is functionally hazardous. The evidence timestamp and lease expiry embedded in the command proposal remain safeguards even over nanosecond-synchronized fieldbuses. The transport budget must reserve adequate headroom for physical actuation to execute, and the real-time permission path must reject any setpoint whose authoritative validity window has expired.

[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus]: **Time-Sensitive Networking**\index{Time-sensitive networking}: IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Sensitive Networking provides bounded Ethernet delivery by configuring time-aware traffic shapers across network switches. High-priority control frames travel inside dedicated, pre-scheduled transmission windows, while asynchronous high-bandwidth traffic (such as uncompressed camera streams) is held back at the switch gates. This scheduled time-division multiplexing lets camera streams and microsecond servo commands share a physical link without packet collisions or switch-queue buildup.

title: Hardware proposal boundary
caption: **Hardware proposal boundary**: (a) The application processor proposes across a black-channel board link into the safety microcontroller's own double buffer; the permission path on that microcontroller is the sole writer of the drive registers and can trip a drive inhibit. (b) When the application processor can write the drive registers directly, an unchecked write reaches the motors, and proposer and drives share a single failure domain.
alt: Two panels. (a) Separate permission path: a dashed bronze application processor box, learned proposers with no drive access, sends proposal p t through a dashed black-channel board link with CRC and sequence into a safety MCU container, which has its own memory and is the sole writer of drive registers. Inside it, an MCU-local double buffer feeds the permission path at a 1 kHz tick, which checks state, freshness, and lease. The permission path sends admitted command u t to drive registers and then drives and motors; a red trip line from the permission path sends drive inhibit to the drives and motors. (b) Collapsed, host writes drives: inside a red dashed box labeled one failure domain, the application processor sends an unchecked register write straight to the drive registers, which feed the drives and motors.
context:
## Actuation Authority {#sec-nervous-actuation-authority}

A shared mailbox cannot protect a mobile manipulator if the host processor retains a diagnostic route, an auxiliary bus master, or a JTAG debug port that writes directly to a drive. The silicon partition established in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning therefore requires exclusive physical control over every electrical path capable of energizing the motor windings. Actuation authority is this exclusive physical ability to modify drive states, encompassing PWM configuration registers, current references, gate-driver outputs, and bridge-enable lines. Under this architecture, the host publishes candidate proposals $\CandidateProposal_t$ and the safety microcontroller's permission path alone turns them into admitted commands $\AdmittedCommand_t$. The difference between holding that authority and merely appearing to is a question of wiring (@fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers). When the permission path is the sole writer of the drive registers and can trip a drive inhibit, every motion passes its checks. When the host can also write those registers, one unchecked write reaches the motors, and proposer and drives share a single failure domain.

title: Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path
caption: **Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path**: Each emergency-stop contact holds its own force-guided relay, and each relay's enable contact holds one of the drive's two STO inputs, so a single welded contact or shorted wire leaves the other channel able to remove torque. The EDM contacts report a relay that failed to release before restart. Removing torque leaves the motor free to coast; the spring-applied brake is a separate circuit that clamps when its supply is removed. The diagram shows a hardware response path, not a certified integrity level or a stopping distance (synthesized from ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2).
alt: Two-channel schematic. A red positive-break E-stop is mechanically linked to two normally closed contacts, S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. S1 feeds the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of relay K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact. K1 sends STO1 enable and K2 sends STO2 enable to two STO terminals on the drive, which feed the gate-drive supply and then the inverter bridge driving motor M. A red tag above the motor reads tau equals 0, and a note below reads may coast. The two EDM contacts are wired in series with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. At the bottom, a brake supply on its own circuit, switched by K1 and K2, contacts not drawn, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft. A note reads hardware only, no processor in this path.
context:
If the safety microcontroller itself hangs or suffers a clock failure, it cannot execute a software-directed stop. A hardwired, out-of-band interlock must therefore supervise the system and enforce a qualified fallback state. Safe Torque Off (STO) accomplishes this by disabling gate-driver optocouplers or charge pumps through hardware logic, preventing the inverter from generating rotating magnetic fields.[^fn-std-iec61800-sto] STO does not isolate the high-voltage DC bus from the mains, nor does it guarantee that momentum will dissipate within the stopping clearance allocated for powered deceleration. Complete electrical isolation requires an upstream safety contactor, and containing gravitational drop or mechanical drift requires a certified electromechanical brake. A dual-channel interlock circuit (the relay network of @fig-real-estop) decouples torque inhibition entirely from the host software stack. Safety qualification must still verify that the system remains resilient against common-cause failures in power rails, clock crystals, and harness wiring.

[^fn-std-iec61800-sto]: **Safe Torque Off (STO)**\index{Safe torque off}: An STO implementation removes torque-producing drive signals through a hardware interlock. An IEC 61800-5-2 integrity rating depends on the actual devices, diagnostic coverage, wiring, and validation, not on the circuit pattern alone [@iec61800part52].

Opening a latch from a nominal centered approach and recovering from an off-axis sideways slip require different physical actions (@fig-05-latch-corridor). Every retained demonstration guides the gripper forward along the narrow corridor centered on the strike plate, which populates the archive with thousands of forward-progress actions. The archive contains zero demonstrations that start from a gripper displaced a few millimeters toward the fixture and return it to the centerline. Because a skilled human operator rarely lets the gripper drift into those boundary regions, and because teleoperation runs that drifted noticeably were aborted or discarded during curation, nothing in the training data constrains the policy's output at such a displaced state.[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch] The **recoverability problem**\index{Recoverability problem} is this absence of demonstrated corrective actions that steer the system back into the nominal corridor.

[^fn-alvinn-recovery-latch]: **ALVINN (Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network)**\index{ALVINN!recovery data}: Pomerleau's road-following network learned to steer from a human driver who kept the van centered, so its training images held almost no off-center views [@pomerleau1989alvinn]. His remedy shifted each camera image sideways in software and corrected the steering label to match, synthesizing recovery examples about 20 years before Dataset Aggregation (DAgger, @sec-data-intervention-recovery) [@pomerleau1991efficient]. A warp could fill that gap because the missing state was only a viewpoint of a flat road, whereas a gripper displaced toward the fixture also lacks contact forces that no image transform can manufacture, so its recoveries must be demonstrated or collected.

title: Four-stream action tap tuple
caption: **Four-stream action tap tuple**: Four places a command can be logged, from raw policy intent on the application processor through to measured plant response. Which tap a dataset records decides what the model learns to imitate. The four-tap decomposition is this book's construct; the teleoperation rigs it instruments follow @zhao2023learning and @wu2023gello.
alt: Block diagram. On the application processor, a policy or operator box feeds a kinematic mapping box; tap 1, a req, sits between them and tap 2, a cmd, sits after the mapping. A black-channel link with no shared memory crosses the dashed proposal boundary to the discrete safety MCU, which holds the permission path at a 1 kHz tick. Tap 3, a enf, sits after the permission path, which feeds the drives that close the current loops and apply the torque limit. The drives move the plant, joint encoders measure the motion over an interval, and tap 4, a meas, leaves the encoders. All four taps run down to a synchronized telemetry log stamped with hardware timestamps.
context:
### The four-stream action tap tuple {#sec-data-four-stream-action-tap}

If a dataset keeps only one signal from those two processing domains, any discrepancy between what the operator asked for and how the arm actually moved becomes impossible to diagnose. A command must therefore be logged at each of the four causal stages it passes through. The **four-stream action tap**\index{Four-stream action tap!definition}\index{Action tap!definition} $(\RequestedActionTap, \MappedCommandTap, \EnforcedCommandTap, \MeasuredResponseTap)$ records all four in one hardware-synchronized telemetry log (@fig-05-action-taps). Two are logged on the unprivileged Linux host before the black-channel link, and two on the discrete safety MCU after the 1 kHz permission check. Logged together, the taps keep interventions and tracking errors auditable.

title: One lag, three verdicts
caption: **One lag, three verdicts**: Pairing an observation with an action across an uncompensated lag displaces the recorded state by speed times lag. At `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_lag_str` the transit pairing is `{python} SyncDisplacement.dx_transit_str` off, the faster latch approach exceeds the `{python} SyncDisplacement.clearance_str` clearance, and the guarded approach stays inside it. The clearance tolerates at most `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str` of lag at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_fast_str` and `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_guarded_str` at `{python} SyncDisplacement.v_guarded_str`; a full-frame rolling-shutter skew alone spans `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` to `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str`.
alt: Log-log plot of pairing displacement in millimeters against observation-to-action lag in milliseconds, 1 to 100 ms. Three straight parallel lines: transit at 0.50 meters per second on top, the faster latch approach at 0.10 meters per second, and the guarded approach at 0.03 meters per second at the bottom. A red dashed horizontal line marks the 2 millimeter latch clearance. A dotted vertical line at 35 ms marks the uncompensated lag, with a dot on each line. Red squares where the latch lines cross the clearance are labeled at most 20 ms and at most 66.7 ms. A gray band from 15 to 33 ms marks full-frame rolling-shutter skew.
context:
:::

When an imitation learning model trains on misaligned pairs, it fits a relationship in which the action appears to precede the visual evidence that prompted it. During closed-loop deployment, that artificial phase lag appears as overshoot, control hunting, and chattering against rigid surfaces. Because displacement grows linearly with lag, each approach speed has a lag ceiling equal to the clearance divided by the speed, and @fig-05-sync-displacement places those ceilings beside a second timing error the notebook did not count. A rolling-shutter sensor exposes its pixel rows one after another rather than all at once, so the bottom row of a frame is captured later than the top (@sec-data-rolling-shutter-skew quantifies the delay). A full-frame rolling-shutter skew of `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_lo_str` to `{python} SyncDisplacement.t_skew_hi_str` is comparable to the uncompensated lag, so a logger that stamps every frame correctly can still breach the faster approach's `{python} SyncDisplacement.lag_max_fast_str` ceiling through readout alone.

title: Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop
caption: **Kinematically isomorphic teleoperation loop**: The operator moves a leader arm whose joints mirror the follower's, and the host copies joint angles across, as in low-cost leader-follower rigs such as GELLO [@wu2023gello]. Because the leader shares the follower's joint structure, the interface needs no inverse kinematics and inherits none of its singularities (configurations where joints align and the arm loses a direction of motion), preserving the operator's direct joint-level coordination. The loop still closes through the operator: human reaction, command transfer, mechanical response, and display delay all enter the recording as phase lag, so the demonstration carries the operator's delay as if it were policy.
alt: Block diagram of a teleoperation loop. An operator box labeled see, decide, move sends an arrow labeled t hum to a small leader arm with joints q1, q2, and q3. The leader feeds a joint copy box stating q follower equals q leader, noted no inverse kinematics, which sends an arrow labeled t cmd to a larger follower arm with the same three joints, reaching toward a latch across a gap labeled t mech. A dashed arrow runs from the follower down to a workspace camera, whose arrow labeled t disp runs left to a display, which feeds back up to the operator.

The cage-door latch campaign illustrates this relational join for the running machine. Its six-cell example records occupancy, without supplying per-cell counts or a minimum-count requirement. Every retained episode approaches the strike plate at the guarded speed of `{python} LatchScenarioTable.v_guarded_str` with the plate aligned within ±`{python} LatchScenarioTable.logged_offset_str` of nominal, and every successful demonstration stays below the illustrative `{python} LatchScenarioTable.f_trip_str` detection threshold. This observation does not itself qualify the collection response. Evaluated against an uncritical table containing only the nominal plate position at the guarded speed, the archive appears exhaustive. Against the scenario table the deployment actually demands, three plate positions (nominal and ±`{python} LatchScenarioTable.plate_offset_str`) crossed with two approach speeds (`{python} LatchScenarioTable.v_guarded_str` and `{python} LatchScenarioTable.v_fast_str`), the identical dataset populates only one cell of `{python} LatchScenarioTable.n_cells_str`. The raw logged telemetry does not change between these two assessments; the difference lies entirely in the standard of audit applied. The `{python} LatchScenarioTable.n_zero_str` unvisited cells therefore travel with the dataset into training as documented operational absences, establishing that the current demonstrations provide no empirical foundation for competence claims in those regimes. Targeted collection can acquire the missing recovery trajectories, but downstream training and closed-loop testing must verify what the resulting policy achieves. @Fig-05-collector-coverage-table sets the two audits side by side and adds a third, the stipulated recovery collection `latch-recovery-02` of @sec-data-intervention-recovery, which fills one more cell and still leaves `{python} LatchScenarioTable.n_zero_recovery_str` known absences.

title: Covariate shift and intervention curation
caption: **Covariate shift and intervention curation**: (a) The learned policy's own actions choose the states it sees next. The worst-case cost bound grows as $\CovariateDriftBound$ for behavioral cloning and as $\mathcal{O}(\DeviationDisadvantage\BehaviorCloningHorizon\AggregatedSurrogateLoss)$ for aggregation on a recoverable task; these are bound orders, not measured drift. (b) One takeover. The `{python} DataLookbackWindow.t_lookback_str` lookback reaches back past the divergence point; states between divergence and takeover are eligible for expert relabeling while the learner's commands there are masked. After takeover, the enforcer's blend and the operator's reorientation are retained for diagnosis but excluded from expert imitation targets, and only the reviewed segment from measured stabilization to recovery becomes an expert demonstration. Based on @ross2011reduction and @spencer2021feedback.
alt: Two panels. Left: a closed loop in which a learned policy sends an action to the plant, a disturbance enters the plant, and the plant state returns to the policy, with the bound orders big-O of S squared epsilon for behavioral cloning and big-O of u S epsilon for aggregation written inside the loop. Right: tracking error against time, flat until t div and rising under the learner to a peak at t takeover. A dashed segment marks the enforcer blend, an oscillating segment marks the operator's reorientation, and from t stabilize the expert's curve falls smoothly to zero at t rec. A bracket marks a 5-second lookback window ending at t takeover and reaching back past t div. Below the axis, a row names the four intervals: drift, blend, re-orient, and stabilized. A states row marks drift as relabel-eligible, blend and re-orient as excluded, and stabilized as expert recovery. A commands row marks drift, blend, and re-orient as masked and stabilized as expert labels.
context:
A team can also avoid online interventions entirely, and this is the wide-tube remedy promised in @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability. Injecting small noise perturbations into the teleoperator's commands pushes the robot off the nominal path during ordinary collection, so the operator's corrections back toward the corridor appear in the initial demonstration set itself [@laskey2017dart]. Each perturbation consumes hardware life from the fatigue budget in @sec-data-yield-fatigue-budgeting and must stay within recoverable bounds. Ingestion pipelines therefore log the collection mode of every episode explicitly (nominal, noise-injected, or gated intervention), because the three modes put different kinds of states and labels into the archive.

[^fn-math-dagger-bound]: **Corrective Aggregation Error Bound**\index{DAgger!linear error bound}: The bound is Theorem 3.2 of @ross2011reduction. It holds for some policy in the sequence of $\AggregationRoundCount$ iterations, with $\AggregationRoundCount$ of order $\DeviationDisadvantage \BehaviorCloningHorizon$ up to logarithmic factors, and $\DeviationDisadvantage$ bounds the change in the expert's cost-to-go after any single action. @Sec-appendix-ml-compounding states the finite-sample form, in which the same constant appears as $\Glyph{u_{\max}}$.

title: Camera-to-robot calibration check on DROID scenes
caption: **Camera-to-robot calibration check on DROID scenes**: Randomly chosen DROID scenes with a robot mask rendered from the robot's URDF mesh at the recorded joint angles and projected through each camera's audited calibration, from the dataset's own post-hoc recalibration [@khazatsky2024droid]. Where the mask and the visible arm coincide, the extrinsics are consistent with the joint encoders; a displaced camera shows up as a mask that misses the arm, before any corrupted trajectory reaches the training pipeline. Source: Khazatsky et al., Fig. 13, CC BY 4.0.

section: Passive covariate shift vs. physical dynamics shift {#sec-data-passive-vs-physical-shift}
context:
calibration!planar target}: In practice $\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix$ is estimated from a few views of a planar checkerboard, the method @zhang2000flexible introduced, and the extrinsics come from a separate hand-eye calibration. Both describe one mounting at one time. The reprojection residual is therefore a calibration test repeated every session, not a setup step performed once.

@Fig-05-camera-calibration displays this verification pipeline across a $7 \times 7$ grid of workspace scenes from the DROID dataset. In each, a colored silhouette of the robot arm, rendered from its Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) kinematic mesh at the recorded joint angles, is projected through each camera's extrinsic calibration matrix and overlaid directly onto the raw photographic frame. Where the mask and the physical arm coincide, camera extrinsics and joint encoders are geometrically aligned; where the colored silhouette departs from the links, the check exposes camera mount slippage before corrupted trajectory pairs enter training. The DROID corpus showed how easily mount drift escapes standard checks. Although its cameras were initially calibrated with checkerboard targets during data collection, independent re-analysis revealed that rendered kinematic masks barely overlapped visible robot links across numerous recorded episodes [@lu2025ctrnetx]. The DROID research team subsequently evaluated stored extrinsics by measuring mask intersection-over-union, discarded failed sessions, re-estimated camera poses using learning-based hand-eye estimators, and published updated calibrations for approximately `{python} StateOfPractice.droid_recal_str` episodes [@khazatsky2024droid]. This calibration error shipped within a major open-source corpus because it was transparent to standard file format parsers. To prevent these silent failures, ingestion architectures must bind every recorded episode to an immutable calibration identifier and real-time clock synchronization metrics. Trajectories collected under conflicting geometric or temporal calibrations force neural policies to average incompatible sensorimotor distributions within identical state spaces.

title: Drift out of the demonstrated states
caption: **Drift out of the demonstrated states**: Behavioral cloning trains only inside the shaded tube the expert visited. Once the learner leaves it, each action is taken from an unfamiliar state and the error compounds. DAgger labels a learner-visited state outside the tube, which supplies recovery experience while a return is still possible. Past the red boundary, actuator and friction limits leave no action that restores the task, so no label can help. The sketch is schematic; its axes carry no units.
alt: Schematic state-space plot with task progress on the horizontal axis and deviation from the demonstrated path on the vertical axis. A shaded band surrounds a solid expert path. A dashed learner path leaves the band and continues upward into a red region at the top. At one point just outside the band, a marker labeled DAgger label has an arrow pointing back toward the band.
context:
:::

Expert availability also does not imply physical recoverability. The machine may lack enough actuator effort or frictional grip to return from a deviation. The simplified force balance $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix\GeneralizedAccelerations = \JointTorque + \ExternalContactTorque$ is Newton's second law written per joint. Here $\GeneralizedCoordinates$ denotes joint positions, $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix$ inertia, $\JointTorque$ actuator torque, and $\ExternalContactTorque$ the torque that contact forces exert about the joints. Other forces are omitted for clarity, and @sec-planning-rigidbody-dynamics develops the full equation. Actuator limits require $|\CommandedJointTorque_i| \le \JointTorqueLimit$ on every joint axis, while available friction bounds tangential force by $\|\TangentialContactShear\| \le \CoulombFrictionCoefficient \NormalContactForce$, with normal force $\NormalContactForce$ and friction coefficient $\CoulombFrictionCoefficient$. These constraints can leave no action that restores the task, and then $\DeviationDisadvantage$ is unbounded and DAgger's linear guarantee no longer applies. Interactive aggregation is therefore most useful where learner deviations can be contained, labeled, and repeated within the operator-time and hardware-exposure budget. The state space divides into three regions (@fig-06-compounding-error). Cloning trains in the tube of demonstrated states. Just outside it lies a band where an expert label on a learner-visited state still restores the task. Beyond the band is an unrecoverable region, where actuator and friction limits leave no restoring action and every further label is vacuous. Interactive aggregation buys experience only in the middle band.

section: The Simulator as a System Component {#sec-training-simulator-component}
context:
A reinforcement learning policy trained on door latching learned an aggressive, unbraked plunge because its simulated strike plate yielded far more than the physical mechanism. Stripping away the simulator during physical deployment does nothing to unlearn that behavior. The physics simulator is not an external sandbox; it is an active component of the training pipeline whose equations, contact approximations, and timing assumptions dictate the exact experience supplied to the optimizer. Accepting simulated task success as evidence of hardware readiness requires measurable, verifiable error bounds on every one of those assumptions.

Like any physical subsystem, a simulator requires a formal interface contract stated in quantities that engineers can measure and budget. This interface contract specifies observation dimensions, action bounds, simulation time step $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$, transport latency between command issuance and physical actuation, actuator torque and current limits, sensor noise distributions, reset distributions, and termination conditions. For instance, if a simulator executes an observation loop at 100 Hz with an assumed zero-delay sensor channel and Gaussian noise of variance $\SensorNoiseStandardDeviation^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ (rad/s)}^2$, the policy tunes its feedback gains to those exact signal statistics. An unmodeled 15 ms bus transport delay on the physical machine then removes $\CrossoverFrequency \PureTransportDelay$ of phase at the loop's crossover frequency $\CrossoverFrequency$ (@eq-nervous-delay-phase), and the loop goes unstable whenever that loss exceeds the phase margin the learned gains left. OpenAI's Dactyl project faced this contract at full scale, with a 24-DoF Shadow Hand in a motion-capture cage and its MuJoCo twin (@fig-06-sim2real-dactyl) [@andrychowicz2020learning]. The team calibrated the simulator against the physical hand and then randomized physical parameters around those calibrated values, so that the policy met the remaining discrepancies as variation it had already seen in training.

title: Contact force against brake onset
caption: **Contact force against brake onset**: Counterfactual constant-drive ramps rise as $\NormalContactForce = \ContactStiffness \SpeedAtDetection \TimeInstant$ from touch. At the fast approach, the tripwire fires at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_trip_fast_str` and braking can begin at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_brake_fast_str`, only `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_left_fast_str` before the ramp reaches the latch limit. At the guarded approach, brake onset is `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_brake_guarded_str`, leaving `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_left_guarded_str`. Each onset includes the same `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_contact_loop_str` response after its own tripwire crossing. Plate stiffness alone gives the shortest deadlines; the lines do not model actual braking trajectories.
alt: Line plot of force against time since touch. Dashed fast and solid guarded constant-drive ramps rise from the origin through a horizontal tripwire toward the latch limit. Separate vertical markers locate fast brake onset at 2.375 milliseconds and guarded brake onset at 3.25 milliseconds. Brackets run from each onset to its ramp's force-limit crossing, with a short 0.125 millisecond fast interval and a longer guarded interval. A red band lies above the force limit.
context:
LatchContactDeadline.t_contact_loop_str`, placing brake onset at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_brake_fast_str`. Only `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_left_fast_str` remains before the counterfactual constant-drive ramp reaches the force limit. At the guarded approach of `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_guarded_str`, the tripwire fires at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_trip_guarded_str` and braking begins at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_brake_guarded_str`, leaving `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_left_guarded_str` before the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_yield_guarded_str` touch-relative limit (@fig-06-latch-contact-force). Neither remaining interval establishes that the actual braking trajectory stays below the limit.

The plate-only deadline leaves too little demonstrated braking margin to credit the reactive force monitor at the fast approach, so protection must act before contact until the contact response is qualified. An independently monitored deceleration envelope, $\SafeApproachSpeedEnvelope(\StoppingBoundaryClearance) \le \sqrt{2 \CredibleBrakingDeceleration \StoppingBoundaryClearance}$, is the stopping inequality of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline applied to the gripper. Here $\StoppingBoundaryClearance$ is the clearance to a stopping boundary placed a short standoff before the plate, after sensing and actuation latencies are charged, and $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ is the credible deceleration of the arm at the tool, not the base's value on the machine card. Because $\SafeApproachSpeedEnvelope$ falls to zero at that boundary, the envelope forbids an unbraked arrival at the plate. Crossing the standoff is a separate act. A guarded contact mode, qualified on its own, takes over inside it and holds the gripper at or below the guarded approach speed of `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_guarded_str` until touch. That mode needs its own evidence about approach speed, force rise rate, loop latency, and deceleration, and a force tripwire works only inside those validated bounds. This contact deadline, not the reward used in training, is what confines the policy's declared ODD to the guarded approach speed (@sec-training-policy-manifest).

title: Sim-to-real reality gap vector
caption: **Sim-to-real reality gap vector**: Illustrative traces for a separate linear-drive scenario distinguish dynamics (a), timing (b), sensing (c), and appearance (d). Panel (a), dynamics, shows force rising later on hardware and overshooting a dashed force limit in red before a current-limit trip drops it to zero, while the simulated force settles at a target. Panel (b), timing, shows two sinusoids offset by an unmodeled delay T d. Panel (c), sensing, shows the hardware reading offset above the simulated one by a bias delta y, with a shaded dropout gap. context: A linear drive approaches a surface at `{python} LinearDriveGap.v_approach_str` and regulates contact force to `{python} LinearDriveGap.f_target_str`. In the dynamics channel, an unmodeled drive delay of `{python} LinearDriveGap.tau_drive_str` and a softer physical contact pad cut the force rise from `{python} LinearDriveGap.rate_sim_str` in simulation to `{python} LinearDriveGap.rate_real_str` on hardware (a rate the force regulator sets as it ramps toward its target, far below the free-impact rate $\ContactStiffness \SpeedAtDetection$ of the latch analysis). The target force therefore arrives at `{python} LinearDriveGap.t_target_real_str` instead of `{python} LinearDriveGap.t_target_sim_str`. The drive overtravels by `{python} LinearDriveGap.d_overtravel_str`, and a hard current-limit shutdown trips. In the sensing channel, a calibration bias of +`{python} LinearDriveGap.range_bias_str` triggers premature deceleration, and a specular dropout burst of `{python} LinearDriveGap.n_dropout_frames_str` frames blinds the controller during final descent. In appearance, a pixel difference of only `{python} LinearDriveGap.pixel_diff_pct_str` hides a `{python} LinearDriveGap.patch_shift_str` lateral shift in the contact-patch estimate, more than the `{python} LinearDriveGap.chamfer_tol_str` chamfer tolerance. In timing, an illustrative p99 actuation delay of `{python} LinearDriveGap.tau_p99_str` carries the mechanism `{python} LinearDriveGap.d_unmodeled_str` past the point the simulator predicts with its idealized `{python} LinearDriveGap.tau_sim_str` observation-to-actuation delay. The simulator's `{python} LinearDriveGap.dt_sim_str` integration step is a numerical parameter, not pipeline latency, and cannot be subtracted from the physical transport delay. Each channel fails in its own units (milliseconds of force rise, millimeters of bias, millimeters of patch shift, millimeters of unobserved travel). A scalar loss can report that hardware departs from simulation but cannot say which channel failed, and separating the channels is what lets @tbl-06-reality-gap give each one its own paired-trace acceptance test and its own permission-path interceptor.

title: Teacher-student privileged state distillation
caption: **Teacher-student privileged state distillation**: A schematic two-phase transfer pipeline. The teacher uses simulator state during training, and the student learns from onboard observations and their history. The training advantage does not establish that every privileged quantity is identifiable from those observations. On the machine, the frozen student renews a proposal every `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str` and crosses the proposal boundary to the independent permission path; it still requires physical validation.
alt: Two-region block diagram separated by a vertical dashed line. On the left, labeled training in simulation, a simulator box holds a privileged state card listing friction, plate offset, and contact wrench, and a simulated sensors card. The privileged state feeds a teacher trained by RL, whose labels pass through an imitation loss whose gradient updates a student fed by an observation history. A dashed return path marks that student rollouts choose the states the teacher labels. On the right, labeled deployment on the machine, machine sensors feed a history box and then the frozen student with the same weights, which renews every 50 milliseconds and sends a proposal with 25 millisecond setpoints across a dashed proposal boundary to the permission path.
section: Teacher-student privileged state distillation and asymmetric actor-critic {#sec-training-privileged-distillation}
context:
Everything privileged stays on the simulation side, and only the frozen student's proposals, built from the machine's own sensor history and renewed every `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str`, cross to the permission path. In Phase 1, the privileged teacher policy $\pi_{\text{teacher}}(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \mid \PrivilegedSimulatorState, \MultimodalObservation_{t})$ learns an effective control strategy via standard reinforcement learning, exploiting full access to contact forces and surface friction. In Phase 2, the student policy $\pi_{\text{student}}(\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \mid \ObservationHistoryWindow)$ is trained via supervised imitation learning (such as DAgger or behavioral cloning) to reproduce the teacher's proposed actions using only a sliding history of onboard observations. While this two-phase approach simplifies reinforcement learning exploration, it introduces a transfer bottleneck. If the teacher's control strategy relies on distinctions that cannot be reconstructed from the onboard observation history $\ObservationHistoryWindow$, the student cannot replicate the teacher's behavior. Privileged information accelerates training convergence, but it cannot make physically unobservable states identifiable on hardware.

Consider the cage-door latch mechanism. A student network equipped with a temporal history can compare commanded motor efforts against observed joint accelerations over recent timesteps, inferring changes in contact stiffness or friction through the resulting mechanical resistance. However, identical joint kinematics can arise from multiple distinct physical causes, and an unobserved geometric offset in the strike plate cannot be inferred simply because the simulation teacher possessed that knowledge. A temporal convolutional network or transformer encoder can output a learned latent embedding of the environment, but its accuracy must be audited against physical ground truth. Adding auxiliary loss functions to predict privileged parameters during distillation regularizes the representation, but an auxiliary loss cannot create physical information that is absent from the underlying sensor stream.

Panel (b) stacks three small traces: a state trace that drifts out of a shaded band of demonstrated states, a contact force whose red spike rises above a dashed force limit, and an oscillation that grows into large chatter where the actuation frequency matches the resonance frequency.
context:
```

Minimizing loss on an offline demonstration split or maximizing cumulative return in simulation measures compliance with training assumptions rather than physical competence on hardware. When an objective rewards behavior that exploits a curated demonstration distribution or a simulator approximation, the ranking of candidates established in training can invert on deployment\index{Deployment!policy ranking inversion}. The candidate that scored highest in simulation finishes lowest on hardware, through unsupported state drift, contact-force spikes past the structural limit, or torque oscillations that grow into resonant chatter (@fig-06-policy-ranking-inversion). Virtual environments forgive maneuvers that physical hardware penalizes with tripwires, resonance, or thermal overload, so the causal assumptions connecting a training metric to physical execution have to be tested before a policy receives actuator authority.

title: Evaluation evidence regimes
caption: **Evaluation evidence regimes**: The regimes vary along causal feedback (open vs. closed loop) and physical realism (logged or synthetic vs. live hardware). Replay cannot observe compounding drift, simulation leaves the reality gap open, shadow operation locks the trajectory to the baseline controller, and constrained testing truncates failures at the constraint boundary $\partial\ConstrainedTestEnvelope$. No single regime tests deployment beyond that boundary.
alt: Two-axis schematic with physical realism on the vertical axis, from logged or synthetic up to live hardware, and causal feedback on the horizontal axis, from open loop to closed loop. Four panels. Shadow mode, top left, feeds the real plant's observations to a baseline controller that drives the motors and to a candidate policy whose actions are only logged. Constrained testing, top right, closes the loop from the candidate policy through the permission path to the real plant, inside a red dashed constraint boundary beyond which lies open deployment. Recorded replay, bottom left, feeds a demonstration dataset to the policy and scores the action error, with no path from action back to state. Simulation, bottom right, closes the loop through a simulated plant whose dynamics differ from the real one.
context:
### The four evaluation evidence regimes {#sec-evaluation-four-regimes}

The first axis, causal feedback, governs whether a candidate's emitted actions alter future states and subsequent sensor observations ($\partial \MechanicalPlantState_{t+1}/\partial \CognitivePolicyAction_{t} \ne \ZeroVector$), or whether the policy merely reads a prerecorded, invariant sensory stream. In an open-loop configuration, execution errors cannot compound because mistakes never propagate into future inputs. In a closed loop, small policy errors perturb subsequent machine states and accumulate into compounding drift at a rate dictated by system dynamics and closed-loop feedback gains. The second axis, physical realism, governs whether sensory observations originate from physical transducers interacting with unmodeled contact dynamics, gear backlash, tire slip, and variable illumination ($\PhysicalPlantDynamics$), or instead emerge from a synthetic numerical simulator or static buffer ($\SimulatedPlantDynamics$). No single testing configuration can maximize both axes simultaneously without exposing expensive hardware, or nearby operators, to an unproven and potentially destructive policy. Each quadrant of @fig-07-evidence-regimes therefore provides evidence for specific claims and carries its own structural blind spot.

title: Inverting a clean record into a bound
caption: **Inverting a clean record into a bound**: The probability that `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_runs_str` independent runs all succeed, $\TrialSuccessProbability^{20}$, against the true per-run success probability $\TrialSuccessProbability$. Candidates left of the crossing with $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha_str` would make the observed record rarer than one campaign in twenty, so the record rules them out; the crossing at $\TrialSuccessProbability =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str` is the lower bound. The one-in-eight policy still logs a clean record in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_clean_one_in_pct_str` of campaigns.
alt: Log-scale plot of the probability of twenty clean runs against the true success probability from 0.70 to 1.00. The rising curve crosses a horizontal dashed line at 0.05 near a success probability of 0.861, marked with a dot and a vertical dropline; the region left of the crossing is shaded gray. A second marker at a success probability of 0.875 sits slightly above the line at about 0.069.
context:
fails one run in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.n_one_in_str` ($\TrialSuccessProbability =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_one_in_str`). That policy still produces an unbroken twenty-run success streak in `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_clean_one_in_pct_str` of evaluation campaigns. An empirical run of twenty successes cannot rule it out. As the candidate success rate $\TrialSuccessProbability$ decreases, a clean record becomes increasingly improbable. When $\TrialSuccessProbability$ drops to `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str`, the probability of observing twenty consecutive successes falls to exactly $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.alpha_str`, which corresponds to the significance level for a 95 percent confidence requirement ($1 - 0.95$). Any underlying success probability lower than `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str` would make the observed twenty-run clean record rarer than a 1-in-20 chance ($\TrialSuccessProbability^{20} < 0.05$). The one-sided lower confidence bound therefore identifies the threshold below which candidate policies become statistically inconsistent with the experimental data. In standard frequentist qualification, "95 percent confidence" describes the long-run coverage of the testing protocol. Across repeated qualification campaigns, the procedure traps the true parameter $\TrialSuccessProbability$ above the calculated bound at least 95 percent of the time. The bound represents a conservative floor under the declared sampling model rather than a point estimate of $\TrialSuccessProbability$ or a Bayesian posterior belief about this specific policy.

Reading the inversion as a curve makes the logic visible. Plotting $\TrialSuccessProbability^{20}$ against every candidate $\TrialSuccessProbability$ (@fig-07-clean-run-inversion) shows the clean record ruling out only the candidates whose curve lies below the $\HypothesisTestSignificanceLevel$ line, the region left of $\TrialSuccessProbability =$ `{python} ClopperPearsonZeroFailure.p_lower_val_str`. The one-in-eight policy sits just above that line, which is why twenty flawless runs cannot reject it.
