title: Standardized robotic evaluation facility
caption: **Standardized robotic evaluation facility**: NIST response-robot test bays photographed in 2013 (Linda Joy/NIST); their test methods are standardized by ASTM subcommittee E54.09 on response robots. A zero-failure run across standardized bays establishes competence inside the arena and says nothing about glare, surface contaminants, or obstacles outside it.
alt: Photograph by Linda Joy/NIST of NIST response-robot test facility bays in 2013. Structured test spaces support repeatable trials within their fixture conditions.
context:
The door latch campaign shows why the contact shock entry in @tbl-07-extreme-value-tails pairs a measurement with an architectural safeguard rather than with a fitted tail. Each trial yields only one block maximum, its peak latch contact force, and twenty maxima cannot fit a generalized extreme value tail that would predict the probability of exceeding `{python} EvalMachine.f_latch_limit_str`. The safeguard therefore comes from the rise-time argument above. The guarded `{python} EvalMachine.v_approach_str` approach is a candidate precontact limit whose adequacy depends on the measured effective mass, contact stiffness, and structural threshold. Reactive force monitoring addresses the sustained load that follows.

Deploying parallel robots across a test fleet does not establish statistical independence, as the pitfall in definition \ref{dfn-evaluation-exposure-wall} warns. Ten identical machines operating concurrently in a single warehouse share the same manufacturing batch, firmware revision, concrete sealant finish, heating and ventilation airflow, and operator handling protocols. Environmental disturbances absent from that facility, such as low-angle winter solar glare, surface water pooling, or floor polishing glazing, affect none of the machines. Standardized physical test fixtures, such as the response-robot test bays captured in @fig-07-nist-test-arena, ensure repeatable benchmark comparisons by strictly constraining the test environment to known, fixed obstacle geometries.

Uncorrected, the skew alone spends about half of the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` localization allowance (dashed line).
alt: Line plot with image row on the vertical axis, zero at the top, and camera position along the direction of travel in millimeters on the horizontal axis, with read time in milliseconds on a second axis above. A straight line runs from zero at the top row to about 25 millimeters at the bottom row, inside a shaded band about 24 millimeters wide. A dashed vertical line at 50 millimeters marks the localization allowance.
section: Rolling shutter distortion and motion compensation
context:
Resolving this spatial artifact requires **rolling-shutter motion compensation**\index{Rolling-shutter motion compensation!definition}: unwarping image coordinates geometrically using an interpolated camera pose for every scanline. The onboard IMU supplies high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) angular velocity and specific-force[^fn-imu-specific-force] samples rather than direct velocity measurements. A fused state estimator integrates these inertial readings with bias estimates, gravity tracking, and wheel odometry to compute continuous body poses. Transforming these poses through calibrated body-to-camera extrinsics yields an estimated optical pose for each scanline, allowing the perception pipeline to rectify the image before running stereo matching or landmark triangulation. Plotted against row index, the uncompensated skew is a straight line, because each row is read a fixed interval after the one above it (@fig-08-rolling-shutter-rows). The line ends halfway to the `{python} RollingShutterSkew.delta_loc_str` allowance, which is why compensation, not a budget row, must absorb it.

[^fn-imu-specific-force]: **Specific Force**: An accelerometer measures non-gravitational acceleration, $\LinearAcceleration-\GravityVector$, so a unit resting on the floor reads one $\Gravity$ upward and one in free fall reads zero. Dead reckoning must therefore rotate specific force into the navigation frame and restore the gravity vector, and an attitude error $\AttitudeError$ leaks $\Gravity\sin\AttitudeError$ into horizontal acceleration, which integrates twice into the per-row poses that de-skewing relies on. \index{Inertial measurement unit!specific force}

title: Rolling shutter distortion geometry
caption: **Rolling shutter distortion geometry**: A phone camera's rolling shutter photographs a turning aircraft propeller. Because scanlines are exposed and read sequentially from top to bottom rather than simultaneously, blades that move appreciably during the frame's readout are recorded as curved, disconnected arcs; each row samples the blade at a later instant. On a moving robot the same row-by-row sampling shears straight structures and biases the geometry downstream estimators triangulate. (Credit: [Dick Lyon](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Propellor_with_rolling-shutter_artifact.jpg) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0).
alt: Photograph from an aircraft window of a propeller and engine nacelle in flight, with sky and ground below. The blades appear as bent, curved shapes, some detached from the hub, instead of straight radial blades.

The sharp building edges and vehicles hold only because every return was placed with the pose at its own firing time; a single sweep is far sparser than this aggregate. (Credit: [Daniel L. Lu](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ouster_OS1-64_lidar_point_cloud_of_intersection_of_Folsom_and_Dore_St,_San_Francisco.png) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0).

context:

In the two-subscript convention, the first subscript names the destination frame and the second names the source: `T_ab` maps coordinates from frame b to frame a, and its inverse maps back. A homogeneous point appends a final coordinate of 1 so that the matrix applies translation as well as rotation. @Sec-appendix-control-spatial develops this representation and composition; @sec-perception-coordinate-chain applies it to the machine's mounting chain. Combining high-frequency (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) inertial data with wheel odometry allows the state estimator to compute the continuous trajectory of the vehicle body frame, $\WorldBodyTransform(\TimeInstant_i)$. Applying the calibrated mounting extrinsic $\BodyLidarTransform$ transforms coordinates from the LiDAR frame to the body frame, yielding the world-frame sensor pose $\WorldLidarTransform(\TimeInstant_i) = \WorldBodyTransform(\TimeInstant_i)\BodyLidarTransform$. Each individual homogeneous point return is then projected back into the LiDAR's coordinate frame at the frame reference epoch $\LidarSweepStartTime$:
$$\CartesianPosition_i(\LidarSweepStartTime) = \WorldLidarTransform^{-1}(\LidarSweepStartTime) \cdot \WorldLidarTransform(\TimeInstant_i) \cdot \CartesianPosition_i(\TimeInstant_i)$$
De-skewing is what makes an accumulated LiDAR map usable. The returns registered in @fig-08-lidar-pointcloud, gathered over about 18 s of driving through a city intersection, keep crisp building facades, road striping, and parked vehicles only because each return was placed with the vehicle pose at its own firing epoch $\TimeInstant_i$. Independently moving obstacles in the environment require separate velocity estimation and clustering. Flash LiDAR architectures avoid sweep distortion altogether by illuminating the entire field of view with a single laser pulse to capture an instantaneous 3D range matrix. Distributing finite optical pulse energy across a wide solid angle, however, sharply limits maximum operational range compared to concentrated, steerable beams.

caption: **Capture-to-brake timing strip**: Time runs from the exposure midpoint of the frame that first shows the hazard. The camera and host lanes carry the navigation camera's serial stages, with link, DMA, and ISP drawn as one segment, to dispatch at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`; the response lane adds the lease, tick, bus, and actuator onset of a stalled proposer to reach `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_str`. The row beneath reads the same axis as base travel at the `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` drive limit. The dashed line at dispatch marks where the dispatch-to-admission interval $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ enters; this chapter does not bound it, so every later event shifts right by its measured value.

The camera lane shows a solid exposure bar centered on the capture line and a readout bar after it. The host lane shows a combined link, DMA, and ISP bar, a longer backbone bar, and a thin IPC bar ending at a dispatch line. A dashed line at dispatch is labeled as the point where unbounded dispatch-to-admission time enters. The response lane starts at dispatch with a long lease bar, a thin tick and bus bar, and an onset bar ending at a brake-onset line. A bracket over the strip spans capture to brake onset. context:
This subtotal is a **partial delay budget** rather than an end-to-end capture-to-response bound. In the timing breakdown of @tbl-04-event-timing, perception governs the first interval from capture to dispatch, while actuator mechanics govern the third interval of physical braking. The observation continues to age across the intermediate second interval while the proposer completes inference, transmits the candidate trajectory, and awaits admission from the permission path. Let $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ denote this dispatch-to-admission interval, encompassing model planning and inter-process communication overheads. Because an active lease takes effect only upon candidate admission, the total delay under a stalled-proposer fault equals the displayed subtotal plus $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$. The transport-budget calculation in @sec-placement-dispatch-admission allocates a budget for $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ that awaits empirical validation on hardware. That allocation includes a full inference after dispatch, and part of that inference overlaps the vision backbone already counted in $\DispatchObservationAge$. Adding the two therefore counts the overlap twice and overstates the delay, which errs on the safe side; timestamping both intervals on the loaded machine removes the overlap.

Laid on one clock, the partial budget shows where the unbounded interval sits (@fig-08-capture-to-brake-strip). Everything before dispatch at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` belongs to perception, while everything after it belongs to the response path that reaches brake onset at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_str`. The dispatch-to-admission interval $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ enters at the dispatch line, so whatever value it takes on the loaded machine shifts every later event to the right.

section: MIPI CSI-2 DMA ingress and zero-copy buffers
context:
[^fn-iommu-dmabuf-sharing]: **IOMMU (Input-Output Memory Management Unit)**: The device-side counterpart of the CPU's MMU. It translates the addresses a DMA engine issues through page tables the kernel controls, so the ISP, CPU, and GPU can share one set of physical pages without copying while each device stays confined to its own mappings. A translation miss on that path is one more source of ingestion delay that the measured budget must include. \index{Memory!IOMMU}

Sharing pages changes the ownership of a captured payload rather than removing the payload's journey through memory. @Fig-08-shared-capture-buffer separates physical storage from device mappings and marks the release that permits the capture engine to reuse that storage.

title: Predict and update on the rack-end range
caption: **Predict and update on the rack-end range**: Each bar spans one standard deviation of the range estimate. Prediction widens the bar from `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_prior_str` to `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_pred_str`; the LiDAR update (gain `{python} AisleKalman.g_lidar_str`) and the stereo update (gain `{python} AisleKalman.g_stereo_str`) each narrow it below both of their inputs, whose own spreads appear as gray bars. The misdated stereo update on the right reports the same `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_fused_str` spread while sitting `{python} AisleKalman.bias_post_str` from the true range, which the variance alone cannot reveal.
alt: Error-bar chart with five columns on a vertical axis of range error in millimeters. Prior, predicted, after LiDAR update, and after stereo update columns are centered on zero, with the bar shrinking sharply after the stereo update. Gray bars beside the two update columns show the LiDAR and stereo measurement spreads. A fifth red column, labeled misdated stereo, has a short bar centered well above zero.
context:
A misdated measurement breaks this estimation algebra silently. Suppose a stereo depth observation is tagged with its host arrival timestamp, which @sec-perception-handoff shows hides exposure, readout, and transport delay, rather than with its physical exposure epoch. The filter erroneously pairs this observation with a robot pose `{python} AisleKalman.bias_misdate_str` further along the aisle than where the photons actually struck the sensor. Consequently, the measured range reads systematically long by that spatial displacement, causing the update to drag the state estimate `{python} AisleKalman.bias_post_str` away from the physical obstacle while reporting the same deceptively tight `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_fused_str` standard deviation. The resulting physical error spans approximately `{python} AisleKalman.bias_in_sigmas_str` reported standard deviations in the hazardous direction, yet the filter's covariance update detects nothing amiss because algebraic variance reduction depends entirely on modeled sensor noise rather than measurement residuals. Corrupt timestamps are therefore far more dangerous than dropped sensor frames. Dropping the stereo frame instead would leave the posterior uncertainty at `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_lidar_post_str`, imprecise but statistically honest.

Set side by side on one range-error scale (@fig-08-kalman-predict-update), the stages read as a single story. Prediction widens the bar from `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_prior_str` to `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_pred_str`, each update narrows it below both of its inputs to a final `{python} AisleKalman.sigma_fused_str`, and the misdated column reports that same tight spread while its center sits `{python} AisleKalman.bias_post_str` from the true range, the only bar that does not contain the truth.

title: Three evidence epochs in one cycle
caption: **Three evidence epochs in one cycle**: The tactile array, the camera's exposure midpoint, and the joint encoders each date their evidence on one clock, at `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t1_str`, `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t2_str`, and `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t3_str` in this illustrative cycle. A fused state dated to the encoder epoch must carry the camera's evidence across the `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str` gap with a kinematic model and a bounded velocity; packing the three readings into one token sequence records none of these epochs.
alt: Timing strip with three lanes labeled tactile, camera, and encoders over a time axis in milliseconds. Each lane has one short sample mark at its own time, with vertical event lines labeled tactile latch, camera exposure midpoint, and encoder sample. A bracket above the strip spans the interval between the camera and encoder marks and is labeled with the gap to project across.
context: MemoryEpochAlignment.t1_str`, an optical tracking camera might have its exposure midpoint at $\TimeInstant_2 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t2_str`, and joint optical encoders might sample angular positions at $\TimeInstant_3 =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.t3_str`. These observations occur at different epochs and cannot be combined through direct tensor concatenation or naive algebraic operations. Multimodal foundation models and vision-language-action (VLA) backbones frequently pack visual patch tokens, proprioceptive vectors, and tactile embeddings into a single sequence under the implicit assumption that all tokens capture a simultaneous physical snapshot. However, nothing in that token serialization records that the camera frame came from $\TimeInstant_2$ and the encoder reading from $\TimeInstant_3$. As a result, representations inferred from unaligned inputs carry unquantified temporal mismatch errors. Fusing a camera observation at $\TimeInstant_2$ with an encoder observation at $\TimeInstant_3$ requires the consumer to project one state across the temporal gap $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant = |\TimeInstant_3 - \TimeInstant_2| =$ `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str`. The projection uses explicit kinematic models and bounded velocities (for example, propagating the historical camera observation along the joint velocity vector to reconcile it with the instantaneous encoder reading). The gap is small in time but not in space; at the arm's `{python} EpochGapTravel.v_cart_str` Cartesian speed limit, the tool moves `{python} EpochGapTravel.d_gap_str` in `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str`, a millimeter-scale error that a fine insertion cannot absorb. Without the true acquisition epoch for each individual signal, the alignment calculation cannot determine the sign or magnitude of $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$, leaving uncorrected temporal offsets to compound geometric errors across every inference cycle. Placed on one shared timeline (@fig-09-epoch-alignment), the three epochs fall at distinct instants, and the camera evidence must be carried across the `{python} MemoryEpochAlignment.gap_str` gap before it can be fused with the encoder state.

section: Coordinate Transform Expiry and Localization Drift {#sec-memory-reference-frames}
context:
:::

Transform state also spans multiple machine words: three floating-point numbers for translation and four for rotation as a unit quaternion. A high-rate control reader racing an asynchronous perception writer can therefore tear a read, observing an old rotation paired with a new translation. The lock-free sequence lock (seqlock) mailbox established in @sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges resolves this concurrency race without blocking hard real-time control threads. Each reader makes a single bounded attempt per tick and never blocks. If the sequence count reveals a torn read, the thread discards the sample and lets the last validated transform age in place.

title: Transform staleness and lever-arm error at the latch-release slot
caption: **Transform staleness and lever-arm error at the latch-release slot**: Illustrative finger error over one frame period, with zero ingestion delay assumed to isolate this contribution. A deployed calculation must use full capture-to-use age. The camera-to-slot edge ages by duration $\\FiniteChange \\TimeInstant$. Lateral drift at the velocity bound $\\DriftSpeedBound$ moves the finger by $\\TranslationalDriftError = \\DriftSpeedBound\\,\\FiniteChange \\TimeInstant$, while the wrist turning at $\\JointAngularRate$ swings the fingertip, a lever arm $\\LeverArmLength$ beyond it, by $\\LeverArmSweepError \\approx \\LeverArmLength\\,\\JointAngularRate\\,\\FiniteChange \\TimeInstant$. Composing the stale edge with the current wrist pose adds both to the initial error $\\InitialTrackingError$, so the finger error $\\ToolPositionError \\approx \\InitialTrackingError + \\TranslationalDriftError + \\LeverArmLength\\,\\FiniteChange\\JointAngle$ exceeds the slot tolerance $\\PositionalTaskTolerance$.
alt: Transform staleness at the latch-release slot. A dashed ghost arm shows the wrist and finger as dated by the stale edge at t0, with a dashed circle marking the slot tolerance r_tol around the finger. The current arm at t0 + Δt shows the wrist shifted laterally by e_trans = v_drift Δt and the link of length r_arm turned by Δθ_joint = ω Δt, which swings the finger by e_rot ≈ r_arm Δθ_joint. A red vector from the stale finger position to the current finger, labeled e_tool ≈ e_0 + e_trans + r_arm Δθ_joint, ends well outside the r_tol circle.
context:
including neural inference, message serialization, and transport. Starting from an initial calibration error $\InitialTrackingError =$ `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e0_str`, lateral motion drifts by at most $\TranslationalDriftError = \DriftSpeedBound\,\FiniteChange \TimeInstant =$ `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_trans_str` under an unobserved lateral velocity bound of $\DriftSpeedBound =$ `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.v_drift_str`.

The kinematic lever arm magnifies this displacement substantially. With the fingertip positioned at a distance $\LeverArmLength =$ `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.lever_str` beyond the wrist joint, an alignment rotation at angular rate $\JointAngularRate =$ `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.omega_str` sweeps the tip through an arc of $\LeverArmSweepError \approx \LeverArmLength\,\JointAngularRate\,\FiniteChange \TimeInstant =$ `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_rot_str`. The optical encoders register the wrist rotation correctly; the error comes from what the rotation is applied to. The cached camera-to-slot transform states where the slot sat relative to the camera at the previous frame, and the camera rides on the wrist. Application code that chains that cached transform with the current wrist pose therefore swings the computed slot along with the wrist, while the real slot, fixed in the door, stays where it was. The result is a hybrid pose that the arm never occupied. Correcting this error requires either querying the kinematic chain at the exact capture epoch of the camera frame or expiring the stale transform outright. Unchecked, the stale transform displaces the estimated finger position by $\ToolPositionError \approx \InitialTrackingError + \TranslationalDriftError + \LeverArmSweepError =$ `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.e_tool_str`, which exceeds the mechanical tolerance by `{python} LatchTransformStaleness.ratio_pct_str`. The lever arm contributes over three times as much error as translational drift alone. Because the matrix multiplications complete without raising a runtime exception, the control loop blindly aligns the tool to an invalid target, driving the finger into the surrounding strike plate.

title: Odometry drift against the localization bound
caption: **Odometry drift against the localization bound**: The UMBmark return error, scaled per meter of path, grows linearly with distance driven. Uncalibrated, it spends the `{python} OdometryDrift.delta_loc_str` localization bound after `{python} OdometryDrift.d_uncal_str`; calibrated, after `{python} OdometryDrift.d_cal_str`, only just beyond one `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle. Both lines extrapolate return errors from a slow laboratory run; deployed correction spacing must be qualified against the machine’s own drift envelope before $\\LocalizationBound$ can be relied on.
alt: Line plot of accumulated odometry error in millimeters against distance driven in meters, from 0 to 60 m. A steep line for uncalibrated odometry leaves the top of the plot within a few meters, and a shallow line for calibrated odometry rises slowly. A red dashed horizontal line marks the localization bound, and markers show where each line crosses it. A gray dashed vertical line marks the length of one aisle.
context:
driven (@fig-09-odometry-drift), even the calibrated line crosses the bound only just past one `{python} OdometryDrift.aisle_length_str` aisle, which makes $\LocalizationBound$ a constraint on how often external map corrections arrive rather than an intrinsic property of the mobile base.

Three physical realities prevent this illustrative calibrated extrapolation from establishing an operational design margin. First, the laboratory benchmark operated at `{python} OdometryDrift.v_test_str` along straight segments to minimize wheel slip, stopping to pivot at each corner; production warehouse bases travel `{python} OdometryDrift.speed_ratio_mult_str` faster under varying operational payloads. Second, kinematic calibration eliminates only deterministic systematic errors. Non-systematic stochastic errors (floor irregularities and micro-slip) produced a run-to-run standard deviation of approximately `{python} OdometryDrift.sigma_run_str`, eclipsing the residual calibrated systematic error of `{python} OdometryDrift.e_cal_str`. Third, a constant per-meter error rate is merely a first-order linearization. An uncorrected heading error $\SmallChange\HeadingAngle$ produces lateral position displacement $\SmallChange\HeadingAngle\,\TraverseDistance$ over a straight traverse of distance $\TraverseDistance$. Because wheel-diameter mismatch causes heading error to accumulate linearly with distance ($\SmallChange\HeadingAngle \approx \HeadingCurvature \TraverseDistance$ for a constant heading curvature $\HeadingCurvature$), the resulting lateral error grows quadratically, about $\tfrac{1}{2}\HeadingCurvature \TraverseDistance^2$, quadrupling each time the straight run doubles. Under this illustrative drift model, reserving localization margin requires external corrections at intervals shorter than the calculated crossing distance; the deployed interval must come from the machine’s qualified drift envelope. In deployed systems, the site parameter $\LocalizationBound$ must be established empirically, by driving the robot past surveyed fiducials at nominal velocity and maximum payload across actual facility flooring, reporting drift rates at a defined operating percentile.

```
title: One range return updates only the cells it touched
caption: **One range return updates only the cells it touched**: Under the qualified coverage and geometric-error assumptions, the cells the ray crosses become free and take the capture epoch $\\TimeInstant_1$ of the return, which also retires a phantom obstacle left on that line; the cell holding the return becomes occupied at $\\TimeInstant_1$. Cells behind the return and every cell off the ray keep whatever epoch their own last evidence gave them, here $\\TimeInstant_0$, so the map's publication time dates none of them.
alt: A grid of square cells with a sensor at the left. An arrow runs from the sensor along one row of cells, which are tinted and labeled t1. One of them holds a dashed square labeled phantom retired. The arrow ends at a black cell labeled return, occupied, t1. The four cells beyond it in the same row are hatched and labeled t0, with a note reading behind return, not renewed. The other rows are blank.
context:
[^fn-voxel-ray-traversal]: **Voxel Traversal**: @amanatides1987fast step a ray from one voxel boundary to the next by comparing the distances to the next crossing on each axis and adding one fixed increment, so each voxel visited costs a few comparisons and one addition. The work per ray is therefore proportional to the number of voxels it crosses, range divided by pitch, which is the $\RayTraversalLength/\VoxelPitch$ factor of @eq-mem-dram-bandwidth. \index{Voxel traversal!Amanatides-Woo}

[^fn-logodds-unknown-prior]: **Log-Odds**: Storing $\ell = \ln\big(\CellOccupancyProbability/(1-\CellOccupancyProbability)\big)$ turns each Bayesian occupancy update into an addition, with an uninformed prior at $\ell = 0$. A cell no ray has touched and a cell that received as many hits as misses both read $\ell = 0$, so the value alone cannot separate never observed from observed and ambiguous. The manifest of @tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief therefore carries an explicit `cell_state`. \index{Log-odds!unknown state}

title: Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graph architecture
caption: **Hierarchical 3D dynamic scene graph architecture**: Five-layer spatio-temporal memory organization bridging continuous 3D-indexed metric state stores to symbolic foundation reasoning. Drawn for the warehouse, Layer 1 captures triangular metric mesh geometry; Layer 2 extracts 3D objects and dynamic agents such as a walking person; Layer 3 models topological places via Voronoi freespace clearance spheres ($\\TopologicalPlaceNode_i$); Layer 4 structures architectural rooms and portals; and Layer 5 establishes global building mission topology. Vertical inter-layer edges coordinate upward abstraction (compressing metric surfaces into symbolic entities) and downward grounding (translating task tokens into metric coordinates) (adapted from Rosinol et al. [@rosinol20203d; @rosinol2021kimera] and Hughes et al. [@hughes2022hydra]).
alt: Five stacked horizontal bands. From bottom to top: layer 1, a triangle mesh; layer 2, boxes for mug, tote, cage door, and a dashed box for person; layer 3, four places p1 to p4 drawn as dashed circles joined in a chain; layer 4, rooms aisle 12, cross aisle, and dock bay joined in a row; layer 5, buildings warehouse and loading dock. Thin lines connect each node to its parent in the band above, and the mesh to three of the objects. An upward arrow labeled abstraction and a downward arrow labeled grounding run beside the bands.
context:
Supplying that identity is the job of semantic scene memory, which sits above the raw metric layer and inherits its physical constraints. Learned neural models infer what an object is, whereas the underlying metric mapping pipeline anchors where that object sits in physical space. Open-vocabulary scene memory bridges these domains using **3D vision foundation models**\index{3D vision foundation models}. A self-supervised visual backbone such as DINOv2 [@oquab2023dinov2] extracts dense patch feature representations. A promptable segmentation model such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [@kirillov2023segment] generates class-agnostic instance masks. Systems such as ConceptGraphs [@kuwajerwala2024conceptgraphs; @jatavallabhula2023conceptfusion] and Hydra [@hughes2022hydra] lift those 2D masks and semantic features through calibrated depth, extrinsics, and visual odometry into an **object-centric 3D scene graph**\index{Object-centric 3D scene graph!definition}. In this structured representation, each node represents an entity parameterized by a 3D centroid, a spatial covariance matrix, and a text-aligned multimodal embedding vector.

Drawn for the warehouse (@fig-09-dynamic-scene-graph), such a graph stacks five layers: a metric mesh, the objects and agents segmented from it (mugs, totes, the cage door, a walking person), topological places linked through free space, rooms such as aisles and dock bays, and the building itself. Edges between layers run both ways, compressing metric surfaces into symbols on the way up and grounding task tokens in metric coordinates on the way down.

title: Free-space erosion at the rack end
caption: **Free-space erosion at the rack end**: (a) Top view. The navigation camera's sightline passes the rack end, so the cross aisle behind the rack is unknown from the moment of capture. A person hidden there can advance at $\\HumanWalkingSpeedBound$ = `{python} RackEndBelief.v_h_str`; the dashed disc is the region that person may occupy when the claim lapses, which stops $\\LocalizationBound + \\ProtectiveClearanceMargin$ short of the hull's front. (b) The depth memory still certifies, $\\FreeSpaceDepth - \\LocalizationBound - \\ProtectiveClearanceMargin - \\HumanWalkingSpeedBound \\TimeInstant$. For the hull's current position it falls from the initial clear distance less localization error and protective clearance to zero at `{python} RackEndBelief.t_exp_ahead_str`, and the frame's `{python} RackEndBelief.t_age_str` age at dispatch is spent before memory receives it; abreast of the rack end, the `{python} RackEndBelief.side_clearance_str` side clearance certifies nothing even at capture.
alt: Two stacked panels. Top panel a, a top view: a hull in an aisle between two racks, the upper rack ending 1.10 m ahead of the hull's front where a cross aisle opens. A dashed teal sightline runs from a camera on the hull's front past the rack end, and the cross aisle above the sightline is hatched and labeled unknown, hidden cross aisle. A pink dashed disc centered on the rack end, clipped to the floor, is labeled reach at T_inv, 0.95 m, and a small ring at its center is labeled at dispatch, 83 mm. Dimensions show D_clear 1.10 m ahead and a side gap of 150 mm between hull and rack. Bottom panel b: certified free depth in millimeters against time since the frame, 0 to 700 ms. A solid blue line falls from 950 mm to zero at 593.75 ms, marked with a red dot. A dashed gray line for the hull abreast of the rack end lies at zero, with a red dot at 0 ms. A gray band covers the first 51.6 ms, labeled frame age at dispatch.
context:
:::

In the open aisle, spatial memory reliably bridges temporary camera frame drops. However, the notebook's deadline is computed for a hull standing at its current pose. A hull that drives toward the rack end at speed $\SpeedAtDetection$ closes on the occlusion boundary while the hidden person closes on it from the other side. The depth certified ahead therefore shrinks at $\SpeedAtDetection + \HumanWalkingSpeedBound$ rather than at $\HumanWalkingSpeedBound$. Each successive swept volume along the planned path starts closer to the boundary, until the horizon reaches zero abreast of the rack uprights. The stopping budget makes the same point in distance. At the `{python} RackEndBelief.v_drive_str` drive limit, the stopping-budget terms charged before memory enters already claim `{python} RackEndBelief.running_total_str` of the `{python} RackEndBelief.d_clear_str` clear distance before anyone moves in the cross aisle. The safety enforcement path must therefore evaluate @eq-mem-free-space-expiry along the entire planned trajectory. The robot must bring itself to a controlled stop, or reacquire line-of-sight visibility into the cross aisle, before any point on the swept path breaches its invalidation deadline. The clear distance the sensors can still see caps the speed at which the hull may approach an occluded rack end, a ceiling that @sec-enforcement-phase-portraits plots against clearance. Memory certifies clearance only to a depth governed by the physical distance to the occlusion boundary. At the rack corner, that geometric depth vanishes completely.

title: Belief uncertainty and invalidation horizon
caption: **Belief uncertainty and invalidation horizon**: Illustrative spatial error bound $\\BeliefErrorBound(\\FiniteChange \\TimeInstant)$ of a gripper finger entering the cage door's latch-release slot, expanding quadratically under unobserved forward propagation until intersecting the slot clearance $\\PositionalTaskTolerance$ = `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e_max_str` at invalidation horizon $\\BeliefInvalidationHorizon$ = `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_str`; the shaded region beyond it is elapsed time for which the belief no longer supports motion. A dashed constant-velocity estimate grows more slowly, and the red marker shows that estimate still admitting the belief at `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_linear_str`, after the bounded error has passed the clearance. Belief has a shelf life governed by physical disturbance dynamics, and only qualified new evidence can renew the relevant state claim.
alt: Belief uncertainty growth and invalidation horizon plot. Spatial error bound E(Δt) plotted against elapsed time Δt since last measurement. The quadratic curve expands from e0 = 0.1 mm to intersect task clearance r_tol = 1 mm at invalidation horizon T_inv = 66 ms, beyond which the plot is shaded light red. A dashed constant-velocity line rises more slowly, and a red marker on the bounded curve shows the belief that estimate still admits after the curve has crossed the clearance.
context:
Evaluating this bounded growth model with the scenario parameters yields `{python} LatchSlotBelief.growth_math`, where elapsed time $\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$ is in seconds and error $\BeliefErrorBound(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant)$ is in millimeters. Setting $\BeliefErrorBound(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant) = \PositionalTaskTolerance$ produces the quadratic characteristic equation `{python} LatchSlotBelief.quad_math`. The positive real root establishes an invalidation horizon of $\BeliefInvalidationHorizon =$ `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_str`. Motion plans relying on this visual estimate must complete or transition to a qualified fallback before this deadline, with deceleration commands dispatched in advance.

If the mechanical slot is machined to a tighter clearance of `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e_max_tight_str`, the invalidation horizon contracts sharply to `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_exp_tight_str` (`{python} LatchSlotBelief.quad_tight_math`). Tightening the mechanical clearance by a factor of `{python} LatchSlotBelief.tol_ratio_mult_str` reduces the available prediction window by a factor of `{python} LatchSlotBelief.horizon_ratio_mult_str`, because the initial error consumes a larger share of the tighter tolerance. Subtracting the unchanged initial error leaves `{python} LatchSlotBelief.slack_str` in the original slot and `{python} LatchSlotBelief.slack_tight_str` in the tighter one, so the usable-slack ratio exceeds the total-tolerance ratio. Acceleration separately shortens both horizons. In contrast, an estimator that naively assumes constant velocity ($\DisturbanceAccelerationBound = 0$) predicts an overly optimistic horizon of $(\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError)/\DriftVelocityBound =$ `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_linear_str`. By that time, the bounded acceleration model permits error up to `{python} LatchSlotBelief.e_linear_str`, exceeding the allowable clearance by `{python} LatchSlotBelief.overshoot_pct_str`. A controller operating on constant-velocity extrapolation would continue unguided insertion for `{python} LatchSlotBelief.t_extra_str` beyond safe physical bounds, risking mechanical jam or tool damage.

## The Belief Record Schema {#sec-memory-spatial-state-schema}

The belief record introduced in @sec-memory-handoff, the seventh record in the record chain, binds each state estimate to its capture epoch, coordinate frame, and error-growth law so that downstream controllers can catch a frozen transform, a chimeric frame chain, or a prediction that has outlived its slot tolerance. This schema unifies discrete tracked entities and continuous volumetric representations (@tbl-09-schema-volumetric-belief) under one set of time and error rules, serving both trajectory planning on the host and bounded local permission checks on real-time microcontrollers. From the observation contracts established in @sec-perception-observation-contract, the record inherits the raw sensor capture epoch, clock identifier, and hardware conversion bound. For differently constrained state components, it preserves separate evidence epochs or a conservative shared epoch and growth bound, as required by @sec-memory-state-epoch. With these fields, the safety permission controller translates the sensor's capture timestamp into its own local monotonic clock with bounded synchronization error before evaluating evidence age. Persistent memory contributes five fields of its own. An estimate epoch dates the propagated state without renewing physical evidence. An uncertainty-growth bound projects error expansion across blind intervals. A validity region defines the operating envelope where that bound holds. The record also carries a physical invalidation deadline. Finally, a query-work allocation is set to at most `{python} RepresentationQuery.t_query_str` per local collision query in the reference design, and it becomes a justified execution bound only after qualification on the chosen hardware. Across its lifetime, each record moves through the four-state lifecycle of @fig-09-spatial-belief-state-machine, whose guards enforce two rules. Only fresh evidence returns a record to `VALID`, and leaving `UNOBSERVABLE` also requires restoring the missing physical constraint.
```

section: What each proposal family leaves to admission {#sec-intent-proposal-families}
context:
open-vocabulary phrase grounding from computer vision and natural language processing [@kamath2021mdetr; @gu2022open; @radford2021learning; @liu2023grounding], yet an embodied machine cannot rely on a model's internal activations for physical safety. For example, a semantic skill ranker like SayCan outputs a discrete skill identifier scored by language affordance and value functions [@ahn2022saycan]. A programmatic generator like Code as Policies produces a control script that calls perception and motion APIs [@liang2023code]. VoxPoser synthesizes 3D spatial value maps (@fig-10-value-map-composition). OK-Robot emits a distribution of sampled grasp poses (@fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding). Because none of these outputs natively carries a bounded wrench envelope, a certified clearance margin, or a hardware lease expiration, choosing one model family over another only shifts where conversion happens and leaves the admission checks in @tbl-10-grounding-paradigms unchanged.

Predicting a syntactically valid coordinate or control script never guarantees physical feasibility. Vision-language and action models are trained to maximize sequence likelihood over offline demonstration datasets. Their loss functions encode neither metric distances, rigid-body collision avoidance, manipulator Jacobian conditioning, nor frictional contact dynamics. Validating a candidate action requires deterministic physical checks evaluated within explicit coordinate frames. These checks include signed-distance queries over robot and environment meshes to verify clearance, numerical inverse-kinematics solvers with joint-limit and singularity screening, and Coulomb friction models to confirm that the planned grasp wrench resists expected gravitational and inertial loads. For contact-rich tasks such as sliding an object, turning a latch, or executing a handover, the system can simulate candidate trajectories in a rigid-body physics engine before committing actuator current. However, simulation fidelity remains bounded by the accuracy of estimated surface friction and inertial parameters. Downstream controllers must still enforce real-time admission checks regardless of simulation outcomes.

In VoxPoser's value-map interface (@fig-10-value-map-composition), an affordance map rewards voxels near the handle the instruction names, an avoidance map penalizes voxels near observed obstacles, and the planner follows the composed cost around the obstacle it can see. section: Dynamic obstacle forecasting and forward occupancy {#sec-intent-dynamic-forecasting}
context:
1. *Short receding horizons:* Screening over the evidence horizon rather than seconds ahead keeps the growth term near `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_occ_tracked_str` instead of meters. The forecast must still cover the entire executed prefix and the physical fallback, including response delay and deceleration; shortening the lease does not shorten an actor's possible motion while the robot stops.
2. *Re-centering on fresh evidence:* A qualified tracker re-centers each set on new measurements ($\MonotonicClockInstant_0 \leftarrow \FreshEvidenceTime$), resetting the growth term and the propagated covariance, provided its accuracy and latency support the required bound.
3. *Interaction-aware prediction:* Trautman and Krause's own remedy predicts the people and the robot jointly, so that each accounts for how the others will respond. Such predictions are learned or modeled proposals, and they may narrow a set only after their error has been bounded by the same kind of evidence the permission path demands of any other input.

title: Intent lease lifecycle
caption: **Intent lease lifecycle**: A proposal waits in `Pending` until admission either refuses it, granting no authority, or arms the lease. While the lease is held, only a renewal with a higher sequence number, a newer capture, and a passing permission check moves it to `Renewed` or keeps it there; a stale renewal is rejected without resetting the timer. The held lease ends in one of three ways: the terminal predicates complete the goal, the timer reaches $\IntentLeaseExpiry$, or a contact limit or evidence loss aborts it. Expiry and abort both start the validated fallback, which the MCU selects for the measured state.

section: The Intent Lease Specification and Contract {#sec-intent-lease}
context:
An intent lease progresses through five discrete lifecycle states on the Safety MCU: `Pending`, `Active`, `Renewed`, `Expired`, and `Aborted`. The controller transitions a proposal from `Pending` to `Active` only after verifying all geometric and dynamic ceilings and confirming that a collision-free stopping path remains executable from the current state. Transitioning to `Renewed` requires a strictly monotonic sequence counter, a newer parent belief record with an updated sensor capture epoch, and a fully passed admission re-check. A complex approach trajectory can span multiple consecutive lease renewals as long as fresh perception evidence continues to justify the motion. Dropping an isolated camera frame does not immediately abort tracking if the current coasting window remains valid. However, absent renewal, the hardware timer continues counting toward expiration. When an anomaly, force limit breach, or evidence timeout revokes tracking authority, the controller immediately engages a pre-calculated deceleration or hold trajectory to manage the kinetic energy of the moving manipulator safely.

@Fig-10-intent-lease-lifecycle draws the same machine. Its one subtle transition is the self-loop on a stale renewal. A packet with an old sequence number or an old capture is discarded without resetting the timer, so a host that keeps talking without new evidence still runs out of authority. Expiry and abort end in the same place, the validated fallback that the MCU selects for the measured state.

```
context:
**Systems insight**: Evaluating torque magnitude alone is an inadequate feasibility screen at a trajectory seam. Actuator drives fail on the rate of change of torque, which grows quadratically ($1/\SeamBridgeDuration^2$) as blending duration compresses. When late trajectory admission forces the system to compress bridge duration $\SeamBridgeDuration$, required jerk and torque slew rates increase fourfold for every twofold reduction in duration. An admission monitor must explicitly re-evaluate the compressed bridge rather than inheriting validity from the uncompressed nominal profile. Furthermore, link inertia, payload mass, gravity, and joint friction compound this inertial baseline, requiring independent peak torque and thermal budget verification. The torque verdict of step 1 depends on that exclusion. With the payload inertia of @eq-plan-one-joint-dynamics included, `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.j_eff_str` in place of `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str`, the one-tick request grows by the same ratio and exceeds even the `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated peak, so the one-tick step fails the torque check as well.

context:
drive limit, the loaded tote rack tolerates the machine's credible `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` deceleration only when that deceleration is ramped gradually rather than applied as an abrupt step. The base's stop is therefore the S-curve of @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix with $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` and a jerk bound of `{python} PlanningC2Stop.j_base_str`. Plotted as velocity against time, the area under each curve is its stopping distance, and the jerk ramps appear as the rounded start and finish that stretch the S-curve and the polynomial past the constant-deceleration line (@fig-11-stopping-profiles). title: What the wheels allow
caption: **What the wheels allow**: (a) A differential-drive base with track width $\WheelTrackWidth$ can move forward at $\BaseForwardSpeed$ and turn at $\YawRate$ about the center of its axle, but its wheels cannot roll sideways. (b) A pure sideways offset is still reachable, as a maneuver rather than a step: turn in place, drive, and turn back. Proportions are schematic.
alt: Two top-view panels of a rectangular base with a drive wheel on each side. In the left panel, a solid arrow points forward along the heading, a curved arrow shows turning, a bracket marks the track width, and a dashed arrow pointing sideways is crossed out. In the right panel, a dashed sideways arrow between a start and a goal pose is crossed out, and a second path shows the base turned a quarter turn in place at the start, driving straight to the goal, and turning back, with the three steps numbered.
context:
The non-integrable relation in @eq-plan-unicycle forms a **nonholonomic constraint**\index{Nonholonomic constraint!differential drive},[^fn-holonomic-hertz-etymology] restricting the instantaneous velocity space without diminishing the dimension of the reachable configuration space $\PlanarSpecialEuclideanGroup$ [@siciliano2009robotics]. The base can reach any planar pose in the aisle, but not with any velocity. It can drive forward at $\BaseForwardSpeed$ and turn at $\YawRate$ about the center of its axle, while the no-slip condition forbids translation along the axle (@fig-11-nonholonomic-base). A pure sideways offset is therefore reached as a maneuver rather than a step: turn in place, drive along the new heading, and turn back. A base planner must therefore search directly over kinematically admissible control trajectories rather than straight geometric paths in configuration space. Furthermore, each wheel's tangential speed equals $\BaseForwardSpeed \pm \YawRate \WheelTrackWidth/2$ for track width $\WheelTrackWidth$, so hardware motor limits constrain linear velocity and turning rate jointly.

[^fn-holonomic-hertz-etymology]: **Holonomic** (Greek *holos*, whole, and *nomos*, law): @hertz1894prinzipien introduced the term for systems whose constraints obey integral laws, relations among positions alone, in contrast to material systems in general, which obey only differential laws. A wheel's no-slip rule is a differential law that cannot be integrated into such a relation. The distinction decides the planner's search space, since a holonomic arm can be planned as a path through configuration space while the base must be planned through its controls.\index{Holonomic constraint!etymology}

title: Planar laser scanner
caption: **Planar laser scanner**: A rotating mirror sweeps a time-of-flight beam across a horizontal fan, so the device reports range over one plane around the base. A safety-rated scanner of this form adds an early warning field and a protective field. The warning field requests earlier deceleration; the protective field's safety output feeds a controller that selects a risk-assessed stop. Protective-field length must include scanner response, controller and drive delay, braking travel, and uncertainty; a moving base does not become safe merely because motor torque is removed. (Photograph: [Björn Heller](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sick_laserscanner.jpg) / Wikimedia Commons, [CC BY-SA 3.0 DE](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/de/deed.en).)
alt: Photograph of a blue industrial laser scanner on an office desk beside a keyboard and mouse. A boxy upper housing carries a small status window and the maker's label; below it a black cylindrical window wraps around the base, behind which the beam sweeps.
section: legend below the axes: inside, the walking-person curve and the clear-distance label run under it
context:
:::

An independent protective safety scanner operates under its own hardware-to-actuation timing budget. When an obstacle breaches a safety-rated zone, the scanner's internal optical sampling, fail-safe output switching, safety controller logic, and drive disconnect delays entirely bypass the perception dispatch and software lease infrastructure. However, the physical response must still reserve the same underlying deceleration distance, mechanical tracking error, localization tolerance, and protective safety cushion; only computational delays bypassed by the safety bus are eliminated from the sum. Industrial mobile bases deploy such protective fields under ISO 3691-4 [@iso3691part4] for driverless industrial trucks and ISO 13849-1 [@iso13849part1] for safety-related control circuits, using a safety-rated planar scanner of the kind in @fig-12-real-laser-scanner, which evaluates programmable warning and protective fields. The physical dimensions of this protective field must be calculated from the dedicated scanner path's verified hardware timing budget, rather than inheriting the software lease and vision latencies of the neural planner. The safety-rated optical scanner is a component of a separately qualified protective function, distinct from the primary perception LiDAR that generates non-safety-rated point clouds for neural proposal generation. Its component rating does not certify the complete sensor-to-stop path. In the running architecture, that path must establish the detection coverage, response time, and physical stopping performance required for protection at rack intersections. @Sec-enforcement-certified-functions maps the software stopping budget onto this certified hardware baseline and shows that industrial vehicle testing standards validate pedestrian detection against the same static-obstacle assumption derived here.

context:
### Phase portraits and speed ceilings {#sec-enforcement-phase-portraits}

Checking velocity against a fixed scalar limit fails as soon as obstacle distance shrinks: a speed that is recoverable two meters from the rack end becomes an inevitable collision eighty centimeters closer. Drawn in the distance--velocity $(\ClearDistance, \SpeedAtDetection)$ phase plane (@fig-12-stopping-envelope-phase-plane), the plotted pre-dispatch envelope separates states whose accounted subtotal fits from states whose subtotal already exceeds clearance. Complete admission contracts that boundary further by charging dispatch travel. Braking alone traces the outer parabola. The inset boundary pulls the viable set, the recoverable set drawn in this plane, inward by the pre-brake travel $\SpeedAtDetection\PrebrakeDelay$, the jerk ramps of the matched stop, and the fixed localization, protective, and tracking allowances. At the rack-end clear distance the height of that plotted boundary is the subtotal speed ceiling, with the candidate aisle speed beneath it. The complete dry-floor ceiling is `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_complete_str`; the governor must use the fully charged boundary. Under the verified delay and deceleration bounds, the envelope is therefore a velocity ceiling that varies with clearance, and a state outside it violates the stopping reservation even if an emergency maneuver might avoid a collision in an edge case.

section: Closed-form quadratic programming and torque projection {#sec-enforcement-qp-projection}
context:
This geometric behavior exposes the distinction between **torque-space and task-space minimal intervention**\index{Minimal intervention!torque vs. task space}: an orthogonal projection $\CertifiedControlAction = \NominalControlCommand + \FiniteChange \ControlInput$ minimizes joint effort deviation $\|\ControlInput - \NominalControlCommand\|^2$, which redistributes multi-axis joint torques and rotates the net Cartesian wrench. While a feasible projection can preserve the safe set $\ForwardInvariantSafeSet$ under the stated model and timing assumptions, it deflects the end-effector trajectory and may arrest task progress. If the upstream neural policy continues emitting unprojected nominal setpoints without awareness of the intervention, the robot can chatter or stall at the boundary. The downstream enforcer must therefore stream the intervention vector $\FiniteChange \ControlInput$ back to the application processor as a telemetry signal, notifying the high-level planner to re-plan around the newly active physical constraint.

The same correction has a picture in state space and one in torque space (@fig-12-cbf-safety-filter). In state space, a trajectory that would breach the velocity-dependent boundary $\SafetyBoundaryManifold$ is turned along it; in the torque plane, the projection places $\CertifiedControlAction$ on the half-space boundary $\BarrierConstraintNormal^\top \ControlInput = \BarrierConstraintBound$, while the per-axis clamp leaves $\ClampedControlCommand$ outside it and skews its direction.

title: Illustrative emergency-stop circuit
caption: **Illustrative emergency-stop circuit**: Stages 1 and 2 are the out-of-band interlock circuit (Chapter 4); Stage 3 maps to the numbered list above. Two linked contacts each hold a force-guided relay, the relays' enable contacts hold the drive's two Safe Torque Off (STO) inputs, and their EDM contacts in series block a restart after a weld. The spring-applied brake runs on its own supply, and a supply contactor, if fitted, provides galvanic disconnection. A moving motor can coast after STO, so the brake's set time and the physical stopping distance must be measured for the load and state.
alt: Two-channel schematic in three labeled stages. Stage 1, dual-channel E-stop: a red positive-break E-stop mechanically linked to normally closed contacts S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. Stage 2, redundant relays with EDM: S1 drives the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact, and the EDM contacts in series run with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. Stage 3, separate stop functions: K1 and K2 send STO1 and STO2 enable to the drive, whose gate-drive supply feeds an inverter bridge driving motor M, tagged in red tau equals 0 and noted may coast. A dashed box above the drive reads supply contactor, if fitted. A brake supply on its own circuit, switched by K1 and K2, contacts not drawn, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft, with a dashed tag reading brake set time: measure.
context:
1.  **Torque removal (Stage 3, drive side):** De-energizing the safety relays drops the drive's STO inputs, which de-energize the gate drive power supply for the three-phase inverter bridge, rendering the power MOSFETs or insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) high-impedance, so the motor can no longer produce electromagnetic torque. STO alone does not apply mechanical braking. An unbraked motor carries momentum and may coast freely.
2.  **Mechanical restraint (Stage 3, brake side):** A separate coil circuit powers the spring-applied electromechanical friction brake. When power is removed, coil magnetic flux decays, allowing internal springs to physically clamp friction pads against the motor shaft, applying the brake without electrical power. A holding-brake rating does not establish the ability to arrest a moving load; dynamic stopping requires separate energy, torque, and response qualification.

title: Fallback responses and the paths that run them
caption: **Fallback responses and the paths that run them**: The plant state and the failed check select one response directly; the four are alternatives, not steps of an escalation. PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP run in the safety MCU's firmware and reach the drives through its arbiter, which here passes the projected command. INHIBIT is the one response that survives loss of the MCU itself, so it bypasses the arbiter on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply and lets the spring brakes set. On a moving machine that path also removes motor braking, and the machine coasts until the separately qualified brakes take hold.
alt: Four rows, each with a condition card on the left joined by an arrow to a response card. The first three responses, PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP, sit inside a dashed box labeled safety MCU firmware, 1 kHz, and feed a multiplexer whose selected input, PROJECT, connects to an output arrow labeled u act entering a tall box labeled drives and brakes. The fourth response, INHIBIT, sits in a separate dashed box labeled hardware interlock and connects directly to the drives box by an arrow labeled STO, brake supply. The PROJECT condition, proposal u nom admitted, is drawn dashed in bronze.
context:
:::

The four rungs run on two paths (@fig-12-fallback-ladder). `PROJECT`, `HOLD`, and `STOP` run in safety MCU firmware at the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.loop_rate_str` tick and reach the drives through one arbiter, which selects a single actuation command $\SelectedActuationCommand$; `INHIBIT` bypasses the firmware on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply (STO) and drops spring-brake holding current when the processor itself fails. The rungs trade response latency, control authority, and recovery cost, and the arbiter selects directly among those whose entry prerequisites still hold. A controlled stop demands verified drive electronics and sufficient stopping clearance; losing drive integrity forces unpowered mitigation with strictly weaker physical guarantees. Selection is also only as sound as the state evidence behind it. The 2023 Cruise pullover, which @sec-boundary-when-fails set beside Tempe as a failure after impact, selected a motion fallback on the strength of a missing track (war story \ref{ws-enforcement-cruise-fallback-dragging}).

title: Tempe detection and braking timeline
caption: **Tempe detection and braking timeline**: The NTSB reports first detection `{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.t_detect_str` before impact and recognition of imminent collision `{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.t_recognize_str` before impact. The ADS suppressed its motion plan for one second and then planned gradual slowing; it did not perform emergency braking. Classification and path prediction failed: at each change of class the ADS discarded the object's tracking history. The Volvo forward-collision warning and automated emergency braking functions were disabled while the developmental ADS operated. (Adapted from NTSB/HAR-19/03 [@ntsb2019uber].)
alt: Timeline from first ADS detection 5.6 seconds before impact to imminent-collision recognition 1.2 seconds before impact, one-second action suppression, gradual-slowdown plan, and impact. Separate note says the Volvo collision-warning and emergency-braking functions were disabled during ADS operation; each classification change discarded the object's tracking history.
context:
**Architect's countermeasure**: Enforce the causal separation of perception and safety by establishing an independent, non-semantic geometric barrier. A safety-rated sensor channel, such as a time-of-flight lidar curtain, radar, or safety scanner, must maintain direct hardware veto authority to command a Category 1 stop. This safety layer evaluates occupancy and closing rate directly, completely bypassing the neural perception pipeline, semantic classifiers, and trajectory forecasting models.
```

```
section: Execution leases and three-position enabling hardware {#sec-intervention-enabling-hardware}
context:
The pendant's red mushroom button is a different device with different semantics. Under ISO 13850, the emergency stop is a complementary protective measure, not a substitute for safeguarding or for the stop the risk assessment selects. It takes priority over every other function in every operating mode, it latches until an operator deliberately resets it at the device, and that reset must not restart the machine [@iso13850emergency]. Which physical response the stop invokes is a stop-category choice that @tbl-12-iec60204-stopping-categories maps to its evidence. The latch and the reset rule matter for supervisory control because they make a human stop sticky in exactly the way a network command is not. A remote packet can request a stop and a lease can lapse into one, but only the local reset of a latched device, followed by the fresh admission this chapter requires, returns the machine to motion.

[^fn-std-reduced-speed]: **Manual Reduced Speed**\index{Manual reduced speed!enabling devices}: ISO 10218-1:2025 limits the tool speed of an industrial robot in manual reduced-speed mode to $250\text{ mm/s}$ [@iso10218part1], the mode in which the pendant of @fig-14-teach-pendant couples motion to a three-position grip. Releasing or over-squeezing the grip only requests a stop from the safety circuit, and the performance level that circuit must reach, graded from PL a to PL e, is set by the machine's risk assessment under ISO 13849-1 [@iso13849part1]. The grip therefore bounds how fast the machine may be moving when a startled operator lets go, not which stop follows.

Two properties of the protocol show only when the states and handshake are drawn together (@fig-14-authority-handshake-fsm). Every active state has an edge to `Fallback`, so no failure of the network or the operator can leave a channel without a defined owner, and the only edge out of `Fallback` is a reset from standstill. The hardwired `Protective` input sits outside the protocol entirely and preempts every state.

section: Initial condition matching and integrator pre-biasing {#sec-intervention-integrator-prebiasing}
context:
[^fn-sys-blend-abort]: **Mid-Blend Re-Intervention Abort**\index{Bumpless transfer!mid-blend abort}: If an operator commands a secondary protective stop while a bumpless transfer blend is actively underway ($0 < \BumplessTransferProgress < 1$), the enforcer does not wait for $\BlendingTransitionWindow$ to complete. It uses the measured plant position, velocity, and acceleration, together with the active command and their uncertainty, to select a qualified state-matched fallback. A new polynomial seeded only from the intermediate command does not establish that the physical plant can execute it.

To verify a transfer, record the command profile, motor current, encoder motion, and chassis inertial response on a shared timebase with bounded alignment error. In the ideal model, a step command has an infinite derivative at the switch, which excites high jerk, unmodeled compliance, and drivetrain ringing in physical hardware. A fixed-endpoint quintic polynomial removes the command discontinuity by zeroing the boundary derivatives, so its command rate stays bounded across the whole window $\BlendingTransitionWindow$ instead of concentrating in one impulse (@fig-14-bumpless-transfer-dynamics). The measured plant response, not the command profile, establishes whether the handover met its physical limits.

section: What each of the four rungs makes physical {#sec-verification-qualification-rungs}
context:
Two operational testing paradigms exist alongside this qualification ladder, but both break the closed loop entirely. Trace replay feeds recorded sensor streams into the candidate controller; while it preserves authentic sensor noise and optical artifacts, the recorded frames reflect the actions of the original historical policy rather than reacting to the candidate's new commands. Shadow operation runs the candidate model in parallel with an incumbent, validated controller. If the candidate proposes an aggressive velocity vector that would drive the base into a storage rack, the logger records the telemetry while the incumbent controller safely halts the base. Because neither approach permits candidate actions to alter future state observations, neither reveals the closed-loop physical consequences of an erroneous command.

A production shadow deployment cannot allow a stalled proposer to drive toward a human worker at a rack end to see if the brakes engage in time. A software simulator cannot expose a timing race between transceiver silicon buffers. An instrumented physical dynamometer cannot execute the tens of millions of randomized runs required to bound extreme distribution tails. Systems engineers must therefore route each fault injection scenario to the specific rung on the ladder that embodies its underlying physical and causal mechanism. Coverage of the causal loop grows with each higher rung, from decision logic alone to drives and floor contact, while trial throughput shrinks, so no rung dominates the others (@fig-15-qualification-ladder).
```

section: Signal temporal logic and quantitative robustness {#sec-verification-stl-robustness}
context:
distance bound.

To illustrate this dual evaluation numerically, consider an F1 trace at aisle speed, timed channel by channel in @fig-15-hardware-fault-injection, where powered deceleration begins `{python} RackEndVerification.late_onset_str` late, occurring `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_late_str` after the last valid renewal. The onset margin against the `{python} RackEndVerification.onset_bound_str` bound evaluates to `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_onset_str`. Because the mobile base travels `{python} RackEndVerification.late_extra_str` further before braking engages, total travel from renewal to rest reaches `{python} RackEndVerification.travel_late_str`, yielding a distance margin of `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_dist_str` against the `{python} RackEndVerification.f1_aisle_stop_bound_str` oracle. The onset predicate fails, while nominal travel remains within the distance allowance. The verification results retain both margins in their native physical units; the tracking inset belongs in the oracle and is not additional travel in the plotted speed integral. Because taking an unweighted minimum across milliseconds and millimeters produces an uninterpretable quantity, synthesizing them into a unified score via `min` requires normalizing each margin by a predeclared positive scale in its corresponding unit. Logging both the raw margins and their normalization factors ensures the synthesized verdict remains physically meaningful. Choosing scales equal to the verification bounds themselves yields normalized margins of `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_onset_n_str` for onset timing and `{python} RackEndVerification.rho_dist_n_str` for stopping distance, making the onset predicate the governing term in the combined score. When several predicates have negative margins, alternative scales can change which one governs the compound score, so test engineers must fix normalization factors before executing verification runs. In this nominal trace only onset fails, so positive rescaling cannot make distance the governing predicate. These numerical values reflect model arithmetic over a stipulated reference trace rather than empirical physical measurements.

context:
restricted subset of the envelope and binds the permission path to those narrower limits. In the running machine, `COND` selects a pre-validated safety configuration, much like industrial safety controllers and protective optical scanners switch between pre-validated field sets[^fn-scanner-field-sets] and speed-monitoring profiles. All restricted kinematic thresholds ($\SpeedBound \le \RestrictedSpeedBound$, $\ProfileAccelerationBound \le \RestrictedAccelerationBound$) and spatial geofences are evaluated and validated as one configuration before release; the runtime verdict selects among these vetted profiles rather than inventing parameters on the fly. A conditional verdict (`COND`) is an offline, predeployment contract that restricts the machine's operating envelope until re-adjudication. A **degraded mode**\index{Degraded mode!definition} is an online runtime fallback, pre-assessed and named in the signed release, that the permission path invokes when an active subsystem loses telemetry or sensor redundancy (@sec-release-blind-travel-limits sizes one for the base). Release then enforces physical, kinematic, or environmental boundaries that exclude unverified hazard states, such as de-rated joint speeds, a restricted illumination range, or a physical barrier that keeps humans outside the manipulator's workspace. Where contact force cannot be bounded for unseparated co-presence, a restricted release case may require physical separation: @fig-16-real-robot-safety-cell illustrates yellow perimeter mesh fencing around an industrial workcell. Crediting that separation requires validated access-interlock and stopping evidence showing that the protective response completes before hazardous access.

[^fn-scanner-field-sets]: **Safety Scanner Field Sets**\index{Safety laser scanner!field sets}: A safety laser scanner stores several protective-field geometries that were configured and validated in advance, and a safety controller selects one of them from encoded speed or position inputs. The scanner never computes a new field at runtime. `COND` borrows the pattern, so the verdict selects a pre-assessed limit set and no untested parameter can reach the permission path.

```
title: Closed causal loop
caption: **Closed causal loop**: The Brain proposes across the proposal boundary, and the permission path in the Nervous System admits, modifies, or refuses each proposal before the Body acts. The Body's current becomes force and motion at the Boundary, the World evolves, and the Boundary returns measurements with capture times to the permission path and the Brain. Not every state of the World reaches a sensor. The governance envelope surrounds all five levels and changes on the timescale of releases rather than control cycles. The labels are this machine's values: the intent model proposes at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.intent_rate_str`, the chunk is renewed every `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.renewal_str`, the application processor sends a setpoint every `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.setpoint_str` over a black-channel link to a discrete safety microcontroller unit (MCU) whose permission path ticks at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.permission_str`, and the drives close their current loops at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.current_loop_str` from a `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.bus_str` bus. Another machine sets its own rates.
alt: Five stacked levels inside a dashed governance envelope: Brain, Nervous System, Body, Boundary, and World, with a dashed proposal boundary between the Brain and the Nervous System. Inside the Nervous System an application processor sends setpoints over a black-channel link to a discrete safety MCU that runs the permission path. Arrows run from the Brain to the application processor, labeled proposal, from the safety MCU to the Body, labeled admitted command, and on to the World, labeled current in a winding and force and motion. A return arrow runs from the World to the Boundary, then up a side lane to the safety MCU, labeled fresh state, and to the Brain, labeled observations. Labels give the intent model 2 Hz with 336 ms inference, chunk renewal every 50 ms, a setpoint every 25 ms, a 1 kHz permission tick, a 20 kHz current loop in the drives, and a 47.7 V drive bus; the Boundary is event-timed, the World is continuous, and governance has no control rate.
context:
```

Assembled, these parts close one causal loop through the physical world (@fig-18-causal-loop-synthesis). The loop runs at rates four orders of magnitude apart: the Brain proposes at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.intent_rate_str`, the permission path on the discrete safety microcontroller admits, corrects, or refuses at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.permission_str`, and the drives close their current loops at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.current_loop_str`. The loop closes only through the World, and the World returns only what its sensors capture, with capture times, to the permission path and to the Brain. A state the sensors never carry, such as the friction under a clear film, is invisible to every level at once. Governance surrounds all five levels and changes on the timescale of releases, so it sets the budgets and standing conditions that the fast loop enforces without taking part in any single control cycle.
