title: Camera ray frustum lifting and BEV splatting
caption: **Camera ray frustum lifting and BEV splatting**: LSS [@philion2020lift] places learned depth hypotheses from each camera in a shared metric BEV frame; that coordinate transform does not resolve monocular depth ambiguity. The final clearance inset requires separately validated metric residuals, bias, and a chosen tail quantile or deterministic error bound before permission. (Architecture adapted from @philion2020lift.)
alt: Four stages show image features, a ray with several learned depth hypotheses, a shared bird's-eye-view grid, and a clearance decision. The last panel labels depth as estimated and the inset as checked; learned depth-bin weights alone do not establish a metric error bound.
context:
The workspace is discretized into a grid of vertical pillars, for example `{python} AppxBevFrustum.bev_cells_str` cells on a side covering a `{python} AppxBevFrustum.workspace_str` square at `{python} AppxBevFrustum.bev_res_str` resolution. The splat sums every frustum feature that falls within pillar $(\BevPillarXIndex, \BevPillarYIndex)$, using accelerated cumulative sums or point-pillar pooling [@philion2020lift; @liu2023bevfusion]:
   $$ \BevPillarFeature(\BevPillarXIndex, \BevPillarYIndex) = \sum_{(\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate, k) \in \text{Pillar}(\BevPillarXIndex, \BevPillarYIndex)} \FrustumFeature $$
   On parallel GPU accelerators, naive scatter-add operations create severe write-port contention and non-coalesced DRAM transactions when hundreds of frustum points map to the identical BEV pillar. Optimized runtimes eliminate this bottleneck by sorting frustum points by pillar index and executing parallel cumulative-sum prefix scans or precomputed index-table indirection [@liu2023bevfusion]. The splat aligns the cameras' hypotheses in one metric frame. It cannot fill a region no camera saw or remove depth-scale error, so the footprint it assigns to a pedestrian still depends on the depth hypotheses and the calibration. That dependence is why the clearance panel closing @fig-08-ray-frustum-voxel-lifting marks depth as estimated and only the inset as checked.

title: Gaussian memory and clearance handoff
caption: **Gaussian memory and clearance handoff**: Camera observations update a Gaussian scene for novel-view rendering. Its visual output does not directly supply conservative collision distance; a separately validated geometry or occupancy conversion and permission check are required [@kerbl20233d; @matsuki2024gaussian].
alt: Three-panel schematic. Panel a: an RGB-D stream feeds pose tracking, which outputs the camera pose. Panel b: a Gaussian scene memory holding 3D Gaussians with mean, covariance, opacity, and spherical-harmonic color, drawn as three oriented ellipses, above an adaptive density control step that splits, clones, and prunes. Panel c: a rasterize arrow leads to novel-view rendering, a visual output; a convert arrow leads to a dashed candidate occupancy or distance field marked not yet validated, which connects to an error-bound-then-clearance step.
context:
Here $\CumulativeTransmittance_i$ represents cumulative optical transmittance along the viewing ray, initialized to $\CumulativeTransmittance_1=1$. In this rendering equation, $\PixelOpacityContribution_i$ is the pixel-dependent opacity contribution, including the projected Gaussian footprint, rather than the stored opacity $\GaussianPrimitiveOpacity_i$. An implementation may terminate when the remaining transmittance is sufficiently small; the error tolerance, scene density, and hardware determine the resulting speed.

However, a physical AI systems engineer must recognize the boundary between visual rendering and physical clearance. The 3D Gaussian parameters are optimized strictly against 2D photometric rendering loss (such as $\ell_1$ color difference and SSIM). Gaussians frequently fit unobserved scene regions with semi-transparent "floaters," hollow shells, or blurred volumetric density. Neither the stored opacity $\GaussianPrimitiveOpacity_i$ nor the spatial gradient $\nabla_{\CartesianPosition} \GaussianPrimitiveDensity_i(\CartesianPosition)$ of its density constitutes a conservative collision surface. @Fig-3dgs-slam-splatam partitions this architectural handoff across three functional panels. Panel (a) tracks camera poses from an incoming RGB-D stream. Panel (b) maintains the 3D Gaussian memory primitives (mean, covariance ellipsoid, opacity, and spherical-harmonic color) under adaptive splitting, cloning, and pruning. Panel (c) decouples photometric rasterization from physical safety, routing Gaussian primitives through an unvalidated candidate occupancy or signed distance field before an explicit error-bounding step admits the clearance envelope.

title: Constructed spatial-memory storage scenarios
caption: **Constructed spatial-memory storage scenarios**: A dense cube uses four bytes per voxel, the octree allocates one 32-byte surface cell per squared grid dimension, and the Gaussian scene holds a fixed count and packing while grid resolution varies. These are storage models, not equal-fidelity or measured runtime benchmarks; Gaussian count must rise if a stricter geometry target requires it.
alt: Log-scale plot of calculated storage against grid cells per dimension for a dense cubic voxel grid, an assumed surface-allocated octree, and a Gaussian scene held at a fixed primitive count. The fixed Gaussian line is an assumption, not a claim of constant cost at equal geometric fidelity.
context:
:::

Storage per primitive depends on its packing and spherical-harmonic degree, so a map's footprint is its primitive count times that packing. A dense cubic grid instead stores $\mathcal{O}(\GridSideCellCount^3)$ cells, and a sparse occupancy map stores only allocated structure, whose size depends on the observed geometry and the accuracy target. @Fig-09-volumetric-memory-scaling plots these three storage scaling regimes on logarithmic axes as grid resolution spans from 10 to $10^4$ cells per dimension. The cubic grid grows steeply as $\mathcal{O}(\GridSideCellCount^3)$ and passes gigabytes at modest resolutions. The surface-allocated octree scales along an $\mathcal{O}(\GridSideCellCount^2)$ trajectory. The stylized Gaussian scene maintains a flat baseline under an assumed fixed primitive count of 500,000 elements.

title: Probabilistic octree volumetric mapping
caption: **Probabilistic octree volumetric mapping**: A corridor traversal reconstructed from raw point cloud into a probabilistic octree and then into explicit free, occupied, and unknown space [@hornung2013octomap]. The third panel is what distinguishes spatial memory from an accumulated point cloud, because raycasting records evidence of emptiness along sightlines, letting the map actively retire a phantom obstacle track instead of waiting for a timeout to expire it. (Image: @hornung2013octomap, Autonomous Intelligent Systems Lab, University of Freiburg.)
alt: Probabilistic 3D Volumetric Mapping and Hierarchical Octree Space Subdivision. Empirical 3D spatial memory representation reconstructed from a physical mobile robot traversing an indoor corridor with a tilting lidar scanner. (a) Raw 3D point cloud acquired during robot motion, subject to sensor noise and finite field-of-view occlusions. (b) Volumetric OctoMap voxel representation modeling 3D space as an 8-ary hierarchical tree, where occupied volumes are probabilistically updated and stored across variable resolutions. (c) Explicit free-space raycasting and lossless octree pruning, differentiating observed free cells (white voxels) from occupied obstacles (dark voxels) and unobserved unknown regions; free evidence alone does not certify traversability for a particular robot. By maintaining explicit free-space evidence along sensor sightlines, spatial memory actively invalidates phantom obstacle tracks without waiting for arbitrary software timeouts. (Image: Hornung et al., Autonomous Intelligent Systems Lab, University of Freiburg.)
context:
#### Octree occupancy and free-space raycasting

Occupancy grid mapping [@elfes1989using] tessellates space into cells and applies this update to every cell a ray touches.\index{Occupancy grid mapping!octree storage} A volumetric raycast walks each return's sightline with the three-dimensional digital differential analyzer (3D-DDA) traversal [@amanatides1987fast].\index{Volumetric free-space raycasting!3D-DDA traversal} Hierarchical stores such as OctoMap [@hornung2013octomap] and OpenVDB [@museth2013vdb] allocate cells only where rays have passed, so storage follows the observed volume rather than the bounding cube. @Fig-09-octomap-volumetric-mapping traces this spatial-memory pipeline across three successive representations during an indoor mobile robot traversal. Panel (a) shows the unorganized, noisy 3D point cloud acquired by a tilting range scanner. Panel (b) shows the hierarchical 8-ary octree that adaptively clusters occupied volumes. Panel (c) shows the explicit ternary classification that differentiates confirmed free-space voxels (white) and occupied obstacle cells (dark) from unobserved unknown volumes. Free-space evidence recorded along ray sightlines lets the map retire a phantom obstacle once the same region is seen empty, while a never-observed cell stays unknown however long the map runs. @Sec-memory-scene-attention-buffers applies this rule to the aisle, where only fresh free-space evidence can vouch that a path is clear.

title: Diffusion policy action chunk denoising and receding-horizon decoupling
caption: **Diffusion policy action chunk denoising and receding-horizon decoupling**: (a) Multimodal resolution: direct regression with mean squared error averages divergent demonstrations into an invalid obstacle collision, whereas conditional diffusion can sample alternative demonstrated modes; generated paths still require clearance checks. (b) Iterative trajectory denoising: starting from Gaussian noise $\ActionChunk^{\DecoderEvaluationCount} \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \IdentityMatrix)$, reverse diffusion progressively resolves a coarse trajectory into a smooth action chunk $\ActionChunk^0$. (c) Dual-rate decoupling: an asynchronous sampler on the application processor sends each chunk over a black-channel link to a discrete $1\\,\text{kHz}$ safety microcontroller, which holds it in its own double buffer and runs the freshness check, spline interpolation, and slew clamping. The two processors share no memory. (Adapted from @chi2024diffusionpolicy).

title: The S·P·A intersection landscape
caption: **The S·P·A intersection landscape**: Sense, Plan, and Act meet pairwise in three physical decisions, locating the object now, checking that proposed motion fits limits, and measuring what changed after acting. Their center is the permission decision, where an independent permission path checks the shared physical budget before actuation.
alt: Three overlapping circles labeled Sense, Plan, and Act. Sense and Plan ask where an object is now. Plan and Act ask whether motion fits physical limits. Act and Sense ask what changed. The center, where all three overlap, is the independent permission decision.
context:
## The Intersection Landscape {#sec-appendix-spa-intersections}

When a mobile manipulator clips a cart that just rolled out of a cross-aisle, the fault often spans more than one subsystem: a voxel layer that held a stale free-space timestamp, a trajectory handoff that delayed braking, or a shared memory bus that stalled the safety check. @Fig-spa-triad diagrams the Sense, Plan, and Act (S·P·A) triad as three intersecting functional domains. Its three pairwise interfaces are $\Glyph{S} \cap \Glyph{P}$ (locating object position in current time), $\Glyph{P} \cap \Glyph{A}$ (verifying that proposed trajectories satisfy dynamic limits), and $\Glyph{A} \cap \Glyph{S}$ (measuring physical state evolution after actuation). The independent permission decision sits at their central three-way intersection ($\Glyph{S} \cap \Glyph{P} \cap \Glyph{A}$), where a qualified permission path gates all motor commands against physical budgets before actuation. Each intersection below pairs its physical handoff contract with a discriminating measurement.
